en: Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery, Scroll One.
Originally translated by the Śramaṇa Huili; annotated by Yancong.
From his birth in Guoshi to his final journey westward to Gaochang. From his birth in Guoshi to his final journey westward to Gaochang.
The Dharma Master’s name was Xuánzàng; his secular surname was Chén, and he was a native of Chénliú.
He was a descendant of Zhònggōng, the Grand Marshal of Tāiqiū during the Hàn dynasty.
His great-grandfather, Qīn, served as the Governor of Shàngdǎng under the Later Wèi.

Zu Kang served the state of Qi due to his excellence in learning, holding the office of State Preceptor (Guozibo). He was granted a fief in Zhounan, where his descendants settled and made their home; thus, they became people of Guoshi.

His father, Hui, was brilliant and pure with refined integrity; he mastered the classical arts at an early age. Standing eight chi tall, with beautiful eyebrows and clear eyes, he wore voluminous robes and wide sashes, embodying the dignified appearance of a Confucian scholar; his contemporaries compared him to Guo Youdao.

By nature he was tranquil and simple, having no ambition for honor or advancement; moreover, as the administration of the Sui dynasty declined, he devoted himself to the study of the ancient classics.

Although the local prefectures repeatedly recommended him as a "Filial and Incorrupt" official and the Office of the Imperial Censor summoned him with an appointment, he declined both on the grounds of illness and did not accept them, earning the admiration of those who understood him.
He had four sons, of whom the Dharma Master was the fourth.
From his youth, he possessed exceptional integrity and talent; his intelligence and insight were beyond his peers.

At the age of eight, while his father sat by a desk orally instructing him in the *Classic of Filial Piety*, when they reached the passage where Zengzi left his seat, the boy suddenly adjusted his robes and rose.
When asked the reason for this, he replied:
"When Zengzi heard his teacher’s command, he left his seat; now that Xuanzang receives your compassionate instruction, how could I remain seated at ease?
His father was greatly pleased and knew that he would surely achieve success.
He summoned the Clan Registrar and spoke with him;
they all congratulated him, saying, "This is the manifestation of your public virtue. Such was his precocity.

Thereafter, he thoroughly mastered the profound depths of the scriptures; he cherished antiquity and revered the worthy, refusing to read anything but elegant and orthodox texts and never practicing anything other than the conduct of sages and philosophers.
He did not associate with the company of children, nor did he enter the gates of marketplaces;
even when bells and drums resounded in the main thoroughfares and the hundred performances and songs echoed through the alleys, with men and women gathering like clouds, he never once went out.
Furthermore, he possessed a modest knowledge of filial care for his parents, being warm, pure, and prudent in his conduct.
His second elder brother, Changjie, had previously left the household life and resided at Jingtu Temple in the Eastern Capital.
Observing that Dharma Master Cha was capable of transmitting the teachings of the Dharma, Changjie brought him to the monastic grounds to recite and study the scriptures.

Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict was issued to ordain fourteen monks in Luoyang. At that time, there were several hundred candidates of superior merit, but because the Dharma Master was too young, he was not included within the quota and stood by the side of the official gate.
At that time, Zheng Shanguo, the Minister of Justice (Daliquan), possessed the discernment of a man of knowledge; seeing him, he marveled at him and asked, "Whose family do you belong to?
He replied with his clan name and personal name.
He asked again,
"Are you seeking deliverance? He replied:
"It is so. However, because my habitual karma was slight and I did not associate with them closely, I have not been granted inclusion among their ranks.
He asked again:
"What is the purpose of your intention to leave the household life? He replied:
"My intention is to propagate the Tathāgata’s teachings far and wide, and to illuminate his bequeathed Dharma in its immediate vicinity."
The Duke deeply admired his resolve and esteemed his character and appearance; thus, he selected him specifically.
He then said to his officials:
"Mastery of recitation is easily achieved, but noble bearing and bone-structure are difficult to find."

"If this youth is ordained, he will surely become a great vessel for the Śākya school; however, I fear that you gentlemen may not witness him soaring through the clouds and skies, sprinkling and expounding the nectar of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, one must not fail to uphold the name of 'home-leaver' (śramaṇa).
Judging by this, it is clear that the words of the Minister of Zheng were not empty.

Having been permitted to leave home and reside with his elder brother, there was at that time a Dharma Master Jing at the monastery lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He took up the scroll and committed it to memory, eventually forgetting both sleep and food.
Furthermore, he studied Master Yan’s commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, his fondness for it growing ever more intense.
Once he had heard it almost entirely, after reading it a second time, there was nothing further that remained to be forgotten.

The assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement; they then had him ascend the seat to repeat his discourse, which he delivered with such eloquence, clarity, and thoroughness that it fully embodied the essence of his master’s tradition.
From this point on, his reputation and fame began to spread far and wide.
At that time, he was thirteen years old.
Subsequently, the Sui dynasty lost its mandate, and the world was thrown into turmoil.
The imperial capital became a nest for Jie and Zhi, while the Yellow and Luo Rivers became dens for jackals and wolves.
Robes and caps were discarded in the funeral rites, and the monastic community perished; white bones littered the thoroughfares, and the smoke of hearths was cut off.

Even during the calamities of Wang Mang and Dong Zhuo’s usurpation and rebellion, or the disasters of Liu Yuan and Shi Le’s turmoil in China, there has never been such a time when the living were so cruelly slaughtered and the land within the seas so utterly ravaged.
Although the Dharma Master was still a youth, his mind was adept at discerning the exigencies of the situation;
he thus addressed his elder brother, saying, "Though this is our parents' home, the world is so ravaged by war and chaos—how could we remain here and die!"

"I have heard that the Emperor of Tang has driven the multitudes from Jinyang and already occupied Chang'an; the whole world turns to him for refuge as if returning to their own parents. I wish to join you, my elder brother, and go there."
The elder brother followed his advice, and they came together; it was the first year of the Wude era.

At that time, the foundations of the state were being laid, and military conflict was still prevalent; the strategies of Sun Wu and Wu Qi were considered urgent matters, while the teachings of Confucius and Śākyamuni had not yet been given leisurely attention. Consequently, there were no lecture halls in the capital, which left the Dharma Master deeply lamenting this state of affairs.
Initially, Emperor Yang established four monastic centers in the Eastern Capital and summoned the renowned monks of the empire to reside therein.
Those who were summoned were all masters of specific arts; thus, eminent Dharma generals gathered like a forest, with Jing, Tuo, Ji, and Xian standing as their preeminent leaders.

In his later years, as the country fell into chaos, the supply of provisions ceased; he traveled extensively through Mian and Shu, where the community of those who knew the Dharma was also flourishing.
The Master then addressed his elder brother, saying:
"There is no longer any work for the Dharma here; it would be a waste to pass the time in vain. I wish to travel to Shu to receive formal instruction."
The elder brother followed his advice.

They traveled together through Jingzi Valley and entered Hanchuan, where they encountered the two Dharma Masters Kong and Jing; both were great virtuous masters of Daochang Monastery, and upon meeting, they were filled with both sorrow and joy.
After staying for over a month, he followed him to receive instruction and continued together toward Chengdu.

Once the eminent masters had gathered, they established a grand Dharma assembly; thereupon, he further studied Daosheng’s and Daoxian’s commentaries on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā*, as well as Dharma Master Zhen’s commentary on the *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma*. Cherishing every moment and exerting himself with untiring diligence, within two or three years he thoroughly mastered all the various treatises.

At that time, the world was suffering from famine and turmoil, but only within Shu was there abundance and tranquility; consequently, many monks from all quarters sought refuge there, and the assembly beneath his lecture seat often numbered several hundred.

The Dharma Master’s wisdom, insight, and vast talent all surpassed those [of his predecessors]; from Wu, Shu, Jing, and Chu, there was no one who did not know or hear of him. Those who yearned for his exemplary influence were like the ancients who revered Li Bing and Guo Tu.
The Elder Dharma Master resided at Konghui Monastery in Chengdu; he was also brilliant and refined in spirit, with a physique that was imposing and majestic, much like his father’s.

He took delight in both Buddhist and secular studies, lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharma*. Furthermore, he was well-versed in the *Shujing* and the *Shizhuan*, and was particularly adept at the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*, earning him the admiration of the people of Shu and the special esteem of the Governor, Lord Zan.
As for composing phrases and conversational discourse, as well as possessing refined elegance and cultivating social graces to guide ordinary people, you are no less than your younger brother.

However, regarding standing tall and unique in excellence, remaining untainted by worldly dust, traversing the eight regions, exhausting the profound principles, broadening one’s ambition to encompass the universe, and making it one’s heart’s intent to succeed the sages and reach the enlightened; in upholding and reviving the collapsing net of order, subduing divergent customs, maintaining an unwearied spirit amidst wind and waves, and increasing one’s integrity even when facing the Son of Heaven—these are indeed things you, elder brother, cannot yet attain.
However, as for these two brothers, their noble deeds and pure regulations, their fragrant reputation and elegant character, could not have been surpassed even by the brothers of Mount Lu.

When the Dharma Master reached the age of twenty, he received full ordination in Chengdu in the fifth year of the Wude era; there he spent the summer retreat studying the Vinaya, mastering the principles of the five categories and seven groups of precepts after only a single recitation.
Having thoroughly mastered the study and synthesis of the sutras and śāstras in the Yi region, he further contemplated entering the capital to inquire about its profound doctrines.

However, as the regulations presented obstacles and he was detained by his elder brother, he could not fulfill his intention; he therefore secretly joined a caravan of merchants, launched his boat upon the Three Gorges, and fled downstream along the river.
He arrived at Tiantai Monastery in Jingzhou. Having long admired his reputation, both the monastics and laypeople there, upon seeing him arrive, all requested that he preach.
The Dharma Master lectured on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* from summer until winter, completing each three times.
At that time, the Prince of Hanyang, being a man of profound virtue and a close relative of the imperial house, was stationed there as a regional governor.
Upon hearing that the Dharma Master had arrived, he was greatly delighted and personally went to pay his respects.

On the day the lectures commenced, the Prince led his officials along with members of the monastic and lay communities who were skilled in the arts, all gathering together to witness the magnificent occasion.

Thereupon, their interrogations arose like gathering clouds and surged forth like rising peaks; yet the Dharma Master responded and explained them all, leaving them without words and their minds in submission.
Among them, some attained profound realization, overcome with grief they could not restrain themselves.
The King also praised him boundlessly and offered gifts as vast as mountains, yet he accepted nothing at all.
After the lecture concluded, he traveled north again to seek out and inquire after the virtuous masters of former times.
Upon reaching Xiangzhou, he visited Dharma Master Xiu to inquire about his doubts and difficulties.
He then traveled to Zhaozhou to call upon Dharma Master Shen and study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
He entered Chang’an again and stayed at Da’jue Monastery, where he studied the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* under Master Sengyue.
He mastered its essential principles after a single reading; whatever passed before his eyes was committed to memory, such that even veteran scholars of advanced age could not surpass him.

As for delving into the profound, reaching the distant, opening up the subtle, and revealing the hidden—to attain an awakening, unique and solitary, to what is obscure and abstruse where the multitudes have not reached—this is certainly not a matter of a single principle alone.

At that time, there were two great virtuous masters in Chang’an named Chang and Bian. They had thoroughly investigated the Two Vehicles and perfected their practice in the Three Studies. They served as preeminent Dharma masters for the capital, to whom both monastics and laypeople turned for refuge. Their Way shook the land of China and their fame spread beyond the seas; students carrying their book-cases followed them like clouds. Although they encompassed and mastered a multitude of scriptures, they specialized in lecturing on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

The Dharma Master had previously achieved great merit in the regions of Wu and Shu; since arriving in Chang’an, he has further pursued his inquiries and investigations, such that all its profound subtleties have been gathered and fully grasped.
Both men were deeply moved and praised him, saying to the Dharma Master:

"You may truly be called a 'thousand-li colt' of the Śākya gate; the re-illumination of the Sun of Wisdom shall rest upon your person. It is our regret that we are old and decrepit and fear we shall not live to see it."
From that time on, his disciples changed their views, and his reputation filled the capital.

Having visited all the masters and fully digested their teachings, the Dharma Master examined their principles in detail; yet each held its own unique system, and when verified against the sacred scriptures, they differed in both explicit and implicit meanings, leaving him unable to know which path to follow. He therefore vowed to travel to the Western Regions to inquire about his doubts and to obtain the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*—which is the present-day *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*—to resolve the various uncertainties.
Furthermore, he said:

"In the past, Faxian and Zhiyan were also contemporaries who were both able to seek the Dharma and guide and benefit all living beings. How could we allow their lofty traces to remain without successors, or their pure influence to be severed for all time?"
"A great man shall surely succeed to this [task].
Thereupon, he formed a fellowship and submitted a memorial.
However, Yao Zhao did not grant permission.
All the others withdrew, but only the Dharma Master did not yield.

Since he was about to travel alone and had heard that the western road was perilous, he tested his own mind by subjecting it to the various sufferings of the human world; thus, he became capable of enduring them without retreating.

Only then did they enter the stupa and offer their prayers, expressing their intent and wishing for the secret assistance of all the sages so that their journey there and back would be free from obstacles.
When the Dharma Master was first born, his mother dreamed that he, dressed in white robes, departed toward the west.
The mother said, "You are my son; where do you wish to go now? He replied:
"I shall depart for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
These were the preliminary signs of his journey abroad.
In the eighth month of autumn in the third year of the Zhenguan era, as he was about to set out upon his path, he again sought auspicious omens.
Then, in a night dream, he saw Mount Sumeru in the midst of a great ocean, composed of the four precious substances and exceedingly magnificent and beautiful.
Desiring to climb the mountain, he found the surging waves turbulent and there were no boats or rafts; yet, undaunted by this, he resolved to enter.
Suddenly, he saw a stone lotus flower emerge from beyond the waves; it appeared as soon as his foot touched it, and when he looked back, it vanished as his foot moved away.
In a short while, he reached the foot of the mountain, which was again so steep and precipitous that it could not be ascended.
He attempted to leap, and his body rose of its own accord; a whirlwind suddenly arrived, supporting him as he ascended.

Upon reaching the mountain peak, he looked in all four directions and found it vast and open, free from any further obstruction. He awoke from this joyful vision and immediately set out on his journey.
At that time, he was twenty-six years old.

There was then a monk from Qinzhou named Xiaoda who was studying the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in the capital; when his studies were completed and he was returning to his hometown, [Sengyai] went along with him.
Upon reaching Qinzhou, he stayed for one night and met his companions from Lanzhou, with whom he continued on to Lanzhou.
After staying there for one night, he encountered a man from Liangzhou returning home with official horses and followed him to that place.

After staying for more than a month, both monastics and laypeople requested that he expound upon the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; the Dharma Master expounded and elucidated them all for them.
Liangzhou was the capital of Hexi and bordered the various kingdoms of the Western Tubo and the regions east of the Pamirs; caravans of merchants traveled back and forth without interruption.

On the days when lectures were held, these people gathered in great numbers, all offering precious jewels and prostrating themselves in praise. Upon their return, each would extol the Master’s excellence to their respective rulers, saying that he intended to travel westward to seek the Dharma in the land of the Brahmins. Consequently, there was no city in the Western Regions that did not anticipate his arrival with joy, preparing the grounds and sprinkling them with water in expectation.

On the day the assembly dispersed, the offerings were abundant and generous; there were countless pieces of gold, silver, and coin, as well as horses and carriages. The Dharma Master accepted half for the purpose of lighting lamps, while the remainder was distributed to various monasteries.
At that time, state administration was still new and the borders were not yet far-reaching; thus, the common people were strictly forbidden from traveling beyond the prefectures.
Li Daoliang, serving as the Governor-General of Liangzhou, received these strict edicts and consequently exercised exceptionally rigorous control over the population.
Someone informed Sengliang, saying:
"There is a monk who has come from Chang'an and intends to go to the Western Regions; we do not know his purpose.
Frightened, Liang pursued the Dharma Master to question him about his reasons for coming.
The Dharma Master replied,
"I wish to travel westward in search of the Dharma.
When Sengliang heard this, he pressured him to return to the capital.

There was the Dharma Master Huiwei, a preeminent leader of Hexi, whose spiritual insight was sharp and discerning. Having already esteemed the Dharma Master’s eloquence and reasoning, and now hearing of his resolve to seek the Dharma, he felt deep sympathetic joy; he secretly dispatched two disciples—one named Huilin and the other Daozheng—to escort him westward in secret.
From then on, he did not dare travel openly; instead, he hid by day and traveled by night until he reached Guazhou.
When the Regional Inspector, Du Gu Da, heard that the Dharma Master had arrived, he was greatly delighted and provided him with generous hospitality and service.
The Dharma Master, while traveling along the western road, was informed by someone who said:

"Traveling north from here for more than fifty *li*, there is the Gourd River (*Alābu-nadī*). It is wide at its lower reaches and narrow at its upper reaches; the swirling currents are extremely swift, and it is so deep that it cannot be crossed."
Above is situated Yumen Pass, which is the essential gateway through which all routes must pass; it is the strategic throat of the western frontier.
To the northwest outside the pass, there are five beacon towers where lookouts reside, each separated by one hundred *li*, with neither water nor grass found in the intervening spaces.
"Beyond the five beacon towers lies the Mo-he-yan desert, which is the border of the kingdom of Yiwu.
Upon hearing this, he was overcome with distress and despondency; his riding horse also died, and not knowing what course of action to take, he remained silent for more than a month.
Before he had even departed, a search warrant arrived from Liangzhou, stating:
"There is a monk named Xuanzang who intends to enter Western Tibet; all local prefectures and counties shall strictly guard for and apprehend him."
Li Chang, a provincial official and a man of devout faith, grew suspicious of the Dharma Master and secretly presented a document, saying:
"Is the Master not this person?"
The Dharma Master hesitated and did not reply.
Chang said,
"The Master must speak the truth."
"If this is indeed so, I, your disciple, shall depict it.
The Dharma Master then answered him with full truth.
Upon hearing this, Li Chang deeply praised it as rare and marvelous, saying:
"If you, Master, can truly do so, then for your sake I shall destroy this document.
He then tore it apart right before him and said:
"The Master must depart early.
From that time on, [Dao'an's] grief and despondency increased all the more.

Of the two young monks who had accompanied him, Daozheng had previously gone toward Dunhuang; only Huilin remained, but knowing that he was unable to travel such a great distance, he also sent him back.
He then traded for a horse, but he suffered from having no one to guide him.
He immediately made a prayer before the Maitreya statue in the temple where he was staying, vowing that he might find a person to lead him across the pass.
That night, a foreign monk named Dharmaruci was at the monastery; he dreamed that the Dharma Master sat upon a lotus flower and departed toward the west.
Dharmaruci felt privately troubled by this and came to report it the following morning.
The Dharma Master was delighted in his heart, taking this as a sign that he would attain the practice;
nevertheless, he said to Dharmatā, "A dream is illusory; what is the need for further words?
He then entered the ritual arena once more to pay homage and make his request.
Suddenly, a man from the Hu region entered to pay homage to the Buddha and followed the Dharma Master for two or three circuits.
When asked his name and surname, he replied that his surname was Shi and his given name was Bantuo.
The Hu man immediately requested to receive the precepts, whereupon [the Master] conferred upon him the five precepts.
The Hu man was greatly delighted and took his leave to return.
After a short while, he came again bringing cakes and fruit.
The Dharma Master, seeing that he was intelligent and vigorous and his countenance was respectful and solemn, informed him of his intention to travel.
The Hu man gave his consent, saying, "I shall escort the Master past the five watchtowers.
The Dharma Master was greatly pleased; he then exchanged his clothing and provisions to purchase horses and made an appointment with him.
As the sun was about to set the following day, he entered the grass; after a short while, that barbarian arrived, pursued by another barbarian old man riding a lean, aged, red horse.
The Dharma Master’s heart was not at ease, so a young Hu man said:
"This old man is extremely familiar with the western road; he has traveled back and forth to Yiwu more than thirty times. That is why we came together, hoping for his counsel."
Lord Hu then said, "The western road is perilous and treacherous;
the Sha River is obstructed and far distant. There are demons and hot winds, such that none who pass through reach their destination.
Even with a large retinue, many still lose their way; how much more so for you, Master, traveling alone? How can you possibly proceed?"
"I pray that you will exercise due caution and not treat your own life and body lightly.
The Dharma Master replied, "I have set out for the Western Land in search of the Great Dharma; if I do not reach the land of the Brahmins, I shall never return to the East."
"Even if I were to die midway, it would not be cause for regret.
The old man Hu said,
"If you must go, Master, you may ride this horse of mine."
This horse has traveled back and forth to Yiwu fifteen times;
it is robust and knows the way.
My master’s horses are few and cannot endure such a long journey.

The Dharma Master then thought to himself: "When I was in Chang'an, on the eve of my resolve to set out for the West, there was a practitioner of arts named He Hongda, who recited incantations and performed divinations that were frequently accurate."
The Dharma Master had him perform a divination, and Da said:
"The Master may go.
The manner of his departure resembles riding an old, red, and emaciated horse; on the front of its lacquered saddle-bridge, there is iron."

Having observed that the horse ridden by the Hu man was lean and reddish, with a lacquered saddle equipped with iron fittings, it coincided with what he had been told by He; thinking this was certainly correct, he proceeded to exchange his own horse for it.
The old Hu man was filled with joy; he paid his respects and took his leave.
Thereupon, he prepared his gear and set out with the young Hu man under the cover of night.
Around the third watch, they reached the river and saw the Jade Gate Pass in the distance.
About ten *li* upstream from the pass, the river was over a *zhang* wide at its banks, with groves of pepper trees growing alongside.
Hu then cut timber to construct a bridge, spread grass and filled it with sand, and drove his horse across.

Once the Dharma Master had crossed over, he was filled with joy; he therefore unyoked his carriage to rest for a while. He remained about fifty paces away from the Hu man, and each lay down upon their mats to sleep.

After a short while, the Hu man drew his sword and rose; he walked slowly toward the Dharma Master, but before reaching a distance of about ten paces, he turned back again. It was unclear what his intention was, and it was suspected that he harbored ulterior motives.
He immediately rose to recite the sutras and invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Upon seeing this, the Hu man lay back down and fell asleep.
As dawn was breaking, the Dharma Master called him to rise, fetch water for rinsing his mouth, and conclude the fast; when they were ready to depart, the Hu man said:

"Disciple, the road ahead is perilous and long, and there is neither water nor grass. There is water only beneath five watchtowers; we must arrive at night to steal the water and pass through. If we are discovered at even a single location, we shall be as good as dead."
"It would be better to return for the sake of peace and security.

The Dharma Master remained firm and did not turn back; he simply walked forward with a composed air. [The pursuers] bared their blades and drew their bows, commanding the Dharma Master to proceed ahead.
The Dharma Master was unwilling to go ahead; the Hu man walked himself for several li and then stopped, saying, "I, your disciple, cannot proceed further.
My family responsibilities are already great, and I may not interfere with the royal law."
The Dharma Master understood his intention and allowed him to return.
The Hu man said, "Master,
you certainly will not reach your destination."
"If we are captured, what can be done about leading each other [into trouble]?
The Dharma Master replied,
"Even if this body were cut into pieces as small as fine dust, I would never lead you into it."
He made a solemn vow to him, and only then did [the spirit] desist.
He gave him a single horse, and after expressing his gratitude for the labor, they parted.
From then on, he traveled alone through the desert, advancing only by following the piles of bones and horse dung as his guide.

Recently, several hundred military units suddenly appeared amidst the desert sands, moving and halting intermittently; they bore the likeness of fur robes, coarse woolen garments, camels, and horses, as well as the forms of banners, standards, lances, and streamers. Their appearances shifted and their substances transformed, undergoing a thousand sudden mutations; when viewed from afar, they were extremely distinct, yet as one drew near, they grew faint.
When the Dharma Master first saw them, he took them for a band of thieves;
as they drew near and he saw them vanish, he realized they were malevolent ghosts.
Furthermore, he heard a voice in the air saying:
"Do not fear, do not fear!
At these words, they were somewhat reassured.
After traveling more than eighty *li*, they saw the first watchtower.
Fearing that sentries might see him, he hid in a sand gully and did not emerge until nightfall.

Upon reaching the west of the beacon tower, he saw water; having drunk from it and washed his hands, he was about to take his leather bag to fill it with water when an arrow whizzed toward him, nearly striking his knee.
After a brief moment, another arrow came flying; realizing he had been seen, he cried out loudly, "I am a monk coming from the capital.
Do not shoot me!"
He immediately led the horse toward the beacon tower.
The man atop the tower also opened the gate and came out; seeing him and recognizing that he was a monk, he escorted him inside to meet the Commandant Wang Xiang.
Xiang ordered fire to be lit so that he might examine him, saying, "He is not a monk from Hexi;
he truly resembles one who has come from the capital.
He questioned him in detail regarding his purpose for traveling.
The Dharma Master replied,
"Does the Colonel have heard people from Liangzhou say there is a monk named Xuanzang who intends to go to the country of the Brahmans to seek the Dharma? He answered:
"I have heard that Master Xuanzang has already returned to the East.
For what reason have you come here?
The Dharma Master then produced the official documents and his name from his horseback, whereupon the other believed him.
He further said, "The western road is arduous and distant; you will ultimately not reach your destination.
Now, I shall not hold you guilty; I am a native of Dunhuang and wish to escort you toward Dunhuang."
"There is a Dharma Master there named Zhang Jiao; he admires the worthy and honors virtue, and he always rejoices upon seeing a teacher. Please go to him.
The Dharma Master replied, "I, Xuanzang, am from Luoyang, my ancestral home; since my youth, I have yearned for the Way."

Among the masters of the Dharma in the two capitals and the monks of singular skill in the regions of Wu and Shu, there were none who did not carry their books to follow him and exhaustively master his interpretations.

In our debates and discussions, we too have attained a status as leading figures of our time; yet, if one wishes to nurture oneself and cultivate a reputation, how could we be inferior to you, the donor from Dunhuang?

However, I regret that the Buddha’s transformation of beings was not exhaustive, that the scriptures are incomplete, and that the meaning [of the teachings] has gaps; therefore, I have no regard for my life or limb and do not fear hardship or peril, vowing to travel to the Western Regions to seek out the bequeathed Dharma.
If you, my patrons, do not urge me on but instead exclusively advise my return, how can this be called sharing a distaste for worldly toil and together planting the seeds for Nirvana?
If you insist on detaining me, I am willing to face whatever punishment; I shall never take a single step eastward to betray my original resolve.
When Xiang heard this, he said with deep compassion, "I am fortunate, my disciple, to have encountered you, Master; how could I not rejoice in your success?
You are weary, so please rest; I shall escort you myself at dawn and point out the way."
He then cleared the mats and prepared the seating.
At dawn, after the Dharma Master had finished his meal, Huixiang sent people carrying water, parched grain, and cakes to escort him for more than ten li.

He said, "Master, take this path toward the fourth watchtower. That man is also of a virtuous mind and is a kinsman of your disciple; his surname is Wang and his given name is Bolong. When you arrive there, you may say that your disciple has sent you."
He wept and bowed before departing.
Once he had left, he reached the fourth watchtower at night; fearing he might be detained, he intended to take water silently and pass through.
Before he had even descended to the water, a flying arrow arrived, reporting the same as before. He immediately hurried toward it, and the other man also came down.
Upon entering the beacon station, the official in charge questioned him, to which he replied:
"I wish to travel to India, and my route passes through here; I have been sent by Wang Xiang, the Commandant of the First Beacon Station, to visit you."
Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy and invited him to stay the night; furthermore, he presented him with a large leather bag, a horse, and barley as parting gifts, saying, "Master,
you need not proceed to the fifth watchtower."
That man was coarse and impulsive; I fear he might harbor ulterior motives.
About a hundred li from here, there is Wild Horse Spring (Yemaquan); you should fetch water from there.

Beyond this point lies the Moheyan Desert, over eight hundred li in length. In antiquity it was called the Sandy River (Shahai): above it, no birds fly; below it, no beasts run; furthermore, it is devoid of both water and grass.
At that time, he was all alone, looking at his own reflection; he did nothing but recollect Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

Previously, while the Dharma Master was in Shu, he saw a sick man whose body was covered in foul-smelling sores and whose clothes were tattered and filthy. Moved by compassion, he took the man to the monastery and provided him with clothing and the funds necessary for food and drink.
Feeling ashamed and remorseful, the sick man bestowed this sutra upon the Dharma Master, who then constantly recited and practiced it.

Upon reaching the Shahe (Sandy River) region, he encountered various malevolent spirits and strange, monstrous beings that surrounded him from front and back; though he invoked Avalokiteśvara, they would not depart, but as soon as he recited this sutra, they all dispersed at his voice. Having escaped danger and obtained salvation, he truly relied upon this [sutra].
After traveling more than a hundred li, he lost his way and could not find Yema Spring.
As he went down to the water to drink, the leather bag was heavy; he lost his grip and overturned it, so that his provisions for a journey of a thousand li were exhausted in a single morning.
Furthermore, having lost his way and wandered in circles without knowing where to go, he intended to return east to the fourth beacon tower.
After traveling some ten li, he thought to himself:
"I previously made a vow that if I did not reach India, I would never take a single step back to the east; why have I come here now?"
"It would be better to die heading west than to live by returning east!
Thereupon he turned his chariot and, single-mindedly recollecting Avalokiteśvara, proceeded toward the northwest.
At that time, looking out in all directions, everything was desolate; both humans and birds had vanished.
At night, malevolent spirits and *chi* demons raised fires that blazed like a multitude of stars; by day, a terrifying wind swept up sand that scattered like seasonal rain.
Although he encountered such things, his mind felt no fear; he suffered only from the exhaustion of the water and the inability to proceed due to thirst.

At that time, for four nights and five days, not a single drop had moistened his throat; his mouth and belly were parched and withered, and he was on the verge of death. Unable to take further food, he lay upon the sand and silently recited the name of Avalokiteśvara, never ceasing despite his exhaustion.
He addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I, Xuanzang, have come on this journey not seeking wealth or profit, nor do I hope for fame; I have come solely for the sake of the unsurpassed True Dharma.
I look up to you, O Bodhisattva, who compassionately regards all living beings and makes the salvation of those in suffering your primary concern."
"This is suffering; do you not know it? When he spoke thus, [the disciple's] mind remained uninterrupted from moment to moment.
At midnight on the fifth night, a cool breeze suddenly touched his body, as refreshing and invigorating as bathing in cold water.
Consequently, his vision was restored and the horse was able to rise.
Once his body had recovered, he fell into a brief sleep.
During this sleep, he dreamed of a great deity several zhang in height, who brandished a halberd and commanded him, saying:
"Why do you not force yourself to proceed, yet lie down again?

Startled awake by these words, the Dharma Master set out. After traveling about ten *li*, his horse suddenly veered off onto a different path; though he tried to restrain it, the horse would not turn back.
After traveling several *li*, he suddenly saw several mu of green grass; he dismounted and ate his fill.

When he was ten paces from the grass and about to turn back, he came upon another pond. Its water was sweet and as clear as a mirror; he immediately went there to drink, and his life was fully restored, so that both man and horse were revived.

Considering this, it was likely not an old pond of water and grass; it must have been created by the Bodhisattva’s compassion for living beings. That his utmost sincerity could communicate with the divine is an instance of precisely this kind.

He rested for one day at the grass pond, and on the following day, he filled his waters and gathered his grass to set out. After traveling for two more days, he finally emerged from the shifting sands and reached Yiwu.
Such perils and hardships could not be fully detailed even in a hundred thousand accounts.
Having arrived at Yiwu, he stayed at a single monastery.

There were three Chinese monks there; among them was an elderly man who, with his robes untied and barefoot, came out to meet him. He embraced the Dharma Master and wept, wailing and sobbing so deeply that he could not stop, saying:
"How could I have expected to see my fellow countryman again today!
The Dharma Master also wept sorrowfully in response.
Other Hu monks and the Hu king all came to pay their respects; the king invited him to his residence and prepared a full array of offerings.
At that time, a messenger of the King of Gaochang, Qu Wentai, was already in Yiwu and was about to return home when he happened to encounter the Dharma Master. Upon returning, he informed his king.

When the king heard this, he dispatched a messenger that very day with an edict ordering the King of Yiwu to send the Dharma Master to him; furthermore, he selected several dozen fine horses and sent a high-ranking official to drive camels and establish rest stations to welcome and escort him.
After staying for over ten days, the King’s envoy arrived; he conveyed the King’s intentions and offered his respectful invitations with great earnestness.

Although the Dharma Master intended to pass through the Kān-futu (Khan-buddha) monastery, since he had been invited by Gaochang, he could not decline the request. Thereupon he set out, traversed the southern desert for six days, and reached Baili City on the borders of Gaochang.
As the sun had already set, the Dharma Master wished to halt, but the city officials and messengers said, "The royal capital is near; please proceed.
They changed to several fine horses and rode on ahead, leaving the red horse the Dharma Master had previously been riding for them to follow later.
That very night, at the hour of cockcrow, he arrived at the royal city.
The gatekeeper informed the king, who commanded that the gates be opened.

The Master entered the city; the king, accompanied by his attendants, personally came out from the palace with torches held before and behind him to welcome the Master into the rear courtyard, where he was seated within a precious canopy in a multi-storied pavilion.
He paid his respects with great sincerity and said,
"Ever since I first heard the Master’s name, I have been so filled with joy that I have forgotten both sleep and food."
"Judging by the distance traveled along the road, I know that the Master will surely arrive tonight; therefore, my wife and I have not yet slept, reading scriptures and waiting with reverence.
After a short while, the Queen, accompanied by several dozen attendants, came again to pay their respects.

At that time, as dawn was gradually approaching, [the Master] spoke of being weary from the long conversation and wishing to sleep; the King then returned to his palace, leaving several eunuchs to attend him overnight.
At dawn, before the Dharma Master had even risen, the King arrived at the door and led his queen and the rest of the entourage to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being.
The King said, "I, your disciple, have reflected upon the hardships and obstacles of the desert road; that you, Master, were able to come alone is truly marvelous.
He shed tears and offered his praises incessantly.

When the meal was served and the breaking of the fast concluded, there was a separate meditation hall beside the palace; the King personally escorted the Dharma Master there and stationed eunuchs to guard him.

A certain Dharma Master Tuan had previously studied in Chang’an and was well-versed in the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); the King held him in high esteem and ordered him to come and meet with the Dharma Master, after which he departed shortly thereafter.
He further summoned the State Preceptor Wang, who was over eighty years of age, to reside with the Master; he even sent messengers to exhort him to stay and not proceed to the Western Regions.
The Master did not consent.
After staying for more than ten days, as he was about to take his leave, the King asked:
"I have already instructed the Commander-in-Chief to consult you; what is your intention?
The Dharma Master replied:
"It is truly by Your Majesty's grace that I am able to remain here; however, it is not fitting for my heart to come [to this land].
The King said, "Tài traveled to the great kingdom with the former king."

From the time of the Sui Emperor, as he traveled through the two capitals of the East and West, and across the regions of Yan, Dai, Fen, and Jin, he encountered many renowned monks, yet his heart felt no particular affinity toward them.

Upon hearing the name of Dharma Master [Seng]cheng, his body and mind were filled with joy; he danced with his hands and stamped with his feet, vowing that once the Master arrived, he would receive him as a disciple and provide for his needs until the end of his life.

He caused all the people of the country to become disciples of the Master, hoping that the Master would provide instruction; although the number of monks was small, there were several thousand of them, all of whom were made to hold scriptures and serve as the assembly listening to the Master.
"I humbly pray that you will examine and accept my humble intentions, and no longer harbor thoughts of traveling to the West.
The Dharma Master declined, saying,
"How could Your Majesty’s profound kindness be something appropriate for one of meager virtue such as this poor monk?"

However, I have not come for the sake of making offerings; rather, I grieve that in my native land the principles of the Dharma are not yet complete and the scriptural teachings are deficient. I harbor doubts and remain mired in confusion, finding no one from whom I may seek instruction.

Thus, I shall devote my life to the West to seek the teachings I have not yet heard, desiring that the nectar of the Vaipulya sutras not only be sprinkled upon Kapilavastu alone, but that these subtle words of definitive discernment may also reach and moisten the Eastern lands. May the resolve of Pāpāṅga to seek the Way and the mind of Sudhana seeking spiritual friends grow ever firmer day by day; how could they be allowed to cease midway?
"I pray that Your Majesty will restrain your intention and not harbor thoughts of providing only general sustenance.

The King said, "I, your disciple, admire and delight in the Dharma Master; I shall certainly detain him to provide for his needs. Even if Mount Cong could be turned back, this resolve of mine would not waver."
"I beg you to believe my humble sincerity and do not doubt its truth.
The Dharma Master replied,
"How could Your Majesty’s profound intention require repeated words before it is known?"
However, I, Xuanzang, have come from the West for the sake of the Dharma; since I have not yet attained the Dharma, I cannot stop midway.
For this reason, I respectfully decline [your invitation], hoping Your Majesty will grant me your understanding.

Furthermore, Your Majesty has cultivated superior karma in the past and now holds the position of sovereign; not only do the common people rely upon you, but the Buddhist teachings likewise depend on you. It is only right that you assist in their propagation; how could it be appropriate for you to create an obstacle?

The King said, "Your disciple would not dare to cause any obstruction; it is simply because our country lacks a teacher that we have humbly requested you, Dharma Master, to remain here and guide those who are ignorant and deluded."
The Dharma Master declined each time, refusing to permit it.
The King then changed countenance, rolled up his sleeves, and spoke in a loud voice:
"If a disciple has a different path for serving his teacher, how can the teacher simply depart on his own?"
"Either you must remain here by mutual agreement, or I shall send my teacher back to his own country; please consider this for yourself.
It would still be better to comply.
The Dharma Master replied:

"I, Xuanzang, have come for the sake of the Great Dharma; now that I am met with such obstacles, my bones may indeed be detained by the King, but my consciousness and spirit will surely not remain here.
Having said this, he sobbed and could speak no further.
The king did not accept this, but instead increased his offerings further.
Every day he presented food, personally carrying the tray himself.
Since the Dharma Master had been detained and his original intention thwarted, he vowed to fast in order to move the king's heart.
Thereupon he sat upright, not taking even water or gruel into his mouth for three days.
On the fourth day, the King perceived that the Dharma Master’s breath was gradually fading; feeling deep remorse and fear, he prostrated himself in apology and said:
"I allow you, Master, to proceed westward; I beg you to accept this early meal."
The Dharma Master, fearing that [the king's words] might not be true, requested that the king swear by the sun as witness.
The king said,
"If it must be so, I pray that we may together make a further karmic bond before the Buddha."

They then entered the dharma hall together to pay homage to the Buddha. In the presence of their mother, Empress Zhang Taifei, they made a covenant with the Dharma Master to become brothers, entrusting themselves to him to seek the Dharma.
They requested that upon his return, he remain in this country for three years to receive the offerings of their disciples.
"If you shall attain Buddhahood in the future, we disciples vow to serve as external patrons (*dānapati*) for you, like King Prasenajit, King Bimbisāra, and others.
We further entreat you to remain for one month to lecture on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, during which time we shall prepare your monastic robes."
The Dharma Master agreed to all her requests.
The Noble Consort was deeply delighted and wished to become the kinswoman of the Master, so that they might deliver one another through successive generations; only then did she begin to eat.
Such was the constancy and firmness of her resolve.

On a subsequent day, the King separately prepared a large pavilion for the lecture; the pavilion could accommodate more than three hundred people. From the Senior Queen (Taifei) downward, including the King, the Commander-in-Chief, and the high ministers, each sat in their respective divisions to listen.
Every time it was time for a lecture, the King would personally carry an incense burner to welcome and lead him.
As he was about to ascend the Dharma seat, the King would again kneel low to serve as a footstool, allowing the Dharma Master to step upon it; this was done every day in this manner.
When the lecture was concluded, he ordained four śrāmaṇeras as attendants for the Dharma Master.
He also prepared thirty sets of dharma robes;
furthermore, because the Western lands are cold, he fashioned several items including face masks, gloves, boots, and socks.

One hundred taels of gold, thirty thousand silver coins, and five hundred rolls of brocade and silk were provided as travel expenses for the Dharma Master’s journey there and back over a period of twenty years.
Thirty horses and twenty-five men were provided;
the Court Attendant-Inspector (Dianzhong Shiyushi) Huan Xin was dispatched to escort them to the headquarters of the Yehe Khan.
Furthermore, twenty-four letters were composed to communicate with the twenty-four kingdoms, including Kucha.
Each letter was accompanied by one roll of fine brocade as a token of sincerity.
Furthermore, five hundred rolls of brocade and silk, along with two wagons of fruit and delicacies, were presented to the Yehe Khan, together with a letter stating:

"This Dharma Master is my younger brother; he wishes to seek the Dharma in the land of the Brahmins. We pray that Your Majesty will regard the Master with the same compassion you show me, and further request that the western kingdoms be ordered to provide escorts and relay horses to send him beyond their borders."

When the Dharma Master saw that the King had sent the śrāmaṇera, along with the state letter, silk, and other gifts, he felt ashamed of the generosity of these parting honors and submitted this petition of thanks:
"I, Xuanzang, have heard that the rivers and seas are vast and deep, yet those who cross them must rely upon boats and oars;
so too, sentient beings are mired in delusion, and those who guide them truly depend upon the Holy Word."
Therefore, the Tathāgata, mobilizing the great compassion for his only child, was born into this defiled land;
he reflects the sun of the wisdom of the three knowledges to illuminate this dark obscurity.

The clouds of his benevolence shade the heavens up to the Akaniṣṭha realm, and the rain of the Dharma moistens the trichiliocosm. Having completed the work of benefiting and pacifying all beings, he relinquishes his manifested form to return to the ultimate truth.

Since the Bequeathed Teachings flowed eastward more than six hundred years ago, Fotudeng and Zhu Fohui have spread its brilliance in the regions of Wu and Luo, while Dharmakṣema and Kumārajīva have concentrated its excellence in Qin and Liang; thus they have not allowed the profound wind to fall into ruin, and all have assisted in upholding this supreme enterprise.

However, as translations were produced by foreigners from afar, their pronunciations and explanations differed; and as the distance from the Sage grew ever greater over time, the meanings and categories became distorted and erroneous. Consequently, the teaching of the single flavor at the Twin Śāla Trees was divided into the two constants of the "present" and the "future," and the Mahāyāna doctrine of non-duality was split into the two paths of the North and the South.
Conflicting debates have persisted for several hundred years;
throughout the land, doubts have been harbored, yet no one has emerged to provide a definitive resolution.
By the grace of past causes, I, Xuanzang, was fortunate to enter the ranks of the monastic community early on; carrying my book-box to follow teachers, nearly twenty-four years have passed.

I have been fortunate to consult with worthy and eminent friends and have gained a general understanding of the tenets of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. Yet, there have been moments when I could not help but hesitate while holding a scroll, or feel despondent while clasping a sutra; I have longed to set foot in the Jetavana Grove and harbored deep thoughts of Vulture Peak, wishing to pay my respects in person and resolve my long-standing doubts.

However, I know that a short bamboo tube cannot peer into the heavens and a small conch shell is ill-suited for scooping up the ocean; yet, unable to cast aside this humble sincerity, I have prepared my gear and set out on the road, and after traveling for some time, I have finally arrived at Yiwu.

I humbly submit that Your Majesty has received the pure harmony of Heaven and Earth and is endowed with the auspicious qi of the Two Polarities. Wearing the robe of ease, you act as sovereign and nurture the masses like your own children. To the east, you reach the customs of the Great Nation; to the west, you pacify the traditions of the hundred tribes. The lands of Loulan and Yuezhi, and the regions of Cheshi and Langwang, are all covered by your profound benevolence and equally moistened by your deep virtue.
Furthermore, he revered the worthy and loved scholars, delighting in goodness and flowing with compassion; he took pity on those who had come from afar and graciously arranged for their reception.
Once they had settled there, his generous favors became even more profound as he granted them his personal discourse and elucidated the principles of the Dharma.

Furthermore, I was graced by the opportunity to form a bond with his younger brother, and he earnestly encouraged our fraternal sentiments; he also dispatched letters to more than twenty kingdoms in the Western Regions, conveying his warmest and most sincere greetings, and ordering them to provide successive escorts for my journey.

Furthermore, out of compassion for his solitary journey to the West and the bitter cold of the snowy roads, he issued a clear edict to ordain four śrāmaṇeras as his attendants. He provided more than fifty items, including dharma robes, cotton hats, fur cloaks, woolen rugs, and boots, along with silk, brocade, gold, silver, and coinage, to serve as provisions for twenty years of travel there and back.

Prostrating myself before you in shock and shame, I do not know where to turn; the waters of the Jiao River compared to your bounty are not more abundant, and Mount Congling lifted up in comparison to your grace is surely not weightier.
The perilous crossing of Lingxi shall no longer be a cause for concern;
the land of the Celestial Ladder and the Bodhi Tree can be visited for worship without delay.
If this request is granted, whose power could it be but yours?
This is the grace of the King.

Thereafter, I shall pay my respects to the various masters, receive the true Dharma, and return to translate it so as to widely disseminate what has not yet been heard. I will clear away the dense forest of various views, sever the forced interpretations of heterodox schools, supplement the omissions of the Semblance Dharma age, and establish a guide for the profound gate. It is my hope that through this modest merit, I may repay his extraordinary bounty.
Furthermore, as my previous journey is long, I am unable to remain for much longer; tomorrow I shall take my leave, which already increases my sorrow and distress.
Unable to bear the weight of your profound kindness, I respectfully submit this letter of thanks.

The King replied, "Since the Dharma Master has consented to be my brother, then whatever the state maintains shall be held in common with you, Master; for what reason, then, should there be any need for thanks?"
On the day of departure, the King, along with the monks, ministers, and common people, emptied the entire city to see him off west of the western gate.
The King embraced the Dharma Master and wailed aloud; both monastics and laypeople were moved to grief, and the sound of their lamentation over the parting shook the surrounding suburbs and towns.

He commanded his consort and the common people to return, while he himself, along with the virtuous monks and those below them, traveled several tens of li on horseback to see them off before returning home.
In all the kingdoms they passed through, the kings and nobles treated him with such profound respect; it was always of this nature.
From here, traveling westward, after passing the cities of Wu-ban and Du-jin, one enters the country of A-qi-ni (formerly called Wu-qi, which is an error).
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci'en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty, Scroll One.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci'en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty,
Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili and annotated by Shi Yancong.
From the Kingdom of Ākīni to the Kingdom of Kanyākubja. From here, traveling westward, one arrives at the Springs of the Father-Master in the Kingdom of Ākīni.
The spring is located on the southern cliff of Sandao; the cliff is several *zhang* high, and the water emerges from its midpoint.
According to tradition, several hundred merchants once traveled along this road when their water ran out. Arriving here exhausted and at a loss as to what to do, they were saved by this source.
At that time, there was a monk among the assembly who did not pack his travel provisions and relied upon the community for alms.
The assembly deliberated, saying:
"This monk serves the Buddha; it is for this reason that we provide for him. Although he has traveled ten thousand *li*, he has carried nothing with him."
"Now we are parched with thirst, yet you show no concern; we should speak to you together.
The monk said, "If you wish for water, each of you should pay homage to the Buddha, receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and I shall climb the cliff for you to create water."
As the assembly was in dire distress, they all followed his instructions.
Once the ordination was completed, the monk instructed them, saying:
"After I have ascended the cliff, you must call out, 'Father Master, please descend for us,' using as many repetitions as you deem necessary."

Not long after he had departed, the multitude made their request as instructed; in a short while, the water flowed down in abundance, and there was no one among the great assembly who was not filled with joy.
The Master never returned, and when the people looked up to observe him, they found that he had already entered parinirvāṇa.
The great and small wailed in grief, and according to the customs of the Western Regions, they cremated him.
At the place where he sat, they gathered bricks and stones to build a stupa; this stupa remains to this day, and the water has not ceased to flow.
Travelers passing through come and go in varying numbers, with the water becoming shallow or deep accordingly;
when no one is present, it flows as a mere stream.
The Dharma Master stayed with the assembly by the side of the spring.
At dawn, he again passed through a silver mountain.
The mountain was exceedingly high and vast, consisting entirely of silver mines; it is from here that the silver coins of the Western Regions originate.
To the west of the mountain, he encountered a band of robbers, who seized his belongings and departed with them.
They eventually reached the banks of a river near the capital city and stayed there for the night.

At that time, several dozen fellow merchants from the Hu lands, greedy to be the first to trade, set out secretly in the middle of the night and traveled some ten or more li ahead. There they encountered bandits who robbed and killed them, with not a single person escaping.
When the Dharma Master and his companions arrived, they saw his remains; as he possessed no further property, they sighed with deep sorrow.
As they gradually drew closer and saw the royal capital from afar, King Ajita came out with his ministers to welcome them, inviting them inside to provide offerings.
That country had previously been harassed by the invasions of Gaochang; harboring resentment, they were unwilling to provide horses.
The Master stayed there for one night and then departed.
He crossed two great rivers and traveled several hundred li across a flat plain to the west, entering the borders of the kingdom of Kuci (formerly called Qiuci, which is a corruption).
As they drew near the royal capital, the King, together with his ministers and the venerable monk Mokṣagupta and others, came out to welcome them.
Furthermore, several thousand other monks had all pitched floating canopies outside the eastern gate of the city, where they installed a processional image and remained there performing music.
When the Dharma Master arrived, the virtuous monks rose to offer him their greetings; once this was concluded, they each returned to their seats.
They sent a monk to carry a tray of fresh flowers and present it to the Dharma Master.
Having received them, the Dharma Master led [the flowers] before the Buddha, scattered the flowers, and after completing his prostrations, took a seat below Moksagupta.
Once seated, he again distributed the flowers.
After the flower procession was completed, they proceeded with the pomegranate juice.

Having received the flowers and the juice at the first monastery, they did the same at each subsequent monastery; thus, by passing from one to another, the day drew to a close before it was finished, and only then did the assembly of monks disperse.
There were several dozen people from Gaochang who had left the household life at Quchi; they resided separately in a monastery located to the southeast of the city.

Because the Dharma Master had come from their native land, they first invited him to stay overnight, so he went there with them, while the King and the various virtuous monks each returned to their own quarters.

The next day, the King invited him to his palace and prepared an array of offerings; however, the food contained the three kinds of "pure meat," which the Dharma Master would not accept, much to the King’s deep astonishment.
The Dharma Master replied:
"This is what has been permitted by the gradual teachings, yet the Mahāyāna, which Xuanzang studies, does not allow for such things."
Having received other special food and finished eating,
he passed beyond the city to the north-west to the Aśokārāma (in the language of Tang, "The Extraordinary"), which was the monastery where Mokṣagupta resided.

Kumāralāta was exceptionally skilled and adept in consciousness; he was the one to whom others looked for guidance. Having traveled and studied in India for over twenty years, although he had encountered many scriptures, he was most proficient in *Śabda-vidyā* (Grammar). He was respected by both the king and the people of the land, and was acclaimed as being peerless.
When he saw that the Dharma Master had arrived, he treated him merely with the courtesy due to a guest and did not yet acknowledge him as one who understood the Dharma.
He said to the Master:

"In this land, all such works as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the *Vibhāṣā* exist; it is sufficient to study them here. There is no need for the trouble of traveling to the West to undergo such hardships."
The Dharma Master replied,
"Is there the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* here? Kuṭadanta said:
"What is the use of inquiring about this book of heterodox views?
A true disciple of the Buddha does not study such things.
When the Dharma Master first held him in deep esteem, upon hearing these words, he regarded him as nothing more than dust.

He replied, "The *Vibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa* already exist in my own country; however, I regret that their principles are coarse and their language shallow, as they do not represent the ultimate teaching. For this reason, I have come specifically to study the Mahayana *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*."
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* was spoken by Maitreya, a Bodhisattva in his final existence; to now call it a heterodox work—is this not to fear falling into a bottomless pit of injustice?
He replied, "The *Mahāvibhāṣā* and other such works are things you have not yet understood; how can you say they are not profound?
The Dharma Master responded:
"Does the Master understand now?
He replied, "I understand it all."

The Dharma Master then cited the opening passage of the *Abhidharmakośa* to question him; the opponent’s initial premise was erroneous, and as the Master pursued the matter further, the man’s complexion changed and he said, "Please ask about another point."
He then showed another passage, which was also not found;
[the opponent] said, "The *Śāstra* does not contain these words.

At that time, Wang Shu Zhimue, who had left the household life and was also proficient in the sūtras and śāstras, was sitting nearby; he immediately testified that the *Śāstra* did indeed contain those words.
He then took up the original text and read it against the commentary; Guptaka felt deeply ashamed and said, "It was merely my failing memory.
He also questioned other schools, but none provided a satisfactory explanation.

At that time, because the snowy roads over Mount Ling had not yet opened, he was unable to set out; he remained detained for more than sixty days. Aside from observing him from afar, he occasionally went to speak with him; upon meeting, [the Master] no longer sat in a haughty posture, but would either stand or move aside to avoid him.
I said to the man:
"This Chinese monk is not easily refuted.
Even if you were to go to India, it is uncertain whether anyone among the youth there would surpass him."
Such was his awe and admiration.
On the day he set out, the King provided him with laborers, camels, and horses; the king, along with monastics and laypeople, emptied the city to see him off.

After traveling west for two days, he encountered more than two thousand horsemen of the Tujue (Turks), who were robbers. These bandits had previously divided the traveling party's provisions and wealth among themselves, but as they disputed over the unequal distribution, they fell into internal strife and dispersed.
Furthermore, traveling six hundred li forward, they crossed a small desert and reached the kingdom of Baluka (formerly called Gumu), where they stayed for one night.
Continuing northwest for three hundred li, they crossed another desert and reached Mount Ling, which is the northern corner of the Pamir Mountains.
The mountain is steep and precipitous, its peaks reaching to the heavens.

Since the beginning of creation, it has been a gathering place for ice and snow; these have accumulated into glaciers that do not melt in spring or summer. Thick with frozen masses and spreading over vast areas, they connect with the clouds above; looking up at them, they appear brilliantly white, their limits invisible to the eye.

Those peaks that had collapsed and fallen across the side of the road were some a hundred feet high and others several tens of feet wide; consequently, the paths became rugged and the ascent arduous and obstructed.
Furthermore, as wind and snow flew together, even with double-soled shoes and heavy furs, one could not avoid shivering from the cold.
When wishing to sleep or eat, there was likewise no dry place to stay; one knew only to hang cauldrons over fires to cook and to lie down upon the ice to sleep.

Only after seven days did they finally emerge from the mountains; among the companions, thirteen or fourteen had perished from exposure to the cold, while the loss of oxen and horses was even more severe.
After leaving the mountains, they reached a clear lake, which is also called the Hot Sea.

Because it was observed that this river did not freeze even when facing Mount Ling, it received its name; its waters are not necessarily warm. It spans fourteen or fifteen hundred *li* in circumference, being long from east to west and narrow from south to north. When viewed from afar, it appears vast and boundless, and its surging waves reach several *zhang* in height even without the aid of a gale.

Traveling northwest along the coast for over five hundred *li*, he reached the city of Suyab, where he encountered the Tujue Yehu Khan, who was then engaged in a hunting expedition with a vast array of warhorses.
The Khan was dressed in a robe of green silk gauze; his hair was unbound, with a length of several feet of white silk cloth wrapped around his forehead and trailing behind.
More than two hundred high-ranking officials, all wearing brocade robes and with their hair braided, surrounded him on his left and right.
The rest of the troops were all clad in furs, coarse wool, and animal hair, carrying spears, banners, and bows; their camels and horses galloped so that the eye could not see their limit.
Upon meeting them, the Khan was delighted and said, "We shall travel together for a short while and return in two or three days; for now, you masters should proceed to the headquarters."
He ordered the high official Dharmaśreṣṭhin to escort him and settle him there.
After three days had passed since his arrival at the capital, the Khan returned and led the Dharma Master inside.
The Khan resided in a great tent adorned with golden flowers, so dazzling that it blinded the eyes of men.
The high officials sat in two rows on long mats in the front, all resplendent in their brocade robes; the remaining guards stood behind them.
Beholding this, even the lords of the felt tents would consider it dignified and magnificent.
The Dharma Master went some thirty paces from his tent; the Khan came out from his tent to meet him with a prostration. After the greetings and inquiries were concluded, he entered and took his seat.
Regarding the Turks, they worship fire and do not provide beds, for wood contains fire; thus, out of reverence, they do not sit upon them, but merely spread thick carpets upon the ground.
He then prepared an iron cross-legged chair for the Dharma Master, spread a mat upon it, and invited him to sit.

After a short while, he further led the Chinese envoys and the envoys from Gaochang inside to present the national letter and the gifts; the Khan examined them with his own eyes, was greatly pleased, and ordered the messengers to be seated.
The Khan ordered wine to be set out and music to be performed; he joined his ministers and envoys in drinking, while separately seeking pomegranate juice to offer to the Dharma Master.

Thereupon, they indulged in mutual toasts and exhortations, as goblets and bowls of various shapes were passed back and forth and filled one after another. The sounds of the *gim-ma* and *tou-li* melodies rang out in harmonious alternation; though these were the songs of the frontier tribes, they greatly delighted the ears and eyes and gladdened the heart and mind.
After a short while, more food arrived; all were the flesh of freshly cooked lambs and calves, piled high before him.
Separately prepared pure food was offered to the Dharma Master, consisting of cakes, rice, ghee, milk, rock honey, flower honey, grapes, and so forth.
When the meal was finished, grape juice was served once more, and he invited the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma.

The Master thereupon instructed him in the ten wholesome paths of action, the cherishing and protection of living beings, and the karma of the pāramitās and liberation; whereupon [the king] raised his hand to touch his forehead in reverence and joyfully accepted the teaching with faith.
He remained there for several days and urged him to stay, saying:

"Master, you need not go to the country of Indataga—that is, India. That land is very hot; the tenth month there corresponds to the fifth month here. Judging by your physical appearance, I fear you would wither away upon reaching it."
That man’s complexion was dark and he lacked dignified deportment; he was not worthy of being looked upon.
The Dharma Master replied, “I am going there now because I wish to seek out sacred traces and yearn for the Dharma.”

The Khan then ordered his army to search for someone who understood Chinese and the languages of various nations. He eventually found a young man who had previously been in Chang’an for several years and was proficient in the Chinese language; he was immediately appointed to the office of Mudu-da and tasked with writing letters to the various nations. He was then instructed to escort the Dharma Master to the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
Furthermore, he presented a set of ceremonial robes made of crimson brocade and fifty rolls of silk, accompanying the ministers for more than ten *li* on their journey.

From here, traveling westward for over four hundred *li*, one arrives at Bingyul, also known as Qianquan (The Thousand Springs). The territory spans several hundred *li*; it abounds in ponds and marshes and is rich with rare trees. Dense, cool, and humid, it serves as the place where the Khan retreats during the summer.
Traveling westward from Zibing for one hundred and fifty *li*, one reaches the city of Talasa.
Continuing southwest for two hundred *li*, one reaches the city of Bai-shui.
Continuing southwest for another two hundred *li*, one reaches the city of Gongyu.
Fifty li further south, one reaches the kingdom of Nu-chi-chieh (formerly read as Nu-nu).
Two hundred li further west, one reaches the kingdom of Cha-shih (the Tang-language name for the Kingdom of Shih), which borders the Ye-ye River to its west.
Traveling another one thousand or more li to the west, one arrives at the kingdom of Sutrishna, whose eastern border abuts the Yeh-yeh River.
This river originates from the northern source of the Pamir Mountains and flows toward the northwest.

Furthermore, traveling northwest into a great desert where there is neither water nor grass, he proceeded for over five hundred li by following the remains of bones until he reached the kingdom of Samarkand (which in the language of Tang is called Kangguo).
The king and the common people did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, taking the worship of fire as their path.

There were two monasteries, but they were remote and devoid of resident monks; whenever visiting monks sought refuge there, the various Hu people would drive them away with fire, refusing to allow them to stay.
When the Dharma Master first arrived, the King received him with lingering arrogance.
After one night had passed, the Master preached to him on the causes and effects of human and celestial realms, praised the merits of the Buddha, and explained the benefits of reverent devotion.
The King was filled with joy and invited him to receive the fast and precepts, treating him with the utmost sincerity.
His two junior disciples went to the temple to pay their respects, but the various Hu people instead pursued them with fire and burned them.

The śrāmaṇera returned and informed the king; upon hearing this, the king ordered that the one who had burned him be captured. Once he was found, the king assembled the common people and commanded that his hands be severed.
The Dharma Master, wishing to encourage virtue, could not bear to see his limbs mutilated, so he rescued him.
The King then severely flogged him and banished him beyond the capital.
From that time on, those above and below were solemn and reverent, all seeking to practice the faith; consequently, he established great assemblies and ordained people to reside in monasteries.
In every place he visited, he transformed depraved minds and enlightened the ignorant masses; such was his influence.
Traveling further west for more than three hundred li, he reached the country of Kustana (pronounced with a falling tone).
Traveling further west for more than two hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Kāpiśī (Tang: Dong'an Guo).
Traveling another four hundred li to the west, one reaches the kingdom of Bamiyan (Tang: Zhong'an Guo).
Traveling further west for more than one hundred li, one reaches the country of Vāḍī (in the language of Tang, Xī'ān Guó).
Traveling another five hundred li to the west, one reaches the country of Hualimiga, which borders the Oxus River (Vakṣu) to its east.
Traveling further southwest for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Karashahr (in the Tang language, the "History Kingdom").
Continuing southwest for two hundred li, one enters the mountains; the mountain paths are deep and perilous, barely passable for human foot traffic, and moreover, there is neither water nor grass.

Traveling over three hundred li through the mountains, one enters the Iron Gate. The peaks and cliffs are narrow and precipitous, and the rocky slopes abound with iron ore; these were used to construct the door leaves, and bells cast of iron were hung upon them in great numbers, hence its name.
This was the frontier pass of the Turks.
Exiting through the Iron Gate, one arrives at the country of Tukhāra (formerly called Tuhuoluo, which is a corruption).

From here, after traveling several hundred *li* and crossing the Oxus River (*Vakṣu*), one reaches the country of Huo (Jiehuo), which is the residence of the eldest son of the Yabghu Qaghan, named Tardu Śāta (Śāta being an official title). Furthermore, he is the brother-in-law of the King of Gaochang.
A letter from the King of Gaochang had arrived at his location.
By the time the Dharma Master arrived, the Princess Khokhan had already passed away.
The Tardu Shad was also ill; upon hearing that the Dharma Master had come from Gaochang and receiving the letter, he, along with his sons and daughters, wept uncontrollably.
He then requested of the Dharma Master, saying, "I have observed that your eyesight is failing; I pray that you will rest for a short while.
Once you have recovered, I shall personally escort you to the country of the Brahmins."
At that time, another Brahmin monk arrived and recited incantations for him, whereby his ailment was gradually eliminated.
