Later, he married a young lady, the Princess Khe-khun; having received the instructions of his former son, she used medicine to kill her husband.

When the Shé died, the Prince of Gaochang’s son was still young, so the former son, the Tegin, usurped the throne and established himself as the new Shé; he subsequently took the Shé’s stepmother as his wife.
Because they were in mourning for the deceased, they remained there for over a month.

There was a śramaṇa named Dharmasaṃgha who traveled to study in India; to the west of the Pamir Mountains, he was esteemed as a master of the Dharma, such that none among the monks of Shule or Khotan dared to engage him in conversation.
The Dharma Master, wishing to ascertain the depth of their learning, sent someone to ask the teacher how many sūtras and śāstras he could explain.
When the disciples heard this, they were all incensed.
Bodhidharma smiled and said:
"I understand everything; you may ask whatever you wish.

Knowing that [the interlocutor] did not study the Mahāyāna, the Dharma Master questioned him on several topics from the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts of the Hīnayāna; however, he was not well-versed in them.
Consequently, he apologized and submitted, and his disciples were all filled with shame.
From then on, whenever they met, they greeted each other with joy; they praised him everywhere, saying that they themselves could not equal him.

At that time, Xinshe had just established himself in office, and the Dharma Master requested from him some attendants and *ulakas* (messengers), wishing to travel south toward the land of the Brahmins.

He said: "In the territory under my jurisdiction lies the kingdom of Bāhīka, bordering the Oxus River to the north; people call it the Lesser Rājagṛha. It contains a great many sacred sites. I pray that you, Master, will go there briefly to pay your respects, and thereafter take a vehicle and travel south."
At that time, several dozen monks from Bāhlika, having heard that the former [monastery] had been destroyed and that the son had rebuilt it, came together to offer their condolences.
When they met with the Dharma Master, he explained his intentions to them.
The other said, "You should depart at once; there is a good road there. If you come here again, it will only be a fruitless detour.
The Dharma Master followed his advice, made his excuses, took his carriage, and departed with that monk.
Upon arrival, he observed that the city and its suburbs were spacious and bright, while the rivers and fields were fertile and lush; it was truly an excellent location.
There were one hundred monasteries with more than three thousand monks, all of whom studied the Hīnayāna.
To the southwest outside the city is the Navā Monastery (translated into Chinese as "New"), which is most magnificently adorned.
Within the monastery’s Buddha hall is the Buddha’s bathing pitcher, with a capacity of slightly more than one *dou*.
There is also a tooth of the Buddha, one cun long and eight or nine fen wide, yellowish-white in color, which constantly emits auspicious light.
There is also the Buddha’s broom, made of kāśa grass, over three chi in length and about seven cun in circumference; its handle is adorned with various precious gems.

These three objects are brought out every fast day (*upoṣadha*), when both monastics and laypeople come to observe and pay homage; those of sincere devotion are moved by the manifestation of divine light.
To the north of the monastery is a stūpa, over two hundred feet in height.

To the southwest of the monastery, there is a meditation hut established many years ago; those who have dwelt within it to practice the Way and realize the four fruits of sainthood have appeared generation after generation without interruption. After their parinirvāṇa, each was memorialized with a stupa, and these foundations now extend in succession for more than several hundred.
Fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city, one reaches the city of Trapuṣa.
Forty *li* north of this city is the city of Bhallika.
Within this city are two *stūpas*, each three *zhang* in height.

In the past, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he received these two elders’ offerings of parched grain and honey. He first taught them the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, and they invited him to accept their offerings.

The Tathāgata then granted them his hair and nail-clippings, instructing them on how to construct stūpas and the rituals for doing so. The two elders took these back to their own country and established sacred shrines; this is precisely that site.
More than seventy *li* to the west of the city is a stūpa over twenty feet high, constructed during the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha.
At the Navasamghārāma was the Tripiṭaka master of the Hīnayāna from the kingdom of Tsa-kia (Takka), named Prajñākara, which in the language of Tang means "Wisdom-Nature."
Having heard that the kingdom of Bamiyan possesses many sacred sites, I have come here to pay my respects.

Its people are intelligent and devoted to learning; they are bright and spirited from their youth, having delved deeply into the Nine Divisions of the Canon and mastered the Four Āgamas. Their reputation for expertise in interpreting the meaning of the scriptures resounds throughout India.
He was thoroughly proficient in all the Hīnayāna Abhidharma treatises, including the *Kātyāyanīputra*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, and the *Abhidharma* texts.
Having heard that the Dharma Master had traveled from afar in search of the Dharma, they were greatly delighted upon meeting.

The Dharma Master then set forth his doubts and difficulties, posing questions based on the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. The master’s responses were exceptionally refined and thorough; consequently, he stayed for over a month to study the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* under him.

In the monastery there were also two masters of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna: Dharmapriya (translated into Chinese as Fǎ’ài, "Dharma-Love") and Dharmakīrti (translated into Chinese as Fǎxìng, "Dharma-Nature"), both of whom were highly revered by those there.
Beholding the Dharma Master’s spiritual countenance, which was bright and elegant, they treated him with the utmost reverence and admiration.
At that time, to the southwest of Bāhīka were the kingdoms of Rāmta and Huśikana.

When their kings heard that the Dharma Master had come from a distant land, they both dispatched high-ranking ministers to pay their respects and invite him to pass through their countries to receive offerings; however, he declined and did not go.
He sent messengers back and forth several times until, having no choice, he went there.
The King was greatly pleased and presented gold, jewels, food, and drink as offerings to the Dharma Master; however, the Dharma Master accepted none of them and returned.
Traveling south from Zabawakhan, he accompanied the Dharma Master Huixing into the kingdom of Jiezhiguo.
To the southeast, they entered the Great Snow Mountains and traveled over six hundred li, exiting the territory of Tukhāra and entering the kingdom of Bāmiyān (Fanyuenna).

The country extends for more than two thousand *li* from east to west and is situated amidst the Snow Mountains (*Himavat*). The roads are perilous and difficult, exceeding those found in the icy wastes (*lingqi*) tenfold; frozen clouds and flying snow never cease for even a moment. When one encounters particularly severe stretches, where the level path is but a few *zhang* wide, this is what King Song referred to when describing the hardships of the West: "Massive ice rises high, and flying snow extends for a thousand *li*. This is precisely it.

Alas! Were one not to seek the unsurpassed True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, what purpose would there be in receiving the physical body bequeathed by one’s parents to wander through this world?
Long ago, when Wang Zun ascended the slope of nine bends, he declared of himself:
"I am a loyal minister of the House of Han."
"The Dharma Master has now traversed the Snowy Ranges in search of scriptures; he may truly be called a genuine son of the Tathāgata.
Thus, he gradually arrived at the capital city of Bamiyan, where there were more than ten monasteries and several thousand monks who studied the Lokottaravāda school of the Hīnayāna.
The King of Bamiyan came out to welcome him and invited him into the palace to provide offerings; it was only after several days that he departed.

There were two monks of the Mahāsāṃghika school, Ācārya Dhava (translated into Chinese as Shengshi, "Holy Messenger") and Ācārya Sna (translated into Chinese as Shengjun, "Holy Army"), both of whom had a profound understanding of the characteristics of dharmas. Upon seeing the Dharma Master, they were struck with wonder and admiration, exclaiming that even in a distant land such as China there were monks of such caliber. They led him about to various places to pay their respects and observe the sights, doing so with unremitting earnestness.
On a mountain slope to the northeast of the royal city, there is a standing stone image one hundred and fifty feet high.
To the east of the image is a monastery, and to the east of the monastery is a standing brass image of Śākyamuni one hundred feet high.
Within the monastery is a reclining image of the Buddha entering nirvana, one thousand feet in length, exquisitely adorned and magnificent.

Traveling more than two hundred li southeast from here, crossing the Great Snow Mountains to a small valley, there is a monastery containing the Buddha’s tooth and the tooth of a pratyekabuddha from the beginning of the kalpa; it is five inches long and slightly less than four inches wide.
Furthermore, there were the teeth of a Cakravartin King, three inches long and two inches wide.
There was also the iron alms bowl, with a capacity of eight or nine *sheng*, and the *saṃghāṭī* robe, dyed a deep crimson, both belonging to Śāṇakavāsa (formerly called Shanhexiu, which is an error).

Throughout five hundred lifetimes, during both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*), this person constantly wore these garments; they emerged from the womb together with him, and later transformed into *kāṣāya* robes. The details of these causes and conditions are as extensive as described in the separate biography.

Thus, after fifteen days, he departed from Bamiyan; on the sixteenth day, he encountered snow and lost his way, reaching a small sandy ridge where he met a hunter who showed him the path. Crossing the Black Mountains, he arrived at the realm of Kapisa.
The country is over four thousand *li* in circuit, with the Snow Mountains to its north.
The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is sagacious, resourceful, and majestic, presiding over more than ten kingdoms.
Upon his approach to the capital, the king, together with various monks, came out of the city to welcome him.
There were more than one hundred monasteries, and the monks were constantly at odds, each wishing to invite [the traveler] to stay at their own residence.
There was a Hinayana monastery named Śālaka, which tradition says was built during the time when the son of the Han Emperor was held as a hostage.
The monks of that monastery said,
"Our monastery was originally built by the son of the Han Emperor.
Now that you have come from there, you ought first to visit our monastery."

Seeing his earnest devotion and noting that his companion, Dharma Master Huixing, was a follower of the Hīnayāna who likewise did not wish to reside in a Mahāyāna monastery, the Dharma Master consequently settled there.

When Prince Jeta was building the monastery, he also buried immeasurable treasures beneath the feet of the Great Devarāja to the south of the eastern gate of the Buddha court, intending them for the future repair of the saṃghārāma.
The monks, bearing his grace, have depicted the prince’s likeness upon the walls of their dwellings in various places.
On the day the summer retreat (varṣā) concludes, they further recite scriptures for him to plant roots of merit.
This tradition has been passed down through generations and continues unabated to this day.
Recently, there was a wicked king, greedy and tyrannical, who sought to seize the Sangha’s treasures. He dispatched men to dig beneath the feet of the deity, whereupon the earth shook violently.
Upon the deity’s head was an image of a parrot; seeing the excavation, it flapped its wings and cried out in alarm.
The king and his entire army were all overcome with fainting; terrified, they retreated.

In the monastery, the parasol of a stūpa had collapsed and been destroyed. When the monks wished to take the precious materials to repair it, the earth shook and roared once more, such that no one dared to approach.
Once the Dharma Master had arrived, the assembly gathered together and collectively requested him to recount the previous events.
The Dharma Master went with them to the deity’s shrine and, burning incense, declared:
“The hostage originally concealed this treasure intending to employ it for the cultivation of merit; now that we open it for use, truly the time has come.”
I pray that you will reflect upon my sincere intentions and slightly restrain your majestic severity.

If you would grant me this permission, I, Xuanzang, shall personally supervise the opening [of the stupa], weigh the contents to determine their quantity before handing them over to the relevant authorities, so that they may be constructed according to the Dharma without any waste.
"Only the spiritual power of Your Divinity can hope to grant its consideration.

Having spoken thus, he ordered men to dig; the ground was leveled without difficulty, and at a depth of seven or eight feet, they found a large bronze vessel containing several hundred catties of gold and dozens of bright pearls.
The great assembly rejoiced, and there was none who did not sigh in admiration and submission.
The Dharma Master immediately entered the summer retreat at the monastery.

As the King held the arts in light esteem but placed great faith in the Mahāyāna, and delighted in observing lectures and recitations, he invited the Dharma Master and the Tripiṭaka Master Huixing to assemble for a Dharma gathering at a major Mahāyāna temple.

Among them were those who were preeminent: the Mahāyāna Tripiṭaka master named Manojñaghoṣa (translated into Chinese as Rúyìshēng), the Sarvāstivāda monk Āryavarman (translated into Chinese as Shèngzhòu), and the Mahīśāsaka monk Guṇabhadra (translated into Chinese as Dèxián). All of these were the foremost among them.

However, as scholars do not master all fields simultaneously, those specializing in either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna each possess distinct limitations; though they may be refined in a single principle, they ultimately excel only in one direction.

Only the Dharma Master possesses comprehensive knowledge of all teachings; according to whatever questions were posed to him, he answered each based on its respective school, such that all were fully satisfied and convinced.
Thus, after five days, the assembly finally dispersed.
The King was greatly pleased and bestowed five rolls of pure brocade upon the Dharma Master as a special gift, while providing other gifts to each of the others according to their rank.
Having completed the summer retreat at Śrāvakasthāna, the Dharma Master Huixing was again invited by the King of Tukhāra to return; the Master then took his leave of him.
Traveling eastward for over six hundred *li*, he crossed the Black Ridge (*Kṛṣṇagiri*) and entered the territory of Northern India, arriving at the kingdom of Lampāka.
The kingdom is over one thousand *li* in circuit.
There are ten monasteries, and the monks all study the Mahāyāna.

After staying for three days, he traveled south to a small ridge. On the ridge was a stūpa, which was built by later generations out of veneration and longing because the Buddha had formerly walked from the south to this spot and stood there.
From this point northward, all territories are called Mleccha, which in the language of Tang means "frontier lands.
Whenever the Tathāgata wished to teach and transform beings there, he traveled through the air and no longer trod upon the ground; for when he walked, the earth would immediately tilt and shake.
From here, traveling south for more than twenty li, one descends a ridge and crosses a river to reach the kingdom of Nāgarahāra, within the borders of North India.

Two li to the southeast of the great city stands a stūpa over three hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. This is the place where Śākya Bodhisattva, during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha; there he spread his deerskin garment and laid out his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction of future Buddhahood.
Although the kalpa of destruction has passed, these traces remain forever; the devas scatter various flowers as a constant offering.
When the Dharma Master arrived there, he prostrated and circumambulated the site, while an elderly monk nearby recounted to him the circumstances of the stupa’s construction.

The Dharma Master asked: "When the Bodhisattva spread his hair, it was already during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. From the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa until the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, immeasurable kalpas passed; within each of these kalpas, worlds underwent many cycles of formation and destruction. When the calamity of fire arises, even Mount Sumeru is reduced to ashes. How is it that this trace alone remains without decay?"
He replied: "When the world is destroyed, this [site] is likewise destroyed; when the world is formed again, its traces shall appear in their original location.
For instance, even though Mount Sumeru is destroyed and then reappears, how could the sacred traces alone be absent?"
"Judging by this, there is no need for further doubt.
This also serves as a definitive response.
Next, about ten li to the southwest, there is a stūpa at the place where the Buddha purchased flowers.
Furthermore, traveling southeast for more than ten li across a sandy ridge, one arrives at the City of the Buddha’s Cranial Bone.
Within the city is a multi-storied pavilion; inside the second story is a small stupa made of the seven precious gems, containing the cranial bone of the Tathāgata.
The circumference of the bone is one chi and two cun; the hair-pores are distinct and its color is yellowish-white. It is enshrined within a precious casket.

Those who wish to know the signs of their own merit and demerit should grind fragrant powder into a paste, wrap it in fine silk, and apply it over the bone; according to what is obtained therefrom, they shall determine good or ill fortune.
The Dharma Master immediately obtained an image of the Bodhi tree;
the two śrāmaṇeras he had brought with him—the elder obtained an image of the Buddha, and the younger obtained an image of a lotus flower.
The Brahmin who was guarding the relics rejoiced, snapped his fingers toward the Dharma Master, scattered flowers, and said:
"The Master's attainment is most rare; this signifies that he possesses the potential for Bodhi.
Furthermore, there is a stupa containing skull-bones, the shape of which resembles lotus petals.
Furthermore, there was the Buddha’s eye, as large as a crabapple, its radiance brilliant and intense, illuminating the space outside the casket.
There was also the Buddha’s saṃghāṭī robe, made of exquisite, fine cotton cloth.
There was also a Buddha’s mendicant staff, with rings made of white iron and a shaft of sandalwood.

The Dharma Master prostrated himself before it all, exhausting his expressions of grief and reverence; he then offered fifty gold coins, one thousand silver coins, four silk banners, two rolls of brocade, and two sets of dharma robes, scattering various flowers before departing after his final salutation.

Furthermore, I have heard that more than twenty li to the southwest of the city of Dīpāvatī, there is a cave where the Naga King Gopala dwells; it was here that the Tathagata subdued this dragon in the past and consequently left his shadow within it.

The Dharma Master wished to go there to pay his respects, but he learned that the roads were desolate and obstructed, and moreover infested with many bandits; for the past two or three years, most people who have gone there have been unable to see him, and for this reason, those who travel there have become sparse.
When the Dharma Master wished to go there to pay his respects, the envoys sent by the kingdom of Kāpiśī, desiring to return quickly and unwilling to linger, urged him not to go.
The Dharma Master replied, "The shadow of the Tathāgata’s true body is difficult to encounter even in hundreds of millions of kalpas; how could one reach this place and not go to pay homage?
You all should proceed slowly for now; I, Xuanzang, shall return as soon as I have briefly visited."
Thereupon, he departed alone.
Upon reaching the city of Dīpāvatī, he entered a monastery to inquire about the route and seek someone to guide him, but not a single person was willing to do so.
Later, he saw a young boy who said, "The temple's manor is near there; I shall now escort you, Master, to the manor.
He then went with him and stayed the night at the manor.
He encountered an old man who knew its location and guided him along the way.
After traveling several *li*, five bandits appeared with drawn blades; the Dharma Master immediately removed his hat to reveal his monastic robes.
The bandits asked,
"Where do you wish to go, Master?
He replied:
"I wish to pay homage to the Buddha’s shadow.
The bandit said,
"Have you not heard that there is a thief here?"

He replied: "A thief is also a human being; now, for the sake of paying homage to the Buddha, even if fierce beasts were to fill the streets, I would not fear them, much less you, O donor, who are a human being!"
The bandits then resolved to follow him and pay their respects.
Upon arriving at the cave, they found it on the eastern wall of a rocky ravine with its entrance opening toward the west; peering inside, it was so dark and deep that nothing could be seen.
The old man said:
"The Master should enter directly and, having struck the eastern wall, retreat about fifty paces. Looking due east, the shadow will be found there."

The Dharma Master entered, stepping forward with faith for about fifty paces until he indeed struck the eastern wall. He then withdrew and stood back, performing more than a hundred prostrations with utmost sincerity, yet he saw nothing at all.

Reproaching himself for his karmic obstructions and afflictions, he wailed with grief and deep remorse. He further performed prostrations and recited various sutras such as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and hymns of praise to the Buddha with utmost sincerity. As he praised and prostrated, he performed over a hundred more bows. Then, he saw a light about the size of an alms bowl appear on the eastern wall, which suddenly vanished.
Filled with both grief and joy, they prostrated themselves once more. Again, a great light as vast as a *pāṇyū* appeared; having manifested, it vanished.
Their sense of longing and veneration increased all the more, and they made a vow: "If we do not behold the shadow of the World-Honored One, we shall never move from this spot."

After performing more than two hundred prostrations in this manner, the entire cave suddenly became brilliantly illuminated; the shadow of the Tathāgata appeared clearly upon the wall like a golden mountain suddenly revealed when clouds and mist part. His wondrous features were radiant and harmonious, his divine countenance shimmering with light. Gazing up in awe and leaping for joy, he could find no analogy to describe his state.

The Buddha’s body and his *kāṣāya* robe are both reddish-yellow; from the knees upward, the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are extremely clear, while from below the flower seat they are somewhat faint. To the left and right of the knees, as well as behind him, the images of bodhisattvas, holy monks, and others are all fully present.
Having seen this, he called six men from outside the gate to bring fire inside to burn incense.
Just as the fire arrived, the Buddha’s shadow suddenly vanished again.
He hurriedly ordered the fire to be extinguished; only after they had requested [his presence] once more did the image reappear.
Of the six people, five were able to see, while one saw nothing at all.

Thus, for about the duration of half a meal, they beheld him with perfect clarity; having offered their prostrations and praises, and finished scattering flowers and incense as offerings, the light vanished, whereupon they took their leave and departed.
The brahmin who had been sent was filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"Were it not for the Master’s utmost sincerity and the thickness of his power of aspiration, this could not have been achieved."
Outside the entrance of the cave, there were many other sacred sites,
as described in detail in separate accounts.
As they returned together, those five bandits all destroyed their weapons and staves, received the precepts, and departed.
From here, he rejoined his companions and traveled southeast for over five hundred li, reaching the country of Gandhāra (formerly called Jiāntuówèi, which is a corruption).
This is the region of North India.
Its territory borders the Indus River to the east, and its capital city is named Puruṣapura.
The country abounds in sages and saints; since ancient times, there have been various masters who composed treatises:
Nārāyaṇa-deva, Bodhisattva Asanga, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, Dharmatrāta, Manoratha, the Venerable Pārśva, and others—all emerged from this [tradition].
To the northeast of the royal city, there is a precious terrace where the Buddha’s almsbowl was once placed.
The bowl has since been transported to various countries and is currently located in the kingdom of Pārāṇasī.

Eight or nine *li* to the southeast of the city stands a Pippala tree, over a hundred feet high; four Buddhas of the past sat beneath it, and there are now images of the four Tathāgatas present. Furthermore, the nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas of the future shall likewise sit there.

Beside it is another stūpa built by King Kaniṣka; it is four hundred feet high, with a base one and a half li in circumference and one hundred and fifty feet high. Upon it rises a twenty-five-tiered gilded copper parasol, within which is one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics.

More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the Great Stūpa, there is a white stone image one zhang eight chi in height, standing facing north. It manifests many miraculous signs; frequently, people see the image walking in circumambulation around the Great Stūpa at night.

More than one hundred *li* to the northeast of the Kaniṣka Monastery, one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkarāvatī. To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; it is the site where the four Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma.

Four or five *li* north of the city, within a monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka. This is the place where Śākyamuni Buddha, in former times when practicing the bodhisattva path, delighted in the practice of giving; it is the site where he gave up his eyes during one of his thousand births as king in this country.
These sacred sites were immeasurable in number, all of which the Dharma Master was able to visit and pay his respects to.

Of the gold, silver, brocade, silk, clothing, and other items bestowed by the King of Gaochang, he distributed portions at every great stūpa and major monastery he reached to offer as sustenance for worship, thereby manifesting his sincerity before departing.
From here he proceeded again to the city of Udakhāṇḍa.

Ascending mountains and crossing rivers north of the city, he traveled over six hundred li and entered the country of Udyāna (which in the language of Tang means "Garden"); this was formerly the garden of King Aśoka.
Formerly called Uḍḍiyāna, this is a corruption [of the name]. It is situated on both banks of the Suvāstu River.
In the past, there were one thousand four hundred monasteries with eighteen thousand monks; nowadays, they have all fallen into ruin and their numbers have diminished.
Regarding the transmission of the monastic discipline (vinaya) for instruction, there are five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka;
second, the Mahīśāsaka; [and so forth].
3. The Kāśyapīya school; 4. The Sarvāstivāda school;
5. The Mahāsāṃghika school.
The king mostly resided in the city of Mung-kie-li (Mukhalinda), which was prosperous in both people and wealth.

Four or five *li* to the east of the city is a great stūpa that has manifested many miraculous signs; this is where the Buddha, in a former life as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin (the Immortal of Forbearance), was subjected to violence by King Kali (translated into Chinese as T’ou-cheng, "Strife").
The old name was Kali, which is an error; it is the place where his body was cut and mangled.
Two hundred and fifty li to the northeast of the city, one enters a great mountain and reaches the spring of the Apsarā Dragon, which is the upper source of the Suvāstu River.
It flows toward the southwest.
The land there is cold; it remains frozen throughout spring and summer, and at dusk snow begins to fall, shimmering with five colors as it swirls and dances like a profusion of various flowers.

More than thirty li southwest of Longquan, upon a flat rock on the northern bank of the river, there are the footprints of the Buddha. Their length varies according to the merit and aspirations of those who view them; these were left by the Buddha when he departed after subduing the dragon Apalāla in the past.
Flowing downstream for more than thirty *li*, there is a stone where the Tathāgata washed his robes; the patterns of the stripes on the *kāṣāya* are still clearly visible.

Over four hundred *li* south of the city, one reaches Mount Kheṭaka (formerly called Jié, a contraction of the Sanskrit term). This is where the Tathāgata formerly heard half a verse. [Note: The term "verse" (*jié*) is a phonetic abbreviation of the Sanskrit word.]
Some say "gāthā," which is a corruption of the Sanskrit term;
following the correct form, it should be called *gāthā*.
*Gāthā* is translated into Chinese as "verse" (*sòng*), consisting of thirty-two syllables. [This refers to the place] where he sacrificed his body to repay the kindness of the yakṣa.

Fifty *li* west of the city of Mung-kie-li, one crosses a great river and arrives at the Lūhika (translated into Chinese as "Red") Stūpa. It is over ten *zhang* high and was built by King Aśoka. This is the place where, in the past, when the Tathāgata was King Maitrībala, he pierced his own body with a knife to feed five yakṣas (the old transcription "ye-xia" is erroneous).

More than thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, one reaches the Adbhuta (translated into Chinese as "Extraordinary") stone *stūpa*, which is thirty feet high. In the past, the Buddha preached the Dharma for humans and devas at this spot; after the Buddha’s departure, this *stūpa* spontaneously sprang up from the earth.
Tāxi crossed the great river and traveled three or four *li* to reach a monastery, where there was an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (translated into Chinese as Guanzizai).
The combined characters and their continuous phonetic rendering in Sanskrit are as stated above.
To analyze the individual components: *avalokita* is translated as "Contemplation," and *īśvara* is translated as "Sovereign."

The old translations—Guangshiyin (Light-World-Sound), Guanshiyin (Contemplating-World-Sound), or Guanshiyinzizai (Sovereign of Contemplating-World-Sound)—are all erroneous. His majestic spiritual power is most manifest.

To the northeast of the city, it is said that there are those who have climbed over mountains and valleys and traveled upstream along the Xidu River; the path is perilous, requiring one to cling to ropes and chains and tread upon flying bridges for over a thousand *li* until reaching the Dali Luo Plain, which is the ancient capital of Ujjayinī.
Beside a great monastery in the middle of that river stands a carved wooden image of Maitreya Bodhisattva, adorned with gold and over a hundred feet in height;
it was fashioned by the Arhat Madhyāntika (formerly called Madhyāndina, a corruption of the name).

By means of his supernormal powers, he took the artisans up to Tuṣita Heaven (formerly called Doushuaituo, which is an error)—there they personally beheld the wondrous marks—and after making three such journeys back and forth, their work was finally completed.

South of the city of Udakhāṇḍa, one crosses the Sindhu River; the river is three or four li wide, its current extremely clear and swift, and many venomous dragons and fierce beasts dwell within its depths. If anyone carrying rare Indian treasures, famous flowers, or śarīra relics attempts to cross, their boat invariably capsizes and sinks.
Having crossed this river, one arrives at the kingdom of Takṣaśilā in the region of North India.
Twelve or thirteen *li* north of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which frequently emits divine light.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path as a great king named Candraprabha (translated into Chinese as "Moonlight"), he sought enlightenment with such resolve that he gave away his own head a thousand times.
Beside the stupa is a monastery where, in the past, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (translated into Chinese as Tóngshòu) composed various treatises.
From here, traveling over seven hundred li to the southeast, one hears of the kingdom of Siṃhapura within the borders of North India.

Furthermore, crossing the Indus River from the northern border of Takṣaśilā and traveling southeast for more than two hundred *li*, one passes through a great stone gate; this is the place where, in the past, Prince Mahāsattva sacrificed his body here to feed a starving tigress and her seven cubs.
The ground there was previously stained with the blood of the prince’s body and remains crimson even now; the same is true for its grasses and trees.
Furthermore, traveling southeast from here for over five hundred li through the mountains, one arrives at the country of Uraśā.
Furthermore, proceeding southeast up a perilous path and crossing an iron bridge for over a thousand li, he arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra (formerly called Jibin, which is a corruption).
The western side of its capital borders a great river. There are one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks.
There are four stūpas, lofty and magnificent, built by King Aśoka; each contains more than a peck of the Tathāgata’s relics.

When the Dharma Master first entered the borders of that country, he arrived at the Stone Gate, which was the western gate of the kingdom; the king had dispatched his younger brother by the same mother to meet him with carriages and horses.
Having passed through the Stone Gate, he visited various monasteries in succession to pay his respects, and eventually stayed overnight at a temple named Huṣkarā.
That night, the assembly of monks all dreamed that a divine being told them:
"This visiting monk has come from the country of Mahācīna; he wishes to study the scriptures in India, visit and pay homage to the sacred sites, and receive teachings on what he has not yet heard."
Since this person has come for the sake of the Dharma, immeasurable benevolent spirits have followed him and are present here now.

You masters possess the merit of past lives and are admired by those from afar; you ought to diligently recite and study so as to inspire the praise and reverence of others. Why then are you indolent, sinking into sleep!

Upon hearing this, the monks were each startled awake; they engaged in walking meditation, seated meditation, and recitation until dawn, after which they all came to recount the circumstances of what had occurred, their reverence becoming even more solemn.

After traveling for several days in this manner, they gradually drew near the royal city; at a distance of about one *yojana*, they reached Dharmāśālā—translated into Chinese as "House of Merit"—which was established by the king's decree to welcome travelers and provide for the poor and destitute.

The King led his ministers and the monks of the capital to the House of Merit to welcome him; more than a thousand attendants followed in his train, with banners and canopies filling the roads and incense smoke and flowers covering the path.

Having arrived, they met with him and offered profound and respectful salutations; having personally scattered immeasurable flowers as an offering, they requested that he mount a great elephant and proceed together with them.
Upon arriving at the capital, he stayed at Jayendrasvāmin Monastery, which had been established by the king’s maternal uncle.
The following day, he was invited into the palace for offerings, along with several dozen eminent monks, including the Venerable Saṃghaghoṣa.
When the meal was finished, the King requested that the Dharma Master deliver a lecture and engage in debate; observing this, he was greatly pleased.

Furthermore, learning that [the Master] had traveled from afar out of a desire for study but lacked the original texts for his research, he provided twenty scribes and ordered them to copy the sutras and treatises.
He assigned five attendants to serve and direct him, providing all necessary provisions and supplies from public funds.
That monk, who was called a Dharma Master, was a man of lofty conduct.

His observance of the precepts was pure and refined, his contemplation of principles profound and far-reaching; he possessed vast learning and the power of dhāraṇī, and his talent was sagacious while his spirit was flourishing. Moreover, by nature he loved the worthy and esteemed scholars; since you were among his most distinguished guests, he looked upon you with admiration and welcomed you with open arms.
The Dharma Master also devoted his heart to receiving instruction from him, tireless by day or night, and consequently requested that he lecture on various treatises.

At that time, the Master was nearly seventy years old and his physical strength had already declined; yet, having joyfully encountered such a vessel of the Dharma, he exerted himself to propagate the teachings. From before noon, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*; from after noon, he lectured on the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*; and during the first watch of the night, he lectured on the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* and the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*.
Consequently, all the scholars within the realm assembled there without exception.
The Dharma Master comprehended everything they taught without omission; he investigated the profound and struck upon the essential points, exhausting their hidden mysteries.
The Duke was filled with joy and praised him boundlessly, saying to the assembly:

"This Chinese monk possesses vast and profound intellectual power; looking throughout this assembly, there is none who can surpass him. His brilliance and nobility are sufficient to carry on the tradition of the brothers Vasubandhu and Asaṅga. My only regret is that he was born in a distant land and did not encounter the lingering fragrance of the sages and worthies at an earlier time."

At that time, among the assembly were Mahāyāna monks such as Viśuddhasena (translated into Chinese as Jing-shizi, "Pure Lion"), Cenanandana (translated as Zuishengqin, "Most Victorious Relative"), Sarvāstivāda monks such as Sugatamitra (translated as Rulaiyou, "Friend of the Tathāgata") and Vasumitra (translated as Shiyou, "World-Friend"), and Mahāsāṃghika monks such as Sūryadeva (translated as Riztian, "Sun God") and Candra-trāta (translated as Zuishengjiu, "Most Victorious Savior"). Although this country had long been devoted to learning, these monks were all firm and steadfast in their spiritual practice and possessed abundant talent and understanding; though they could not yet match the renown of the [Indian] monks, they more than sufficed when compared to other people.

Having seen the Dharma Master praised by the Great Master, there were none who did not exert themselves to challenge and interrogate him; yet the Dharma Master responded with clear insight, without any hesitation or impediment, whereby these worthies also yielded in shame and submitted.

This country was formerly a dragon pond. Fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika, a disciple of Ānanda, converted the dragon king, causing him to relinquish the pond and establish five hundred monasteries. He then summoned various worthies and sages to dwell therein, where they received the offerings of the dragons.

Subsequently, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, four hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, King Kaniṣka, at the request of the Venerable Pārśva, assembled four hundred and ninety-nine noble monks who had mastered the Tripiṭaka internally and the five sciences externally, together with the Venerable Vasumitra, totaling five hundred sages and saints, to compile the Tripiṭaka there.

First, he composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas (formerly called *yōubótīshè*; this is an error) as an exposition of the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (formerly called *xiūdúoluó*; this is an error).
Next, he composed the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas, which provides an exposition on the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (the old translation "Viyaya" is erroneous).
Next, he composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas, which provides an exposition of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (or, as it is erroneously called, the *Abhidharma*).
The entire work consists of three hundred thousand stanzas, amounting to nine hundred and sixty thousand words.
The King had copper plates of red metal cast and engraved with the treatise; he sealed them within a stone casket and enshrined them inside a great stūpa, commanding a yakṣa deity to guard it.
The profound meaning was clarified once again through this power.
Having stayed in this manner for two years from beginning to end, he studied various sūtras and śāstras; after paying homage to the sacred sites, he then took his leave and departed.
Traveling southwest across mountains and streams for seven hundred li, one arrives at the ancient kingdom of Panunnu.
From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Āḷasapura, within the borders of North India.
From here, traveling southeast down the mountain and across rivers for over seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Lāḍaka, within the borders of North India.

From Lampā to this land, as the customs of its inhabitants dwell in a remote and desolate region, their dress and language differ somewhat from those of India, and there is a prevailing air of vulgarity and disdain.

After departing from the kingdom of Aṭaliptapura, he traveled for three days, crossed the Candrabhāgā River (which means "Divided by the Moon"), and arrived at the city of Jayapura, where he stayed overnight at a monastery of non-Buddhist practitioners.
The monastery was located outside the western gate of the city; at that time, there were more than twenty companions in his party.

On a later day, they proceeded to the city of Śākala, where there was a monastery with over a hundred monks. It was here in the past that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Paramārthasatya-śāstra*.
Beside it stands a stūpa two hundred feet high, which is the site where four past Buddhas preached the Dharma; traces of their walking paths (caṅkrama) are still visible there.

Departing from this place toward the city of Nālaṃgaha, he traveled eastward into the great forest of Pārśa, where he encountered a band of more than fifty robbers. They plundered all the clothing and provisions belonging to the Dharma Master and his companions, leaving them destitute. Furthermore, they brandished their swords and drove them toward a dried-up pond to the south of the road, intending to slaughter them all.

The pond was overgrown with many weeds, thorns, and creepers; the śrāmaṇera accompanying the Dharma Master then spotted a water hole on the southern bank of the pool large enough for a person to pass through. He privately informed the Dharma Master, who immediately accompanied him in escaping through it.

Running swiftly toward the southeast for two or three *li*, he encountered a Brahmin plowing a field. He informed him that he had been robbed by bandits; hearing this, the man was struck with alarm and immediately unyoked his oxen to give them to the Dharma Master. He then blew a conch shell toward the village and beat drums to summon others, gathering more than eighty men who each took up weapons and hurried to the location of the bandits.
When the bandits saw the multitude, they scattered and fled into the forest.
The Dharma Master then went to the pond and untied the bonds of the people; he further accepted robes from them to distribute among them, and they escorted one another to a village to stay the night.
The others wept with grief, but the Dharma Master alone laughed without any sorrow or distress.
His companions asked him, "Our clothing and provisions have been plundered by bandits along the way until they are completely exhausted; we have barely escaped with our lives."
In our current state of exhaustion, hardship, and peril, matters have reached their ultimate limit; this is why I am reflecting back upon the events in the forest and cannot help but feel sorrowful.
For what reason do you, O Dharma Master, not share in this grief, but instead laugh with such joy?
He replied: "The nobility of living consists solely in one's nature and destiny (*xingming*).
Since nature and destiny already exist, what else is there to worry about?"
Therefore, the secular books of our land say:
"The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life.
Once life exists, the Great Treasure does not perish.
"A few minor garments and requisites—what is there to worry about or begrudge?
Thereupon, his companions were moved to realization.
Such was the depth of his character; though stirred, it remained undisturbed and pure.
The next day, he arrived at the eastern border of the kingdom of Līkā and reached a great city.

To the north of the road west of the city was a large mango grove. Within the grove lived a Brahmin who was seven hundred years old; yet when [the Master] went to observe him, he appeared to be only about thirty years of age. He was of robust and imposing stature, possessed profound discernment, and was well-versed in the *Madhyamaka* and *Śataśāstra* treatises, as well as the *Veda* and other scriptures.
He had two attendants, each over a hundred years old.
When the Dharma Master met them, they welcomed him with great joy.

Learning that he had been robbed by bandits, they immediately dispatched one attendant to summon those in the city who were believers in the Buddha and the Dharma, ordering them to prepare food for the Dharma Master.
The city had several thousand households; those who believed in the Buddha were few, while those who followed non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) were extremely numerous.

While the Dharma Master was in Kaśmīra, his reputation had already spread far and wide, such that all the kingdoms were aware of him. His messenger then went throughout the city to proclaim: "A monk from the land of China has arrived;
he was recently robbed by bandits and his clothing is completely exhausted. All people should take this as an opportunity to assist him."

Moved by the power of his merit, the members of the heterodox faction were ultimately transformed in heart. More than three hundred eminent individuals, having heard of this, each brought a piece of variegated cotton cloth and offered food and drink; they arrived with reverence, piling their offerings before him, prostrating themselves, kneeling, and inquiring after his well-being.

The Dharma Master offered prayers of blessing and expounded upon retribution and the law of cause and effect, causing all the people to resolve their minds upon the Way, abandon heterodoxy, and return to the orthodox path; they then returned home laughing, conversing, and leaping with joy.
The Elder sighed, "This is truly unprecedented.

Thereupon, he distributed cotton cloth to the people; each received the value of several sets of robes, yet even after using it, they could not exhaust the supply. Thus, he offered fifty rolls of cloth as a gift to the Elder.
He remained there for another month to study the *Śataśāstra* and the *Viṃśatikā-śāstra*.
This master was a disciple of Nāgārjuna and had received the teachings directly from his teacher; his explanations were exceptionally clear and lucid.
Furthermore, traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Navattha.

He visited the Tuṣasana Monastery, where there was the Venerable Vinītābhara (translated here as Tiàofùguāng, "Tamed Radiance"), who was a prince of North India, possessed of elegant demeanor, and well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. [The Master] composed commentaries on the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* and the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-bhāṣya*. He stayed there for fourteen months to study the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra*, and other texts.
Traveling over fifty li southeast from the great city, one arrives at the Damasuvana Monastery (translated into Chinese as Ān-lín, "Dark Forest").
There are more than three hundred monks, who study and expound the Sarvāstivāda school.
The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa shall all assemble at this site to preach the Dharma to humans and devas.

Three hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, there will be the śāstrin Kātyāyanīputra (formerly called Jiāzhānyán, which is an error) who will compose the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here.
From here, traveling northeast for one hundred and forty or fifty *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrīnālanda, within the borders of North India.

Upon entering the country, he went to the Nālandā Monastery, where there was a great virtuous master named Candravarma (translated here as "Moon Armor"), who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. He stayed there for four months to study the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā*.
From here, traveling northeast and traversing perilous heights for over seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kulu (also read as Qujulu), within the borders of North India.
From the kingdom of Kulu, traveling south for over seven hundred *li*, crossing mountains and rivers, one reaches the kingdom of Śatadru, also within the borders of North India.
From here, traveling southeast for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Pāriyātra, within the borders of Central India.
From here, traveling east for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Mathurā, within the borders of Central India.

The stūpas containing the remains of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s noble disciples, such as Śāriputra—formerly called Shelizi (舍梨子) or Shelifu (舍利弗), both of which are corruptions—and Maudgalyāyana—formerly called Mujianlian (目乾連), which is a corruption—are all extant today.

*Dalieyanini futuo* (Tang for Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra); formerly called Mìduōluónízǐ, which is an erroneous abbreviation; *Upāli*; *Ānanda*; *Láohùluó* (formerly called Luóhòuluó, also called Luóyún—both are erroneous); and *Mañjuśrī* (Tang for Wondrous Auspiciousness); formerly called Róushǒu, also called Wénshūshīlì, or Mañjūśrī, translated as Wondrous Virtue (which is an error).
Regarding these various stūpas, on the annual day for cultivating merit, the monastic community leads one another to perform offerings according to their respective objects of devotion:
those belonging to the Abhidharma school offer to Śāriputra,
while those who practice meditative concentration offer to Maudgalyāyana.
Those who recite and uphold the sūtras shall make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra;
the assembly studying the Vinaya shall make offerings to Upāli;
and the bhikṣuṇīs shall make offerings to Ānanda.
Those who have not yet received full ordination make offerings to Rāhula;
those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various Bodhisattvas.
Five or six *li* east of the city, one reaches a mountain monastery, which was established by the Venerable Upagupta (translated into Chinese as Jìn-hù).
Among these are the relics of his fingernails and hair.
To the north of the monastery, on a rocky cliff, there is a stone chamber twenty-odd feet high and thirty-odd feet wide, its interior filled with fine wooden tally-sticks four inches long.
Whenever the Venerable Upagupta preached the Dharma and led someone to enlightenment such that both husband and wife together realized the fruit of Arhatship, he would place a tally stick;
however, for those who were single individuals or from other clans, even if they attained realization, he did not record it.
From here, traveling northeast for over five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Sātavīra within the borders of Central India.
Traveling further east for over four hundred *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Ruluna within the borders of Central India.
To the east it borders the Gaṅgā River, and to the north it is backed by great mountains; the Yamunā River flows through its center.

Furthermore, traveling more than eight hundred *li* eastward from here, one reaches the source of the Gaṅgā, which is three or four *li* wide; where it flows southeast into the ocean, it is over ten *li* wide. Its water is sweet and delicious, with fine sand flowing along with the current.
In their secular records, it is called "Water of Blessings.
By bathing therein, one's transgressions are eliminated;
by sipping its waves and rinsing with its currents, one's calamities and misfortunes are utterly extinguished.
Those who die and sink [into the water] are immediately reborn in heaven to receive blessings.
Fools and simple women constantly gather at the riverbanks; these are all the false words of non-Buddhists and possess no reality.
Later, when Bodhisattva Deva demonstrated the correct principles to him, he finally ceased [the practice].
In the kingdom there was a great virtuous one named Jayagupta, who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka.
The Dharma Master stayed for one winter and half a spring, completing his study of the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sautrāntika school.
He then crossed to the eastern bank of the river and arrived at the country of Mathurā.
Its king is of the Śūdra caste.
There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.
Four or five *li* to the south of the great city, there is a small monastery with more than fifty monks.

Formerly, the master of śāstras Guṇaprabha (translated into Chinese as Déguāng, "Virtuous Light") composed here over a hundred treatises, including the *Tattvasaṃdeśa* (translated as *Biànzhēn*, "Discerning Reality").
The Master was a native of the country of Pārvatī; he originally studied the Mahāyāna but later regressed to study the Hīnayāna.

At that time, the Arhat Devasiṃha (translated into Chinese as Tiānjūn, "Celestial Army"), who traveled between Tuṣita Heaven and this world, wished to see Maitreya to resolve his lingering doubts and obstructions. He thus requested Devasiṃha to use his supernatural powers to transport him up to the celestial palace.
Having seen Maitreya, he merely bowed and did not prostrate, saying:
"I have left the household life and received the full precepts, whereas Maitreya dwells in the heavens like a layman; therefore, formal prostration would be inappropriate."
Thus he went back and forth three times, yet none of them offered him salutation.
Since his pride was so great, his doubts remained unresolved.
Three or four *li* to the south of the Deguang Monastery was another monastery with more than two hundred monks, all of whom studied the Hīnayāna.
This is the place where the master of śāstras, Saṃghabhadra, passed away.
Originally a native of Kaśmīra, the master was profoundly learned and highly talented, being well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, who likewise possessed profound wisdom and vast learning, first composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. It refuted the tenets held by the Vaibhāṣika masters; its principles were profound and its prose elegant. Among the students of the Western Regions, there was none who did not praise and revere it, such that even ghosts and spirits studied and recited it.

Upon reading this, Saṃghabhadra was filled with indignation; twelve years later, he applied himself to profound reflection and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-śataka-śāstra* (The Hundred-Verse Treatise on the Abhidharmakośa) in twenty-five thousand stanzas, totaling eight hundred thousand words.
Having completed it, he wished to personally settle the points of contention with Vasubandhu, but he passed away before his purpose was fulfilled.
Later, when Vasubandhu saw that treatise, he marveled at its understanding and insight,
remarking that the power of its reasoning was no less than that of the *Vibhāṣā* masters.
"Although it is highly consistent with my own doctrine, it should be titled the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise in Accordance with Correct Reasoning). Thereupon, he acted accordingly.
After Saṃghabhadra passed away, a stūpa was erected in the Āmrapālī Grove, which remains visible even today.
Beside the grove there is another stūpa, marking the place where the master of śāstras, Vimalamitra (translated into Chinese as Wugoucheng), left his body.

This master was a native of Kaśmīra who entered the monastic order within the Sarvāstivāda school. Having traveled throughout the five regions of India, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka. On his way back to his home country, he passed by the stūpa of Saṃghabhadra; moved by the fact that Saṃghabhadra’s writings had not yet been fully propagated, he suddenly passed away. Thereupon, he vowed to compose further treatises to refute the Mahāyāna doctrines, to eliminate the fame of Vasubandhu, and to ensure that the teachings of this master of śāstras would be transmitted far into future generations.

Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged; five tongues protruded from his mouth, and blood flowed from his entire body. Realizing that this suffering originated from his evil views, he composed a letter of repentance, exhorting his fellow practitioners not to slander the Mahāyāna. As soon as he finished speaking, his breath ceased.
At the place where he was to die, the earth sank to form a pit.
In that country lived a man of great virtue named Maitrasena, ninety years of age; he was a disciple of the master Guṇaprabha and was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka.

Furthermore, during the latter half of spring and the summer, the Dharma Master studied the *Tattvasaṃdeśa-śāstra* (translated into Chinese as the *Vibhaṅga-satya-śāstra*) in two thousand five hundred verses, composed by Guṇaprabha according to the Sarvāstivāda school, as well as the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and other treatises.
Furthermore, traveling north from here for more than three hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Brahmapura in Central India.
Again, traveling southeast from here for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Hicchatra in Central India.
Traveling south again for more than two hundred *li*, he crossed the Gaṅgā River and reached Vīranara, within the borders of Central India.
Traveling eastward again for more than two hundred *li*, he arrived at Kapitha, also in Central India.

More than twenty *li* to the east of the city is a great monastery (*mahāvihāra*). Within its courtyard are three jeweled staircases arranged from south to north, descending toward the east and west; these are the places where the Buddha, having finished preaching the Dharma for his mother, Queen Māyā, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, descended back to Jambudvīpa.
The central path was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of white silver.

When the Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and descended with the assembly of devas, he stepped upon the central staircase. Mahābrahmā, holding a white fly-whisk, trod upon the silver staircase and took his place on the right; Śakra, Lord of Devas, holding a precious parasol, stepped upon the crystal staircase and remained on the left.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts and great bodhisattvas accompanied him as he descended.

Although there were still steps remaining from several hundred years ago, they have now all been submerged; a later king, out of longing and devotion, built a structure of brick and stone modeled after their original form and adorned it with various jewels, which stands over seventy feet high.

Above, he erected a vihāra containing a stone Buddha image; to its left and right were images of Śakra and Brahmā, all modeled after ancient precedents to manifest the sense that the Buddha was truly present.
Beside it stands a stone pillar seven *zhang* high, erected by King Aśoka.
Beside it is a stone foundation over fifty paces long and seven feet high;
this is the place where the Buddha formerly walked.
From here, traveling northwest for two hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kanyakubja (translated into Chinese as Quǔnǚchéng).
It is located in Central India.
The kingdom is four thousand *li* in circuit; its capital city borders the Gaṅgā River to the west, being over twenty *li* long and five or six *li* wide.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Its king is of the Vaiśya caste; his name is Harṣavardhana, which in the language of Tang means "Increasing Joy."
His father’s name was Prasenajit, which in the language of Tang means "Increaser of Action. His elder brother’s name was Ajātaśatru, which in the language of Tang means "King Increaser.
King Priyottara reigned with benevolence and compassion, and the people of the realm sang his praises.

At that time, King Śaṃkara (translated into Chinese as the same) of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as Jīn'ěr, "Golden Ear") in East India detested his [the king's] brilliant strategy because it posed a threat to his neighbor; he therefore lured him in and killed him.

The minister Bāṇi (translated into Chinese as Liáomíng), along with the various officials, lamenting that the common people were without a ruler, together established his younger brother Śīlāditya (translated into Chinese as Jièrì) to succeed to the ancestral temple and govern the realm.

The King possessed a heroic and distinguished bearing and possessed far-reaching strategic insight; his virtue moved heaven and earth, and his righteousness touched both spirits and men. Consequently, he was able to avenge his brother’s grievance and bring India under his sway; wherever his majesty reached and wherever his rites and teachings permeated, all submitted to his virtue.

Once the world was settled and the common people were at peace, he then laid down his weapons and ceased hostilities to cultivate meritorious deeds; he issued an edict throughout his realm that no living beings were to be killed, and commanded all his subjects to universally abstain from meat.
Wherever there were sacred traces, they constructed monasteries; for twenty-one days each year, they provided offerings to the assembly of monks.

Once every five years, they held an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*paṃcavārṣika-mahāpariṣad*), wherein all accumulated funds from the treasuries were bestowed as alms. Examining their conduct, they were of the same caliber as Sudatta.

To the northwest of the city is a stūpa over two hundred feet high; six or seven li to the southeast, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā River, there is another stūpa over two hundred feet high. Neither was built by King Aśoka; both were sites where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma.

The Dharma Master entered that country and stayed for three months at the Vatsalavihāra Monastery; there, relying on the Tripiṭaka Master Viryasena, he completed his study of the *Buddhadūta-vibhāṣā* and the *Sūryavaṃśa-vibhāṣā*.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty, Volume II.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty,
Volume III.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili and annotated by Shi Yancong.

From the Kingdom of Ayodhyā to the Kingdom of Ilāvrata. From the Kingdom of Ayodhyā to the Kingdom of Ilāvrata. From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li and crossing the Gaṅgā River, one arrives south at Ayodhyā in Central India. There are over a hundred monasteries with several thousand monks who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Within the great city is an ancient monastery where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu—translated into Chinese as Shiqin (World-Kinsman); formerly called Basoubandou, which is a corruption of the meaning "Heavenly-Kinsman"—composed Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises and gave public lectures.

Four or five *li* to the northwest of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River within a great monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka at the site where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for three months.
Beside it, there are also the walking paths of four past Buddhas.
Five or six li to the southwest of the city is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga preached the Dharma.

At night, the Bodhisattva ascends to Tuṣita Heaven, where he receives the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra* from Maitreya Bodhisattva; by day, he descends from heaven to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
Asaṅga, also known as Wu-zhuo (Maitreya), was a native of the kingdom of Gandhāra.
He appeared in the world during the millennium following the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha; he initially left the household life within the Mahīśāsaka school but later came to believe in the Mahāyāna.
His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, entered the monastic order within the Sarvāstivāda school before later converting to the Mahāyāna.
Both brothers possessed the capacity for sagely wisdom and the talent for composition; they extensively authored various treatises to explain the Mahāyāna, becoming the preeminent masters of India.
Works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* were all his compositions.

The Dharma Master, having paid homage to the sacred sites in the country of Ayodhyā, traveled eastward down the Gaṅgā River by boat with more than eighty companions, intending to proceed toward the country of Ayomukha.
After traveling some one hundred li or so, both banks of the river were lined with Aśoka groves that were exceptionally deep and lush.
Within these groves, on both banks, there were more than ten boats of pirates who, beating their oars against the current, came forth all at once.

The boat was thrown into a state of panic, and several people threw themselves into the river; the bandits then steered the vessel toward the shore and ordered everyone to strip off their clothes so they could search for precious treasures.

However, those bandits had long been devoted to the deity Tuka; every autumn, they would seek out a person of handsome appearance and fine features, killing them to take their flesh and blood for sacrifice in order to pray for good fortune.
Seeing that the Dharma Master’s appearance was magnificent and his physical frame imposing, they looked at one another with joy and said:

"Our time for sacrificing to the deity is about to pass, yet we could not find anyone suitable. Now this śramaṇa’s countenance is so refined and beautiful; if we kill him to offer as a sacrifice, would that not be auspicious!"
The Dharma Master replied:
"That my wretched and lowly body should serve as an offering for the sacrifice is truly not what I would dare begrudge.

However, having come from afar with the intention of paying homage to the Bodhi tree and the image at Vulture Peak, as well as to inquire about the scriptures and the Dharma, this purpose remains unfulfilled. If you, O donor, were to kill me now, I fear it would not be auspicious."
All those on board the ship joined in their plea, and some even offered to take his place; however, the pirates would not permit it.

Thereupon, the pirate leader sent men to fetch water, cleared a space within a flower grove to establish an altar, mixed mud to plaster and sweep the ground, and ordered two men to draw their swords and drag the Dharma Master onto the altar, intending to strike him with their blades immediately.
The Dharma Master’s countenance showed no sign of fear, which left the bandits utterly astonished.
Realizing they could not escape, he said to them:
"I pray you grant me a brief moment; do not press or harass me, so that I may attain parinirvāṇa with a peaceful mind and joyful heart."

The Dharma Master then concentrated his mind on the Tuṣita Heaven, calling to mind Maitreya Bodhisattva, vowing to be reborn there to pay respectful homage and offerings, receive the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, hear the sublime Dharma, and achieve supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*). He further vowed that upon returning to this world, he would descend to convert these people, leading them to cultivate superior practices, abandon all evil karma, and widely proclaim the various Dharmas for the benefit and peace of all beings.
Thereupon, he paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and sat with right mindfulness, focusing his mind on Maitreya without any further distractions.

Within his mental visualization, it was as if he had ascended Mount Sumeru and passed beyond the first, second, and third heavens, seeing the Tuṣita Palace where Bodhisattva Maitreya dwells upon a sublime jeweled terrace, surrounded by a host of devas.
At that moment, his body and mind were filled with such joy that he was unaware of being at the altar and did not even remember the presence of the bandits.
His companions broke out into loud wailing.

In an instant, a black wind arose from all sides, snapping trees and scattering sand; the river surged with waves, and the ships were tossed about and overturned. The bandits were utterly terrified and asked their comrades:
“From where have you śramaṇas come,
and what are your names? They replied:
"This is one who has come from the land of China to seek the Dharma.
If you kill him, you will incur immeasurable sin.
Furthermore, observe the state of the wind and waves; the heavenly deities are already incensed. You should quickly repent."
The bandits were terrified; they led one another in repentance and apology, prostrating themselves to take refuge [in him].
At that time, he was still unconscious; only when the bandits touched him with their hands did he open his eyes and say to them, "Has the time arrived?"
The bandit said, "I dare not harm you, Master; I pray that you accept my repentance.

The Dharma Master accepted his prostrations and thanks, and for him he explained how the unwholesome karmas of killing, stealing, and improper worship lead to the suffering of the Avīci Hell in the future.
"Why do you take this body, which is as transient as a flash of lightning or a morning dew, and plant the seeds of suffering for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*)?
The thieves bowed their heads and apologized, saying, "We were deluded and inverted; we have done what should not be done and engaged in what should not be engaged in."
Had it not been for meeting you, Master, whose merit moved the spirits of heaven and earth, how could I have heard your instructions?
From this day forward, I shall immediately sever this karma; I pray that you, Master, will bear witness to this.

Thereupon, they exhorted one another to collect their various implements of plunder and cast them all into the river; the clothing and provisions they had seized were each returned to their original owners. They all received the five precepts, and the wind and waves subsided once more.
The bandits were filled with joy; they prostrated themselves in farewell.
Their companions marveled at them with a reverence far exceeding the ordinary.
Those who heard of this from near and far could not help but express their astonishment and wonder.
Were it not for his profound and earnest quest for the Dharma, how could he have reached this point?
From here, traveling eastward for more than three hundred *li* and crossing the Gaṅgā River, he arrived at the kingdom of Ayodhyā in Central India.
From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred *li*, crossing the south bank of the Gaṅgā River and the north bank of the Yamunā River, one arrives at Prayāga in Central India.
To the southwest of the city, within a grove of *campaka* flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the Buddha formerly subdued the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Beside it is a monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Śata-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Extensive Hundred Treatise) and defeated the Hīnayāna non-Buddhists.

To the east of the great city, at the confluence of two rivers, there is a level plateau to the west, fourteen or fifteen *li* in circumference. The ground is flat and even; since ancient times, kings and noble clans who were benevolent and charitable have all come to this place, which is therefore known as the "Great Field of Almsgiving" (*Mahādānasthāna*).

Now King Śīlāditya has also followed this precedent: having accumulated wealth for five years, he bestowed it in charity for seventy-five days; from the Triple Gem above down to the orphaned and the destitute below, there was no one to whom he did not give.
From here, proceeding southwest into the Great Forest, one frequently encounters wild beasts and wild elephants.
After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī (formerly called Jushanmi, which is an erroneous transcription).
In Central India, there are more than ten monasteries with over three hundred monks.

Within the old palace in the city is a great vihāra, over sixty feet in height, containing a sandalwood image of the Buddha. Above it hangs a stone canopy, which was commissioned by King Udayana (translated into Chinese as Chuchi, formerly called You-tien; this is a corruption).

Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven spending the summer retreat preaching the Dharma for his mother, the King, filled with longing and yearning, requested Maudgalyāyana to lead skilled artisans up to heaven to observe the Buddha’s venerable countenance and deportment. Upon their return, they carved a likeness of his true features from red sandalwood. When the World-Honored One descended, this very image went out to welcome him; it is this very one.
To the south of the city there is an old residence; this was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (formerly called Jushi-luo, a corruption of the name).
Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, which was the site of the elder’s garden.
Within it stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
To the southeast is a multi-storied pavilion, the place where Vasubandhu composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Next, to the east, within the Āmra grove, there is an old foundation; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Traveling more than five hundred li east from here, one arrives at the kingdom of Viśoka.
There are more than twenty monasteries with approximately three thousand monks, who study the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.

To the southeast, on the left side of the road, there is a great monastery where, in the past, the Arhat Devaśarman composed the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, asserting that there is no self (ātman) or person (pudgala). There, the Arhat Gopa composed the *Siddhānta-śāstra*, asserting that there is a self and a person. Because of these differing attachments to doctrine, they subsequently engaged in profound disputes.
Furthermore, this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla subdued one hundred masters of the Hīnayāna treatises during seven days.
Beside it is also the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for six years.
There is a tree over seventy feet high; long ago, when the Buddha was cleaning his teeth, he discarded a remaining twig, which took root and has flourished until the present day.
Heretics have come many times to cut it down, yet as soon as it is felled, it grows back again, flourishing as luxuriantly as before.
From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (formerly called Shewei, which is a corruption).
It is over six thousand *li* in circuit. There are several hundred monasteries with several thousand monks, all of whom study the Saṃmitīya school.

When the Buddha was in the world, there was a city called Pāṭaliputra (translated into Chinese as Shèngjūn, "Victorious Army"; formerly transcribed as Bōsìní, which is erroneous), the capital where King Śaiśunāga resided.

Within the city are the ruins of the former royal palace; not far to the east of these is another site with ruins upon which a stūpa has been erected, marking the place where King Śaiśunāga built a great lecture hall for the Buddha.

Next there was another stūpa, which was the vihāra for the bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī—the Buddha’s maternal aunt (translated into Chinese as Shēngzhǔ, "Mistress of Beings"; formerly called Bōshèbōtí, which is a corruption).
To the east of this is a stūpa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (translated into Chinese as Lèshī; formerly called Xūdá, which is an error).
Beside the residence is a large stūpa, marking the place where Aṅgulimāla (formerly called Yāngjuémóluó, which is an error) abandoned his heterodox ways.
Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana—translated in Chinese as "Victorious Forest" (Yanshenglín); the old transcription "Jita" is an error.
This is the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
Formerly it was a monastery, but now it has fallen into ruin.
To the left and right of the eastern gate stand stone pillars, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka.
All the other buildings have completely vanished, leaving only a single brick chamber remaining, within which there is a golden image.

Long ago, when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit conceived a deep sense of longing and devotion; hearing that King Udayana had carved an image out of sandalwood, he subsequently commissioned the creation of this one.
Not far behind the monastery is the place where a non-Buddhist brahmin killed his wife and slandered the Buddha.
More than a hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta, having attempted to harm the living Buddha with poison, fell into hell.
To the south of that is another great pit, the place where the bhikṣu Kokālika slandered the Buddha and entered hell alive.
More than eight hundred paces to the south of this pit is the place where the brahmin woman Cañcā slandered the Buddha and entered hell alive.
