All three of these pits are so deep that their bottoms cannot be seen when looked into.
Over seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a lofty and grand vihāra.
Inside it sits a Buddha image facing east; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly engaged in debate with non-Buddhists.

Next to the east is a deva temple, equal in size to the vihāra; as the sun’s rays shift, the shadow of the deva temple does not reach the vihāra, while the shadow of the vihāra constantly covers the deva temple.
Three or four *li* further to the east is a stūpa, the site where Śāriputra debated with the non-Buddhists.
Over sixty *li* to the northwest of the great city is an old city; this was the father’s city of Kāśyapa Buddha during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
To the south of the city is the place where the Buddha first beheld his father after attaining perfect enlightenment.
To the north of the city is a stūpa containing the entire bodily relics (śarīra) of Kāśyapa Buddha, which was erected by King Aśoka.
From here, traveling southeast for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Kapilavastu (formerly called Jialipoluowei).

The country is over four thousand *li* in circuit, and its capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference; both are now largely in ruins. The palace city is fifteen *li* in circuit, built of brick, and is extremely solid.
Within, there is an old foundation, the main hall of King Śuddhodana; a vihāra has been built upon it, and within it is an image of the king.
To the north of that is another old foundation, the bedchamber of Queen Māyā; a vihāra has been built upon it, and within it is an image of the queen.
Beside it is a vihāra, which is the place where Śākyamuni Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb; inside is an image of the Bodhisattva’s descent into birth.

The Sthavira school states that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttara-āṣāḍhā, which corresponds here to the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
According to other schools, these twenty-third days correspond to the eighth day of the fifth month.
To the northeast is a stūpa, the place where the seer Asita performed the physiognomy of the Prince.
To the left and right of the city were the places where the Prince contended in feats of strength with the Śākyas;

the place where he mounted his horse and leaped over the city walls; and the place where, having previously seen an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa at the four gates, he grew weary of and renounced the world, turning his carriage back.
From here, traveling east through a wilderness for over five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Rāmagrāma in Central India.
The inhabitants are sparse.

To the southeast of the old city stands a brick *stūpa* over fifty feet high, which was built by a former king of this country after he received a portion of the relics following the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; it frequently emits radiance.

Beside it is a dragon pond; the dragon frequently transforms itself into human form to circumambulate the stupa and practice the Way. Wild elephants often come to offer worship, carrying flowers in their trunks.
Not far from there is a monastery, which is managed by a śrāmaṇera.

It is traditionally related that in the past, there was a bhikṣu who invited his fellow practitioners to visit and pay their respects. Upon arriving, they saw a wild elephant carrying flowers in its mouth and placing them before the stūpa; it further used its tusks to clear away weeds and its trunk to sprinkle water. When the assembly witnessed this, there was none who did not feel moved with deep admiration.
A certain bhikṣu then renounced his full ordination, wishing to remain and offer service;

he said to the crowd, "An elephant is but a beast, yet it knows to revere the stūpa by offering flowers and sweeping it clean. I am a human being who has left the household life in reliance upon the Buddha—how could I behold its ruin and neglect to serve it!"

He then took his leave of the assembly and settled there, constructing a dwelling by a shallow pond, planting flowers and fruit trees; though he endured both cold and heat, he never grew weary of his labors.

Hearing of this, neighboring kingdoms each donated wealth and treasures to jointly build a monastery, whereupon they requested him to take charge of monastic affairs. This tradition was passed down from then on and eventually became a long-standing custom.

Traveling more than a hundred *li* eastward from the Śrīgupta monastery through the great forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the Prince, having reached this spot after crossing the city walls, removed his precious robes, celestial crown, and topknot jewel, and entrusted them to Chandaka (formerly called Chen-duo-ka, a corruption), returning them to him.
At each site where his hair was shaved, there is a stupa as a memorial.
Having emerged from this forest, he arrived at the kingdom of Kuśinagara,
which was extremely desolate and overgrown.
In the northeastern corner of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This was the former residence of Cunda (formerly called Chuntuo, which is an error);
within the house is a well that was dug at the time he was about to prepare his offerings, and its water remains clear and limpid.
Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (translated into Chinese as "Invincible"; formerly called the Aravati River, which is an error).

Not far from the riverbank, one reaches the Śāla forest; its trees resemble the oak, with green bark and white leaves that are exceedingly lustrous. Four pairs stand at equal heights; this is the place where the Tathāgata entered *nirvāṇa*.
There is a great brick vihāra containing an image of the Tathāgata in the state of parinirvāṇa, lying with his head toward the north.
Beside it stands a great stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka.
Furthermore, a stone pillar was erected to record the events of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; however, it does not record the year or month.

According to tradition, the Buddha remained in the world for eighty years and entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the second month.
The Sarvāstivādins further state:
"The Buddha entered nirvana during the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month in this calendar.

Since his nirvana, it has been said to be either one thousand two hundred years, or one thousand three hundred, or one thousand five hundred; or it is said to have passed nine hundred years but not yet reached a full millennium."

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata sat within the golden coffin to preach the Dharma for his mother, he extended his arm to question Ānanda and displayed his feet to Śāriputra; his body was cremated with fragrant wood, and the eight kings divided his relics, each of which has its own memorial stupa.
From here, traveling again through the great forest for over five hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī (the local pronunciation is "Nü Dian").
The kingdom is over four thousand *li* in circuit. To the west of the capital city lies the Gaṅgā River; it is over ten *li* long and five or six *li* wide.
There are more than thirty monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna.

Crossing the River of Vārāṇasī and traveling northeast for more than ten li, one arrives at the Mṛgadāva Monastery, where the terraces and pavilions reach the clouds and long corridors enclose it on all four sides.
There are one thousand five hundred monks who study the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
Within the great enclosure is a vihāra over a hundred feet high, featuring stone steps and brick niches arranged in hundreds of tiers, all of which contain gilded Buddha images in relief.
Inside the hall is a brass image of the Buddha, equal in size to the body of the Tathāgata, depicted in the posture of turning the Wheel of Dharma.
To the southeast of the vihāra is a stone stūpa built by King Aśoka, over one hundred feet in height.
In front stands a stone pillar over seventy feet high, marking the place where the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Beside it is Maitreya (translated into Chinese as Cishi; formerly called Mile, which is an error), the Bodhisattva’s site for receiving his prophecy.

To the west of this is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Buddha, in a former life as the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāpāramitā (Huming), received a prophecy from Kāśyapa Buddha during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.

To the south of where Śākyamuni received his prediction, there is the place where four past Buddhas walked back and forth; it is over fifty paces long and seven feet high, constructed of piled blue stones, and bears images of the four Buddhas walking upon it.

To the west of the monastery is a bathing pool for the Tathāgata, as well as a pool for washing vessels and a pool for laundering robes; all are guarded by divine nāgas, so that no one may defile them with impure contact.
Beside the pond is a stūpa marking the place where the Buddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path, gave his six tusks to a hunter.

Furthermore, it marks the place where, while he was a bird, he made a pact with a monkey and a white elephant beneath a nyagrodha tree to determine their seniority, and then traveled about to convert people.
He was also born as a king of deer, and this is the place where he saved the five men, including Kauṇḍinya.
From here, traveling eastward for more than three hundred li along the course of the Gaṅgā River, one arrives at the kingdom of Yodheya.
From here, traveling northeast across the Gaṅgā River for one hundred forty or fifty *li*, one arrives at the country of Vaiśālī (formerly called Bisheli, which is an error).
The country is over five thousand *li* in circuit; its soil is fertile and rich, and it abounds in *āmra* (mango) and *moca* fruits.
The capital city lies in ruins.
Its old foundations extend sixty or seventy *li* in circumference, and there are very few inhabitants.
Five or six *li* to the northwest of the palace city is a monastery, beside which stands a stūpa; this is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Next, three or four *li* to the northeast, there is a stūpa at the site of the former residence of Vimalakīrti; this house still abounds in miraculous wonders.
Not far from here is a chamber constructed of piled stones, which was the place where Vimalakīrti manifested illness and preached the Dharma.
Beside it are also the former residences of Ratnākara and the girl Āmrapālī.

Three or four *li* further to the north is a stūpa, marking the place where the Buddha stood while his celestial and human followers gazed upon him as he was about to depart for Kuśinagara to enter parinirvāṇa.

To the west of that, there is again the place where the Buddha made his final observation of Vaiśālī; to the south of that, there is the place where the woman Āmrapālī offered her grove to the Buddha; and there is also the place where the Buddha granted the Māra king permission to enter parinirvāṇa.
Traveling more than one hundred *li* south of the border of Vaiśālī, one reaches the city of Vaidiśapura, where the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* was obtained.
Crossing the Gaṅgā River again to the south, one arrives at the kingdom of Magadha (formerly called Mojieduo; this is an erroneous transcription).
It is over five thousand *li* in circuit.
The local customs revere learning and honor the worthy.
There are more than fifty monasteries with over ten thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna.
To the south of the river is an old city, over seventy *li* in circumference; though it is now dilapidated and in ruins, its battlements still remain.
In the past, when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable, this was known as the city of Kusumapura, which in the language of Tang means "Fragrant Flower Palace City."
Because the royal palace abounded in flowers, it received this name.
Later, when the human lifespan reached several thousand years, the city was renamed Pāṭaliputra (formerly called Xīliánfúyì, which is a corruption).
Furthermore, it was named after the Pāṭalī tree.
One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was King Aśoka—translated into Chinese as Wúyōu (Sorrowless); the former name Āyù (A-yù) is an error.
He was the great-grandson of King Bimbisāra (translated into Chinese as Yǐngjiān), who moved the capital from Rājagṛha to this location.
As the years have passed since then, only the old foundations remain today.
There were once several hundred monasteries, of which only two or three remain.

To the north of the old palace, bordering the Ganges River, lies a small city containing over a thousand households. North of the palace stands a stone pillar several tens of feet high, marking the site where King Aśoka established a hell.
The Dharma Master stayed in the small city for seven days to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites.
To the south of the hell [site] is a stūpa, which is one of the eighty-four thousand.
The king established this structure through human labor; within it lies one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s śarīra, which constantly emits divine light.

Next is a vihāra, within which is a stone upon which the Tathāgata walked. On the stone are the Buddha’s two footprints: one foot is one chi and eight cun long and six cun wide. Beneath both feet are the marks of thousand-spoked wheels; on the tips of the ten toes are the patterns of the *svastika*, as well as vases, fish, and other symbols, all clearly and vividly manifest. This was where the Tathāgata, when about to enter *nirvāṇa*, traveled from Vaiśālī and stood upon a large square stone on the southern bank of the river.
He looked back and said to Ānanda: "This is the final trace I have left here, gazing toward the Vajrāsana and the city of Rājagṛha."

To the north of the vihāra stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, inscribed with a record that King Aśoka thrice offered the continent of Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and thrice redeemed it with precious treasures.

To the southeast of the old city are the ruins of the Kuṭāgāra-saṃghārāma—translated into Chinese as Jīyuán (Chicken Garden)—founded by King Aśoka; it was the place where he summoned a thousand monks and provided them with the four requisites of support.
At these holy sites, he stayed for a total of seven days until his prostrations were complete.
Then, traveling southwest for six or seven *yojanas*, he arrived at the Tiladhaka Monastery.
In the monastery there were several dozen masters of the Tripitaka; hearing that the Dharma Master had arrived, they all came out to welcome and escort him.
From here, he traveled south again for over a hundred li and reached the Bodhi Tree.
The enclosure wall is constructed of piled bricks, high and steep, and extremely solid.
It is long from east to west and somewhat narrow from south to north.

The eastern gate faces the Nairañjanā River; the southern gate adjoins the Great Flower Pond; the western side is backed by precipitous fortifications; and the northern gate leads to the Great Monastery. Within, sacred sites are interconnected—consisting of vihāras and stūpas—all built by various kings, ministers, wealthy elites, and elders out of devotion to the Sage, serving as monuments to his memory.
In the center is the Vajrāsana.

Formed at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, it arose simultaneously with the great earth; situated at the heart of the trichiliocosm, it extends downward to the golden wheel and upward to the surface of the earth. Composed of diamond, it measures over a hundred paces in circumference.
Regarding the term "Vajra," it is taken to mean that which is firm, indestructible, and capable of resisting all things.

If one does not rely upon the fundamental limit (bhūtakoṭi), the earth cannot provide stability; if one does not take the Vajra as a seat, there is no ground upon which one can give rise to the Vajra-samādhi.

Now, as he intends to subdue Māra and attain enlightenment, he must dwell here; if it were any other place, the earth would tilt and incline. Therefore, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all come to this very spot.
Furthermore, the place where enlightenment was attained is also called the Bodhimaṇḍa; while the world trembles and shakes, this alone remains unmoved.
For the past one or two hundred years, sentient beings have lacked merit, and though they go to the Bodhi tree, they do not see the Vajrāsana.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various kings established two images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries; they sit facing east.

It is traditionally said that when the bodies of these bodhisattvas sink and disappear, the Buddha-dharma shall come to an end. Now, the bodhisattva on the southern side has already sunk down to his chest.

That Bodhi tree is the Pippala tree; when the Buddha was present, it stood several hundred feet high, but having been repeatedly felled by wicked kings, it now measures only about five zhang. It is beneath this tree that the Buddha sat and attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and for this reason it is called the Bodhi tree.

The trunk of the tree is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are lush and verdant; they do not wither in autumn or winter, falling only on the day of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, after which they grow back as before overnight.
On this day each year, the various kings and their ministers gather beneath the tree together to wash it with milk, light lamps, scatter flowers, and then collect the leaves before departing.

When the Dharma Master arrived, he prostrated before the Bodhi tree and the image of the Buddha at the moment of his enlightenment created by Maitreya Bodhisattva. Having gazed upon them with utmost sincerity, he cast himself to the ground in five-limbed prostration, filled with grief and distress, lamenting to himself:
"When the Buddha attained enlightenment, I did not know where I was drifting and sinking among the realms of existence."
"Now, in this age of the Semblance Dharma, it has finally reached such a point.
Reflecting deeply on how profound and heavy his karmic obstacles were, tears filled his eyes with sorrow.
At that time, as the monks concluded their summer retreat, thousands gathered from near and far; among the spectators, there was none who did not sob and choke with emotion.
That site, one *yojana* in extent, was filled with sacred traces; he stayed for eight or nine days, and only then did he complete his circumambulation and prostrations.
On the tenth day, the community of Nālandā Monastery dispatched four venerable elders (*sthavira*) to welcome him, and he departed with them immediately.
After traveling for about seven *yojana*, they arrived at a monastery estate.
This estate was the village where the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had been born.

Having eaten at the estate, after a short while, more than two hundred monks and over a thousand lay donors (*dānapati*) arrived, carrying banners, parasols, flowers, and incense to welcome and lead them forward; they entered Nālandā amidst praise and circumambulation.
Upon their arrival, the entire assembly gathered together.
Once the Dharma Master had finished greeting them all, a separate seat was prepared at the head of the elders' row; he was invited to sit there, and his disciples likewise took their seats.
Once they have finished sitting, the *karmadāna* is dispatched to strike the *ghanṭī* and make the proclamation.
When the Dharma Master resides in the monastery, all the ritual implements and articles used by the monks residing in the monastery are held in common.

He further dispatched twenty men—neither old nor young, well-versed in the Sutras and Vinaya, and possessed of perfectly composed deportment—to accompany the Dharma Master and consult the Treasury of the True Dharma, namely the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra. As the entire assembly held him in such high esteem, they did not mention his personal name, but referred to him as the "Treasury of the True Dharma" (Saddharmakośa).
Thereupon, he followed the assembly to pay his respects.

Having seen him, the Master began the relationship of teacher and disciple; [the disciple] was intent on exhausting every mark of reverence, following the prescribed ritual by crawling on his knees and elbows, kissing the Master’s feet and prostrating with his head at them, and after completing his inquiries and praises.
Dharmakara had wide seats and mats spread out and commanded the Dharma Master and the assembly of monks to sit.
Once they were seated, he asked the Dharma Master, "From where have you come?
He replied:
"I have come from the land of China, wishing to study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* under your guidance.

Upon hearing this, [Vasubandhu] wept and summoned his disciple Buddhabhadra—whose name means "Awakened Wisdom" in the language of Tang—who was the nephew of Dharmatrāta. He was over seventy years of age, profoundly versed in the sūtras and śāstras, and highly skilled in discourse.
Dharmakṣema said:
"You may relate to the assembly the causes and conditions of my illness and suffering from three years ago.
Having heard this, Dharmakṣema wept; wiping away his tears, he recounted the past events, saying:

"In the past, my preceptor suffered from a wind-related illness; whenever it flared up, his hands and feet would contract and stiffen with a pain like being burned by fire or pierced by knives, alternating between bouts of acute pain and remission for more than twenty years."
Three years ago, his suffering was even more intense; he loathed this body and wished to end his life by ceasing to eat.

During the night, he dreamed of three celestial beings—one of golden hue, one of lapis lazuli hue, and one of silver hue—whose features were upright and handsome, and whose robes were light and radiant. They came and addressed the Upādhyāya, saying:
"Do you wish to cast off this body?"
The Sūtra says:
"One speaks of suffering within the body, but does not speak of wearying of or renouncing the body.
In the past, you were once a king who caused much distress to sentient beings; therefore, you have invited this retribution.

Now you should examine and reflect upon your past transgressions and repent with utmost sincerity; by enduring suffering with equanimity and diligently proclaiming the sutras and śāstras, these [transgressions] shall naturally be extinguished.
Merely becoming weary of the body will never bring an end to suffering.
Having heard this, the Upādhyāya prostrated with utmost sincerity.
The golden man pointed to the one of azure color and said to the Upādhyāya,
"Do you recognize him?"
"This is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara," he said. Then,
pointing to the silver-colored one, he said,
"This is the Bodhisattva Maitreya."
The Upādhyāya immediately prostrated before Maitreya and asked, "Śīlabhadra has always aspired to be born in your presence; I do not know whether he will attain this or not.
Maitreya replied:
"You shall be reborn after you have widely propagated the True Dharma.
The one of golden hue then said of himself, "I am the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī."
"We have seen that you intend to abandon your body in vain, which would bring no benefit; therefore, we have come to exhort you.

You should follow our words and propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises on the True Dharma, reaching those who have not yet heard them. Then your body will gradually become peaceful and secure; do not worry that it will not recover."
"There is a monk from the land of China who delights in penetrating the Great Dharma and wishes to come to you to study; you may wait for him and instruct him.
Upon hearing this, Dharmakara prostrated himself and replied, "I respectfully abide by your instructions."
Having spoken these words, he vanished from sight.
From that time forward, the illness that had afflicted the Venerable One was completely cured.
Among the monastic community, there was no one who did not praise this as a rare and marvelous occurrence.
Having personally received this prophecy, the Dharma Master was overcome with a mixture of grief and joy that he could not restrain; he prostrated once more in gratitude and said:

"If it is as you have described, I, Xuanzang, shall devote my utmost efforts to hearing and studying [the teachings]. I pray that your Honored One will compassionately accept me and provide instruction."
Dharmākara asked again:
"Dharma Master, how many years have you been on this road?
He replied:

"Three years. Since this accorded perfectly with his previous dream, [the King] offered various exhortations and instructions to make the Dharma Master rejoice, thereby expressing the affection between teacher and disciple.

Having finished speaking, he took his leave and departed, escorting him to the courtyard of the King of the Rising Sun (Kōniku-ō-in), where he was settled in the fourth-story pavilion of the Gakken (Bodhibhadra) quarters.
After making offerings for seven days, he further assigned him an upper room to the north of the room of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and increased his provisions.
Daily, he received one hundred and twenty *campaka* fruits, twenty betel nuts, twenty nutmegs, one *liang* of camphor, and one *sheng* of "rice for great men" (*mahāpuruṣa-taṇḍula*).

The grains of this rice are larger than black beans; when cooked as a meal, it is fragrant and fresh, surpassing all other varieties. Only in the kingdom of Magadha does this non-glutinous rice exist, and nowhere else. It is provided exclusively for the king and those of great learning and virtue; therefore, it is called "Rice for Great Beings."
He was granted three *śoṇa* of oil per month, with butter, milk, and other provisions provided daily as needed.
He was assigned one attendant and one Brahmin, exempted from all monastic duties, and traveled by elephant carriage.
At Nālandā Monastery, there were ten thousand resident and visiting monks; those who participated in these provisions included ten *dharmabhāṇakas*.
That he traveled through such distant lands and was accorded such honor is evident from this.
Nālandā Monastery is translated here as "The Monastery of Insatiable Giving.

According to tradition passed down by the elders, there was a pond within the mango grove (āmra-vana) to the south of this monastery; because the pond had a dragon named Nālandā and the monastery was built adjacent to it, it took its name from that.

It is further said that when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he established his capital here as a great king; out of compassion for the orphaned and the destitute, he constantly practiced giving and renunciation. Because people remembered his kindness, this place was named "Never-Tiring in Giving" (Śīlavatī).

The Jotivana, the mango grove of the householder Jeta, was purchased by five hundred merchants for ten billion gold coins and offered as a gift to the Buddha. There, the Buddha stayed for three months preaching the Dharma, and many of the merchants attained the fruits of realization.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the former king of this country, Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as Dìrì, "Sun of the Emperor"), out of his deep devotion to the Buddha, constructed this monastery.

After the king passed away, his son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as Juéhù, "Awakening Protector"), succeeded to the great enterprise and subsequently built another monastery to the south.
His son, King Tathāgata (translated into Chinese as Rúlái), built another monastery to the east;
his son, Brahmaditya (translated into Chinese as Yòurì), built another monastery to the northeast.
Later, seeing the holy monks departing from this land of China to attend that offering, his heart was filled with joy; he abdicated his throne and entered the monastic life.
His son, Vajra—translated into Chinese as "Vajra" (Jingang)—succeeded him on the throne and subsequently established another monastery to the north.
Subsequently, a king of Central India constructed another monastery beside it.
Thus, as six successive emperors inherited the throne, each added to its construction; they further encased the exterior with brick, merging them into a single temple with a unified main gate.
The courtyards and sequences open separately, divided into eight central precincts.

Precious terraces are arrayed like stars, and jade towers stand as lofty as mountains; the pavilions soar above the mists, and the halls fly amidst the rosy clouds. Winds and clouds are generated within the doors and windows, while the sun and moon intersect at the eaves and porches. Furthermore, green waters meander through the grounds, and blue lotuses bloom in full splendor; *karnikāra* trees radiate brilliance among them, and *āmra* groves spread their dense foliage beyond.

The monastic quarters of all the courtyards consist of four-storied pavilions with coiled-dragon rafters and rainbow-colored beams; their crossbeams are embroidered and their pillars vermilion, while the columns are carved and the railings are inlaid. The jade bases are patterned and ornate, the roof ridges catch the brilliance of the jade-like light, and the eaves are linked by silken-colored cords.
The monasteries in India number in the tens of thousands; this [monastery] is the pinnacle of their magnificence and loftiness.

There are always ten thousand monks, both residents and guests, who study the Mahāyāna as well as the eighteen schools of the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, they also study secular texts such as the *Vedas*, as well as the sciences of logic (*hetuvidyā*), grammar (*śabdavidyā*), medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and mathematics (*kalāvidyā*).

In total, there were over one thousand people who had mastered twenty treatises, over five hundred who had mastered thirty treatises, and ten individuals, including the Dharma Master himself, who had mastered fifty treatises.
Only the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra has exhaustively mastered all fields of knowledge; distinguished in virtue and advanced in years, he serves as the preeminent master for the multitude.
Within the monastery, there are more than a hundred lecture halls daily, where students practice their studies without wasting even a moment of time.
The abode of this multitude of virtues is naturally solemn and majestic.
Since its establishment more than seven hundred years ago, not a single person has committed an offense or incurred reproach.

The king holds it in high esteem and has granted more than a hundred villages to provide for its sustenance; each village consists of two hundred households, which daily contribute several hundred *shí* of non-glutinous rice, clarified butter, and milk.
Consequently, this student sat with hands folded, seeking nothing, yet the four requisites were naturally provided for him; that his arts and studies were perfected was due to this very power.
Once the Dharma Master had settled at Nālandā Monastery, he proceeded toward Rājagṛha to pay homage to the sacred sites.

The king abandoned the old city for that which they call Kuśāgrapura (in the language of Tang, "City of the Palace of Superior Thatch"), situated in the center of the kingdom of Magadha; in ancient times, many kings resided within it.
The ground there also produces fragrant *māṣaparṇī* grass, hence it is named after this.

It is surrounded on all four sides by mountains that are steep and sheer as if carved; a small path leads westward, and there is a great gate to the north. It is long from east to west and narrow from south to north, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty *li*.

Within it there is another small city, its foundations measuring more than thirty *li* in circumference; *karṇikāra* trees form groves everywhere, their buds bursting forth and their flowers blooming without interruption throughout the four seasons, their leaves being like the color of gold.
Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, which marks the place where Devadatta and King Ajātaśatru released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla with the intent to harm the Buddha.
To the northeast of this is a stūpa, the place where Śāriputra heard the Dharma preached by the bhikṣu Aśvajit and realized the fruit [of Arhatship].

Not far to the north is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Śrīgupta (translated into Chinese as Shengmi, "Victorious Secret"), having received false teachings from non-Buddhists, intended to harm the Buddha by means of a fire pit and poisoned rice.

Next, at the bend of the mountain city to the northeast of the fire pit, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the great physician Jīvaka (formerly transcribed as Qipo, which is an error) built a preaching hall for the Buddha.
Beside it stands the former residence of Tyavaka.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one reaches Mount Kṣitagarbha-kuṭa—translated into Chinese as Vulture Peak (Jiùfēng) or also as Vulture Terrace (Jiùtái); its former name, Qishajue Mountain, is a corruption.
The mountain’s ridges and northern peaks are loftily elevated and exceptionally high; its shape resembles that of a vulture and it also looks like a lofty terrace, hence it is so named.

Its springs and rocks are pure and extraordinary, and its forests and trees are lush and dense. While the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently resided on this mountain to preach immeasurable sūtras, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

Traveling over one li from the north gate of the city of Śrāvastī, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. There currently exists a brick chamber where the Tathāgata frequently resided in the past and formulated the various precepts.
The owner of the grove was named Kalandaka; he had previously offered this grove to various non-Buddhist teachers.
Later, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the profound Dharma, he regretted not having been able to offer the grove to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Earth Deity, knowing his intention, manifested ominous portents to terrify the non-Buddhists, driving them away and saying to them:
"The householder wishes to offer this grove to the Buddha; you should depart at once."
The non-Buddhists departed filled with resentment.
The elder was filled with joy; having completed the construction of the vihāra, he went in person to invite the Buddha, who accepted his offering.
To the east of Zhuyuan is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru (translated into Chinese as Wèishēngyuàn, "Unborn-Enmity"; formerly called Āshéshì, which is an error).
After the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, the various kings divided his relics. King Ajātaśatru, having obtained a portion, brought it back and erected a stūpa to make offerings to it.
King Aśoka conceived the aspiration to construct stūpas everywhere; he opened [the stūpa] to take the relics, yet a small remnant still remains, which now constantly emits radiance.

Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Garden, there is a separate bamboo grove by the side of a mountain containing a large stone chamber. This is the place where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety-nine great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
When the council was convened, an immeasurable assembly of noble ones gathered. Kāśyapa addressed them, saying:

"Those among you who know for yourselves that you possess the three types of higher knowledge and the six supernormal powers, and who can uphold the entire Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata without error, remain; let the rest each go wherever they find comfort."
At that time, nine hundred and ninety-nine people were selected.
Ānanda was still at the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), so Kāśyapa said to him:
"Your outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted; do not defile this pure assembly."
Ānanda, filled with shame and remorse, departed.
Having practiced diligently throughout the night, he severed the fetters of the three realms, attained arhatship, and returned to knock at the door. Kāśyapa asked:
"Have your fetters been exhausted?
He replied, "Indeed they have!"
He spoke again, saying, "If one's fetters are exhausted, there is no need to trouble oneself by opening the door; enter as you please.
Ānanda then entered through a crack in the door and prostrated at the feet of the monks.
Kāśyapa took his hand and said, "I wished for you to sever all outflows and realize the fruit of sainthood; that is why I drove you out—you should understand this."
"Do not harbor resentment.
Ānanda said, "If one harbors resentment, how can one be said to have exhausted all fetters?"
Thereupon, they paid their respects, took their leave, and sat down;
it was then the fifteenth day of the initial *varṣā* retreat.
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:

“The Tathāgata has always praised you among the assembly for your great learning and your mastery of the dharmas through total retention (*dhāraṇī*). You should now ascend this seat and recite for the assembly the *Sūtrapiṭaka*, which comprises all the sūtras.”

Ānanda, having received this command, rose and paid homage toward the direction of the mountain where the Buddha was entering parinirvāṇa. Having completed his prostrations, he ascended the seat and recited the sūtra, while the assembly recorded it as it issued from his lips.
When the recording was finished, he further commanded Upāli to recite the *Vinayapiṭaka*, which comprises all the precepts and discipline.
When that was finished, Kāśyapa himself recited the *Abhidharmapiṭaka*, which comprises all the treatises and exegeses.
After two or three months, during the *varṣā* retreat, the compilation of the Tripiṭaka was completed; it was then inscribed upon palm leaves and widely circulated.
The various sages said to one another, "We have compiled this in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness; that we are able to hear it today is due to the power of that effort."
Because Mahākāśyapa was the foremost elder (*sthavira*) among the Saṃgha, his followers were called the Sthavira-vāda (Elder School).
Furthermore, twenty *li* to the west of this place is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the site where the Mahāsāṃghika-vāda (Great Assembly School) gathered together.

Thousands of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who had not been included when Mahākāśyapa convened the council gathered together in this place and said to one another:
"When the Tathāgata was alive, we studied under the same teacher."
"The World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa and has excluded us; how could we not compile the Dharma-piṭaka to repay the Buddha’s kindness?

They subsequently compiled the *Sūtra-piṭaka*, the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*, and the *Mantra-piṭaka*, establishing them as five distinct piṭakas. Because ordinary persons and noble ones assembled together therein, it was called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly School).
Proceeding three or four *li* northeast from here, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (translated into Chinese as Wángshèchéng, "King’s Abode City").
The outer walls have already crumbled, but the inner city remains lofty; it is over twenty *li* in circumference, with a single gate on each side.
Formerly, when King Bimbisāra resided in the Upper Thatched Palace, the populace was dense and dwellings were packed together like fish scales.
Having repeatedly suffered from fire disasters, he established a strict regulation: anyone who was negligent and the first to cause a fire would be banished to the Śītavana cemetery.
The Śmaśāna was the foul place in that country where corpses were discarded.
Shortly thereafter, the royal palace suddenly caught fire again.
The king said:
"I am a ruler of men; if I myself commit offenses and fail to practice [virtue], there will be no means to discipline my subordinates.
He commanded his crown prince to remain and pacify the realm, while the King moved his residence to the Śītavana (Cold Forest).
At that time, the King of Vaiśālī heard that Bimbisāra was dwelling in the wilderness outside the city and intended to select troops to launch a surprise attack upon him.
The scouts learned of this and reported it; the King then established a city there.
Because the King had first taken up residence here, it was named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence), which is the New City.
Later, King Śaśāṅka succeeded to the throne and made it his capital.
When King Aśoka moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra, he bestowed this city upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Today, there are no people of mixed origin within the city; there are only some one thousand households of Brāhmaṇas.

In the southwest corner of the palace grounds, there is a stūpa; this was the former residence of the householder Sudarśana (translated into Chinese as Xīnglì, formerly called Shùtíjiā, which is an error). Beside it is the site of Rāhula, the son of the Buddha.
To the northwest of Nālandā Monastery, there is a great vihāra over three hundred feet high, built by King Balāditya.
Its adornments are exceedingly magnificent, and the Buddha image within it is identical to the one at the Bodhi tree.
To the northeast of the vihāra is a stūpa, the site where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days.
To the northwest is further the place where the four past Buddhas sat.
To its south is a brass vihāra built by King Śīlāditya; although its construction is not yet complete, according to its plans and measurements, it is intended to be over ten zhang in height.

More than two hundred paces to the east of the city is a standing bronze Buddha image, over eighty feet in height; it requires a six-story multi-storied pavilion to cover it, and it was made in the past by King Pūrṇamukha.

Traveling eastward again for several *li*, there is a stūpa at the place where the Buddha, having first attained enlightenment, was heading toward Rājagṛha when King Bimbisāra and a multitude of hundreds of thousands of his subjects came out to welcome and see him.
Traveling eastward again for more than thirty *li*, one reaches Mount Indrāśila-kuha.
Before the monastery on the eastern peak is a stūpa, which is called Saṃsa (the Chinese translation is "wild goose").

In the past, this monastery followed the gradual teachings of the Hīnayāna and consumed the three kinds of pure meat. On one occasion, when they were unable to purchase or redeem any for their meal, the overseer was anxious and at a loss as to what to do. Seeing a flock of geese soaring through the sky, he looked up and said in jest:
"Today there is a deficiency in the monastic provisions; Mahāsattva, you should know that now is the time."
Having finished speaking, the one leading the way turned back at the sound of his words; he clipped his wings high in the clouds and threw himself down from above.

When the bhikṣu saw this, he was filled with shame and fear, and he announced it to the entire assembly of monks. Those who heard it were struck with amazement, and there was none among them who did not sigh and weep in response.
They said to one another, "This is a bodhisattva.
What kind of people are we that we would dare wish to devour him?"

Furthermore, the Tathāgata established his teachings with gradual stages of protection; yet we clung to those initial words of guidance as being the ultimate doctrine, remaining in ignorance without reform, which led to this injury.
"From this day forward, you should follow the Mahāyāna and must no longer eat the three kinds of pure meat.
He then erected a spirit-stupa and buried the dead goose within it, inscribing a record of his resolve so that its noble legacy might be perpetuated forever; thus, this stupa exists.

Having thus completed his circumambulation and worship of all such sacred sites, the Dharma Master returned to Nālandā Monastery, where he then requested the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra to lecture on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; several thousand people attended together.
When the introductory discourse was finished, after a short while, a certain Brahmin outside the assembly wept with grief and yet spoke with laughter.
The Master sent someone to ask him the reason for this,
and he replied:
"I am a man from Eastern India who once made a vow before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Pūṭaka to become a king. The Bodhisattva manifested his form to me and rebuked me, saying:
'Do not make such a vow!'"

On such-and-such a day in such-and-such a month in the future, the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra of Nālandā Monastery will lecture on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for the monks of the land of Cīna; you should go there to listen.
"Therefore, having heard the Dharma, I have now been able to see the Buddha; what use is there for kingship!
Now, seeing that the monks from China have arrived and that the Master has again preached for them, his words are the same as those of old, which is why I am both grieved and filled with joy.
The Dharma Master Śīlabhadra consequently allowed him to stay and listen.
After fifteen months, when the lectures were completed, he sent someone to escort the Brahmin to King Śīlāditya, who granted him three villages as a fief.

While at the monastery, the Dharma Master listened to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* three times, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* once, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* once each, the treatises on Hetuvidyā, Śabdavidyā, and Pramāṇasamuccaya twice each, and the two treatises, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*, three times each.

As for the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, the *Abhidharma* treatises, and so forth, since I had already finished listening to them in various kingdoms of Kaśmīra, I merely consulted and read them here to resolve my doubts.
He also studied the Brahmanical scriptures.
The Indian Sanskrit texts are called *smṛti* (treatises on tradition); their origin is beginningless, and no author is known.

At the commencement of every eon (*kalpa*), the Brahmā King first expounds them and transmits them to the devas and humans; because they were spoken by the Brahmā King, they are called "Brahmanical books" (*brahmalipi*).
Its discourse is extremely extensive, consisting of one million stanzas; this is what was formerly translated as the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*. However, its phonetics were not correct;

if they were corrected, it should be called *Vyañjanā* (the "n" sound being pronounced with the *nvǎn* rhyme). This is translated as the *Śabdavidyā-vidhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Rules of Phonology). It is named the *Śabdavidyā-vidhi-śāstra* because it extensively records the various dharmas that serve as expressive designations (*vyañjana*).
In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa of formation, Brahmā first expounded it in one million verses.
Later, at the beginning of the kalpa of endurance, Śakra further abridged it into one hundred thousand verses.

Subsequently, in the city of Tāṇḍula in the kingdom of Gandhāra in North India, the Brahmin sage Pāṇini further abridged it into eight thousand verses; this is the version currently in circulation in India today.

Recently, a Brahmin from South India further abridged it for the King of South India into two thousand five hundred stanzas; this version has become widely circulated in the bordering countries, though it is not followed or studied by the learned scholars of India.
These are the fundamental phonemes and characters of the Western Regions (India).
As for the auxiliary branches that assist them, there is also the *Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī-sūtra*, consisting of one thousand stanzas.

Furthermore, there is a work on letter-forms (*akṣara*) in three hundred stanzas; there are also two types of works on the etymological derivation of letters (*akṣaramūla*): the first is named *Kātantra*, consisting of three thousand stanzas, and the second is named *Cāndra*, consisting of two thousand five hundred stanzas. These separately explain the etymological derivation and the forms of letters.
Furthermore, there is the *Aṣṭadhātuvāda* in eight hundred stanzas, which briefly synthesizes the conditions and the substance of syllables.
Among these various treatises, there are two types of exegesis that distinguish between the signifier and the signified.

The first is called *ṭi-vṛtta* (pronounced *di-yan-duo*), which has eighteen inflections; the second is called *sūmantra*, which has twenty-four inflections. The *ṭi-vṛtta* style is employed in passages where the composition is grand and magnificent, and it is also used sparingly in general prose.
The twenty-four case endings (vibhakti) are used in common for all [grammatical] texts.
As for the eighteen case endings of the *ṭyadādi* [pronouns], there are two types:
first, the *sarvanāmasthāna*, and second, the *asarvanāmasthāna*; each has nine endings, thus totaling eighteen.
Regarding the first nine variations: as when discussing a single matter in general, that single matter has three aspects.
There are three ways of speaking of others, and three ways of speaking of oneself; within each of these three, one may speak of one, speak of two, or speak of many—thus there are three.
Both lines are thus; however, because their phonemes differ, they are divided into two sets of nine.
According to the explanation based on the *Bhramarasa* phonetics, there are various dharmas such as existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "existence" (bhava), there are three names for it: first, bhavāgra; second, bhavāgra-śuddha; and third, bhavānta.
Regarding the three [terms] spoken of for others: first is *bāhus*, second is *bāhuṣaṭ*, and third is *bāhuṣṭha*. Regarding the three spoken of for oneself:

first is *bāhumī*, second is *bāhukṣa* (with the final syllable pronounced as a departing tone), and third is *bāhumā*; this third term is explained according to the *Catuḥ-veda-śāstra*, where it is mostly called *bāhumatsya*.
Regarding the nine inflections of *ādarman*: for each of the aforementioned nine inflections, the word *viyaṭi* is placed beneath them; the rest is as above.
This is established to make the phrasing elegant and skillful, without any other specific meaning, and it also expresses the sense of being "extremely beautiful."

Regarding the twenty-four inflections (*vyañjana*) of the *saman* chant: this refers to a total of eight inflections, each of which is further divided into three—namely, the singular, the dual, and the plural—thus resulting in twenty-four.
Within each of the twenty-four [vocal qualities], there are three types:
namely, male voice, female voice, and neither-male-nor-female voice.
As for what are called the "eight modulations":

1. Denoting the essence of phenomena; 2. denoting the action performed; 3. denoting the instrument and the agent; 4. denoting the purpose for which something is done; 5. denoting the cause from which something arises; 6. denoting that to which something belongs; 7. denoting that upon which something depends; 8. denoting the act of calling.
Furthermore, regarding the eight inflections (*vibhakti*) applied to the masculine gender (*puruṣa*), the term for "man" in the Indian language is *puruṣa*.
Its three primary cases (*tri-vibhakti*) are: first, *puruṣa*; second, *puruṣau*; and third, *puruṣāḥ* (with the departing tone).
The three types of actions performed are: first, *puruṣa-śāna*; second, *puruṣa-śau*; and third, *puruṣa-śrama*.

The three types of instruments and performers are: first, *puruṣa-kṣaṇa*; second, *puruṣa-kṣi* (the character *kṣi* is pronounced with the *bǐ* and *jiàn* tones); and third, *puruṣa-kṣavi*, or alternatively called *puruṣa-kṣahi*.
The three matters to be performed are: first, *pruṣāya*; second, *pruṣābhi*; and third, *pruṣāvi*.
The three causes are: first, *puruṣa*; second, *puruṣaka*; and third, *puruṣakāra*.

There are three types belonging to this category: first, *bhrūṣaṇīya* (pronounced with the *zi* and *ye* finals); second, *bhrūṣaṇā*; and third, *bhrūṣaṇān* (the final *an* pronounced with the *an* rhyme).
As for the three bases: first, *pruḍa* (pronounced with the *ji* rhyme); second, *pruṣālu*; third, *pruṣātru* (pronounced with the *cu* rhyme).
Regarding the three types of invocations: first, *kṣepapūrakṣa*; second, *kṣepapūraka*; and third, *kṣepapūraka*. These two or three examples have been cited briefly;
the remaining cases may be inferred accordingly, as it would be difficult to describe them in full detail.
The Dharma Master thoroughly mastered their language; his discourse with those people was elegant and classical, even more exquisite [than theirs].
In this manner, he investigated various treatises and studied Sanskrit texts for a total of five years.
From here, he proceeded again toward the country of Ilāṃdabhata.
On the way, he reached the Kapota Monastery.

Two or three *li* to the south of the monastery was a solitary mountain, its cliffs and peaks towering high; the shrubs and trees were dense and lush, the springs and ponds were clear and fresh, and the flowers and plants were fragrant.
As it is a preeminent sacred site, its numinous shrines are truly numerous, and its manifestations of spiritual response are marvelous, with many kinds of divine wonders.

Within the central vihāra is a sandalwood statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, whose majestic power is exceptionally venerable. There are always several dozen people who, for seven days or fourteen days, abstain from grain and cut off all liquids to pray for their various aspirations. Those whose sincerity reaches its peak immediately see the Bodhisattva, adorned with all his marks and radiant with brilliant light, emerge from within the sandalwood image to console them and grant their wishes.
As such, people were frequently seen coming to behold it, and consequently, those who returned grew ever more numerous.

Fearing that the visitors might defile the sacred image, the patrons erected wooden railings about seven paces away from each side of the statue; thus, when people came to prostrate themselves, they all remained outside the railings and were not permitted to approach the image.
The incense and flowers they offered were likewise scattered from afar.
Those whose hands the flowers remained upon, or those to whom they hung upon their arms, considered it an auspicious omen and believed their wishes had been fulfilled.

The Dharma Master, wishing to go and make his request, purchased various kinds of flowers and strung them into garlands. Taking them to the place where the image was located, he performed prostrations and offered praise with utmost sincerity. Then, kneeling before the Bodhisattva, he made three vows:
"First, if after completing my studies here I may return safely to my own country without hindrance, may these flowers remain upon your hands.

Second, regarding the merit and wisdom I have cultivated, if I am to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven to serve the Bodhisattva Maitreya as I desire, may these flowers hang suspended from your two arms."

Third, the holy teachings state that within the realm of sentient beings there are some who lack the Buddha-nature; I, Xuanzang, now harbor doubts as to whether this is so or not. If there indeed exists the Buddha-nature such that through cultivation one may attain Buddhahood, I pray that this flower garland may hang upon Your Honored Neck.
Having finished speaking, she scattered flowers from afar, and everything occurred exactly as she had said.
Her wishes being fulfilled, her joy was immeasurable.
When those beside her who were performing prostrations together with the keepers of the vihāra saw this, they snapped their fingers and clapped their hands, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented!
Should you attain the Way in the future, we pray that you will remember this present circumstance and deliver us first.
Having said this, they gradually departed for the kingdom of Irāṇa.
There are ten monasteries with more than four thousand monks, most of whom study the Hinayana teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and donated the capital city to the Sangha; he established two monasteries therein, each housing one thousand monks.

There were two venerable masters: the first was named Tathāgatagupta, translated as "Tathāgata Secret," and the second was named Kṣāntisimha, translated as "Lion Patience"; both were well-versed in the Sarvāstivāda school.
He stayed there for another year, studying the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and other treatises.
To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma to devas and humans for three months; nearby are the remains of the four past Buddhas.
On the western border of the kingdom lies the Gaṅgā River, and to the south is a small isolated mountain where the Buddha formerly spent the three-month summer retreat and subdued the yakṣa Bakula.

On a large rock at the foot of a cliff to the southeast of the mountain is the footprint of the Buddha; it is indented into the stone by more than one inch, measuring five chi and two cun in length and four chi and one cun in width.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha image holding a kuṇḍika—this is a water vessel; the old term "junchi" is a corruption.
It is over an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled floral design.
To the south of the kingdom lies a wilderness forest where there are many elephants, both powerful and of great stature.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll Three.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll [Three].
Compiled by the Fourth Śramaṇa Huili, with annotations by Shi Yancong.

From the Kingdom of Campā to the Invitation of the King of Kāmarūpa. From here, traveling east along the southern bank of the Gaṅgā for over three hundred *li*, one reaches Campā, within the borders of Central India.
There are ten monasteries with more than two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
The city walls are built of brick, several *zhang* high, with foundations and moats so deep and wide that they are extremely lofty and secure.

In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, all humans lived in caves. Later, a celestial maiden descended among men and went to bathe in the Ganges River; when the water-spirit touched her body, she gave birth to four sons. These sons divided rule over Jambudvīpa, demarcated boundaries, and established villages and towns; this was the capital of one of those sons.

Several tens of yojanas to the south of the kingdom lies a great mountain forest, dense and lush, stretching for more than two hundred li. Within it dwell many wild elephants, numbering several hundred in their herds; thus, the two kingdoms of Ilāṇḍa and Campā possess the largest elephant armies. Elephant trainers are regularly sent to this forest to tame and capture them for the state's use as mounts.
Furthermore, it abounds with dholes, rhinoceroses, and black leopards, such that no one dares to travel there.

According to tradition, before the Buddha had appeared in the world, there was a cowherd tending several hundred head of cattle whom he drove into the forest. One ox left the herd and went off alone; it was constantly lost and its whereabouts unknown. When evening came and he wished to return home, the ox would rejoin the herd, its luster and complexion exceptionally radiant and its bellowing extraordinary. All the other cattle were terrified of it, and none dared to stand before it.
After many such days, the cowherd marveled at the reason for this and secretly waited to observe him. After a short while, he returned and departed; the cowherd then followed to watch him.

He saw the ox enter a stone cavern, and the man followed after it. After traveling about four or five *li*, there was a sudden, vast brightness; the forests and fields were radiant with splendor, filled with extraordinary flowers and fruits so brilliant they overwhelmed the eyes—none of which could be seen within the mundane world.
The ox grazed on grass in one place; its color, fragrance, and succulence were such as not even to be found in the human world.

When the man saw the various fruit trees, their yellow and red hues like gold, fragrant and massive, he plucked a single fruit. Although his heart was filled with craving and attachment, he remained fearful and did not dare to eat it.

After a short while, the oxen emerged and the men followed them back home. While they were at the stone hole and had not yet fully emerged, a malevolent spirit snatched away one of the fruits and kept it.
The cowherd asked a great physician about this and described the appearance of the fruit; the physician said, "It must not be eaten immediately; you should employ a skillful means to bring one out."

On a later day, he again followed the oxen inside and once more plucked a fruit, intending to carry it home; the ghost again blocked him and snatched it away. The man placed the fruit in his mouth, and the ghost again pinched his throat so that he immediately swallowed it. Once the fruit had entered his belly, his body became vast and immense; though his head managed to emerge, his body remained stuck within the hole, and he was ultimately unable to return home.

Later, when his family members went to search for him, they were all struck with terror upon seeing that his physical form had been transformed; yet he was still able to speak and explain the circumstances of what had occurred.
When the family returned home, they mobilized many laborers to try and pull him out, but in the end, he could not be moved at all.
Upon hearing this, the king personally inspected it; fearing it might become a source of future trouble, he dispatched men to dig it up and pull it out, yet they were unable to move it.
As many years and months passed, it gradually turned into stone, though it still retained the form of a human being.
Later, there was another king who knew that [the stone] had been transformed by the fruit of an immortal; he said to his attendants:

"Since his body has been transformed due to the medicine, his very body is the medicine. Although it appears as a stone, its essence is ultimately divine and spiritual. You should send someone to take a hammer and chisel to extract a small portion and bring it here."

The minister, obeying the king’s command, went with the craftsmen and exerted all his strength in carving and chiseling; after ten days had passed, not a single piece could be obtained, and it remains as it was even now.
From here, traveling east for more than four hundred *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Karmārgira within the borders of Central India.
He visited the holy sites there; there were six or seven monasteries with more than three hundred monks.
From here, traveling east across the Ganges for more than six hundred *li*, he arrived at the kingdom of Puṇḍravardhana, within the borders of South India.
He visited the sacred sites there; there were over twenty monasteries with more than three thousand monks who studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vakṣu-vihāra, with its lofty and magnificent towers and pavilions, where seven hundred monks reside.
Beside it stands a stūpa built by King Aśoka at the site where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma for three months; from time to time, it emits brilliant light.
Furthermore, there are the traces where four Buddhas walked.
Beside them is a vihāra containing an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; if one prays with utmost sincerity, no wish shall go unfulfilled.
From here, traveling southeast for more than nine hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa, within the borders of Eastern India.
There are over ten monasteries with more than three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are three other monasteries where they do not consume milk or curd; this tradition follows the bequeathed instructions of Devadatta.

Beside the great city is the Lokottaravādin Monastery (translated into Chinese as Chini), which was established by the king in the past when the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached this country, after a śramaṇa from South India, while traveling as a guest in this land, had defeated the heterodox arguments of the Tāmraparṇīya heretics.
Beside it is another stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days.
From here, proceeding southeast, one arrives at the country of Samataṭa, within the borders of East India.
Bordering the great ocean, the climate is mild and pleasant.
There are more than thirty monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the doctrines of the Sthavira school.
The devalayas and the followers of the non-Buddhist paths are also numerous there.
Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, at the site where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days to gods and humans.

Not far from here there is another monastery, within which is a statue of the Buddha made of blue jade, eight feet in height. Its marks and signs are dignified and serene, and it constantly emits a natural, wondrous fragrance that permeates the entire courtyard.
Auspicious omens of five-colored light frequently illuminated the heavens;
all who witnessed or heard of this were deeply moved to resolve upon the Way.

From here, proceeding northeast, there is the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra among the coastal mountains and valleys; further east, at the southeastern corner of the sea, is the kingdom of Kāmarūpa; further east is the kingdom of Dvāravatī; further east is the kingdom of Īśānapura; further east is the kingdom of Mahācampā—here called Lin-yi; and further west is the kingdom of Yamunadvīpa.
These six kingdoms are all situated deep within mountains and seas; although one does not enter their borders, their customs can still be known.
From this country of Samataṭa, traveling westward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Damalipta, which lies within the borders of East India.
Situated near a corner of the sea, there are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks.
Beside the city stands a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka; nearby are the traces left where the four past Buddhas once walked.

At that time, he heard that in the midst of the ocean there was the kingdom of Siṃhala—here translated as "Lion-Holder"—where there were masters of the Tripiṭaka of the Sthavira school who were also learned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. It required traveling seven hundred yojanas by sea to reach it.
Before he had departed, he encountered a monk from South India who urged him, saying:

"Those traveling to the Kingdom of Siṃhala need not take the sea route; there are many dangers at sea, such as fierce winds, yakṣas, and turbulent waves. You may instead go from the southeastern corner of South India by water, and you will arrive in three days."
"Although we must tread over mountains and rivers, we shall do so with a sense of security, and furthermore, we shall be able to behold the sacred sites of various countries such as Oḍra.
Thereupon, the Dharma Master turned toward the southwest, heading for the kingdom of Oḍra within the borders of East India.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks who study the Mahāyāna teachings.
There are also deva temples and non-Buddhists, with those of heterodox and orthodox views living together.
There are more than ten stūpas, all built by King Aśoka, from which miraculous signs frequently manifest.

On the southeastern border of the kingdom, bordering the great ocean, lies the city of Cīlāla (translated into Chinese as Chūfángxíng, "Departure and Setting Out"), which serves as a station for the arrival and departure of sea-going merchants and travelers from distant lands; it is situated more than twenty thousand *li* to the south of the kingdom of Siṃhala.

Every night, when it was still and cloudless, one could see from afar the precious jewel atop that stūpa housing the Buddha’s tooth relic; its radiance was brilliant, appearing like a star or a candle in the sky.
From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than one thousand two hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Koṅgoda in Eastern India.
From there, traveling southwest through a vast wilderness for one thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa in the territory of Southern India.
There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks who study the teachings of the Sthavira school.

In the past, the population was extremely dense; however, because they disturbed a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the seer became enraged and used malevolent incantations to bring about their destruction. Consequently, the people—both old and young—died, and those who remained later gradually migrated from other places to settle here, yet the region is still not fully populated.
From here, traveling northwest for more than one thousand eight hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of South Kośala, within the borders of Central India.
The king is of the Kṣatriya caste;
he reveres the Buddha-dharma and prizes learning and the arts.
There are one hundred monasteries with ten thousand monks.
Temples of the gods and followers of external paths are also quite numerous and mixed therein.
Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, beside which stands a stūpa erected by King Aśoka.
In the past, the Tathāgata manifested great supernatural transformations at this site to subdue and defeat the non-Buddhists; later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna resided in this monastery.

At that time, the king of this country was named Śatavāhana (translated into Chinese as Yǐnzhèng, "Leading the Right"), who revered Nāgārjuna and provided him with exceptionally generous offerings and protection.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva arrived from Siṃhala Island seeking a debate; he went to the gate and requested an audience, and the gatekeeper reported this to him.
Nāgārjuna, who had long known his reputation, filled a bowl with water and ordered a disciple to carry it out and show it to him.
When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it as his disciple was about to depart.
Upon seeing this, Nāgārjuna expressed deep joy and admiration, saying:
"The clarity and fullness of the water are used as a metaphor for my own virtue."
"He came here to cast a needle and has now reached its very bottom.
A man such as this may be discussed with regarding the profound mysteries of the Way; he is fit to be entrusted with the transmission of the lamp.
He then ordered him to be led inside.
When they had finished sitting, they engaged in a dialogue, both of them filled with joy as if fish and water had met.
Nāgārjuna said, "I am now advanced in years; that you shall illuminate the sun of wisdom lies in you."
Deva rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of Nāgārjuna, and said:
"Though I am not quick-witted, I venture to receive your compassionate instruction.
In that country there was a Brahmin who was skilled in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*); the Dharma Master stayed with him for over a month to study the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
From here, traveling southeast through a great forest for over nine hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Andhra, within the borders of South India.
Beside the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma), its construction grand and magnificent, with a majestic and solemn appearance.
In front stands a stone stūpa several hundred feet high, built by the Arhat Ajita (translated into Chinese as Suoxing, "That Which Is Practiced").

About twenty li to the southwest of the Arhat’s monastery is an isolated mountain, upon which stands a stone stūpa; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dignāga (translated into Chinese as Shou, "Bestowed") composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic).
From here, traveling south for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Dhānakaṭaka in South India.

To the east of the city, situated against a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (translated in Chinese as "Eastern Mountain") Monastery; to the west of the city, also situated against a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (translated in Chinese as "Western Mountain") Monastery. These were established by a former king of this country for the sake of the Buddha. They exhaust the architectural standards of grand palatial halls and encompass the finest beauty of forests and springs. Protected by celestial deities, they are inhabited by sages and holy ones.

Within the first millennium after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, every year a thousand ordinary monks would come together to observe the rains retreat; once the retreat was completed, they would all realize arhatship and depart, soaring through the air.

A thousand years later, ordinary people and sages dwell together; however, for over a hundred years, the mountain deity has changed his form and harassed travelers, causing them all to be struck with fear. Consequently, no one dares to go there anymore, and thus the place is now entirely desolate and abandoned, with not a single monk remaining.

Not far to the south of the city is a great stone mountain; this is the place where the master of treatises, Bhāviveka (translated into Chinese as Qingbian), resided in the palace of the Asuras to await the future Buddha Maitreya, intending to resolve his doubts once he had attained enlightenment.

In that country, the Dharma Master met two monks, one named Subhūti and the other named Sūrya, who were well-versed in the Tripiṭaka of the Mahāsāṃghika school. The Dharma Master stayed with them for several months to study Mahāsāṃghika treatises such as the *Mūla-abhidharma*. They, in turn, studied various Mahāyāna treatises under the Dharma Master; thus, having formed a bond of shared resolve, they traveled together on a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
From here, traveling west for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Cūḷika in South India.

To the southeast of the city is a stupa built by King Aśoka; this is the place where the Buddha in former times manifested great supernatural powers, subdued the heretics, and preached the Dharma to deliver humans and devas.

To the west of the city is an old monastery where the Bodhisattva Deva engaged in debate with the Arhat Uttara (translated into Chinese as *shàng*, "Superior") of this temple. When they had reached the seventh turn of the argument, the Arhat remained speechless; he then secretly employed his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to travel to the Tuṣita Palace to consult the Bodhisattva Maitreya. The Bodhisattva explained the matter for him and said:
"That Deva has cultivated merit for a long time and shall attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) during the Bhadrakalpa; you must not underestimate him."
Having returned, he again raised his previous objection.
Deva said, "This is the doctrine of Maitreya Bodhisattva; it is not something that can be attained through your own wisdom alone."
The Arhat, filled with shame and submission, rose from his seat to pay his respects and offer thanks.
From this point, traveling south through a great forest for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, he reached the country of Draviḍa, within the borders of South India.

The capital city of the kingdom was called Kāñcīpura; this city of Kāñcī was the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (translated into Chinese as Hufa), who was the son of a high minister of this country.
From his youth, he was exceptionally bright and intelligent; after reaching the age of twenty, the King, admiring his talent, wished to give him his daughter, a princess, in marriage.

The Bodhisattva had long cultivated detachment and was free from any mind of craving or defilement; yet on the eve of his impending accomplishment, he felt a particular sense of anxiety and distress. He then prayed before a Buddha image for protection, vowing to escape this peril. Moved by the sincerity of his devotion, a great divine king carried him out and escorted him several hundred li beyond the city, placing him within the Buddha hall of a mountain temple.

When the monastics came upon him and saw him, they took him for a thief; the Bodhisattva then explained the circumstances of his situation. Those who heard this were struck with wonder and admiration, and there was none who did not revere his lofty resolve, whereupon he immediately left the household life.

Thereafter, he devoted himself exclusively to the True Dharma and was eventually able to master all its various schools. Skilled in composition, he authored the *Vyākaraṇa-saṃkīrṇa-śāstra* in twenty-five thousand stanzas, and further wrote commentaries on the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratā-siddhi*, and several dozen works on *Hetuvidyā*, all of which were widely propagated.
His flourishing virtue and eminent talent have separate biographies of their own.
Jianzhicheng is the mouth of the southern sea of India; traveling by water for three days from there, one arrives at the kingdom of Siṃhala.
Before they had departed, that king passed away, and famine and chaos broke out within his realm.

There was a monk of great virtue named Bodhimaccheśvara (translated as "Cloud of Sovereign Enlightenment") and Avayadaṃṣṭra (translated as "Fearless Tusk"; these were the names of two leaders among more than three hundred monks who came to seek refuge in India and arrived at the city of Kañcī.
After the Dharma Master had finished meeting with them, he asked the monks:

"I have heard that the Venerable Ones of that country are proficient in the Tripiṭaka of the Sthavira school as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. I now wish to go there to study; for what reason have you masters come here?"
He replied, "The king of my country has died, and the common people are suffering from famine and have no one to rely upon.
I heard that Jambudvīpa is prosperous, peaceful, and secure, being the birthplace of the Buddha and containing many sacred sites; for this reason, I have come."
Furthermore, he said, "Among those who understand the Dharma, none surpass our own school. Elder, if you have any doubts, feel free to ask as you wish.

The Master then cited essential passages and major sections from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to challenge him, yet [the opponent] was unable to produce an interpretation that surpassed that of Śīlabhadra.
From here, across more than three thousand *li* of territory, one hears of the kingdom of Malakūṭa in the region of South India; situated on the seacoast, it abounds exceedingly in rare treasures.

To the east of that city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; it is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and manifested great supernormal powers to deliver immeasurable multitudes.

To the south of the kingdom, bordering the sea, lies Mount Malaya. Its cliffs and valleys are lofty and deep, and within them grow white sandalwood trees and *candana-nimba* trees; these trees resemble the white poplar, their substance being cool and cold, and many snakes cling to them, hibernating only during winter—this serves as a means to distinguish true sandalwood.
