There is also the *karpūra* tree, which has a pine-like trunk but distinct leaves, and its flowers and fruits are likewise unique. When moist, it has no fragrance; however, after being harvested and dried, if one breaks it open, there is fragrance within. Its appearance resembles mica, and its color is like ice and snow; this is what is called *nāgakesara* (camphor).

Furthermore, I have heard that on the eastern shore of the great sea there is a city; from the southeast of this city, after traveling more than three thousand *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Siṃhala (translated into Chinese as Zhíshīzǐ, "Lion-Holder").
This is not within the territory of India.

The kingdom is over seven thousand *li* in circumference, and its capital city is over forty *li* in circumference. The population is dense and prosperous, and the crops are abundant and well-ripened; the people are dark-complexioned, small in stature, and impetuous by nature—such are their customs.

The kingdom was like a precious island, abounding in rare and wondrous things. Later, a woman from South India was being escorted as a bride to a neighboring country when she encountered a lion king on the road. Her attendants fled in terror, leaving her alone in the carriage. When the lion saw her, he carried her away into the deep mountains, where he gathered fruits and hunted game to provide for her.
As the years passed, they gave birth to sons and daughters; though their forms resembled those of humans, their natures were violent and evil.
When the sons gradually grew up, they asked their mother, "To what category do we belong?"
"The father was a beast and the mother was human.
The mother then recounted the events of the past to him.
Her son said:
"Since humans and animals are so different, why do you not abandon him and go your separate ways instead of staying together?
The mother replied, "It is not that I have no heart to leave; it is simply that there is no way for me to escape."
The son subsequently followed his father up mountains and across valleys, observing the places he traversed.

On another day, when he waited until his father had gone far ahead, he took his mother and sister with him, descended into a human settlement, and reached his mother’s native country. He sought out his maternal uncle’s family, but found that their lineage had already been extinguished; they were living as dependents among the village folk.

When the lion king returned and did not see his wife and children, he emerged from the mountain in a fit of rage and roared through the villages and hamlets; many men and women passing by were harmed by him.
The common people reported the matter to the king, who led his fourfold army and selected brave warriors, intending to surround and shoot him with arrows.
Upon seeing this, the lion let out a roar of rage; men and horses fell prostrate, and none dared to advance.
Thus many days passed, yet no success was achieved.
The king again announced a reward, proclaiming that anyone capable of killing the lion would be granted a hundred million pieces of gold.
The son said to his mother:
"It is difficult to endure hunger and cold; I wish to join the King's recruitment—what do you think?
His mother said, "You must not."
"Although he is a beast, he is nonetheless your father; if one were to kill him, how could such a person still be called human?
The son replied, "If it were not so, he would never leave; he might even pursue us and come into our village."
Once the King learns of this, we shall surely die and he will not spare us either.
Why? For the lion is a fierce beast; for the sake of our mother and me, how could one cause distress to many people?
"Reflecting on this for a moment or two, it would be better to respond to the call. Thereupon, he set out.

Upon seeing him, the lion became docile and joyful, harboring no intent to harm at all. The son then used a sharp blade to slit its throat and tear open its belly; though subjected to such agony, the lion’s affection remained so deep that it endured it without moving, and consequently, its life came to an end.
When the king heard this, he was filled with joy; yet, wondering at it, he asked, "What is the cause of this?
but she ultimately did not speak the truth.
Having experienced various forms of distress and desperation,
he then recounted everything in detail. The King said, "Alas!"
"One who is not of the animal species—who could have conceived such a thought?
Nevertheless, although I previously promised you a reward, I shall never go back on my word.
However, as a person who has murdered his father and committed such a rebellion, you may no longer reside within my kingdom."

The Emperor commanded the relevant officials to provide him with abundant gold and jewels, banishing him to the remote wilderness. They immediately prepared two ships, loading them with much gold, provisions, and other necessities, and sent him out into the middle of the sea to drift wherever the currents carried him.
A man traveling by ship across the sea arrived at this precious island and, seeing its abundant and wondrous curiosities, settled there.
Later, when merchants with their families came to that place to gather treasures, he killed the merchants and kept their women.
Thus, through generations of procreation and raising offspring, after countless kalpas had passed and the population had gradually increased, they established the offices of ruler and minister.
Because their distant ancestor had seized and killed a lion, it became the name of the kingdom.

A woman traveling by ship across the sea reached the western region of Persia, where she was seized by a malevolent spirit (rākṣasī). She gave birth to a multitude of daughters, who constitute the present-day kingdom of the Great Western Women.

Furthermore, it is said that Siṃhala was the name of a merchant’s son; because of his great wisdom, he escaped the harm of the rākṣasīs, later became king, and arrived at this island of jewels. Having slain the rākṣasīs and established a capital city there, the land was named after him. This account is recorded in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions).

Formerly, there was no Buddha-dharma in that country. One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka’s younger brother, Mahendrasena, grew weary of and renounced sensual desires, attaining the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. He traveled through the air to and fro, wandering and transforming this country to glorify and praise the Buddhist teachings and manifesting supernatural powers. The people of the nation came to believe in and admire him, and they established monasteries.
I visited more than a hundred monasteries with ten thousand monks who followed the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira schools.
The clergy were solemn and dignified, their observance of the precepts pure and bright, as they exhorted one another to remain diligent and untiring.

Beside the royal palace was a Tooth Relic Shrine (Dantadhātu-vihāra), several hundred feet in height, adorned with various precious gems. A stūpa pillar was erected above it, with a great *padmarāga* jewel placed at its pinnacle; its radiance illuminated the sky, so that even ten thousand *li* away, all could behold it on a cloudless, tranquil night.
Beside it there is another vihāra, likewise adorned with various precious stones.
Within it is a golden image made by a former king of this country; its topknot contains a precious gem whose value no one knows.

Later, there was a person who wished to steal this pearl; however, as the guards were vigilant and the entry points secure, he had no means of gaining access. He then secretly tunneled through the earth to enter the chamber intending to take it, but the form of the image gradually rose higher, so that the thief could not reach it.
He spoke again, saying:

"When the Tathāgata formerly cultivated the path of a bodhisattva, he did not spare his own life for the sake of all sentient beings, nor was he stingy with his kingdoms or cities; why then, on this day, do you instead act with such parsimony and stubbornness?"
Reflecting on this, he feared that his previous words were untrue.
The image then bent its body and handed over the pearl.
Having received it, the man took it to sell; someone who recognized it captured him and brought him before the King.
The king asked what he had obtained,
and the thief replied,
"The Buddha gave it to me himself."
He then related the circumstances in detail.
The King observed for himself that the head of the image was still bowed low.
Witnessing this spiritual miracle, his profound resolve was further awakened; he redeemed the pearl from the thieves with various precious jewels and returned it to adorn the topknot of the image.
It still exists today.
In the southeastern corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā-dvīpa, where many spirits and ghosts dwell.
It was here that the Tathāgata formerly preached the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (formerly called *Lengqie*, which is an error).

Sailing several thousand li southward from the kingdom across the sea, one reaches the island of Nalakaīra. The people of this island are short and small, standing barely over three feet tall; they have human bodies with bird-like beaks. They do not cultivate crops, but subsist on coconuts.
The ocean waves of that country are vast and long; I was unable to reach it myself, but such is the general account obtained from the people there.

From Dvāravatī, together with more than seventy monks from Siṃhala, I returned toward the northwest to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites. After traveling over two thousand li, I arrived at the kingdom of Kanyākubja in the territory of South India.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than ten thousand monks who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Non-Buddhist temples and heretics are also very numerous.
Beside the royal palace city is a great monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom are men of extensive learning and profound erudition.
Within that vihāra was the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha—formerly called Prince Siddhārtha, which is a corruption—standing less than two feet in height.

It was enshrined within a precious casket; whenever a fast day arrived, it was brought out and placed upon a high platform, and those who beheld it with utmost sincerity often perceived wondrous radiance.

Beside the city is a monastery containing a shrine, within which is a sandalwood image of Maitreya Bodhisattva over ten feet high; it has also frequently manifested auspicious radiance and was fashioned by the Arhat Śrutasvabhāva.

To the north of the city is a grove of *tāla* trees, over thirty li in circumference; their leaves are long and glossy, and they are held in the highest esteem for copying scriptures by various kingdoms.

From here, traveling northwest through a great forest and a wilderness of fierce beasts for two thousand four or five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Mahārāṣṭra, within the borders of South India.
The customs of this people regard death lightly but value integrity and high principle.

The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is fond of martial arts and prizes military prowess. Consequently, the kingdom’s troops and horses are well-maintained, and its laws and decrees are strict and clear. Whenever he dispatches a general to fight the enemy, even if they suffer a defeat or lose their army, he does not impose criminal punishment; instead, he bestows women's clothing upon them to make them feel ashamed. Out of such shame and remorse, many of those men commit suicide.

He constantly maintained several thousand brave warriors and several hundred fierce elephants; when about to face the enemy in battle, he would drink heavily until he was nearly intoxicated, and only then would he wave his banner to charge forward. There was never one who did not break and flee. Relying on this, he became arrogant and insolent, paying no heed to neighboring enemies.

King Śīlāditya considered his own wisdom and strategy to be far-reaching and his military forces to be powerful; yet, despite personally leading expeditions to punish and suppress [the rebels], he was unable to subdue them.
There are over one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
There are also deva temples and followers of the path of smearing ashes with ash.
Within and without the great city are five stūpas, each several hundred feet high; these are traces of the places where the four past Buddhas traveled, built by King Aśoka.
From here, traveling northwest for more than a thousand *li* and crossing the Narmadā River, one arrives at the kingdom of Valabhī in the territory of South India.
From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Mālava, also known as the kingdom of Lāṭa, in the territory of South India.

The customs there are mild and gentle, and they hold arts and learning in high esteem; among the five regions of India, only the two kingdoms of Mālava in the southwest and Magadha in the northeast are renowned for their love of learning, their reverence for the worthy, their eloquence in speech, and their refined elegance.
In this country, there are more than one hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
There are also followers of heterodox paths, such as those who smear themselves with ashes and worship the gods.

Tradition relates that sixty years ago there was a king named Śīlāditya, who was of lofty talent and broad learning, benevolent, compassionate, and harmonious. He cherished and nurtured the common people and venerated the Triple Gem. From the time he first ascended the throne until his passing, his mouth never uttered a harsh word and his countenance never showed a trace of anger; he did not wound the feelings of his ministers and subjects, nor did he harm the bodies of even mosquitoes or ants.
Whenever elephants or horses drink water, they strain it before drinking, fearing they might harm the lives of creatures dwelling in the water.
This principle extends even to the common people, who are likewise commanded to abstain from killing.
Consequently, wild beasts relied upon humans, jackals and wolves ceased their venomous ways, and the realm became peaceful and tranquil, with auspicious signs arising daily.

He constructed a refined monastery, reaching the pinnacle of architectural splendor; he fashioned the ritual images of the Seven Buddhas and established an unrestricted assembly (*pañcavārṣika*). Such meritorious deeds continued without interruption for more than fifty years of his reign; the people’s longing and remembrance for him persist to this day.

More than twenty li to the northwest of the great city, beside a Brahmin village, there is a sunken pit; this is the place where a greatly arrogant Brahmin, having slandered the Mahāyāna, entered hell alive. The account is recorded in the *Xiyu ji*.
From here, traveling northwest for two thousand four hundred or five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Aṭali, within the borders of South India.
The soil produces pepper trees, whose leaves resemble those of the Chinese pepper (shu jiao);
it also produces frankincense trees, whose leaves are similar to those of the crabapple (tang li).
From here, traveling northwest for three days, one arrives at the kingdom of Kheṭa, within the borders of South India.
From here, traveling north for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Valabhī, within the borders of South India.
There are more than one hundred monasteries with over six thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna.
During the lifetime of the Tathāgata, he frequently traveled to this country; King Aśoka erected monuments at every place where the Buddha had visited.
The present king is of the Kṣatriya caste;
he is the son-in-law of King Śīlāditya of the kingdom of Kanyākubja, and is named Dhruvabhaṭa, which in the language of Tang means "Imperial Scion."

By nature he was impetuous and his deportment was coarse; nevertheless, he esteemed virtue and honored learning, and with sincere devotion he took refuge in the Triple Gem. Every year he convened a great assembly for seven days, inviting monks from various countries and providing them with the finest delicacies and rare treasures, as well as beds, seats, clothing, and even medicinal supplies—nothing was left unprovided.
From here, traveling northwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Ānandapura, within the borders of Western India.
Traveling further northwest for more than five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Surāṣṭra, within the borders of Western India.
From here, traveling northeast for one thousand eight hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kukkuṭa.
Continuing southeast for more than two thousand eight hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Ujjayanī, within the borders of South India.
Not far from the city is a stūpa, which marks the site where King Aśoka established a hell.
From here, traveling northeast for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Takka, within the borders of South India.
From here, traveling northeast for over nine hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Mahīśvarapura within the borders of Central India.
From there, one returns westward to the country of Surāṣṭra.
From here, traveling further west, one arrives at the kingdom of Aḍakavata in the territory of Western India.
During the time of the Tathāgata, he frequently visited this land; King Aśoka erected stūpas at every location where there were sacred traces, all of which remain intact to this day.
From here, traveling west for more than two thousand li, one arrives at the kingdom of Langkala, within the borders of Western India.
It borders the great ocean and lies on the road leading toward the kingdom of the Women of the West (Oḍiviśa).

From here, traveling northwest to the kingdom of Persia within the borders of North India, I heard it said that the land abounds in precious gems, fine brocades, and delicate woolens; its products include excellent horses and dromedaries.
There are two or three monasteries with several hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna. The alms bowl of Śākyamuni Buddha is kept here in the royal palace.

On the eastern border of the country is the city of Khost; to the northwest it borders the kingdom of Bolor, and to the southwest there is the island of Oṛṇīdvīpa (the Kingdom of Western Women), where all are women and no men reside; they possess much precious wealth and are tributary to Bolor.
King Boliṅ annually dispatches men to provide for them; it is their custom not to raise male children once born.
Furthermore, traveling over seven hundred li northeast from the country of Langjialuo, one reaches the country of Biduśila, within the borders of Western India.
Within it stands a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka; it contains relics that frequently emit brilliant light.
This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life as a rishi, was killed by a king.
From here, traveling northeast for more than three hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Arbuda, within the borders of Western India.
In a great forest to the northeast of the city, there are the ruins of a monastery where the Buddha formerly permitted the bhikṣus to wear *upānaha* (in the language of Tang, boots).
There is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
Beside it is a vihāra containing a standing image of the Buddha carved from green stone, which frequently emits radiance.

Further south, some eight hundred paces into a great forest, there is another stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the Tathāgata once stayed; as the night was cold, he covered himself with his three robes layered over one another. By the following morning, this had become the place where the bhikṣus put on their *nāṃsi* (patchwork) robes.
From here, traveling east again for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Sindhu, within the borders of Western India.
The land produces gold, silver, brass, cattle, sheep, camels, red salt, white salt, black salt, and so forth; these are taken from other places to serve as medicines.
During the lifetime of the Tathāgata, he frequently visited this country; King Aśoka erected stūpas at all the sacred sites to serve as monuments.
Furthermore, there are traces of the travels and conversions of the great arhat Upagupta.
From here, traveling east for more than nine hundred *li* and crossing to the eastern bank of the river, one arrives at the kingdom of Maula-tapu-lo, within the borders of Western India.

The inhabitants worship celestial deities; their temples are magnificent and lofty. The images of these deities are cast of gold and adorned with various precious gems; people from many countries come here in great numbers to offer prayers and petitions.
Flower groves and lotus ponds border the paved walkways and wind around the steps;
all who behold them cannot help but admire and cherish them.
From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Bālbhāṭa, within the borders of North India.

Beside the city is a great monastery with more than a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. This is where the master of śāstras Śrībhadra (translated into Chinese as Zuìshèngzǐ, "Son of the Most Victorious") formerly composed his *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*; it was also the original place of ordination for the masters Bhadrapāla and Guṇaprabha.
Furthermore, that country had two or three great virtuous masters (*bhadanta*), whose learning and conduct were worthy of emulation.
The Dharma Master stayed there for two years to study the *Mūla-abhidharma* of the Saṃmitīya school, as well as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, and other treatises.
From here, proceeding again toward the southeast, I returned to the Anavatapta Monastery in Magadha and completed my prostrations and offerings to the Treasury of the True Dharma.

I heard that three *yojanas* to the west of the monastery lay the Tiladhaka Monastery, where there resided a virtuous monk named Prajñābhadra. He was originally from the country of Vārāṇasī and had gone forth in the Sarvāstivāda school; he was highly proficient in the Tripiṭaka of his own sect, as well as in *Śabdavidyā* (grammar) and *Hetuvidyā* (logic).
The Dharma Master stayed for two months to resolve his doubts.
From there, he proceeded to Mount Daṇḍaka to visit the lay master Vīrasena.
Vīrasena was originally a native of the country of Sūrata, belonging to the Kṣatriya caste.

From his youth, he was fond of learning; first, under the virtuous and beloved teacher Śīlabhadra, he studied *Hetuvidyā* (Logic); furthermore, he studied the *Śabdavidyā* (Grammar), as well as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises, under the Bodhisattva Sthiramati; and he studied the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* under the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra. Extending even to the various foreign texts, the four *Vedas*, astronomy, geography, medicine, and the arts and mathematics, there were none whose fundamental sources he did not investigate and whose branches and leaves he did not exhaustively master.

Having mastered both internal and external studies, his virtue was honored by his contemporaries. King Śīlāditya, the sovereign of Magadha, who revered the worthy and esteemed the scholar, heard of his reputation and rejoiced. He dispatched an envoy to invite him, appointing him as National Preceptor and granting him twenty large districts as fief; however, the Master of Shastras would not accept.

After the death of Pūrṇavarman, King Śīlāditya again invited him to serve as his teacher and conferred upon him eighty great towns of the kingdom of Oḍra; however, the Master of Śāstras declined and would not accept them.
Although the king repeatedly and earnestly entreated him, he likewise firmly declined each time, saying to the king:
"Śrīvijaya has heard that one who receives another's stipend must concern himself with that person's affairs."
"Now that I am currently striving to rescue myself from the urgent entanglements of birth and death, how could I have the leisure to attend to the affairs of kingship?
Having spoken thus, he bowed and departed; the king was unable to detain him.

From then on, he resided at Yaṣṭivana Mountain (Zhanglin Shan), where he nurtured disciples and taught them, constantly lecturing on Buddhist scriptures. Monastics and laypeople alike took refuge in him, numbering always over several hundred.

The Dharma Master attended upon him for two full years, studying the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra*, the *Abhayapaddhati-śāstra*, the *Apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, and the *Sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*. Furthermore, he resolved his doubts regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Hetuvidyā*.
During the night, he suddenly dreamed that the courtyards and chambers of Nālandā Monastery were overgrown and filthy; water buffaloes were tethered there, and no monks remained.

The Dharma Master entered through the western gate of the King Aruṇavata’s courtyard and saw a golden figure atop the fourth story of a multi-storied pavilion, its countenance dignified and majestic, with radiance filling the chamber.
His heart was filled with joy, yet he had no means to ascend; he therefore requested that the other reach out his hand to lead him up.
The other said, "I am the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī."
"Because of the karma you have accumulated, you cannot come here yet," he said,
and pointing outside the temple,
added, "Look at this."
The Dharma Master followed the direction of the finger and looked out; he saw that outside the monastery, fire was burning the villages and towns, reducing them entirely to ashes.
The golden man said, "You should return home at once."
"Ten years from now, King Śīlāditya shall pass away; India will fall into chaos and disorder, and wicked men will harm one another—you should know this.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Having awakened, the Dharma Master marveled and sighed in wonder, then spoke of this to Jayasena.
Jayasena said, "There is no peace in the three realms; it may well be thus."
"Since this has been said, it is up to you, O benevolent one, to decide for yourself.
Thus we know that all the deeds of a Mahāsattva are protected by the mindfulness of Bodhisattvas.
When he was about to depart for India, he informed Śīlabhadra and remained there to wait for him.
While he remained there without returning, he manifested impermanence to urge [the king] to return home.
Had his actions not accorded with the Sage’s heart, who could have moved him to such a display?
By the end of the Yonghui era, King Śīlāditya indeed passed away, and India suffered from famine and desolation, exactly as he had foretold.
The state dispatched Wang Xuance to observe these events firsthand.

It was at the beginning of this first month that, according to the custom of the Western Kingdoms, the *bodhi* temple would produce the Buddha’s *śarīra*. Monastics and laypeople from various nations all came to pay their respects; the Dharma Master then went there together with Śaṅkara.

He saw śarīra relics, some large and some small; the larger ones were like round beads, red and white in color and lustrous, while other flesh-relics were the size of mung beans, moist and crimson in appearance.
After the immeasurable assembly had offered incense and flowers and completed their prostrations and praises, they returned the relics to the stupa.
When about one watch of the night had passed, Jayasena discussed with the Dharma Master the discrepancy regarding the size of the śarīras, saying:
"I have seen śarīras elsewhere that were as large as grains of rice; why are those we see here so exceptionally large?"
"Does your reverence have any doubts?
The Dharma Master replied,
"I, Xuanzang, also have this doubt."
After a short while had passed, suddenly the lamp within the chamber was no longer visible, and both inside and out it became brilliantly illuminated.

Alarmed, he went outside to look and saw that the light of the Śarīra stūpa was radiating upward; its soaring flames reached the heavens, its colors containing the five hues. Heaven and earth were so brightly clarified that the stars and moon were no longer seen, and moreover, a wondrous fragrance was perceived, wafting through the courtyard.

Thereupon, they informed one another that the śarīra had manifested a great supernatural transformation; the multitude then took notice, gathered once more to pay their respects, and praised its rarity.

After the duration of a meal, the light gradually withdrew; when only a small portion remained, it circled the overturned bowl several times before finally entering it entirely. Heaven and earth returned to darkness, and the celestial bodies reappeared.
Having witnessed this, the assembly was entirely freed from the net of doubt.
They paid homage at the Bodhi tree and various other sacred sites; after eight days had passed, they returned once more to Nālandā Monastery.
At that time, the Master Śīlabhadra dispatched the Dharma Master to lecture for the assembly on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-viniścaya*.

Meanwhile, the Venerable Siṃhaprabha had previously been lecturing for the assembly on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*, expounding their tenets to refute the principles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The Dharma Master was exquisitely proficient in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*, and was also well-versed in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. He maintained that when the Sages established their teachings, each followed a particular intention, yet these did not contradict or obstruct one another. Those who are deluded are unable to synthesize them and thus claim they are inconsistent; this failure lies with the transmitters of the tradition, for how could it concern the Dharma itself?

Pitying their narrow-mindedness, he went to them several times to challenge and interrogate them; yet they were unable to provide adequate answers. Consequently, his disciples gradually dispersed and came to follow the Dharma Master.

Furthermore, the Dharma Master held that the essential purport of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* was solely to refute the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), and did not state that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) were to be negated. Siṃhaprabha failed to properly understand this;

seeing that the treatises stated, "all things are non-apprehendable," he claimed that even the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* and other categories established in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* must likewise be discarded, and thus he frequently expressed this view in his speech.

The Dharma Master, in order to harmonize the two schools and demonstrate that their teachings were not contradictory, composed the *Treatise on the Harmonization of the Schools* (*Huizong lun*) in three thousand stanzas.
When the treatise was completed, he presented it to Śīlabhadra and the great assembly; there was no one who did not praise its excellence, and they all circulated it together.

Siṃhaprabha was filled with shame and departed for Bodhivihāra; he then summoned a fellow student from East India named Candrasena to engage in debate with him, hoping thereby to clear his previous humiliation.
When the man arrived, he was intimidated by the Master’s majesty and remained silent, not daring to speak; thus, the Dharma Master’s reputation grew even greater.
Previously, before Śīlabhadra had departed, King Śīlāditya had constructed a brass vihāra beside Nālandā Monastery, over ten *zhang* in height, which was known throughout all kingdoms.

Later, the King personally led an expedition to conquer Koṅgoda. While traveling through the country of Oḍra, he found that the monks there all studied the Hīnayāna and did not believe in the Mahāyāna; they regarded it as the "sky-flower" heresy and claimed it was not the teaching of the Buddha.
Having seen the King arrive, they criticized him, saying:

"We have heard that Your Majesty has constructed a brass vihāra beside Nālandā; its work is truly magnificent. Why did you not build it at the monastery of the Kāpālika heretics, instead of here alone?"
The king said, "Why are these words so extreme? He replied:
"The Nālandā monastery is like a 'sky-flower' heresy; it is no different from the Kāpālikas.

Previously, there was a Pāśupata Brahmin named Prajñāgupta, the consecration preceptor to the King of South India, who was well-versed in the doctrines of the Saṃmitīya school. He composed the *Mahāyānaparibhava-śāstra* (Treatise Refuting the Mahāyāna) in seven hundred stanzas, which all the Hīnayāna masters praised and esteemed.
He took it and showed it to the king, saying, "Such is my school; how could anyone of the Mahāyāna be able to refute even a single word?
The king said:
"Your disciples heard of the foxes and the swarms of mice and considered themselves superior to the lions;
yet when they actually saw them, their souls fled and their spirits were scattered.
Likewise, because you have not yet encountered those of great virtue who uphold the Mahāyāna, you stubbornly cling to your own ignorant tenets."
"If we see it only once, I fear it will turn out to be just like that. He replied,
"If Your Majesty has doubts, why not assemble them for a face-to-face adjudication to determine right from wrong?"
The King said, "This is not difficult either. On that very day,
he dispatched an envoy with a letter to the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, the Upādhyāya and Keeper of the True Dharma (Saddharmapiṭaka) at Nālandā Monastery, stating:

"While traveling through Oḍra, my disciple encountered a teacher of the Hīnayāna who relied upon his own limited views to compose a treatise slandering the Mahāyāna. His arguments were harsh and unreasonable; nevertheless, he still wished to display his prowess and debate with you, Master, and the others."

Your disciple knows that the great virtuous ones (mahāśramaṇas) of this monastery all possess abundant talent and wisdom, and there is nothing they have not mastered in their studies; thus, I have readily granted my permission and respectfully send this report.

I pray that you will appoint four great virtuous ones who are well-versed in both their own and other schools, as well as in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings, to accompany me on my journey to the kingdom of Oḍra.

When the Treasury of the True Dharma received the letter, he assembled the multitude to deliberate and select; he then appointed Haihui, Zhiguang, Shiziguang, and the Dharma Master as the four men to respond to the King’s command.
Sāgaramati and the others were all filled with anxiety, so the Dharma Master said to them:

"As for the Tripiṭaka of the various schools of the Hīnayāna, I have studied them all thoroughly since my time in my own country and until my arrival in Kaśmīra; I am fully conversant with their tenets."
If one wishes to refute the meaning of the Mahāyāna through their doctrinal principles, such a thing is ultimately impossible.
Although my learning is shallow and my wisdom meager, I shall certainly understand it upon confronting it.
I pray that the virtuous ones will not trouble themselves with anxiety.
"If he should be defeated, he is merely a monk from the land of China; it shall have no bearing on this matter.
Everyone was delighted.
On a later day, the King sent another letter, saying:
He said, "The Venerable One previously invited me; you need not depart immediately, but wait for my further instructions.
At that time, a Lokāyata heretic arrived seeking to engage in debate. He then wrote down forty points of doctrine and hung them at the gate of the monastery, declaring:
"If anyone can refute even a single point, I shall cut off my own head in apology."
After several days had passed, no one came forward to respond.
The Dharma Master sent out a lay attendant from his room, had the treatise taken away and destroyed, and trampled it underfoot.
The brahmin was greatly incensed and asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am Mahāyanadeva’s slave. The brahmin, who had long heard of the Dharma Master's reputation, felt ashamed and would no longer speak with him. The Dharma Master ordered him to be summoned inside;

he then brought him before the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra and commanded the assembly of virtuous ones to serve as witnesses, engaging him in debate to examine the foundations of his own school and the various tenets established by the non-Buddhist sects.
The text says:
"For instance, the Pūraṇa heretics, the Nirgrantha heretics, the Kāpālika heretics, and the Śuṅgika heretics—these four differ in their physical appearance and dress;
furthermore, the Sāṃkhya heretics (formerly called *Saṃkhya*) and the Vaiśeṣika heretics (formerly called *Vaiśeṣika*)—these two schools differ in their established doctrines."
The Pāṣaṇḍas smear their bodies with ashes, taking this as the practice of the Way; their entire bodies are covered in white ash, resembling cats or wildcats sleeping by a hearth.

As for the Nirgranthas, they expose their naked bodies to display their eccentricity and pluck out their hair as a virtue; their skin cracks and their feet become chapped, appearing like withered trees on the riverbank.

Those such as the Skull-Garlanded ones wear garlands made of skulls, adorning their heads and hanging them from their necks; with their sunken, withered, and rugged forms, they resemble yakṣas by the side of a cemetery.
Those of the Piṅgala class don robes of rags from refuse heaps and consume excrement and urine; foul-smelling and repulsive, they are like mad pigs in a latrine.
For you to take this as the Way—is it not foolish?

As for the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists, they establish the doctrine of twenty-five principles (*tattva*): from *prakṛti* (primordial nature) arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One arises ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*); next arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); next arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and next arise the eleven faculties (*indriya*).
These twenty-four together serve me; what I enjoy is "mine. Only when one is separated from these does the self attain purity.

The Vaiśeṣika masters establish six categories (padārtha): namely, substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karman), existence (sattā), generality (sāmānya), and inherence (samavāya). These six are the instruments of my experience; until liberation is attained, one experiences these six.
Once liberation is attained, one becomes dissociated from these six, which is termed nirvāṇa.

Now, I shall refute what is established by the Sāṃkhya school. Among your twenty-five principles (*tattva*), the single principle of the Self (*puruṣa*) is a distinct nature, while the remaining twenty-four are mutually identical as a single essence. Furthermore, the single principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has three factors as its essence, namely: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

These three [subtle elements] combine with one another to form the twenty-three principles, beginning with the "Great" (mahat). Each of these twenty-three principles has these three factors as its essence.

If each of the "Great" and the others were to be composed of these three, like a multitude or a forest, they would be merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*); how then could it be said that all of them are real?
Furthermore, since each of these [elements], such as earth and the rest, is composed of all three [qualities], it follows that one is everything.
If one were everything, then each individual thing would necessarily possess the functions of all things.
Since this is not permitted, for what reason do you maintain that the three [faculties] constitute the essential nature of all?
Furthermore, if one were identical to all, then the sense organs such as the mouth and eyes would be identical to the passages for excrement and urine.
Furthermore, if each individual sense faculty possessed all functions, then the faculties of the mouth, ears, and so forth would hear odors and see forms.
If this were not the case, how could one maintain that these three constitute the essence of all phenomena?
How could a wise person establish such a doctrine?

Furthermore, if the self-nature (*svabhāva*) were eternal, it would be like the essence of the self (*ātman*); how then could it undergo transformation to produce phenomena such as the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Moreover, if the nature of the conceived self were eternal, it would be like the self-nature and thus ought not to be the self.
If, like intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its essence were not the self (*ātman*), it should not experience the twenty-four truths (*tattva*).

In that case, the self would not be the experiencer and the twenty-four truths would not be the objects experienced; since both subject and object would be non-existent, the meaning of "truth" could not be established.
After this exchange had been repeated several times, the brahmin remained silent and said nothing; he rose and apologized, saying, "I am now defeated;
let it be according to our prior agreement."
The Dharma Master said, "We, the sons of the Śākya, never harm others; I now make you my slave, and you shall follow my instructions.
The Brahmin joyfully and respectfully complied, and he was immediately led to his quarters; all who heard of it offered their congratulations.
At that time, as the Dharma Master was about to travel to Oḍra, he sought out and obtained a seven-hundred-verse work titled *Mahāyānārthabheda*, composed by followers of the Hīnayāna.
Upon examining it, the Master found several points of doubt and said to the Brāhmaṇa he had subdued:
"Have you ever heard this doctrine?"
He replied, "I have heard it five times.
The Dharma Master wished for him to lecture upon it.
He said, "I am currently a slave; how could it be appropriate for me to lecture for you, sir?
The Dharma Master replied:
"This is the doctrine of another school; I have never seen it before. You need only say that there is no suffering.
He replied, "If that is so, please wait until nightfall, for I fear outsiders might hear that you are learning the Dharma from a slave, which would defile your noble reputation."
Thereupon, when night fell, he cleared away all people and had [the opponent] lecture once more; thus he fully grasped the essence of his arguments.

He then sought out the fallacious points and refuted them by expounding the meaning of the Mahāyāna, composing one thousand six hundred stanzas titled the *Dūṣaṇasamudghāta-śāstra* (Treatise on the Refutation of Evil Views).
He presented it to Dharma Master Śīlabhadra and showed it to his disciples; all without exception praised it, saying:
"If one investigates with such thoroughness, what enemy could possibly remain unsubdued?
The treatise is as presented elsewhere.
Māṭhara said to the brahmin, "Virtuous one, you have been defeated in debate and reduced to slavery; this is sufficient cause for shame. I now release you to go wherever you please."
The Brahmin departed with joy, traveling to the kingdom of Kāmarūpa in eastern India, where he spoke to King Kumāra of the Dharma Master’s virtue and righteousness.
Upon hearing this, the King was greatly pleased and immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll Four.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll [Four].
The Fifth [Chapter], composed by the Śramaṇa Huili and annotated by Shi Yanzong.

From the episode of the Nirgrantha’s divination regarding the return to his native land, ending at the western canal of the Imperial City: During the interval before Kumārajīva’s envoy had arrived, a naked Nirgrantha named Vajra suddenly entered the Dharma Master’s chamber.
The Dharma Master, having previously heard that the Nirgrantha was skilled in divination, immediately invited him to sit and asked about his doubts, saying:
"I am Xuanzang, a monk from the kingdom of China, who has come here to study for a long time now."
Now I wish to return home, yet I do not know whether I shall arrive safely.
Furthermore, between departing and staying, which is most auspicious?
And what will be the length of my lifespan?
"I pray that you, O Virtuous One, will perform a divination.
The Nirgrantha then sought a piece of white stone and drew lines on the ground to cast the lots, reporting to the Dharma Master:
"The time for the Master to reside here is most auspicious; throughout the five regions of India, there are no monastics or laypeople who do not hold you in high esteem."
It is good that you have reached your destination and are treated with respect; however, it is not as well as remaining here.
As for the teacher’s lifespan, from this point forward, he may live for another ten years.
"If it is sustained by remaining merit and continues on, that is beyond my knowledge.
The Dharma Master asked again, for he wished to return home; however, as his scriptures and images were so numerous, he did not know how to transport them successfully.
The Nirgrantha said, "Do not worry;
King Śīlāditya and King Kumāra will personally send people to escort you, Master, so that you will surely arrive without hardship.
The Dharma Master replied:
"Those two kings have never met before; how could such a favor be bestowed?
The Nirgrantha replied, "King Kumāra has already dispatched an envoy with an invitation; he will arrive in two or three days. Once you have seen King Kumāra, you will also see Śīlāditya."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
The Dharma Master then intended to return and prepared the scriptures and images for his journey.
When the virtuous monks heard of this, they all came to urge him to stay, saying:
"India is the birthplace of the Buddha.

Although the Great Sage has passed away, his traces remain intact; to travel there to pay homage and offer praise would have been sufficient for a lifetime's fulfillment. Why have you come here and yet abandoned it?"

Furthermore, as for the land of China, it is a territory of Mlecchas where people are held in low esteem and the Dharma is despised; this is why the Buddhas are not born there. Their aspirations are narrow and their defilements deep; thus the sages and worthies do not travel thither. With its cold climate and rugged terrain, what is there even worth considering!
The Dharma Master replied:
"The Dharma King established his teachings so that their meaning might circulate; how could he have personally attained peace of mind while neglecting those who have not yet awakened?

Moreover, in that country, the attire and decorum are magnificent and the laws may be followed; the ruler is sagacious and the ministers loyal, fathers are kind and sons are filial; they value benevolence and righteousness, and honor the aged and the worthy."
Furthermore, his consciousness penetrated the profound and subtle, and his wisdom was in harmony with the divine.
He embodied the Way of Heaven to establish the norms; the seven luminaries could not conceal their patterns within him.
He devised instruments to divide time; the six pitch-pipes could not hide their tubes from him.
Thus, they were able to command birds and beasts, invoke spirits and deities, regulate the yin and yang, and bring benefit and peace to all things.
Since the Bequeathed Dharma spread to the East, everyone has esteemed the Mahāyāna; the water of meditative concentration is clear and bright, and the fragrance of the precepts is rich and pervasive.
Having resolved to cultivate practice, one vows to equal the merit of the Ten Stages; by folding the palms in meditative cultivation, one aims to reach the ultimate goal of the Three Bodies.

Having been graced by the descent of the Great Sage, who personally manifested his transformative teachings, we have heard his wondrous discourse with our ears and beheld his golden countenance with our eyes. It may well be that we shall travel the long road alongside him; how then can it be said that the Buddha does not come, and thus be treated with such negligence?
He replied: "The sutra says:
'The various devas, according to their respective merits, differ in what they eat together.'"

"Now, while we dwell together with the Dharma Master in Jambudvīpa, and yet the Buddha was born here and not there, this must be because that place is considered a remote borderland and a land of evil."
"Since this land possesses no merit, I did not urge you, O Benevolent One,
to return. The Dharma Master replied, "Vimalakīrti said:..."
"By what cause does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?
He replied: "To dispel the darkness for its sake."
"What I now contemplate as my place of refuge is simply to follow this intention.
When the virtuous ones saw that he would not comply, they called out to one another and went to the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra to recount their thoughts in detail.
Śīlabhadra said to the Dharma Master,
"What is your settled view? He replied:
"This country is the birthplace of the Buddha; it is not that I do not cherish it.
However, the purpose of my coming, Xuanzang, is to seek the Great Dharma in order to extensively benefit all living beings."

Since arriving here, I have had the honor of hearing the Master expound the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which has resolved all my webs of doubt; I have paid homage at sacred sites and heard the profound tenets of the various schools. My heart is comforted and rejoices, for my journey has truly not been in vain.

I wish to take what I have heard back and translate it, so that those with the karmic affinity may likewise hear and see it, thereby repaying the kindness of my teacher; for this reason, I do not wish to remain here.
Śīlabhadra said with joy:
"This is the intention of a bodhisattva.
It was my heart's hope for you, and you have acted accordingly."
"You may prepare your travel gear as you wish; there is no need for anyone to detain you against your will.
Having said this, he returned to his quarters.
After two days had passed, King Kumāra of Eastern India dispatched an envoy bearing a letter to the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, which read:
"The disciple wishes to see a Great Virtuous One from the land of China; I pray that you, Master, will dispatch him to console my longing.
Upon receiving this letter, Śīlabhadra addressed the assembly, saying:

"King Kumāra wishes to invite Xuanzang, yet this man has been assigned by the community to go to King Śīlāditya to debate with the followers of the Hīnayāna. If he were now to depart for that king's court, what would become of him should King Śīlāditya require his presence?"
"It is not appropriate to send him away.
He then said to the envoy,
"The Chinese monk intends to return to his own country and is unable to comply with Your Majesty's command."
When the messenger arrived, the King sent him back again with this invitation:
"Even if you wish to return home, please come to visit me for a moment; it will not be difficult for you to depart afterward.
I earnestly hope you will grant me your presence and do not refuse my request once more."
Since Śīlabhadra would not allow him to go, the king became greatly incensed and dispatched another envoy bearing a letter to the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, which said:
"I, your disciple, am an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) habituated to worldly pleasures; I have not yet known how to turn [my merit] toward the Buddha-dharma."

Now, upon hearing the names of the foreign monks, my body and mind are filled with joy; it is as if the sprouts of the Path have begun to emerge. Yet, since you, Master, do not permit them to come, this would surely cause sentient beings to sink forever into the long night of ignorance. How could this be the way for a Great Virtuous One to succeed and flourish the bequeathed Dharma, and to draw forth and uplift all beings?
Unable to overcome my yearning and longing, I respectfully send this further inquiry.

If you do not come, I, your disciple, shall surely be deemed an evil person. Recently, King Śaśāṅka was even able to destroy the Dharma and ruin the Bodhi tree; does the Master then consider that I lack such power?
"I shall certainly marshal an elephant army and gather like clouds at that place, trampling Nālandā Monastery until it is crushed to dust.
These words are as true as the sun; you, Master, may test them for yourself."
When Śīlabhadra received the letter, he said to the Dharma Master, "That king’s virtuous mind has always been thin; the Buddha-dharma did not flourish much within his realm.
Now that he has heard your name, it seems a profound intention has been awakened."

"Ren may have been his virtuous friend from a previous life; you must strive to go forth as a monk, for benefiting sentient beings is the very foundation of our practice, and now is precisely the right time.
It is like felling a tree: if one merely cuts its root, the branches and twigs will perish of their own accord."
"Go there and cause the king to resolve his mind [on enlightenment], and the common people will follow his transformation.
If you suffer in your refusal to go, there may be demonic obstacles.
Do not shrink from this slight labor."
The Dharma Master took his leave and departed with the envoy.

Upon arriving there, the king was greatly delighted at the sight of him; he led his ministers to welcome and prostrate before him, offering praise, and invited him into the palace. Day after day, music was performed and offerings of food, drink, flowers, and incense were presented in full abundance, as the king requested that he receive the precepts of the fast.
After more than a month had passed in this manner, King Śīlāditya returned from his campaign against Koṅgoda. Hearing that the Dharma Master was with Kumāra, he said in astonishment:
"I previously invited him repeatedly, yet he did not come; for what reason is he now there?"
He dispatched a messenger to King Kumāra, saying:
"Send the Chinese monk here immediately!
King Kumāra held the Dharma Master in such deep reverence that his affection for him was boundless; he could not bear to part with him.
He said to the messenger,
"My head may be obtained, but the Dharma Master must not come yet.
The messenger returned and reported this.
King Śīlāditya was greatly incensed and said to his attendants:
"King Kumāra has slighted me; how could he utter such coarse words for the sake of a single monk!"
The messenger was sent again with this reprimand:
"Since you said your head could be obtained, you should now hand it over to the messenger and bring it here.

Kumārajīva was deeply terrified that his word would fail him; he immediately ordered twenty thousand elephant troops and thirty thousand ships to be prepared, and set out together with the Dharma Master. They traveled upstream across the Gaṅgā River to reach the kingdom of Kajuṅghira, where they finally presented themselves before the king.
When King Kumāra was about to set out on his journey, he first ordered men to construct a temporary palace on the north bank of the Ganges.

On that day, having crossed the river and reached the palace, he settled the Dharma Master there; thereafter, he went with his ministers to pay his respects to King Śīlāditya on the south bank of the river.
When Śīlāditya saw him coming, he was greatly pleased; knowing that [the king] held the Dharma Master in deep respect and affection, he did not reproach him for his previous words, but simply asked:
"Where is the Chinese monk?"
He replied, "It is in a certain pleasure palace.
The king said:
"Why have you not come?
He replied, "The Great King reveres the worthy and loves the Way; how could he send the Master here to visit him?"
The king said, "Very well.
You may go now; I shall come myself tomorrow."
Kumārajīva returned and said to the Dharma Master, "Although the King says he will come tomorrow, I fear he may arrive this very night; we must remain on watch and wait.
If he comes, you, Master, need not move."
The Dharma Master said,
"Xuanzang’s understanding of the principles of the Buddha-dharma is naturally such.
When it was about the first watch of the night, the king indeed arrived.
Someone reported, saying:
"There are several thousand torches in the river, along with the sound of marching drums.
The King said:
"King Śīlāditya is coming!
he exclaimed, immediately ordering torches to be raised and personally going out with his ministers to welcome him from afar.
As King Śīlāditya traveled, he would carry several hundred golden drums; for every step he took, one drum was struck, which was known as the "rhythmic-step drum."
Only King Śīlāditya possessed this [quality]; other kings could not share in it.
Upon his arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the Dharma Master, scattered flowers before him in reverent gazing, and after offering praise with immeasurable verses, he said to the Master:
"Why did you, my disciple’s teacher, not come when I previously invited you?"
He replied, "Xuanzang traveled from afar in search of the Buddha-dharma specifically to hear the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
While awaiting your command, I had not yet finished listening to the treatise; for this reason, I was unable to go to visit Your Majesty."
The King asked again:
"Master, you have come from China. I have heard that in that country there is a song and dance called 'The King of Qin’s Victory over the Arrayed Enemy. I do not yet know who this King of Qin was."
"What further merits does he possess to warrant such praise?
The Dharma Master replied, "In my native land,

when I see one who harbors the virtues of sages and worthies, who can eliminate the wicked and prune away the violent for the sake of the common people, and who provides shelter and nourishment to all living beings, I then sing and chant their praises."
Above, it prepared the music of the ancestral temple; below, it entered the songs of the villages and neighborhoods.
As for the "King of Qin," he is the present-day Son of Heaven of the land of China.
Before ascending the imperial throne, he was enfeoffed as the King of Qin.

At that time, heaven and earth were thrown into turmoil, and the common people were left without a ruler. Human flesh was piled upon the plains and wilds, while human blood flowed through the rivers and valleys. Malevolent stars gathered in the night, and pestilential vapors coagulated at dawn; the Three Rivers suffered from the greed of the great boar, and the Four Seas were oppressed by the venom of the long serpent.

By virtue of his kinship as the Son of Heaven and in response to the mandate of the Celestial Strategy, the King raised his troops and marshaled his forces to strike down and exterminate the great sea-monsters; wielding his battle-axe and brandishing his halberd, he purified the coastal regions and brought peace once more to the universe, causing the Three Luminaries to shine forth again.
"The six directions harbor gratitude; therefore, this hymn exists.
The King said, "A person such as this is precisely what Heaven has sent forth to be the lord of all things."
He further asked the Dharma Master, saying, "I, your disciple, shall return for now.
I will come to welcome you tomorrow; I hope you will not find the journey too fatiguing."
Thereupon, he took his leave and departed.

At dawn the next day, the messenger arrived; the Dharma Master went with Kumārajīva to the side of King Śīlāditya’s palace. The King, accompanied by more than twenty of his gate-attendants, came out to welcome them and led them inside to be seated. He provided an abundant array of delicacies and, after performing music and scattering flowers as offerings, the ceremony was concluded.
The King said, "I have heard that you, Master, have composed the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (The Refutation of Evil Views); where is it?
The Dharma Master replied:
"Here it is," he said, taking it up for inspection.
Having finished his examination, the King was greatly pleased and said to his gatekeeper and other attendants:
"Disciple, you have heard that once the sun has risen, the light of fireflies and candles is eclipsed; when the thunder of heaven resounds, the sound of hammers and chisels ceases.
The tenets maintained by you and your teachers have all been refuted; try now to save them."
None among the virtuous dared to speak.
The King said:

"The Elder Devaśarman, your masters, claims that his understanding surpasses all the eminent men and his learning encompasses all the sages; yet he was the first to promote heterodox views and constantly disparaged the Mahāyāna."

Upon hearing that a guest of great virtue had arrived, he immediately went to Vaiśālī to pay homage to and observe the sacred sites, using this as a pretext to escape and hide; thus, you may know that you, masters, are incapable.
The king had a younger sister who was intelligent and of sharp faculties, well-versed in the doctrines of the Saṃmitīya school; she sat behind the king.

Hearing the Dharma Master’s introduction to the Mahāyāna—its tenets profound and vast, while the Hīnayāna teachings were limited and shallow—she was filled with serene joy, unable to stop praising it.
The King said:

“Your discourse is most excellent, and my disciples as well as these various masters all believe in and submit to it. However, I fear that those in other small kingdoms who follow the Hīnayāna and the non-Buddhists still cling to ignorance and delusion. I hope you will convene an assembly for yourself at Kanyākubja, summoning the śramaṇas, brahmins, and non-Buddhists of the five Indias, to demonstrate the subtle and profound principles of the Mahāyāna, to sever their hearts of slander, to manifest the loftiness of your eminent virtue, and to crush their prideful arrogance.”

On that day, an imperial edict was issued to all the kingdoms and to those versed in the exegesis of the scriptures, commanding them to assemble at Kanyākubja to examine the treatise of the Dharma Master from the land of China.
From the beginning of winter, the Dharma Master had traveled upstream with the king; it was not until the twelfth month that they reached the venue.

From throughout the five regions of India, eighteen kings arrived; more than three thousand monks, well-versed in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, arrived; more than two thousand Brahmins and Nirgrantha heretics arrived; and more than one thousand monks from Nālandā Monastery arrived.
These worthy men were all profoundly learned in both literary expression and doctrine, and possessed abundant eloquence; desiring to hear his virtuous voice, they had all gathered at this assembly.

They were accompanied by attendants, some on elephants, some in carriages, and some bearing banners or streamers, each surrounded by their own retinue. Towering and imposing, they surged like rising clouds or billowing mists, filling the area for several tens of li. Even if the sleeves of those from the Six Qi states were raised to form a curtain, or the sweat of those from the Three Wu regions were waved to become rain, it would not suffice to compare with the magnitude of this gathering.
The King had previously ordered that two grass huts be constructed at the assembly site to accommodate the images and the assembly; by the time [the Master] arrived, both were completed.
These halls were lofty and spacious, each capable of seating over a thousand people.
The royal palace was five li west of the assembly grounds.
Every day, a golden image was cast within the palace; it was mounted upon a large elephant, over which a precious canopy was spread, and the Buddha was installed therein.

King Śīlāditya assumed the form of Śakra, holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right; King Kumāra assumed the form of Brahmā, holding a precious parasol and attending on the left; both wore celestial crowns and flower garlands, with jeweled pendants and jade ornaments hanging down.
Furthermore, two great elephants were adorned and laden with precious flowers;
they followed behind the Buddha, scattering the flowers as they went.
The Dharma Master and the Gate Masters were each mounted upon great elephants, following in succession behind the King.

Furthermore, he had three hundred great elephants upon which various kings, ministers, and men of great virtue were mounted; they proceeded in formation along the sides of the road, offering praises as they went.

Having prepared their attire from dawn, they proceeded from the palace toward the assembly hall; upon reaching the temple gate, each was ordered to dismount, and they carried the Buddha statue into the hall, placing it upon the precious throne.
The King, together with the Dharma Master and others, made offerings in succession.
Thereafter, he commanded the kings of eighteen countries to enter;
he also sent more than a thousand monks from various kingdoms—those whose reputations were most eminent and whose mastery of both text and meaning was most extensive—to enter as well.
More than five hundred practitioners from among the Brahmins and non-Buddhist sects entered,
as did more than two hundred ministers from various kingdoms.
All those outside, whether from non-Buddhist traditions or the laity, were ordered to be stationed in formation outside the gates of the courtyards.
The King ordered food to be prepared both inside and outside [the palace].

When the meal was finished, he offered the Buddha one golden plate, seven golden bowls, one golden water pitcher, one golden mendicant’s staff, three thousand gold coins, and three thousand pieces of fine cotton cloth.
The Dharma Master and the various monks were each given appropriate offerings.

Once the distribution was complete, a precious throne was specially provided for the Dharma Master, who was invited to sit as the presiding master of the discourse. He then extolled the Mahāyāna and explained the intent behind composing the treatise; subsequently, he dispatched the Śramaṇa Mingxian of Nālandā Monastery to read it aloud for the assembly.

Have another copy transcribed and hung outside the gate of the assembly hall to show all people; if anyone can challenge and refute even a single word as being illogical, please sever my head in apology.
Thus it continued until evening, and not a single person uttered a word of objection.

King Śīlāditya was delighted; he adjourned the assembly and returned to his palace, while the various kings and the monks each departed for their respective quarters. Subsequently, the Dharma Master, together with King Kumāra, also returned to his own palace.
The next morning they came again, gathering to welcome and escort the image as they had done before.
After five days had passed, the followers of the Hinayana and the non-Buddhists, seeing their own doctrines being disparaged, harbored resentment and plotted to do him harm.
The King, becoming aware of this, issued a proclamation, saying:
"The heterodox factions have long since confounded the truth.
They have buried the orthodox teachings and deluded the masses. Were it not for those of supreme virtue, how could falsehood be discerned?"

The Dharma Master from China possesses a spirit and countenance that are profound and expansive, and his understanding and practice are deep and vast. Having come to this land to subdue the various heretics, he has propagated the Great Dharma and guided the ignorant and deluded. Yet these followers of sorcery and falsehood, knowing no shame or repentance, have plotted treason and even given rise to murderous intent; if such as these can be tolerated, whom could one not forgive?
If anyone among the assembly should harm or offend the Dharma Master, his head shall be severed; if anyone should revile or abuse him, his tongue shall be cut out.
However, those who wish to present arguments or defend the principles of the teaching are not subject to these restrictions.
From that time on, the heretics withdrew their wings, and for eighteen days in total, not a single person proposed an argument.

On the evening before the assembly was to disperse, the Dharma Master further extolled the Mahāyāna and praised the merits of the Buddha, causing immeasurable people to turn from heterodoxy to orthodoxy and abandon the Hīnayāna to return to the Mahāyāna.
King Śīlāditya increased his esteem and honor for the Dharma Master, bestowing upon him ten thousand gold coins, thirty thousand silver coins, and one hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth;
the eighteen kings likewise each presented him with precious jewels.
The Dharma Master would not accept any of these at all.

The King commanded his attendants to adorn a great elephant and offered it with a ceremonial banner, requesting the Dharma Master to mount it; he then ordered high-ranking officials to escort him as he toured the assembly, proclaiming that his established doctrine was invincible.
According to the custom of the Western lands, when one emerges victorious in debate, it is done in this manner; however, the Dharma Master declined and would not proceed.
The King said, "This has been the law since antiquity; the matter must not be contravened."
Thereupon, he took the Dharma Master’s kashaya and proclaimed it everywhere, saying:

"The Dharma Master of the land of China has established the principles of the Mahayana and refuted all heterodox views; since the eighteenth day, no one has dared to debate him. All should take this to heart."
The assembly rejoiced and vied with one another in bestowing beautiful names upon the Dharma Master. The Mahāyāna community called him "Mahāyanadeva," which means "Mahāyāna Deva";
the Hīnayāna community called him "Mokṣadeva," which means "Liberation Deva."
Having burned incense and scattered flowers, they paid their respects and departed; from then on, his virtuous fame spread ever further.

To the west of the King’s traveling palace was a monastery maintained by the King, within which was a Buddha-tooth relic approximately one and a half inches long, yellowish-white in color, which frequently emitted radiance.
In the past, when the Kṛttivāsas clan in the kingdom of Kaśmīra had destroyed the Buddha-dharma and the monastic community was dispersed, a certain bhikṣu traveled far away to India.

Later, the King of the Snow Mountains in the kingdom of Tukhāra became enraged that the low-caste tribes were destroying the Buddha-dharma; he therefore feigned the guise of a merchant caravan, leading three thousand brave warriors and carrying a great quantity of precious jewels, under the pretext of making an offering.
The king was naturally greedy; hearing this, he was greatly pleased and dispatched an envoy to welcome him.

However, the King of the Snowy Mountains possessed a majestic and fierce nature, with a majesty as solemn as that of a deity. Once he reached his seat, he removed his cap and rebuked him; upon seeing this, King Kṛtīna was struck with terror and prostrated himself upon the ground.
The King of the Snowy Mountains pressed down upon his head and executed him, addressing his ministers:
"I am the King beneath the Snowy Mountains.
Considering that you slaves have destroyed the Buddha-dharma, I have come to punish you."

"In that case, the fault lies with one individual and does not concern you; each of you should remain at ease. Only those who incite delusion and lead the king astray—those who are the primary evildoers—shall be banished to another land; as for the rest, no inquiry shall be made."
Having utterly destroyed the wicked and established a monastery, he summoned the assembly of monks, offered them gifts, and returned home.

A monk who had previously traveled to India heard that his country was pacified and set out on his staff to return; on the road, he encountered a herd of elephants approaching with loud roars. Upon seeing them, the monk climbed a tree to hide, but the elephants sprayed water onto the tree, uprooted it with their tusks, and in an instant, the tree fell.
The elephant used its trunk to coil the bhikṣu and placed him upon its back to carry him away.
Upon reaching a great forest, there was a sick elephant lying down, suffering from a wound.

The elephant led the bhikṣu’s hand to touch the painful spot; seeing that a bamboo splinter had entered the wound, it pulled out the splinter, drained the pus and blood, and tore its own garment to wrap the injury. Thus, the elephant gradually found relief.

Tomorrow, the elephants will compete to seek out various fruits to offer as alms to the bhikṣus. After the bhikṣus have eaten, one elephant will take a casket of gold and give it to the sick one. Once the sick elephant has received it, he will hand it over to the bhikṣu. Having accepted it, the bhikṣu will be carried out of the forest by the elephants. Upon reaching the former site, they will set him down on the ground; then, after kneeling and prostrating, they will depart.
The bhikṣu opened the casket and found it to be a tooth of the Buddha; he intended to take it back for veneration.
Recently, King Śīlāditya, having heard that a tooth of the Buddha was in Kaśmīra, personally went to the border to request to see and pay homage to it.
The local people were stingy and refused to let it be taken out, so he hid it elsewhere.

However, the king there feared the power of King Śīlāditya and searched for it everywhere; having found it, he presented it [to Śīlāditya]. When Śīlāditya saw it, he felt deep reverence for it; relying on his great strength, he eventually seized it and brought it back for worship—this is that very tusk.
After the assembly had dispersed, the King entrusted the cast golden image, robes, money, and other items to the monastery, ordering the monks to guard them.

Having first taken leave of the virtuous masters of Nālandā and completed his collection of scriptures and images, and having finished his debates, on the nineteenth day the Dharma Master took leave of the King, intending to return home.
The King said:

"As a disciple who has succeeded to the ancestral temple and serves as the sovereign of the world for over thirty years, I have constantly feared that my merit and virtue would not increase or expand, and that the causes of the Dharma would not continue. For this reason, I have accumulated wealth and treasures to establish a great assembly site between the two rivers in the kingdom of Prayāga. Every five years, I invite śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the five regions of India, as well as the poor, the orphaned, and the solitary, to perform a great unrestricted almsgiving (*mahādāna*) lasting seventy-five days."
"Five assemblies have already been completed, and now you wish to hold a sixth assembly; why do you not take a moment to look upon them and rejoice?
The Dharma Master replied, "The conduct of a Bodhisattva consists in the dual cultivation of merit and wisdom; when a wise person attains the fruit, they do not forget its source."
"If even the King does not begrudge his precious wealth, how could Xuanzang possibly decline?
Please stay for a short while; I request that you accompany the King.
The King was greatly pleased.
On the twenty-first day, the procession set out toward the country of Prayāga to reach the site of the Great Almsgiving.
The Gaṅgā River was to the north and the Yamunā River was to the south; both flow from the northwest toward the east, meeting at this country.

At the confluence of these two rivers, to the west, there is a great level plain fourteen or fifteen *li* in circumference, as smooth and level as a mirror. Since ancient times, various kings have all performed acts of almsgiving upon this ground; consequently, it is known as the "Field of Almsgiving" (*Dānasthāna*).

It is traditionally said that if one gives even a single coin at this site, it is superior to giving a hundred thousand coins elsewhere; for this reason, it has been held in common esteem since antiquity.

By royal decree, an almsgiving hall was constructed upon the sacrificial ground, enclosed by a fence of reeds each side measuring a thousand paces. In its center, several dozen thatched huts were built to store various treasures, including gold, silver, pearls, red crystal, *indranīla* gems, and great *mahānīla* gems. Beside these, several hundred long sheds were constructed to store *kauśeya* silk, variegated cotton cloth, gold, silver, and coins.

Outside the fence, he constructed a separate kitchen area; in front of the treasure storehouse, he further built more than a hundred rows of long halls, resembling the market stalls of this capital city, with each long hall capable of seating over a thousand people.

Previously, the King had issued an edict summoning the śramaṇas, non-Buddhist practitioners, Nirgranthas, and the poor, the orphaned, and the solitary from throughout the five regions of India to assemble at the site of almsgiving to receive offerings.

There were also those who, having failed to return from the assembly at Kanyākubja due to the Dharma Master’s influence, proceeded directly to the place of almsgiving; eighteen kings likewise followed the King there.
By the time they reached the assembly grounds, more than five hundred thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, had arrived.

King Śīlāditya established his camp on the north bank of the Gaṅgā; King Dhruvabhaṭa of South India established his camp on the west bank of the river; King Kumāra established his camp beside a flowering grove on the south bank of the Yamunā; and the various recipients of alms established their camps to the west of King Bhaṭa.

At dawn, King Śīlāditya and King Kumāra set out with their naval forces, while King Bhaṭa followed with his elephant corps; each arrayed his ceremonial guards as they assembled at the venue, where the kings of the eighteen nations took their places in order.

On the first day, they installed a Buddha image within the thatched hall at the site of the almsgiving; they offered superior jewels, fine robes, and exquisite food, performed music, and scattered flowers, returning to their camp at evening.
On the second day, he installed an image of Sūryadeva and bestowed jewels and robes half as much as on the first day.
On the third day, he installed an image of Īśvaradeva and bestowed gifts equal to those for Sūryadeva.

On the fourth day, he made offerings to more than ten thousand monks seated in a hundred rows; to each person he gave one hundred gold coins, one pearl, and one set of cotton garments, as well as food, drink, incense, and flowers, and having completed these offerings, he departed.
The fifth round of giving to the brahmins lasted over twenty days before it was complete.
The sixth round of giving to the non-Buddhist practitioners lasted ten days before it was complete.
The seventh round of giving to seekers from distant regions lasted ten days before it was complete.
The eighth distribution was to all the poor, destitute, and solitary, which took a full month to complete.

By this time, the treasuries accumulated over five years were entirely exhausted; only elephants, horses, and weapons were retained for the purpose of suppressing rebellions and guarding the ancestral temples.

Furthermore, he gave away all his remaining treasures, as well as the clothing on his body, necklaces, earrings, armlets, jeweled wreaths, neck beads, and the bright pearl within his topknot, offering them all without leaving a single thing behind.
