When all [wealth] was exhausted, he requested coarse and tattered garments from his younger sister, prostrated before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and with leaping joy and palms joined, spoke thus:
"I have recently accumulated wealth and treasures, yet I was always afraid they would not enter a secure treasury."
Now that these have been stored within the field of merit, they may be said to have entered the treasury.
I pray that in every birth, I may always provide the gifts of wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness to sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the ten masteries and fulfilling the two adornments.

When the assembly had concluded, each of the kings took various precious objects and money from among the multitude to redeem the necklaces, topknot jewels, royal robes, and other items bestowed by the King, returning them to him.
After several days, the King’s robes and his finest precious ornaments returned to their former state.
When the Dharma Master took his leave to return home, the King said, "I am only now beginning to propagate the Bequeathed Dharma together with you, Master; why do you wish to return so abruptly?"
Thus they lingered for another ten days or so, and King Kumāra was likewise earnest in his persistence.
He said to the Dharma Master, "If you, Master, would stay in my domain to accept my offerings, I shall build one hundred monasteries for you."
Seeing that the kings’ minds were not yet convinced, the Dharma Master addressed them with these earnest words:

"The land of China is far removed from here and heard the Buddha-dharma late; although we have received its general outline, we cannot possess its full details. It is for this reason that I have come to seek out what is extraordinary."
That we have now fulfilled our vows is entirely due to the profound sincerity and earnest longing of the worthy ones in our native land; for this reason, I dare not forget them for even a moment.
As the Sūtra says:
"Those who obstruct the Dharma shall be without eyes for generation after generation."
"If you detain Xuanzang, it will cause those countless practitioners to lose the benefit of knowing the Dharma; how could I not fear such a retribution for being sightless!

The King said, "I, your disciple, admire and revere your virtue, Master, and wish to always attend upon you. Since detaining you would harm the interests of so many people, I truly harbor this fear; I leave it to you, Master, whether to go or stay."
"Nevertheless, I do not know by which route you intend to return.
If you are going to the South Sea, I shall dispatch an envoy to escort you.
The Dharma Master replied:

"Xuanzang has come from China and reached the western border of your kingdom. There is a country named Gaochang, whose king is wise and delights in the Dharma. Upon seeing that I had come here to seek the Way, he felt deep sympathetic joy and provided me with abundant provisions. He expressed his wish for me to visit him on my return day; I could not refuse his sincere request. Now, however, I must return by way of the northern route."
The King asked,
"How much requisites does the Master require?
The Dharma Master replied:
"I have no need for anything.
The king said, "How can this be?"
Thereupon, he was commanded to bestow gold coins and other items, and King Kumāra also offered various treasures; however, the Dharma Master accepted none of them.
He accepted only a *kṣaumalī* robe from King Kumāra, which was made of the finest, softest wool.
Intending to apply it as a rainproof coating on his robes, he then took his leave. The King and the multitude escorted him for several tens of li before returning.
At the moment of parting, they wept with such choked sobs that none could restrain themselves.
The Dharma Master entrusted his scriptures, images, and other belongings to the army of King Uditas of North India, and proceeded gradually by means of horseback.
Later, King Śīlāditya further provided King Uditas with one large elephant, three thousand gold coins, and ten thousand silver coins to supply for the Master’s travel expenses.

After three days had passed, King [Wang] again accompanied by the kings Kumāra and Bhaṭa, each leading several hundred light cavalry, came once more to see him off; their earnest courtesy was such as this.
He further dispatched four high-ranking officials—titles such as *mahattara*, which correspond to the Chinese *san guan* (dispersed officials)—to accompany the Master.

The King wrote the letter on plain cotton cloth and sealed it with red wax. He commanded these officials to carry the letter to all the kingdoms through which the Dharma Master would pass, ordering that relay stations be established to transport him until he reached the borders of China.

Setting out from the great forest southwest of the kingdom of Prayāga, he traveled for seven days and arrived at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. At the site where the elder Ghoṣila had offered a garden to the Buddha south of the city, he paid homage to the sacred traces; having finished this, he again traveled northwest with King Udayana.
After traveling through several kingdoms for over a month, he paid renewed homage to the sacred traces of the Heavenly Ladder (Devakīla).
Continuing northwest for three *yojanas*, he arrived at the capital city of the kingdom of Viraṇā.

After staying for two months, he met two fellow students, Simhaprabha and Simhacandra, who were lecturing on the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; they all came to welcome him with great joy.
When the Dharma Master arrived, he further expounded the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* and the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, completing them in two months before taking his leave to return.
He then traveled northwest for over a month, passing through several kingdoms until he reached the kingdom of Śrughna, the capital of North India, where he stayed for another month.

King Udita sent men to escort him; after traveling westward for more than twenty days, they reached the kingdom of Siṃhapura. At that time, there were over a hundred monks, all from the north, who were carrying scriptures, images, and other items back home in accordance with the Master’s instructions.

In this manner, they traveled for over twenty more days through mountain torrents; as the area was infested with bandits, the Dharma Master feared they might be plundered. He would constantly dispatch a monk to precede them, instructing him that if they encountered bandits, he should say: "We have come from afar in search of the Dharma. All that we currently carry consists of scriptures, images, and śarīra relics. We pray that you, O donors, will protect us and harbor no ill intent."
The Dharma Master led his disciples from behind;
they encountered [the tiger] several times along the way, yet in the end, no harm befell them.
After traveling in this manner for more than twenty days, they reached the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, where he again paid homage at the site where King Candraprabha had sacrificed his thousand heads.

Fifty yojanas to the northeast of the kingdom was the country of Kaśmīra; its king dispatched an envoy to invite him, but the Dharma Master did not go because his baggage train was traveling by elephant.

After staying for seven days, they traveled northwest again for three days until they reached the great river Sindhu. The river was five or six li wide; the scriptures, images, and fellow companions all proceeded by boat, while the Master crossed on an elephant.

At that time, he dispatched one person to guard the scriptures and various Indian seeds of exotic flowers on board the ship. When they reached midstream, a sudden storm arose with turbulent winds and waves, rocking the vessel so violently that it was on the verge of capsizing. The guardian of the scriptures fell into the water in terror; though the others rescued him, he had lost fifty fascicles of the scriptural texts as well as the flower and fruit seeds, while the remainder were barely preserved.
At that time, the King of Kāpiśī was staying in the city of Udakhāṇḍa. Upon hearing that the Dharma Master had arrived, he went in person to the riverbank to welcome him, asking:
"I have heard that you lost your scriptures in the river; did you not bring seeds of Indian flowers and fruits?"
He replied, "I shall bring it. The king said:
"The drum's surge capsized the ship; this was due to that very circumstance.
Since ancient times, those who have wished to cross with flower seeds have all met with the same fate.

Consequently, they returned to the city with the Dharma Master and stayed at a monastery for over fifty days. Because the original texts of the scriptures had been lost, he sent someone again to the country of Ujjayinī to transcribe the Tripiṭaka of the Kāśyapīya school.
When the King of Kaśmīra heard that the Dharma Master was drawing near, he forgot his distance and came in person to pay his respects; it was only after several days that he returned home.
The Dharma Master traveled northwest together with the King of Kāpiśī for over a month before reaching the borders of the kingdom of Lampāka.

The King dispatched the Crown Prince to go on ahead, commanding the citizens and the assembly of monks to prepare banners and streamers to go out of the city to welcome him; the King and the Dharma Master then set forth gradually.

By the time they arrived, several thousand monastics and laypeople were present with a magnificent display of banners and streamers; upon seeing the Dharma Master, the multitude prostrated themselves with joy, surrounding him before and behind as they proceeded while chanting praises.
Upon arriving at the capital, he stayed at a Mahāyāna temple; at that time, the King was also performing an unobstructed great almsgiving for seventy-five days.
From there, he traveled due south for fifteen days to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to pay homage to the sacred sites.
Furthermore, to the northwest, one goes to the country of Abhagana.
Again to the northwest, one goes to the country of Jāguḍa.
Traveling northward for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Vṛji-Sattala.
From here he traveled eastward to the territory of Kāpiśī, where the king again held a great almsgiving for seven days.
When the distribution was concluded, the Dharma Master took his leave and departed.
Traveling one *yojana* to the northeast, he reached the city of Gholasanda and bid farewell to the king, proceeding northward.
The King dispatched a high minister leading over a hundred men to escort the Dharma Master across the Snow Mountains, providing him with fodder, grass, and provisions.
After traveling for seven days, they reached the summit of a great mountain.

The mountain features overlapping ridges and perilous peaks of various irregular forms; some are level while others rise steeply, their shapes never uniform. The difficulty of ascending it is such that it can hardly be fully described.
From then on, he was no longer permitted to ride a horse, but proceeded on foot, leaning upon a staff.
After another seven days, he reached a high ridge; at the foot of the ridge was a village of some one hundred households, which raised sheep and livestock, the sheep being as large as donkeys.
That day he stayed overnight in this village and departed at midnight, ordering the villagers to mount mountain camels to lead the way.
The terrain was filled with snow, torrents, and frozen streams; had it not been for the guidance of the local people, there would have been great fear of falling into the abyss.
When the following day dawned, they finally crossed over the mountain passes; at that time, there were only seven monks along with twenty-odd hired laborers, one elephant, ten mules, and four horses.
The next day, we reached the foot of the ridge; following the winding path, we ascended another ridge that appeared like snow from afar, but upon reaching it, we found it was entirely white stone.
This ridge is the highest of all; even when clouds gather and snow flies, they cannot reach its summit.
As the sun was about to set, they reached the mountain peak; the cold wind was piercing and biting, such that none among the companions could stand upright.
Furthermore, the mountain was devoid of vegetation, consisting only of piled rocks and clustered peaks that rose steeply like bamboo shoots from a forest.

Since the mountain at that location was high and the wind was fierce, birds attempting to cross could not fly; only after traveling several hundred paces south of the ridge or north of the ridge could they finally spread their six feathers.
Upon examining the heights of the mountain ranges within Jambudvīpa, none exceed this one.

The Dharma Master descended from the northwest for several *li* until he reached a small stretch of level ground, where he pitched a tent and stayed overnight. At dawn he set out again; after traveling for five or six days, he descended the mountain and arrived at the kingdom of Andarābha, which is the ancient site of Tukhāra.
There were three monasteries with several dozen monks who studied the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
There was also a stūpa built by King Aśoka,
where the Dharma Master stayed for five days.
Traveling northwest down the mountain for over four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kustana, which was also formerly part of the territory of Tukhāra.

From here, traveling northwest again by mountain for over three hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Huo, situated on the banks of the Oxus River (*Vakṣu*). This is the eastern frontier of Tukhāra; its capital city lies on the southern bank of the river.
Upon seeing the grandson of the Yabghu Khan, Wang Duohuoluo, who styled himself Yabghu, [the author] stayed at the capital for one month;
the Yabghu then dispatched an escort, and they traveled eastward together with a group of merchants.
On the second day, he arrived at the kingdom of Mang-kien.
Adjacent to it were also the kingdoms of A-li-ni, Ho-lo-hu, Ki-li-se-mo, and Po-li-ho; all of these were formerly territories of Tukhāra.
From Mung-kan, traveling eastward into the mountains for more than three hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Himatala, which was also formerly part of the territory of Tukhāra.

The customs are largely the same as those of the Turks; however, a particularly distinctive feature is that the women wear wooden horns on their heads over three feet high, with two prongs in front. These represent the husband’s father and mother: the upper prong represents the father and the lower prong represents the mother. As each passes away, one prong is removed;
if both the maternal uncle and the father-in-law have died, the entire crown is discarded.
From here, traveling east again for more than two hundred li, he reached the kingdom of Parvata, which was also formerly part of the territory of Tukhāra.
Because of the cold snow, he stayed there for over a month.
From here, traveling southeast by mountain for over two hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Yinpobian.
Continuing southeast, traversing perilous heights and treacherous precipices for over three hundred *li*, one reaches the kingdom of Gulangna.
From here, traveling northeast for over five hundred li by mountain path, one arrives at the kingdom of Dharmasthiti, also known as Gomati.
The country lies between two mountains and borders the Vaksu River; it produces excellent horses that are small in stature but robust.
The local customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people are violent by nature and coarse in appearance. Their eyes are mostly greenish-blue, differing from those of other nations.
There are more than ten monasteries.
The city of Huṇḍā is the capital of the kingdom; within it stands a monastery established by a former king of this country.

Upon a stone Buddha image within the monastery was a circular canopy of gold and copper, inlaid and polished with various jewels; it hovered naturally in the air directly above the Buddha’s crown. When people circumambulated it in prostration, the canopy would turn accordingly, and when they stopped, the canopy would come to rest. No one could fathom its spiritual power, and the origins of the temple’s establishment are detailed extensively in a separate biography.
From this country, traveling north from the great mountain to the kingdom of Hukini;
then crossing the kingdom of Dharmasthiti to the kingdom of Śāmbī.
From there, proceeding eastward through the mountains for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the Pāmira Valley.

The river flows east and west for over a thousand *li*, and north and south for over a hundred *li*. It lies between two snow mountains and is situated in the midst of the Pamir Range; wind and snow swirl and fly there without ceasing from spring through summer. Because of its piercing cold, vegetation is sparse, crops do not flourish, and the region is desolate, with no further trace of human habitation.

In the midst of the river is a great dragon pond, three hundred li from east to west and over fifty li from south to north; situated in the center of Jambudvīpa, its terrain is high and elevated, appearing vast and undulating, such that the eye cannot reach its limits.
The various species of aquatic creatures numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands; their clamor and chatter were so tumultuous as to resemble the workshops of a hundred artisans.
Furthermore, there were various birds, some over ten feet in height, whose eggs were as large as jars.
What was formerly called the "giant eggshell" of Tiao-wei likely refers to this very place.

To the west of the lake, a river branches off and flows westward to the eastern border of the kingdom of Darmasitida, where it joins the Oxus River (Vakṣu) and flows west into the sea; all the rivers to its right likewise converge there.

To the east of the lake, a great river branches off and flows eastward to the western border of the kingdom of Kāśa, where it joins the Sītā River and flows east into the sea; all the waters on its left likewise converge there.
To the south of the mountains beyond the river lies the kingdom of Paruṣa, which abounds in gold and silver; the color of its gold is like fire.
Furthermore, the north and south of this lake correspond exactly to those of Lake Anavatapta.
From here, traveling eastward along the river, ascending precipices and treading through snow for over five hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāpiśī.

The city rests upon a steep ridge, with its northern side backed by the Oxus River (Sītā). This river flows eastward into the Salt Lake (Lop Nor), where it subsides underground; emerging from Mount Jīmūta (Jiashishan), it serves as the source of this kingdom’s river.

Furthermore, this king is wise and sagacious; his dynasty has been established through successive generations for many years. He claims that his lineage is originally that of the *Cīnadevagupta*—which in the language of Tang means "Han-Sun-of-Heaven. Within the former palace of the king, there is the monastery of the venerable master Kumāralāta.

The Venerable was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. He possessed a brilliant and sagacious mind; he could recite thirty-two thousand words daily, and his proficiency in writing was equal. He sported with the various teachings and was refined and at ease in composition. He authored some dozens of treatises, all of which were widely circulated and propagated; he was the founding master of the Sautrāntika school.

At that time, there was Aśvaghoṣa in the east, Deva in the south, Nāgārjuna in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north; they were known as the "Four Suns," capable of illuminating the delusions of sentient beings.
Because the reputation of Dharmatrāta was already so high, the former king personally led an expedition against his country to welcome him and provide for his needs.

Over three hundred li to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stone cliff where there are two stone chambers; in each, an Arhat has entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Seated upright and motionless, they appear as if frail men, yet they have not decayed or crumbled at all, having remained thus for over seven hundred years.
The Dharma Master stayed in that country for more than twenty days.

Traveling northeast again for five days, he encountered a band of robbers; the merchant caravan was struck with terror and fled up the mountain, while the elephants were pursued and perished by drowning.

After the bandits had departed, he gradually proceeded eastward with the merchants; braving the cold and traversing perilous terrain for over eight hundred li, he emerged from the Pamir Mountains and reached the kingdom of Wusha.
Two hundred *li* to the west of the city is a great mountain with extremely steep and jagged peaks, upon which stands a stūpa.

According to ancient accounts, several hundred years ago, the mountain collapsed due to a thunderclap; inside was a bhikṣu of immense stature, sitting with his eyes closed, his hair and beard growing long and hanging down to cover his shoulders and face.

A woodcutter saw this and reported it to the king; the king personally went to observe and pay his respects. News spread among the officials and commoners, and people gathered from near and far to offer their worship, piling up flowers until they formed a great mound.
The king asked,
"Who is this person? A bhikṣu replied:
"This renunciant arhat who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation has remained there for many years; therefore, his hair has grown long.
The king asked, "How can he be awakened and made to rise?"

He replied, "A body sustained by solid food will deteriorate as soon as one emerges from meditative absorption; it would be best first to sprinkle it with ghee and milk to moisten the pores and tissues, and only then strike the *gandī* bell to rouse and awaken him—perhaps he may then rise."
The king said, "Excellent!
He then followed the monk's words, pouring milk and striking the mallet.
The Arhat raised his eyes and looked at them, saying,
"Who are you people, dressed in the robes of the Dharma? They replied:
"We are bhikṣus," they replied. He asked,
"Where is my teacher, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, now?"
He replied, "He entered nirvana long ago. Upon hearing this,
[the king] was deeply moved with sorrow.
He asked again:
"Has Śākyamuni Buddha attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? He replied:
"Having already attained perfection, he asked this for the benefit of sentient beings; he too shall follow into quiescent extinction.

Having heard this, [the king] lowered his gaze for a long while, then with his hand lifted the hair [of the remains], rose into the void, and performed great supernatural transformations. He manifested fire to cremate his body, and his skeletal remains fell to the ground.
The king, together with the great assembly, collected the bones and erected a stūpa; this is the very tower [in question].
From here, traveling north for more than five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Kāśa (formerly called Shule), which is named after its capital city.
The correct pronunciation is *śrīkṛtita*, as declared by Xuanyun;
the term from Shule is a corruption.
From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, crossing the Sita River and over a great mountain range, one arrives at the kingdom of Cīnakya (formerly known as Juchü).

To the south of the kingdom is a great mountain with many grottoes; many Indians who have realized the fruits of the path exercise their supernormal powers to dwell there, and thus those who enter nirvana in this place are numerous.

Even now, there are three arhats dwelling in mountain caves who have entered the meditative concentration of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); as their hair and beards gradually grow long, the monks go there from time to time to shave them.
Furthermore, this country possesses many Mahāyāna sūtras; those consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas form a single collection, of which there are several dozen.
From here, traveling east for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the kingdom of Gostana (which in the language of Tang is called Diryu; this is its refined local appellation).
The common people call it the kingdom of Huanna, the Xiongnu call it Yudun, the various Hu peoples call it Hedan, and in India it is called Kustana.
Formerly called Yutian, this is a corruption [of the original name].
Although the desert wastes cover more than half the land, it is well-suited for grain and yields abundant fruit.
It produces woolen carpets and fine felts; its cotton fabrics are woven with exquisite fineness.
Furthermore, the land abounds in white jade and black jade (yi-yu).

The climate is temperate and harmonious; the people understand propriety and righteousness, esteem learning, and delight in musical tones. Their deportment is refined and orderly, differing from the customs of other Hu peoples.
The script follows that of India from afar, with only slight modifications.
They revere the Buddha-dharma; there are over a hundred monasteries and more than five thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna.
The king was heroic, wise, brave, and martial, and he held those of virtue in high esteem; he claimed himself to be a descendant of Vaiśravaṇa.

The king’s ancestor was the crown prince of King Aśoka, who, while residing in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, was later banished to the north of the Snowy Mountains. There he raised livestock, following the water and grass, until he established his capital at this site. After a long time, he had no son, so he prayed at the temple of Vaiśravaṇa. The deity of the temple split open its forehead, producing a male child. Furthermore, a marvelous substance grew from the ground before the temple, sweet and fragrant like milk; taking it, they nourished the child, and he eventually grew to adulthood.
After the king passed away, his successor ascended the throne; his majesty and virtue spread afar, and by his might he unified the various states—the current king is his descendant.
Because his ancestors were originally sustained by the milk of the earth, Khotan is called the "Land of Earth-Milk" (*Diyu*) in its authentic pronunciation.

The Dharma Master entered its territory and arrived at the city of Bōjiéyí. Within the city was a seated Buddha image, over seven feet in height, wearing a jeweled crown upon its head, with a majestic and perfect countenance.
According to the accounts of former masters, the original image was in the kingdom of Kaśmīra and was subsequently invited here.

In the past, there was an arhat who had a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) suffering from an illness; as the novice was about to pass away, he requested sour rice cakes. The master, observing with his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) that they existed in Gostana, secretly employed his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) to beg for them and give them to him.

Having finished his meal, the śrāmaṇera was filled with joy and took pleasure in being born in that land; through the power of his vows, which were unyielding, he was reborn into a royal family immediately upon the end of his life.
After succeeding to the throne, his talent and strategy were preeminent and heroic, and his ambition was to annex all lands; he thus crossed the Snowy Mountains to strike at his former kingdom.
At that time, the King of Kaśmīra also selected generals and trained his troops, intending to repel the invaders.
The Arhat said, "There is no need for the exertion of raising blades; I shall send them away myself."
He immediately went to the King of Kustana and spoke to him of the faults of King Mūrdhaja’s greed and violence, while also showing him the robes he had worn as a śrāmaṇera in a previous life.

Upon seeing these, the king attained the knowledge of his past lives and was deeply filled with shame and remorse. He then established friendly relations with the King of Kaśmīra and withdrew, subsequently escorting the image he had previously venerated back to his own country along with his army.

When the statue reached this city and remained there without proceeding further, the King and his entire army exerted all their strength to move it, yet in the end they could not budge it. He immediately constructed a refined hermitage atop the statue, invited monks to reside there, and offered his beloved crown as an adornment for the Buddha’s head.
The crown is still extant; it is composed of an immense quantity of precious gems, and all who behold it utter words of praise.
The Dharma Master stayed for seven days. When the King of Khotan heard that the Dharma Master had arrived within his borders, he came in person to welcome and pay his respects.
On a later day, when the funeral procession set out, the King first returned to the capital, leaving his son behind to attend upon him.
After traveling for two days, the King again dispatched high-ranking officials to welcome him back; they stayed forty li outside the city.
The next day, the King, together with monastics and laypeople, welcomed him on the left side of the road with music, incense, and flowers.
Upon his arrival, they escorted him into the city and lodged him in the Sarvāstivāda monastery of the Hīnayāna.
More than ten li south of the royal city, there is a great monastery built by a former king of this country for the arhat Vairocana (translated into Chinese as Biàozhào, "Universal Illumination").
Formerly, when the teachings of the Dharma had not yet reached this country, an Arhat came here from Kaśmīra and sat in meditative seclusion within a forest.
At that time, someone who saw him was struck by his appearance and attire and reported the matter to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king went in person to observe his deportment and asked,
"Who are you, dwelling alone in the forest wilds? He replied:
“I am a disciple of the Tathāgata; it is the natural law for me to dwell in seclusion.
The king asked, “What further meaning does the term ‘Tathāgata’ convey?”
He replied: "The Tathāgata is an epithet for the virtue of a Buddha."

In the past, Prince Sarvārthasiddha, son of King Śuddhodana, took pity on all sentient beings who were submerged in the ocean of suffering, without rescue or refuge. He thus renounced his seven treasures, his thousand sons, and his status as a Wheel-Turning Monarch over the four continents; he entered the secluded forest to pursue the Way, and after six years, he achieved fruition. He attained a golden-hued body and realized the Dharma without a teacher. He sprinkled the nectar of immortality in the Deer Park and shone the mani-jewel upon Vulture Peak. For eighty years, he taught, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened others. Now that his transformative conditions have been exhausted, he has ceased his response to the world and returned to the Truth. Yet the legacy of his image and the legacy of his scriptures remain transmitted and accessible. Your Majesty, by virtue of past merit, holds the position of sovereign; you are the one to whom the turning of the Dharma wheel was entrusted and the refuge for all who possess consciousness. That you remain in darkness and do not hear this—what logic can explain such a thing?
The king said,
"My sins have accumulated over many lifetimes, and I had never heard the name of the Buddha.
That I now receive the descent of the Sage’s virtue is surely due to my remaining merit."
"Since there are already surviving images and scriptures, we request that you receive and practice them.
The Arhat replied, "If you truly desire this, you must first establish a monastery; then the sacred image will arrive of its own accord."

The King then turned his carriage back and, together with his ministers, carefully selected an auspicious site. He commissioned master craftsmen and inquired of the Arhats regarding the architectural style for its construction, whereupon it was built.
When the temple was completed, the King requested again, saying, "The monastery is now finished; where is the image of the Buddha? He replied:
"The King need only be sincere, and the appearance of the image will not be far off.
The King, together with his ministers, officials, and commoners, each burned incense and held flowers, standing with single-minded devotion.
In a brief moment, a Buddha image descended from the sky onto the precious throne; its radiance was brilliant and its countenance solemn.

Upon seeing this, the king rejoiced and celebrated with boundless joy. He then invited the Arhat to preach the Dharma for the assembly, whereupon he and the people of the nation extensively offered worship and offerings.
Therefore, this monastery was established at the very beginning.

Previously, while crossing a river, the Dharma Master had lost his scriptures; upon arriving here, he sent men again to Kucha and Kashgar to seek out the original texts. However, because he was detained by the King of Khotan, he could not obtain them and returned immediately. Consequently, he composed a memorial and dispatched a young man of Gaochang to accompany a merchant caravan to the imperial court, stating that he had previously traveled to the land of the Brahmins to seek the Dharma and had now returned safely to Khotan.
The preface reads:
"I, the śramaṇa Xuanzang, state:

I have heard that Ma Rong was so profoundly learned that Zheng Xuan went to him as a teacher in Fufeng; and because Fu Sheng was so clear-minded and quick-witted, Chao Cuo personally studied under him in Jinan."

It is known that even the ancients sought far and wide for the proximate arts of the Confucian scholars; how much more so, then, would anyone dare to feel weary of the distance and fail to seek and admire the profound traces of the Buddhas in benefiting sentient beings, or the wondrous teachings of the Tripiṭaka that unravel the bonds of affliction?

Xuanzang previously considered that although the Buddha arose in the Western Regions and his bequeathed teachings were transmitted to the East, while these excellent scriptures had indeed arrived, the perfect system was still lacking. He constantly contemplated seeking out and studying them, regardless of his own life or limb.
Thereupon, in the fourth month of the third year of the Zhenguan era, he disregarded the established laws and regulations and traveled privately to India.

He traversed the vast expanse of the shifting sands and ascended the towering heights of the Snowy Mountains; he followed the treacherous paths of the Iron Gate Pass and the surging waves of the Sea of Heat.
Beginning from the ancestral capital of Changshan and ending at the new city of Rājagṛha, the distance traversed in the interim was over fifty thousand *li*.

Although local customs differed in a thousand ways and hardships were encountered in myriads of layers, by relying on the celestial majesty [of the Emperor], there was no obstruction wherever we went.

Still receiving generous hospitality, my person was spared from hardship and my heart’s wishes were fulfilled; I was thus able to behold Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and pay homage to the Bodhi tree, to see traces that had not been seen before and hear sutras that had not been heard before. I exhausted the spiritual wonders of the universe and the generative transformations of yin and yang, proclaiming the virtuous bounty of the Imperial Wind and inspiring the reverence and longing of foreign lands. I traveled and toured extensively for seventeen years.
Having now traveled from the kingdom of Prayāga through the territory of Kapīśa, crossed the Pamir Mountains, and traversed the Pamir Valley, I have returned and reached Khotan.

The elephant I was leading has drowned; as there are many versions of the scriptures and I have not yet obtained a saddle or mount, I must pause for a short while. Thus, I am unable to hasten to the imperial presence for an early audience, and I can do nothing but express my utmost longing and reverence.
"I respectfully dispatch Ma Xuánzhì, a layman of Gaochang, to accompany a merchant caravan to present this memorial first.

Thereafter, for the sake of the monks of Khotan, he lectured on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*. Day and night, these four treatises were proclaimed in succession; the King, along with the monastics and laity, took refuge and listened to them, with those in attendance numbering in the thousands each day.
After seven or eight months had passed, the envoy returned. Having received the Emperor’s gracious decree, an imperial messenger was sent down to welcome and honor him, saying:
"I have heard that you, Master, sought the Way in distant lands and have now returned; my joy is immeasurable. You may come at once to have an audience with me."

As for those monks in that country who understand Sanskrit and the meaning of the scriptures, they may also be brought along. I have already issued an imperial decree to the envoys of Khotan and other states to send teachers; there will certainly be no shortage of manpower or pack animals for transport. I order the officials at Dunhuang to welcome them at Liusha, and the officials at Shanshan to welcome them at Jumu.
Having received the imperial decree, the Dharma Master set forth immediately; the King of Khotan provided him with a very generous send-off.
After traveling more than three hundred li from the capital, he arrived at the city of Hu-mo to the east.
In the city there is a standing image of the Buddha carved from sandalwood, over twenty feet in height. Its physical form is dignified and majestic, and it manifests many miraculous responses.
When people suffer from ailments, they apply gold leaf to the specific part of the image corresponding to their place of pain, and the illness is immediately cured;
for all those who make petitions or seek blessings, their desires are mostly fulfilled.

It is traditionally said that this [image] was originally made by King Udayana of Kauśāmbī when the Buddha was still in the world. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it flew from there and arrived at the city of Halahala in the north of this country; subsequently, it moved again of its own accord to its present location. The circumstances of these events are recorded in a separate tradition.
Furthermore, according to a traditional record, it is said that when the Dharma of Śākyamuni perishes, the Image will enter the Dragon Palace.
From the city of Pāmā, one enters a desert to the east and travels over two hundred li to reach the city of Nīraṅga.

Furthermore, proceeding east from here, one enters the Great Flowing Sands. There, the wind stirs and the sands flow; the land is devoid of water or grass and is plagued by many hot poisons and malevolent spirits.

There are no paths, and travelers going back and forth must rely on the remains of humans and animals as their markers. The terrain is so parched and treacherous that it is difficult to traverse, as described in the preceding introduction.
Traveling another four hundred-odd *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Tukhāra.
Traveling another six hundred-odd *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Jarmadana, which is the land of Jumi.
Traveling northeast again for over a thousand *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Navapa, which is the territory of Loulan; from there, he proceeded by stages until he arrived at his own borders.
Having obtained saddled mounts, he released the messengers from Khotan along with the pack horses to return home.
An imperial edict was issued to reward them for their labors, but they all declined and departed.
Upon arriving at Shazhou, they again submitted a memorial to the throne.
At that time, the Emperor was residing in the Luoyang Palace.

Upon presenting the memorial, he learned that the Dharma Master was drawing near; the Emperor then issued an edict for Fang Xuanling, Duke of Liang and Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs serving as the Imperial Resident of the Western Capital, to instruct the relevant authorities to welcome and attend to him.

When the Dharma Master learned that the Emperor intended to launch a punitive expedition to the Liaodong coast, he feared that any delay would cause him to miss the opportunity; he therefore redoubled his pace and proceeded forward, arriving suddenly at the Cao Canal.

The officials were unaware of his arrival and had no leisure to arrange the ceremonial regalia; yet those who heard of him naturally flocked together, and the streets were so crowded with those coming to pay their respects that they trampled one another, unable to advance, and thus he was forced to stay overnight on the canal bank.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty, Scroll Five.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty,
Scroll Six.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili and annotated by Shi Yanzong. From the first month of spring in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era to the sixth month of summer in the twenty-second year: An account of the arrival in the Western Capital, the expression of gratitude for the Imperial Preface to the Sūtra, and the response thereto. On the *jingzi* day of the first month of spring in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Fang Xuanling, Duke of Liang and Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs serving as the Metropolitan Governor, along with others, received news that the Dharma Master had brought sūtras and images to the capital. They immediately dispatched Houmochen Shi, General of the Right of the Imperial Guard; Li Shushen, Magistrate of Yongzhou; and Li Qianyou, Magistrate of Chang’an County, to welcome them. The party entered through the waterway and took up residence at the Duting Post Station, their retinue gathering like clouds.

On this day, the officials distributed the materials to various monasteries, providing canopies, litters, flowers, banners, and other items intended for the transport of the scriptures and images to Hongfu Monastery; everyone was filled with joy and vied with one another to adorn them.
The following day, a grand assembly was held south of the Zhuque Street, where several hundred items were arrayed in military formation.
Therein were placed one hundred and fifty grains of the Tathāgata’s flesh-relics obtained by the Dharma Master from the Western Regions;
and a golden image of the Buddha’s shadow from the Dragon Cave on Mount Prāgbodhi in the kingdom of Magadha, including its halo and pedestal, measuring three feet and three inches in height.

One sandalwood Buddha image, including its halo and pedestal, three feet five inches in height, modeled after the image of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;

one sandalwood Buddha image, including its halo and pedestal, two feet nine inches in height, modeled after the sandalwood portrait carved by King Udayana of Kauśāmbī out of longing for the Tathāgata;

and one silver Buddha image, including its halo and pedestal, four feet in height, modeled after the image of the Tathāgata descending the jeweled stairs from the celestial palace in the kingdom of Kapitha.

He fashioned a golden Buddha image, one *zhang* in height including its halo and pedestal, modeled after the images of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Magadha;

he also fashioned a sandalwood Buddha image, one *chi* and five *cun* in height including its halo and pedestal, modeled after the image left behind by [the Buddha] when subduing the venomous dragon in the kingdom of Nagaraḥāra;
and he fashioned sandalwood images and others, modeled after [the Buddha’s] processions through the city for the sake of conversion in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Furthermore, he established the Dharma Master with two hundred and twenty-four Mahāyāna sūtras and one hundred and ninety-two Mahāyāna śāstras obtained in the Western Regions,
as well as fifteen sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the Sthavira school, fifteen sūtras, vinayas,
and śāstras of the Mahāsāṃghika school, and [texts] of the Saṃmitīya school.
Fifteen sections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra; twenty-two sections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra from the Mahīśāsaka school;
seventeen sections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra from the Kāśyapīya school;
forty-two sections of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra from the Dharmaguptaka school; and [sections of] Sūtra and Vinaya from the Sarvāstivāda school.
There were sixty-seven treatises on logic (*hetu-śāstra*), thirty-six treatises on causes (*hetu-śāstra*),
and thirteen treatises on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), totaling five hundred and twenty fascicles and six hundred and fifty-seven works,
which he brought back carried by twenty horses.

On that day, the relevant authorities issued a general order to all monasteries: whatever ritual implements for offerings there may be—such as precious canopies, banners, and streamers—are required to assemble at Zhuque Street by dawn on the twenty-eighth day of the following month, in preparation for welcoming the newly arrived scriptures and images to Hongfu Monastery.

Thereupon, the people redoubled their zeal and vied with one another to adorn themselves, exhausting every form of beauty. Banners, canopies, precious tables, and jeweled carriages were brought forth from each monastery and distributed; the monks and nuns followed in formal attire, with refined chanting preceding them and incense burners arrayed behind. Arriving there, these items were all displayed within the streets, numbering several hundred in total.

As the sutras and images were carried forth, the jeweled pendants jingled with sound and the golden flowers scattered their brilliance; among those who accompanied the procession, there was none who did not sing praises of this rare occurrence, casting off worldly dust and dispelling all burdens as they marveled at such an extraordinary encounter.

Beginning from within Zhuque Street and ending at the gate of Hongfu Monastery, for a distance of several tens of *li*, the common people, officials, and civil and military bureaucrats lined both sides of the road, standing in reverent gazing. The crowds were so dense that the authorities, fearing they might trample one another, ordered incense to be burned and flowers to be scattered at every spot, forbidding anyone to move; thus, clouds of smoke and sounds of praise merged together everywhere.

In the past, when the Tathāgata first descended upon Kapilavastu and Maitreya first ascended to Tuṣita, they were honored by nāgas and devas and surrounded by hosts of celestial beings; although this occasion does not equal those times, it is nonetheless a period of flourishing for the Bequeathed Dharma.

On that day, the multitude saw together five-colored, variegated clouds appearing in the sky to the north of the sun; they curled and turned directly above the sutras and images, shimmering and dense for several li in circumference, as if welcoming or seeing off [the scriptures], until they reached the temple and faded away.
Shi Yancong’s commentary states:
"I have examined maps and histories; this is surely what is meant by the auspicious qi of Heaven, which those who discern it rejoice in.

In the past, when the Tathāgata first descended into Kapilavastu and Maitreya was about to ascend to Tuṣita, the dragon spirits made offerings and the celestial hosts welcomed them. Although we do not equal those former times, there has never been such a flourishing state for the Bequeathed Dharma as it is now in its eastward flow."
On the *renchen* day, the Dharma Master paid a visit to Emperor Wenwu Sheng at the Luoyang Palace.
On the *jihai* day of the second month, he was received in the Yiluan Hall; the Emperor welcomed him with great courtesy and comforted him most generously.
Once they were seated, the Emperor said,
"Why did you not inform me of your departure?
The Dharma Master apologized, saying:
"When I was about to depart, I submitted my petition three times; however, because my sincere aspiration was but slight, I did not receive permission.
Driven by the utmost longing for the Way, I have ventured to travel privately. For this crime of acting on my own authority, I am deeply ashamed and fearful."
The Emperor said:

"Master, you have left the household life and are thus fundamentally distinct from the laity; yet, you were able to entrust your life to seek the Dharma for the benefit and welfare of all living beings.
I greatly admire this, and you need not feel any sense of shame."

"However," they said, "we have only thought that those mountains and rivers were so vast and distant, and the customs of the people so different, that we find it strange that you, Master, could reach them.

The Dharma Master replied, "Xuanzang have heard that one who rides the swift wind finds even the Heavenly Lake not far away; likewise, for one who relies on the power of the Way, no distance is too great."
Those who pilot dragon-boats find it no hardship to traverse the waves of the Yangtze River.

Since Your Majesty grasped the Mandate of Heaven and purified the four seas, your virtue has encompassed the nine provinces and your benevolence has spread across the eight regions. The pure wind of your reign fans the lands south of the scorching sun, and your sacred majesty resounds beyond the Congling Mountains. Thus, when the chieftains of the barbarian tribes see birds soaring through the clouds from the east, they still suspect them to have originated from the Central Kingdom and bow their bodies in reverence; how much more so for one like Xuanzang, with a round head and square feet, who has personally received your nurturing transformation.
"Since we rely upon the majesty of Heaven, we have been able to travel back and forth without difficulty.
The Emperor said, "These are merely the words of you, Master and Elder; how could Your Majesty dare to accept them?"
He then questioned him extensively regarding those matters.

From west of the Snow Mountains to the borders of India, concerning the harmonious climate, the products of the land, the local customs, the ancient traces of the Eight Kings, and the remaining sites of the Four Buddhas—none of these had been transmitted by Zhang Qian (Bo Wang), nor could they have been recorded by Ban Gu or Sima Qian.

Since the Dharma Master had personally traveled to those lands and observed their territories and cities, what he had heard and seen remained vividly in his memory without omission; thus, in responding to questions as they arose, his answers were always systematic and well-ordered.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said to his attendants:
"In the past, Fu Jian praised Shi Dao’an as a 'divine vessel,' and the entire court held him in high esteem.
Now, observing the Dharma Master’s elegant discourse and his upright, austere character, he not only does not fall short of the ancients, but indeed surpasses them by far."
At that time, the Duke of Zhao, Changsun Wuji, replied:
"Truly as Your Majesty’s decree suggests.
I have previously read the *Spring and Autumn Annals of the Jin Dynasty* and observed the account of Master Dao’an; he was indeed a monk of lofty conduct and vast erudition."

However, at that time, the Buddha-dharma had only recently arrived, and the sūtras and śāstras were not yet numerous; thus, although there was research and study, it was largely confined to the branches and leaves, rather than like the Dharma Master, who personally gazed upon the Pure Realm, investigated the source of all wonders, and traced the footprints of Nirvāṇa.
The Emperor said,
"What you say is correct.
The Emperor then addressed the Dharma Master, saying:

“The Buddha-lands are remote, and their sacred traces and Dharma teachings cannot be recorded in full detail by previous histories. Since you, Master, have personally witnessed them, it is fitting that you compose a biography to show those who have not yet heard of them.”

The Emperor further observed that the Dharma Master was worthy of being entrusted with the role of a high minister; he therefore urged him to return to secular life to assist in governing worldly affairs.
The Dharma Master declined, saying:

"I, Xuanzang, entered the monastic gate in my youth and have devoted myself to the Buddhist Way. I have practiced the profound principles of the Buddha, but I have not yet heard the teachings of Confucius."

To now dismiss them to follow worldly ways is no different from taking a boat that follows the current and forcing it to abandon the water for land; not only will it be ineffective, but it will also cause it to rot in vain.
"I wish to devote my entire life to practicing the Way in order to repay the kindness of the state; this would be the greatest fortune for Xuanzang.
Having thus firmly declined, [the Emperor] desisted.

At that time, the Emperor was about to launch a punitive expedition against Liaodong, and the armies of the empire had already assembled at Luoyang. Amidst the urgency of military affairs, upon hearing that the Dharma Master had arrived, he ordered him to be ushered into the court, expecting only a brief meeting. However, once their pure discourse began, they were unaware that the sun had already passed its zenith.
The Duke of Zhao, Changsun Wuji, submitted a memorial stating that the Dharma Master was staying at the Court of State Ceremonial and feared he might not arrive in time by dusk.
The Emperor said:

"In our hurried conversation, my thoughts have not yet been fully expressed. I wish to travel east with you to inspect the regions and observe the customs, so that beyond the matters of state administration, we may further engage in discourse. What is your intention?"
The Dharma Master declined, saying, "I, Xuanzang, have come from afar and am moreover afflicted by illness; I fear I shall not be able to accompany Your Majesty.
The Emperor said:
“The Master was once able to travel alone through remote frontiers; this current journey is but like taking a single step—how could it be a cause for refusal?
The Dharma Master replied:

“When Your Majesty marches eastward, the six armies shall provide protection. To punish the chaotic state and execute the treacherous ministers, you will surely achieve the merit of Muye and the victory of Kunyang.”

I, Xuanzang, have personally assessed that I shall ultimately be of no assistance in the efficacy of military formations; I am merely carrying the shame of having needlessly incurred the expenses of the journey.
Furthermore, during times of armed conflict and warfare, the monastic discipline prohibits one from observing such scenes.
"Since the Buddha has spoken these words, I dare not fail to honor them.
I prostrate myself and pray that Your Majesty’s divine compassion will take pity on me; for Xuanzang, this would be most fortunate.
The Emperor accepted his plea and desisted.
The Dharma Master further submitted a memorial, saying:
"I, Xuanzang, have obtained over six hundred Sanskrit texts from the Western Regions, not a single word of which has yet been translated.

I now know that to the south of Mount Song and north of Mount Shaoshi lies Shaolin Monastery; it is secluded from the secular world, with its springs and rocks offering pure tranquility. It was founded by Emperor Xiaowen of the Later Wei dynasty and is the very place where the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci translated the scriptures."
Xuanzang expressed his hope to travel there on behalf of the state to perform translations, humbly awaiting the Imperial Decree.

The Emperor said, "There is no need for you to remain in the mountains. After you have departed for the West, I shall establish Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital on behalf of Empress Dowager Mu. That monastery contains a Chan courtyard that is exceptionally secluded and tranquil; the Dharma Master may proceed there to perform the translations."
The Dharma Master further petitioned, saying:

"The common people are ignorant; seeing that Xuanzang has come from the West, they have gathered to gaze upon me in vain until it has become a bustling marketplace. This not only violates the legal statutes but also obstructs and ruins my religious duties. I hope to be permitted to station guards at the gate to prevent such transgressions."
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "Master, this intention of yours may truly be called 'words for preserving one's person. I shall arrange it accordingly.
You may stay for three or five days to rest; then you shall return to the capital and be accommodated at Hongfu Monastery."
"Whatever you may require, let us deliberate upon it together with Xuánlíng.
From this point on, he took his leave and returned home.
On the *jisi* day of the third month, the Dharma Master returned from Luoyang to Chang’an and immediately resided at Hongfu Monastery.

As the project of translation was about to commence, he drafted a detailed list specifying the required number of scholars for verifying the meaning, those for composing the text, scribes, and copyists, and submitted it to the Guardian of the Realm, Minister of Works, Duke of Liang, Xuánlíng. Xuánlíng then dispatched his relevant officials to prepare a formal petition and send an envoy to Dìngzhōu to present it to the Emperor.
An imperial decree was issued to provide all necessary supplies, ensuring they were fully and adequately prepared.

On the *wùxū* day of the sixth month of summer, twelve virtuous monks (*dégǔ*) arrived who were experts in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, and who were highly esteemed by their contemporaries. They were: Śramaṇa Língrùn of Hongfú Monastery in the Capital; Śramaṇa Wénbèi; Śramaṇa Huìguì of Luóhàn Monastery; Śramaṇa Míngyán of Shíjì Monastery; Śramaṇa Fǎxiáng of Bǎochāng Monastery; Śramaṇa Pǔxián of Jìngfǎ Monastery; Śramaṇa Shénfǎng of Fǎhǎi Monastery; Śramaṇa Dàoshēn of Fǎjiǎng Monastery in Kuò Prefecture; Śramaṇa Xuánzhōng of Yǎnjué Monastery in Biàn Prefecture; Śramaṇa Shéntài of Pǔjiù Monastery in Pú Prefecture; Śramaṇa Jìngmíng of Zhènxiàng Monastery in Mián Prefecture; and Śramaṇa Dàoyīn of Duóbǎo Monastery in Yì Prefecture.

Furthermore, nine eminent monks skilled in composition arrived: the śramaṇa Xixuan of Puguang Temple in the capital; the śramaṇa Minghui of Hongfu Temple; the śramaṇa Bianji of Huichang Temple; the śramaṇa Daoxuan of Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan; the śramaṇa Jingmai of Fojusi Temple in Jianzhou; the śramaṇa Xingyou of Pujiusi Temple in Puzhou; the śramaṇa Daozhuo of Qiyansi Temple; the śramaṇa Huili of Zhaorensi Temple in Bīnzhou; and the śramaṇa Xuance of Tiangongsisi Temple in Luozhou.
Furthermore, one virtuous monk specializing in etymology arrived; he was the śramaṇa Xuanying of Dazongchi Monastery in the capital.
Additionally, one virtuous monk proficient in Sanskrit language and script arrived; he was the śramaṇa Xuanmu of Daxingshan Monastery in the capital.
The remaining scribes, copyists, and all necessary provisions provided by the relevant authorities arrived.

On the day of Dingmao, the Dharma Master finally took up the palm leaves to expound the Sanskrit texts, beginning the translation of four works: the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the *Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. The translation of the *Ṣaṇmukha-sūtra* was completed on that very day; the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* was finished in the year of Xinsi; and the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* were only concluded at the end of the year.
On the *jiazi* day of the first month in the spring of the twentieth year, he again translated the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, completing it in the second month.
He also translated the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
On the *xinmao* day of the seventh month in autumn, the Dharma Master presented the newly translated sūtras and śāstras that had been completed, submitting a memorial which stated:
"Śramaṇa Xuánzàng speaks.

I have humbly heard that the purport of the Eightfold Path is truly the bridge and ferry for crossing the ocean of suffering, and the doctrine of the One Vehicle is indeed the ladder and steps for ascending to Nirvāṇa."

However, because the capacities of sentient beings had not yet ripened, [the Dharma] remained stored to the west of Mount Cong; it passed through the era of Xuting without being heard, and traversed the Zhou and Qin dynasties without arriving.
It was only when Kāśyapa Mātanga entered Luoyang that it first reached the Three Rivers, and when Saṃghadeva traveled to Wu that it finally moistened the lands of Jing and Chu.

From this time forward, people have finally been able to cultivate the causes for liberation and establish the practice of Bodhi within their own households; one can thus know with certainty that the benefit of transmitting the Dharma is truly vast.

Subsequently, Yan and Xian sought out the scriptures, while Fotudeng and Kumārajīva followed in succession with their translations; although the profound wind of the Dharma fanned ever more widely, they all remained under the reigns of illegitimate courts.
Only Xuanzang, disregarding his own life, alone encountered an enlightened sovereign, so that all the sūtras and śāstras he brought back were permitted to be presented to the imperial court.

Having been favored by Your Majesty’s high esteem for the sacred words and granted permission to translate them, I have, together with various monks specializing in the study of meaning, applied myself with diligence day and night, never allowing even a moment of time to go to waste; yet, although I have held the pen for a long duration, I have not yet succeeded in completing the task.

As for those works already completed, I have obtained five sections totaling fifty-eight fascicles, namely: the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in twenty fascicles, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* in one fascicle, the *Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* in twenty fascicles, and the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā-śāstra* in sixteen fascicles. These have been bound into eight volumes, transcribed as specified elsewhere, and are now respectfully presented at the Imperial Palace.

I, Xuanzang, have also humbly observed that when the sacred images at Hongfu Monastery were first completed, Your Majesty personally descended from the imperial carriage to open their blue-lotus eyes. Now that these sutras and treatises have been translated for the first time as new literary works for this sagely age, I venture to rely on the precedent of former instances and hope that Your Majesty will graciously deign to bestow your divine calligraphy by composing a preface to praise and extol the ultimate truth.

I hope that these profound words and deep principles will shine as brightly as the sun and moon, and that these jade-like characters and silver hooks will endure as firmly as heaven and earth, so that for a hundred generations to come, their recitation shall never cease, and for a thousand years beyond, the gaze of reverence shall never end.
"Previously, during my audience at the capital of Luoyang, I was commanded by Imperial decree to compose the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), which has now been completed.
On the day of Yiwu, I again submitted a memorial, stating:
'The Śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.'"
I have humbly investigated how the *Yunguan* records the lands of Emperor Xuan under the *Panmu* and *Youling* mountains;
how the *Shangshu* chronicles the realms of Yao and Yi under the *Liusha* and *Canghai* seas;
and how the White Rings of the Queen Mother of the West were presented to the Sovereign who governs by "hanging robes" (non-action).

The *gǔ* arrows of the Eastern Barbarians were presented to the Sovereign who had laid aside punishments; thus his brilliance has flown through former ages, serving as a model for the auspicious precedents of antiquity.

We humbly reflect that Your Majesty grasps the cosmic order and rides upon the opportune moment, holding the balance and establishing the standard. You hollowed out boats and strung wood to command all under heaven and deliver the multitude of living beings; you used the legs of giant tortoises and reed ashes to fill the square earth and repair the circular canopy. You have illuminated the military arts within the Seven Virtues and propagated civil culture throughout the Ten Relationships. Your grace pervades the springs and sources, and your transformation reaches even the *xiāo* and *wěi* grasses. Medicinal fungi flourish in the chambers of the mountains, and flowers bloom from the surging well.

In the pleasure groves, herds of animals roam in harmony; in the mountain ravines, birds nest and their songs resonate with the musical scales. Purple essences float upon the pearl palaces, and white clouds drift over the jade seals.

Thus, one gardens by the Weak Tree and pools at the Mōngfàn Sea; one cultivates the Fiery Fire Mountain and illuminates the accumulated ice; one ascends the Red Slope to receive the northern winds and crosses the Azure Trench to reach the distant shores. These matters exceed the records of former sages and are beyond the archives of old offices—how could they be compared to the Han dynasty’s opening of Zhang’an, which merely bordered the Golden Wall, or the Qin garrisons at Guilin, which only reached the Pearl Bay?

I, Xuanzang, am fortunate to have lived during the upright reign of the Heavenly Sovereign and the Earthly Ruler, when both the Chinese and the barbarians enjoy tranquility. I dare to align my mind with the realm of the Brahmā-world, seeking to fulfill this noble endeavor; yet my life is as fleeting as morning dew, and my strength is but like that of an autumn locust.

Relying solely upon the majestic spiritual power of the Emperor, my body drifted and my shadow advanced as I wandered through lands of prostration and roamed beyond distant postal stations; there, the giant eggs of Tiaozhi finally verified what I had previously heard, and the solitary luan bird of Jibin allowed me to confirm ancient truths.

As time passed and years accumulated, human aspirations were answered by Heaven; thus, we were able to descend from the snowy peaks to float upon the Tīrthika River, gaze upon the Crane Grove, and behold Vulture Peak. The paths of Jetavana still exist in their general outlines, and the foundations of the Royal City remain as undulating mounds.

In my quest for travel and observation, as the seasons have passed and time has shifted, I have returned to the imperial capital after more than twelve years; during this period, I have heard of and visited one hundred and twenty-eight kingdoms.
I humbly consider that while Zhang Yan’s account merely sets forth vast distances in the void, and Kuafu’s exploits merely traverse the land without describing its local customs;
Ban Chao has been enfeoffed as a marquis yet remains far from his destination, and Zhang Qian has gazed upon distant lands yet his knowledge is not comprehensive.
What is now recorded differs from what was previously heard.

Although I have not yet reached the furthest reaches of the Great Thousand Worlds, I have explored the regions beyond the Pamirs; all of this is based on factual records, and I dare not employ flowery embellishments.
I have respectfully compiled and edited this work, entitled *The Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, in twelve volumes, transcribed as presented here.

I hope that it may be circulated by the imperial scribes and adorned with the refined language of the court, so as to eclipse the encyclopedic learning of the ministers of the Jin dynasty and expand the legacy of the Nine Mountains under Your Majesty’s reign.

"However, Xuanzang’s intellectual capacity and knowledge are shallow and limited; my omissions are truly many, and moreover, I am unskilled in composition. I fear there is nothing here worth perusing.
On the Bingshen day, the Emperor personally replied in his own hand, writing:
"I have examined your letter and fully understood your intent."

The Dharma Master early on displayed lofty conduct and emerged from the mundane world at an early age. He launched the precious vessel to reach the other shore and sought the wondrous Way to open the gates of the Dharma. He propagated the Great Design and washed away the multitude of transgressions. Therefore, when the clouds of compassion were about to roll up, he unfurled them to provide shade across the four voids; when the sun of wisdom was about to dim, he brightened it to illuminate the eight extremities. That which unfurls and brightens—can it be anyone other than the Dharma Master?

"My learning is shallow and my mind is clumsy; I am still deluded regarding worldly affairs, let alone the profound and subtle mysteries of the Buddha-dharma, which I could never hope to fathom. To request that you provide a title for this scripture was not something I ever imagined."
Furthermore, it was said: "The newly compiled *Record of the Western Regions* should be perused by Your Majesty; I request that you issue an imperial decree for Master Xuanzang.
On the day of Dingyou, the Dharma Master submitted a second memorial, saying:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks."
I have humbly received Your Majesty’s written edict, which graciously bestows encouragement and instruction; I reverently uphold these imperial words and maintain them with utmost devotion.

As for Xuanzang, my religious practice is empty and sparse, yet I have by chance joined the ranks of the monastic community. Fortunately, the nine seas are now unified and the four quarters are free from peril; thus, relying on the Imperial majesty, I have traveled afar, and depending on the state’s prestige, I have sought the Way. Though I have braved distant frontiers and perils to exert my humble sincerity, and though I have compiled rare texts and harbored thoughts of the remote lands, this was truly made possible through the transformative influence of the Court.
The sutras and śāstras that have been obtained and commissioned for translation have already been completed as scrolls, yet they remain without commentaries or prefaces.

We humbly observe that Your Majesty’s sagely thoughts unfold like spreading clouds and your celestial brilliance blazes like radiant flowers; your principles encompass the *Xi* and *Xiang* trigrams, and your diction is so transcendent it forms a masterpiece. You have spread your fame across the ages and surpassed a hundred kings with your enduring achievements. We venture to suggest that since spiritual power is boundless, nothing short of divine thought is sufficient to evaluate its principles; and since the holy teachings are profound and remote, nothing but sacred composition can elucidate their source.

Therefore, I have ventured to offend Your Majesty’s august dignity by daring to hope for a title; yet Your Imperial Mien remains profound and remote, and you have not deigned to grant me your compassionate favor. As I reflect upon myself, my breath falters repeatedly, and looking about, I am at a loss for what to do.

Xuanzang has heard that when the sun and moon adorn the heavens, they already distribute their radiance through doors and windows; when rivers and streams mark the earth, they likewise flow with moisture over rocky cliffs. The music of the Yunhe court does not withhold its resonance from the deaf and ignorant, nor do gold, jade, and rare treasures conceal their brilliance from the foolish and blind.
Venturing to rely upon this principle, I again offer my earnest entreaty.

I humbly beseech you to extend your grace like rain and thunder, and to look down with your celestial brilliance; may [the Emperor] endure as long as the Two Polarities and hang suspended together with the Two Luminaries.

Thus, the subtle words of Vulture Peak were made far-reaching by relying on the divine pen, and the profound scriptures of the Chicken Garden were proclaimed through inspired compositions; how could it be that only the limited assembly of Brahmā alone bears this grace and glory, when all sentient beings, however deluded, are now able to transcend the burdens of the mundane world?
From this point on, he was finally permitted [to proceed].
In the spring of the twenty-second year, the Emperor visited the Yuhua Palace.
On the day of Jiawu in the fifth month of summer, the translation of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* was completed, totaling one hundred fascicles.
On the day of Gengchen in the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued summoning the Dharma Master to the palace.
From the time he set out until his arrival on the road, messengers arrived repeatedly,
ordering him to proceed slowly and not to exhaust himself.
Upon his arrival, he was received in the Yu Hua Palace, where the Emperor was greatly pleased.
The Emperor said:

"While in the capital, I suffered from the summer heat; therefore, I have come to this mountain palace. Since the springs and rocks here are cool, my physical strength has improved somewhat, allowing me to attend to the affairs of state."
"However, as I am mindful of the Dharma Master, I have sent word to request your presence; you will surely undergo great fatigue traveling the road.

The Dharma Master declined, saying, "The common people of the four seas depend upon Your Majesty for their livelihood; if Your Holiness is not at ease, the entire realm will be filled with trepidation."
I humbly hear that Your Imperial Majesty has arrived here and that Your Majesty’s meals are now at ease; among all sentient beings who share in this life, who would not leap for joy?
I pray that Your Majesty may forever preserve your exalted station, enduring as long as heaven itself.
"Xuanzang am humble and unworthy, yet I have been undeservedly summoned; bearing this honor, I do not perceive it as toil.

The Emperor, noting that the Dharma Master’s learning was comprehensive and his deportment profound, frequently considered pressuring him to return to secular life so that he might be kept at his side to deliberate on state affairs.
When I previously had the honor of an audience at the Luoyang Palace, we discussed this in person.
On this occasion, he spoke again, saying:

"In the past, among the sovereigns such as Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, and the rulers of the Great Zhou and the Flourishing Han, there were none who did not consider that the realm was vast and the myriad affairs of state were numerous. Since two eyes cannot survey everything and a single mind is difficult to employ for solitary discernment, Zhou relied upon the 'Ten Chaos' and Shun entrusted himself to the 'Five Ministers,' so that they might assist in illuminating the imperial policies and harmonize the governance of the state."
If even those enlightened kings and sagely rulers relied upon the multitude of worthies, how much more so should I, a solitary and ignorant one, not entrust myself to the assembly of the wise?

It is my wish that the Dharma Master might cast off the dyed robes of Subhūti and don the plain garments of Vimalakīrti; ascending the path of the prime minister to present counsel, and sitting in the court of the *huái* trees to discourse on the Way. What do you think of this?
The Dharma Master replied:
"Your Majesty speaks truly.

The realm is vast and its affairs manifold; even the sovereigns of the Three Dynasties and Five Emperors could not maintain it alone. It was entrusted to worthy sages and philosophers, who together brought it to completion."
Zhongni also said that when the ruler fails, the minister succeeds; thus, the ruler is the head and the minister is the limbs.
Xuanzang maintains that these words were intended as a warning for those of mediocre capacity, not for those of superior wisdom.

If it were the case that all ministers must be capable, how could Jie and Zhou have had no ministers? By this reasoning, it is not necessarily so. I humbly reflect that Your Majesty is a sovereign of supreme wisdom; as the sole arbiter of the state’s governance, all affairs naturally find their proper order.

Moreover, since You began your reign, Heaven and Earth have been at peace and prosperous, and both the inner and outer realms have enjoyed tranquility and serenity. All of this is due to Your Majesty’s avoidance of negligence, licentiousness, vanity, and extravagance; Your constant vigilance and earnestness, Your refusal to rest even when there is cause for rest, and Your contemplation of danger while dwelling in safety—all of which result from Your practice of virtue in receiving the Mandate of Heaven. What else has anything to do with it?
Please distinguish between two or three points to clarify this matter.

Your Majesty’s strategic mastery over the eight expanses, your ability to harness the talents of heroes and sages, your merit in quelling calamities and rebellions, your promotion and expansion of the era of peace and prosperity, your virtue of sagacity, literary brilliance, and profound reflection, and your physical bearing that embodies the primal source and accords with the ultimate—these are all bestowed by Heaven and do not depend on others; in their significance, they are one and the same.

To honor the fundamental while discarding the peripheral, to esteem benevolence and ritual, to transform the decadent customs of later times and restore the pure governance of the High Sovereign; to follow parsimonious regulations in taxation and apply lenient statutes in criminal law, so that all sentient beings throughout the nine provinces and the four seas may alike bathe in the waves of grace and achieve peace and happiness—this is yet another instance where the Sage’s supreme transformation relies on nothing other than his own person; this is the second principle.

The Ultimate Way is universally pervasive and profound benevolence reaches far and wide: to the east it surpasses the realm of the sun; to the west it extends beyond Mount Kunlun; to the south it exhausts the Land of Fire; and to the north it reaches the furthest dark frontiers. Among the customs of those who pierce their feet and drink from their noses, and among the people who wear grass garments with lapels on the left—there are none who do not await the wind and observe the rain, prostrating themselves with bowed heads and kneeling knees, offering rare treasures and precious gems that fill the guest houses of the barbarians. This, moreover, is moved by the majesty of Heaven and requires no human artifice; this is the third significance.

The Xianyun have been a source of affliction for a long time; they were subjects whom even the Five Emperors could not bring under their sway, and a power that the Three Kings could not restrain. Consequently, the regions of the Yellow and Luo Rivers became lands of disheveled hair, and Feng and Hao became fields for whistling arrows. As the Central Kingdom declined, the Xiongnu gained the upper hand—a situation that has remained unaltered since the Shang and Zhou dynasties.
When Emperor Wu of Han exhausted his military forces and Wei Qing and Huo Qubing exerted their utmost efforts, although they cleared away the branches and leaves, the root still remained.
Since that time, no sound strategy has been heard of.

When Your Majesty took up the task of governance, this [rebellious] faction was utterly exterminated in a single campaign; their nests were overturned and their lairs demolished, leaving not a single soul remaining. The regions of the Washed Sea and Mount Yanran were all incorporated into the imperial domains, and the archers and cavalry of the Shanyu were all enrolled as subjects.
