If one were to say it depends on ministers, then since the times of Yu and Xia there have been many worthy aides; why then was [the Way] not attained?
Therefore, we know that when the Way exists, it is attained, and it does not depend on others—this is the fourth principle.

Goryeo was a minor vassal state that failed to observe the rites due to the Superior State; the Emperor of Sui assembled the armies of the entire world and campaigned against it three times to punish them. Yet, he could not damage even half a battlement in his sieges, nor did he capture a single person during his raids on the wilds; his six armies were wasted in vain, and he returned in a state of desperate disarray.

Your Majesty briefly led several tens of thousands of cavalry, crushing the formidable array at Zhubì and breaching the impregnable fortresses of Liáo and Gài; returning in triumph with the army, you captured three hundred thousand of the enemy.

The methods for employing troops and commanding generals do not differ; yet the Sui dynasty perished because of them, while the Tang dynasty gained [the empire] because of them. Thus we know that it depends upon the sovereign and requires no other person; this is the fifth principle.

Furthermore, it was as when heaven and earth are in harmonious balance (tai), the sun and moon radiate their brilliance, and the vital energy (heqi) swirls in abundance; auspicious clouds gather in profusion, the five spiritual creatures manifest their forms, and the single-horned unicorn displays its wonders. White wolves, white foxes, vermilion pheasants, and vermilion grasses appeared in such dazzling profusion that they could not be fully enumerated—countless billions of them. All these arrived in response to virtue, without depending on human artifice.
To wish to emulate the former kings and entrust your achievements to ten ministers is, in my humble opinion, something Your Majesty should not adopt.
Even if you require such men, there are currently many who are the equals of Yi Yin and Lü Shang.
I, Xuanzang, am mediocre and unworthy; how could I be deemed fit to participate in this?

Nevertheless, to observe the precepts within the monastic community and to propagate the bequeathed Dharma is my lifelong aspiration. I humbly beseech Your Majesty’s compassionate grace to grant me leave to fulfill it until the end, without depriving me of this opportunity.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.

He said to the Dharma Master, "What you have just described was entirely due to the grace bestowed from on high by the Supreme Mystery, the spiritual power of the ancestral temple, and the efforts of the ministers; how could I, the Emperor, have been able to achieve it?"
"Since you wish to propagate the wondrous Way and do not contravene your lofty aspirations, you may exert yourself; from this day forward, I shall also assist you, Master, in spreading the Way.
Shi Yancong’s commentary states:

"The Dharma Master’s talent encompasses both the inner and outer teachings. His eloquence in responding to immediate challenges is as refined and comprehensive as this—how difficult it is to find such a person!"

In the past, when Dao’an offered his remonstrance, Fu Jian’s carriage did not halt; when Daoheng and Daobiao exerted their eloquence, Yao Xing’s mind would not be turned. In the end, they suffered the disgrace of a defeated army and the hardship of flight.

How could it be otherwise? As soon as the Dharma Master’s elegant discourse was set forth, the Emperor’s heart was fully satisfied; his pure influence became ever more refined, and his noble aspirations surpassed all in their integrity.
Speaking from this perspective, one need not trouble oneself with further deliberation for the superiority or inferiority to become manifest.
At that time, the Director of the Secretariat, Chu Suiliang, memorialized, saying:

"Now that the four seas are cleared of turmoil and the nine provinces are peaceful and tranquil, all is due to Your Majesty’s sagely virtue. This truly accords with the Master’s words; we ministers merely occupy our positions."
"Under the sun and moon, what merit can a firefly or a torch possibly have?
The Emperor smiled and said, "It is not so."
Now, a precious fur robe is not made from the armpit of a single fox, and a great mansion must necessarily be completed by many materials combined.
How could there be a ruler who can achieve success alone?
Your Teacher wishes to preserve his own refined integrity; therefore, he has merely allowed himself to be lavishly adorned by you.
The Emperor again asked the Dharma Master,
"What sutras and śāstras have you recently translated? He replied:
"Having recently finished translating the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it consists of one hundred fascicles.
The Emperor asked, "This treatise is extremely vast; which sage did it proclaim?"
Furthermore, what meaning does this clarify? The answer is:
"This treatise was spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva; it clarifies the meaning of the Seventeen Grounds."
He asked again:
"What are called the seventeen stages? He replied:

That is to say: the stage associated with the five consciousnesses, the stage associated with the mental consciousness, the stage with vitarka and vicāra, the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra, the stage without vitarka and without vicāra, the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita), the stage not in meditative equipoise, the stage with mind, the stage without mind, the stage consisting of what is heard (śruta-maya), the stage consisting of what is reflected upon (cintā-maya), the stage consisting of what is cultivated (bhāvanā-maya), the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, the stage with remainder (sopadhi-śeṣa), and the stage without remainder (nirupadhi-śeṣa).
He then set forth the fundamental principles and key points, enumerating the great meanings.
The Emperor held him in profound esteem and dispatched an envoy to the capital to fetch the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

When the *Śāstra* arrived, the Emperor examined it in detail himself; beholding its profound and far-reaching terminology and meaning, which was unlike anything he had ever heard before, he sighed and said to his attendants:
"In my study of the Buddhist scriptures, it is like gazing at the heavens or looking out upon the sea—I cannot fathom their height or depth."

That you, Dharma Master, were able to obtain this profound Dharma in a foreign land is truly remarkable. Lately, as military and state affairs have been so pressing, I have not had the opportunity to investigate the Buddhist teachings in depth.

Now, observing them, I find their fundamental source to be vast and remote, its limits impossible to fathom; when compared with the nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism, they are like small ponds and marshes set against the vast expanse of the ocean.
"Furthermore, the worldly claim that the three teachings lead to the same goal is but a false discourse.

Thereupon, he issued an edict to the relevant authorities to have the scribes of the Secretariat copy the newly translated sutras and treatises in nine versions. These were to be circulated sequentially throughout the nine provinces of Yong, Luo, Bing, Yuan, Xiang, Jing, Yang, Liang, and Yi, so that all people within the realm might together receive the meanings they had never before heard.
At that time, Minister of Education Duke Zhao, Changsun Wuji, and Chief Secretary Chu Suiliang, among others, submitted this memorial:
"Your servant has heard that the Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious, beyond the comprehension of gods or men; its essence is extremely deep, and its gates are difficult to enter."

We humbly observe that Your Majesty’s supreme Way is brilliantly illuminated, its soaring radiance outshining the sun; your bounty moistens the farthest realms, and your transformation overflows the central lands. You uphold the five vehicles and establish the Three Jewels; thus it was that the Dharma Master, possessing an eminent nature during this age of decline, emerged as a prodigy after a millennium of separation, traversing treacherous obstacles to seek the scriptures and braving perilous paths to inquire after the Way.

Having beheld rare and extraordinary customs and obtained the authentic scriptures in their entirety, I have returned to my country to translate and proclaim them; they are as if the teachings were first expounded in the Jeta Grove, and their refined phrasing and profound meanings are as if newly opened by the Golden Mouth—this is entirely due to the inspiration of Your Majesty’s sagely virtue.
We, your humble and ignorant servants, having been privileged to witness and hear this, find a vessel upon which to rely amidst the surging waves of the sea of suffering.
Furthermore, through Your Majesty’s vast and far-reaching compassion, it is being spread throughout the nine provinces, so that all the teeming masses may partake together in the wondrous Dharma.
"We ministers have encountered this with great rarity over billions of kalpas; we cannot express our boundless fortune," they said.
The Emperor replied, "This is due to the power of the Dharma Master’s great compassion and vow, as well as the accumulated merit of you all from past lives; it is not something achieved by me alone."

The Emperor had previously promised to compose a preface for the new translation of the sutra, but as his official duties were so numerous and pressing, he had not yet found the opportunity to apply his mind to it.
Upon the Dharma Master’s renewed request, he finally took up the brush.

In a short while it was completed, titled "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang," consisting of seven hundred and eighty-one characters. Written in his own divine hand, the Emperor decreed that it be placed at the head of all the scriptures.

The Emperor was residing in the Qingfu Hall, attended by his officials and guards. He ordered the Dharma Master to take his seat and commanded Shang Guan Yi, a scholar of the Hongwen Academy, to proclaim the preface he had composed before the assembly of ministers. It was as radiant as clouds and as expansive as brocade, reaching the height of laudatory expression.
The text says:

"I have heard that the Two Polarities possess form, manifesting their covering and bearing to contain all living beings; the Four Seasons possess no shape, secretly alternating cold and heat to transform all things."

Therefore, when observing heaven and examining earth, even the mediocre and the ignorant can recognize their general outlines; yet when clarifying the yin and penetrating the yang, even the wise and the sagacious rarely exhaust their numerical permutations.
Nevertheless, heaven and earth encompass yin and yang and are easily recognized because they possess form;
yin and yang reside within heaven and earth but are difficult to exhaustively fathom because they are formless.

Thus we know that when the manifestations of the Buddha’s image are visible and can be verified, even the ignorant are not deluded; yet when his form is hidden and cannot be seen, even the wise remain confused. How much more so for the Buddha-way, which honors the sublime void and rides upon the profound to govern the silent; it broadly saves the myriad species and presides over the ten directions. Its majestic spirit is unsurpassed, and its divine power is beyond measure. On a grand scale, it pervades the universe; on a minute scale, it encompasses even a hair’s breadth. It is without cessation and without birth, remaining as ancient as ever through a thousand kalpas. Whether hidden or manifest, it mobilizes a hundred blessings to endure forever. The wondrous Way is concentrated and mysterious—those who follow it do not know its limits; the flow of the Dharma is deep and tranquil—those who draw from it cannot fathom its source. Therefore, one knows that even the most dull-witted and common folk, if they cast themselves into its essential purpose, can surely be free from doubt.

Thus, the rise of the Great Teaching was founded in the Western Land; it leaped across to the Han court, illuminating it through a brilliant dream, and shone upon the Eastern Realm, flowing with compassion.

In former times, when its forms and traces were yet divided, transformation was achieved even before words could spread; in an age where the eternal and the manifest were ever-present, people looked up to its virtue and knew how to follow it.

When the shadows fade and he returns to the Truth, and his physical form passes into another age, the golden countenance hides its luster and no longer mirrors the light of the three thousand worlds; yet when the beautiful image is revealed in the painting, the thirty-two marks of perfection appear at the tip of the void.

Thus, the subtle words spread far and wide, rescuing all sentient beings from the three miserable paths; the bequeathed instructions were proclaimed to distant lands, guiding the multitudes of living beings toward the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Nevertheless, the true teaching is difficult to look up to, as none can unify its ultimate aim; whereas deviant studies are easy to follow, whereby the heterodox and the orthodox become thereby entangled and confused.

Thus, regarding the debates between emptiness and existence, people have alternately judged them right or wrong according to custom; and as for the Great and Small Vehicles, they have flourished or declined in accordance with the times.
There was a Dharma Master named Xuanzang, who was a leader of the Dharma gate.

In his youth, he harbored integrity and acuity, early on awakening to the mind of the Three Emptinesses; as he grew, he harmonized with the spirit of the Way, first encompassing the practice of the Four Endurances.

The pines, waters, moonlight, and mists are insufficient to compare with his purity and brilliance; how could the dew from the immortals or bright pearls equal his radiant lucidity? Thus, through wisdom he attained freedom from entanglement, and through his spirit he fathomed the unmanifest; transcending the six sense-objects, he stands far beyond them, and throughout the ages, he remains without peer.

Concentrating his mind upon the inner realm, he grieved at the decline of the True Dharma; dwelling his thoughts within the profound gateway, he lamented the errors and corruptions of the deep scriptures.

Desiring to categorize the sections and analyze the principles, he sought to broaden what had been heard before, cutting away the false and continuing the true, thereby opening the way for future students.
Therefore, with a mind uplifted toward the Pure Land, he journeyed to the Western Regions; braving perils, he traveled afar, and leaning on his staff, he marched alone.

In the mornings, accumulated snow flew, obscuring the path and causing him to lose his way; in the evenings, startled sands rose, clouding the sky and disorienting him regarding the heavens. Across ten thousand li of mountains and rivers, he pushed forward through mist and clouds; through a hundred cycles of cold and heat, he pressed on through frost and dew.
Valuing sincerity above all and regarding toil as light, he sought what was profound with the aspiration that his wishes be fulfilled.
He traveled throughout the Western regions for seventeen years, traversing to the limits of the lands where the Way prevails, inquiring after and seeking the True Teaching.

At the Twin Trees and the Eight Waters, we tasted the flavor of the Way and feasted upon its breeze; at the Deer Park and Vulture Peak, we gazed upon wonders and looked up to marvels. We received the ultimate words from the former sages and accepted the true teachings from the supreme worthies. Probing the subtle gates of the Dharma, we exhaustively mastered its profound practices;
the path of the One Vehicle and the Five Vinayas gallops through the field of the mind, while the texts of the Eight Collections and Three Baskets surge like billows within the ocean of our speech.

From the countries he visited, he brought back a total of six hundred and fifty-seven essential texts from the Tripiṭaka, which he translated and disseminated throughout the Middle Kingdom to propagate these supreme works.

He draws the compassionate clouds from the western extremity and pours down the rain of Dharma upon the eastern borders; the sacred teachings that had been fragmented are restored to their wholeness, and the sentient beings who were burdened by sin are returned to the state of blessing. He moistens the parching flames of the burning house so that all may be extricated from the path of delusion, and he clarifies the murky waves of the waters of craving so that all may together reach the further shore.
Thus we know that one falls due to the karma of evil causes, while one ascends by virtue of wholesome conditions; the point of ascent or descent depends solely upon what a person relies upon.
It is like the cassia tree growing on a high peak, which only when drenched by clouds and dew can its blossoms be moistened;
or the lotus emerging from green waves, whose leaves cannot be defiled by flying dust.

It is not that the nature of the lotus is inherently pure or that the substance of the cassia is fundamentally upright; rather, it is because when that which one is attached to is lofty, even minute things cannot defile one, and when that which one relies upon is pure, even turbid things cannot taint one.
Now, if even insentient plants and trees depend upon goodness to become good, how much more so should sentient human beings rely upon auspicious conditions to achieve auspiciousness?
I hope that this scripture shall spread its influence as boundlessly as the sun and moon, and that these blessings shall extend afar, remaining eternally vast alongside heaven and earth.
At that time, the Dharma Master, having received the Imperial composition, submitted a memorial of thanks, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.

I have humbly heard that while the six lines of the *Yi* explore the subtle, they are confined to the realm of birth and extinction; and while the correct naming of the hundred things has not yet reached the sphere of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Yet, even so, when one looks back to the records of Fuxi from afar, though one perceives their profundity, one cannot fathom their divine mystery; and when one contemplates the diagrams of Xuanyuan from afar, though one selects through the ages, all return to his excellence."

I humbly submit that Your Majesty, the Emperor, has manifested his essence from the jade-hair radiance and governs the heavens with the golden wheel. You have expanded the nine provinces of the former kings and eclipsed the light of hundreds of thousands of suns and moons; you have broadened the territories of successive dynasties and encompassed the dharma-realm as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Consequently, the Jetavana Vihāra has been incorporated into the imperial domain, and the sacred texts upon palm leaves have all been returned to the Imperial Library.

When I, Xuanzang, previously traveled with my staff raised to pay homage at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, though the journey spanned ten thousand *li*, I relied upon Your Majesty’s divine majesty so that it felt like a mere step; and without riding upon the thousand-petaled lotus, I reached the Twin Śāla Trees as if in the time of a single meal.

He searched through and exalted the Tripiṭaka, exhausting all that was stored in the Dragon Palace; he researched the One Vehicle, fathoming the bequeathed teachings from Vulture Peak. All of these were subsequently carried upon the White Horse and presented back to the Purple Palace.
I have recently received an imperial edict granting me permission to translate these works.
My understanding falls short of that of Nāgārjuna, yet I have mistakenly been honored with the glory of transmitting the Lamp;
my talent differs from that of Aśvaghoṣa, and I feel deep shame regarding my lack of the agility required for pouring from one vessel into another.

The sutras and śāstras I have translated contain many errors and omissions; consequently, I have been graced by Imperial favor, as Your Majesty has deigned to bestow His attention upon composing this preface.
Its prose transcends the *Xiang* and *Xi* hexagrams, and its principles encompass the gateway to all wonders.

Suddenly, by virtue of my meager life, I have personally received these sublime sounds; I leap for joy with boundless delight, as if hearing a prophecy of enlightenment, and I cannot contain the height of my gratitude.
I respectfully submit this memorial to the Imperial Palace to express my thanks and bring it to Your Majesty’s attention.
The Emperor reviewed the memorial and replied in his own hand with this letter:
"My talent falls short of the refined jade of the scholar-officials, and my speech is ashamed of its lack of broad erudition; as for the Inner Scriptures, I am particularly unacquainted with them."
The preface I composed yesterday was profoundly crude and clumsy; I feared only that it might defile the golden tablets with my calligraphy or cast mere rubble upon a grove of jewels.
Suddenly receiving your letter, I am mistakenly honored by your praise; yet as I examine my own conduct and reflect upon my thoughts, my embarrassment grows ever greater.
"It is truly not worthy of mention; you have needlessly troubled yourself by offering thanks.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll Six.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll [Six].
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili, with annotations by Shi Yanzong.

From the sixth month of the twenty-second year [of Zhenguan] to the second month of spring in the fifth year of Yonghui. The Emperor’s “Record in Commemoration of the Sage” begins from the sixth month of summer in the twenty-second year and ends with the Master’s letter in response in the second month of spring in the fifth year of Yonghui. In the sixth month of summer in the twenty-second year, while the Great Emperor resided in the Spring Palace (as Crown Prince), he reverently beheld the Sacred Text and further composed the “Record in Commemoration of the Sage. Its words are as follows: [The Record follows... *Note: The original text contains a lacuna where the actual content of the "Record in Commemoration of the Sage" would have been placed.*
"To propagate the sublime teaching, there is nothing that can broaden its texts except wisdom;
to honor and expound the subtle words, none but the worthy can determine their purport.
Indeed, the holy teaching of True Suchness (Tathatā) is the profound essence of all dharmas and the guiding track of all sūtras."

Comprehensive and far-reaching in its scope, its profound principles are remote and deep; it exhausts the subtle refinements of emptiness and existence and embodies the essential pivot of arising and ceasing.

Its diction is luxuriant while its Way is vast, such that those who seek it cannot fathom its source; its phrasing is manifest while its meaning is obscure, such that those who practice it cannot measure its limits.

Thus we know that wherever the Sage’s compassion reaches, there is no wholesome karma that does not arrive; wherever his wondrous transformation is spread, there is no evil condition that is not severed.

He unfurls the mainstay of the Dharma-net and propagates the orthodox teaching of the Six Perfections; he rescues the masses from their plight like those mired in mud and fire, and opens the secret bolt of the Tripiṭaka.
Therefore, the Name has no wings yet flies forever; the Way has no roots yet remains eternally firm.
The Way and the Name flow forth blessings, remaining constant throughout the vastness of antiquity;
their responsive bodies appear according to conditions, enduring through kalpas as numerous as dust motes without decay.
Morning bells and evening chants intermingle their two sounds upon Vulture Peak; the Sun of Wisdom and the Dharma-stream turn their twin wheels in the Deer Park.
Jewel canopies reaching to the void fly together with soaring clouds; the spring forests adorning the wilds blend their colors with celestial flowers.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty, the Emperor, has received blessings from the High Mystery and governs the eight wildernesses with ease;
your virtue covers the common people, and the myriad nations bow their heads in court.
His grace bestowed upon these decaying bones as the texts of the *palm-leaf* scriptures returned to the stone chambers;
his bounty extended even to insects as the verses of the *Brahma-teachings* flowed from the golden caskets.
Thus, the waters of Lake Anavatapta were made to join the eight rivers of the divine realm, and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was brought to touch the verdant ridges of Mount Song and Mount Hua.
I humbly consider that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and tranquil; there is nothing that does not respond to a devoted heart.
The ground of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*) is mysterious and abstruse; it becomes manifest through the arousal of sincere earnestness.

How could one have expected that the light of the torch of wisdom would illuminate the night of deep darkness, or that the moisture of the Dharma rain would descend upon the morning of the burning house?
Thus, the myriad streams of a hundred rivers flow differently yet converge together in the sea; the distinct meanings of ten thousand regions are synthesized into a single reality.
How could this be compared to weighing the merits of Tang and Wu, or matching their sagely virtue with that of Yao and Shun?

Master Xuanzang was innately endowed with sagacity and refinement; he established his resolve in a state of simplicity and detachment. Even in his childhood, his spirit was pure, and his character transcended the world of vanity and ostentation. He concentrated his mind within the chamber of meditative concentration and concealed his traces in secluded crags. Dwelling in the third dhyāna and traversing the ten stages (*bhūmi*), he transcended the realm of the six sense-objects and walked alone through Kapilavastu. Having realized the purport of the One Vehicle, he transformed sentient beings according to their capacities.
Relying on the lack of substantiality in China, I sought the true texts of India; traveling far across the Ganges, my ultimate aim was the *pūrṇa-akṣara* (the full syllable).
Ascending the Snowy Mountains repeatedly, I further obtained the *ardha-ratna* (the half-jewel).
He traveled back and forth between China and India for seventeen years, thoroughly mastering the Buddhist scriptures with the aim of benefiting all beings.

On the sixth day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he received an imperial decree to translate essential texts of the Holy Teachings at Hongfu Monastery, totaling six hundred and fifty-seven works.

Drawing forth the dharma-streams of the great ocean, they wash away the dust of worldly toil without exhaustion; transmitting the long-flaming torch of wisdom, they illuminate the profound darkness with eternal clarity. Were it not for those who have long planted superior roots of merit, how could this profound purpose be so widely proclaimed?

That which is called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding, equaling the brilliance of the three luminaries; our Sovereign’s fortune has reached its zenith, sharing the stability of the two polarities.

I humbly observe the Imperial Prefaces to the Various Sutras and Treatises, which illuminate antiquity and soar through the present; their principles possess the resonance of metal and stone, and their prose embraces the moisture of wind and clouds.
I have treated this by adding a light speck of dust to a mountain peak and a falling drop of dew to a flowing stream; I have briefly set forth the general outline to compose this record.
The Dharma Master submitted a memorial of thanks, saying:
“Xuanzang has heard that when the seven luminaries spread their radiance, they rely upon the high heavens to disperse their brilliance;”
The waters of the Nine Rivers spread their moisture and flow through because they rely upon the thick earth.

Thus we know that the beauty of mutual dependence is evident even in the realm of material things; how much more so when the propagation of the Dharma relies upon people—the principle here is beyond doubt.

I humbly observe that Your Highness, the Crown Prince, has brought forth your sagely compositions and once again recounted the celestial texts, extolling the Mahāyāna and adorning the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Like pearls revolving and jade turning, like radiant clouds and unfolding brocade, you join in splendor with the sun and moon and harmonize in melody with the *Xian* and *Shao* music.
"I, Xuanzang, am fortunate to have lived long enough to be bathed in Your Majesty’s extraordinary grace; I am overwhelmed with gratitude and offer this memorial to express my thanks.
At that time, an imperial decree was issued, stating:
"I, [the Emperor], have always lacked talent and learning, and by nature am not quick-witted."
I have not yet had the opportunity to examine the various texts of the Inner Canon; thus, the prefaces and records I have composed have been particularly crude and prolix.
Having suddenly received your letter, which offers such praise and commendation, I look upon myself with self-reflection, and a mixture of shame and trepidation overwhelms me.
"That you, Master Lao and others, have traveled from so far away, fills me with deep shame. Shi Yancong’s commentary states:

"Since the two Sages’ Prefaces were issued, princes, high officials, monastics, laypeople, and the common folk have danced for joy and chanted the virtuous edict. Both within and without, it was proclaimed and celebrated; in less than ten days, it had reached the six directions of the world. The cloud of compassion once again provided shade, and the sun of wisdom shone brightly once more; those who took refuge in the Dharma came in waves and gathered like mist."
What is called "the superior transforming the inferior" is like the wind bending the grass—is this not precisely what that refers to?
It is for this very reason that the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to kings.
At that time, Yuan-ding, the abbot of Hongfu Monastery, along with the monks of the capital city, requested that both prefaces be engraved upon metal and stone to be preserved within the monastery.
The Emperor approved this.
Subsequently, the temple monks Huai-ren and others collected the calligraphic works of Wang Xizhi, the Right Army General of the Jin dynasty, and engraved them upon stone steles.

On the day of Gengchen, the Crown Prince, because Empress Wen-de Sheng had departed this world while he was still young, sought to repay her boundless grace by promoting meritorious works in her honor. He dispatched the Grand Master of the Palace (Zhongdafu), serving as Right Attendant-in-Ordinary (Youshuzi), His Subject Gao Jifu, to proclaim an edict, saying:

"I, your servant, am unfortunate; the weight of calamity and reproach has fallen upon me. Before I had reached the age of reason, my compassionate countenance abandoned me. This lifelong sorrow pierces my heart ever more deeply; the bitterness of 'wind and tree' (the mourning for one's parents) cuts to the bone, its depth unfathomable."

Whenever the anniversary of his passing arrived, I was moved by seasonal sentiment; my longing to ascend the hill to see him remained empty, and my grief for the "cold spring" grew ever more poignant.

Soon, however, the music of the flute and song faded away, and I could no longer attend to his needs; I could only contemplate repaying the vast bounty of Heaven, with no way to manifest the affection of a filial crow.
I humbly consider that the great compassion of the Path of Enlightenment truly relies upon the merit of the unseen realm; thus, wishing to express my filial devotion, I take refuge therein.

It is fitting that the relevant authorities select one of the former abandoned temples within the capital and, for the sake of Empress Dowager Wen-de, promptly establish it as a monastery for the Sangha.
On the day the temple is completed, I shall specially ordain monks.
Furthermore, I command that it incorporate forests and springs, striving to exhaust every scenic excellence.
Thus, I look up to the fruit of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, fulfilling this boundless filial devotion.

Thereupon, the officials carefully selected an excellent site and proceeded to construct it within Jinchang Ward to the south of the palace city, facing the Quqi Pond and relying upon the former Jetavana Monastery.

Observing the stars and measuring the terrain, it was modeled after the celestial palaces and patterned after the Jetavana Garden; the exquisite craftsmanship of Bān and Chuí was exhausted, and the finest timbers from Mount Héng and Mount Huò were utilized. Stones with intricate patterns, cypress, camphor, *lǔ*, paulownia, and *bīngzhū* trees provided its materials, while pearls, jade, cinnabar, vermilion, gold, and emeralds furnished its adornments.

There were multi-storied towers and double-tiered halls, cloud-like pavilions and cavernous chambers, comprising some ten or more courtyards in total, with one thousand eight hundred and ninety-seven rooms; beds, bedding, and utensils were all fully provided and abundant.
The Emperor Wenwu Sheng further read the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* presented by the Dharma Master; admiring it, he consequently commanded the Heir Apparent to compose a postscript for the sutra.
The words therein say:
"We have heard that from the time of Fuxi down to the most recent emperors, the essence of their wisdom was exhausted in the patterns upon tortoise shells;
from the time of Emperor Xuanyuan, who penetrated the profound, the subtle mysteries were fully explored in the bird-script characters."
Examining the "Cinnabar Books" to seek out their hidden mysteries, one remains profoundly ignorant of the source of actual reality;
consulting the "Green Anomalies" to investigate the subtle nuances of things, this is clearly not the Way of eternal bliss.
Nevertheless, these matters have illuminated the annals and histories, spreading the fragrance of the "Warm Wind" across the eight extremities of the earth.
Your Virtue permeates all living beings, stirring waves of influence that ripple through ten thousand generations.

We humbly reflect: Your Majesty, the Emperor, turns the wheel of Dharma while sitting with hands folded, and your transformation gradually reaches the Kukkutārāma; you occupy the sublime palace with the jade crown upon your brow, yet your spirit communes with Vulture Peak. To encompass the title of "Tamer of Men" (Vināyaka) is beyond what mere literary thought can fathom;
to integrate the Prajñāpāramitā into your imperial edicts is something no depiction in symbols could ever emulate.

Consequently, as this teaching spread beyond the reaches of the ocean, the sounds of the Eight Liberations were transmitted everywhere; as its instruction permeated the world within the universe, all followed the path of the Four Dhyānas.
Thus, it came to pass that throughout the three thousandfold dharma-realm, every living being was worthy of being enfeoffed;
and across the ten billion Mount Sumerus, each entered the imperial domain to serve as a guardian of the realm.
The waters of the Nairañjanā River are near the azure pools of the royal capital; the Jetavana Grove at Śrāvastī adjoins the lush gardens of the Imperial Forest.
Although the nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, it necessarily responds to conditions; though the True Vehicle is profound and subtle, there is no hidden depth that it does not illuminate.
What is called the Great Power presiding over the throne guides the flow of the Dharma without end;

the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) sustains the destiny of the age, brushing against the kalpa-stone without exhaustion. Their essence is equally endowed with the marks of perfection and is inconceivable; when compared to former kings, how can they be spoken of as being of the same rank?
Since the beginning of creation, the land was bounded by shifting sands, and while China had not yet been unified, the sacred texts remained hidden.
King Han’s refined resonance invoked a dream of the profound heavens;
Emperor Jin’s earnest sincerity brought the Sūtras down upon the White Horse.
To take a sip from a single conch shell, how could one reach the shores of the four seas?
To employ the analogy of peering through a tube, how could one exhaustively fathom the depths of the seven luminaries?
Yet, as imperial majesty spreads afar, its power extends beyond the Iron Ring Mountains;
The Most Holy One has brought forth his illumination, and his virtue extends even to the limits of the Vajra realm.

Throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all have universally adopted the scholar’s robes and caps; the gate of liberation has been opened, and the path of reality has been trodden. Verses expounded by Brahmā in the Dragon Palaces have surely gathered at the Hall of Clarity, and the texts of the Lion’s Roar upon the *Baiye* (Palm) leaves have all returned to the Imperial Library.

Sprinkling this nectar of immortality, it universally moistens sprouts and stalks; hanging down these clouds of wisdom, they pervasively drench all that flies and crawls. Is this not indeed the sublime karma of taking refuge, and the miraculous response of sagely governance?
Now, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* is the essential tenet of the Great Awakened One’s doctrinal tradition.
By practicing this path, the Buddha realized non-arising;
by receiving and upholding it, Bodhisattvas all attain the stage of non-retrogression.
These serve as the essential supports for the six *pāramitās* and fully equip one with the roots and powers of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Indeed, they are the ferry for crossing to the other shore and the ladder and vessel for attaining perfect enlightenment.
During the Zhèngguān era, the land of India submitted to our rule; crossing the Hot Slope, they received the imperial calendar, and traversing the Hanging Bridge, they brought tribute.
As the civilizing system and written tracks became unified, the roads were free of congestion.

The Śramaṇa Xuanzang, shaking his mendicant’s staff in search of the Truth, departed from the Jade Pass and traveled far across the Nālanda Garden until he reached India, the birthplace of the Malla warriors. There he sought out and obtained this scripture, which he brought back to present to the Emperor. An imperial edict was issued for its translation, and thus the work was completed.

In the intervals between my inquiries after [the Emperor's] well-being, I have clarified my mind upon the jewel of the wondrous Dharma; I respectfully transmit the Imperial Decree and offer a modest expression of praise, ordering the relevant officials to append it to the final volume.

From that time on, as the Emperor’s personal faith grew ever more profound, he deliberated upon the principles of the Dharma; his mouth never ceased praising the merit of the field of blessings. He was never for a moment separated from the Dharma Master, and by imperial decree, his provisions were increased, with robes and bedding being ordered to be replaced frequently as needed.
On the jingshen day of the seventh month in autumn, the summer retreat concluded; he further bestowed upon Dharma Master Shi a set of monastic robes (kāṣāya) worth one hundred pieces of gold.
Observing their craftsmanship, one could not discern where the needle and thread had entered or exited.

Within the Imperial Treasury, there were many offerings from previous dynasties, none of which were particularly fine; therefore, he personally instructed the ladies of the inner palace to create this [image] for his own satisfaction. After several years of labor, it was finally completed, and whenever the Emperor undertook his four great tours, he always carried it with him.

In the twenty-second year, the Emperor traveled to the Luoyang Palace. At that time, Dharma Master Daogong of Suzhou and Dharma Master Huixuan of Changzhou both possessed noble conduct; their learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular classics, and they were highly esteemed by both the court and the common people.
The Emperor summoned them.
Once they had arrived, he led them inside, seated them, and finished his address.

At that time, each of the two monks wore a *nāṃsa* robe; these had been bestowed upon their former teacher by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and were cherished as a joint treasure passed down through their lineage.
Having come to pay his respects to the Imperial countenance, he took up the monk’s robe.
The Emperor smiled at its lack of elegance, took out his own inner garment to show him, and further commanded him to compose a poem in praise of it.
The poem by Duke Gong reads:
"The field of merit supports the virtue of the image; the seeds of the Sage are cultivated through subtle, profound fragrance.
Not using gold to form the threads, yet employing colored silks to create the patterns."
"Vermilion and azure shade one another, while emerald brocades swirl in profusion; only the scattered leaves remain, forever parting along the rice terraces.
At the end of his poem, Duke Xuan wrote:
"If I might receive even a single robe from you, only then would it truly merit the name of a 'field of merit.'"
He desired them, but the Emperor granted neither; instead, he bestowed fifty rolls of silk upon each, which were used for these robes.
Their exquisite beauty was such that they were surely not fit for ordinary persons to wear, but only the Master’s profound virtue was worthy of them.
At that time, the Emperor also bestowed a razor upon the Dharma Master. The Dharma Master submitted a letter of thanks, stating:
"The śramaṇa Xuánzàng humbly acknowledges the imperial bestowal of one cassock for wearing and one razor."
Extraordinary honors have arrived in succession, and your gracious majesty is most magnificent; facing this with reverence, I am filled with trepidation, as if treading on spring ice.

Fortunately, Xuanzang has encountered your harmonious transformation and early joined the ranks of those who have stilled their minds. Yet my three karmas remain unregulated and the four debts of gratitude remain unpaid; thus, I have falsely drawn upon your heavenly regard and unworthily received your cloud-like bounty.
The robe of forbearance has its colors blending with the flowing clouds; the blade of wisdom is sharper than what cuts jade.
I shall reverently wear it to subdue the demons of affliction and fasten it on to sever the net of worldly toil.
Fearing that others would find fault with me for my own sake, and apprehensive of appearing hollow while presuming upon honor, I was filled with shame and trepidation;
I hurried along with bowed head and stooped form, my heart cowering in distress as my spirit soared away in agitation.
I am overcome with the utmost sense of awe and gratitude.
I respectfully submit this memorial of thanks for Your Majesty’s consideration.
Having troubled Your Sacred Inspection, I am deeply trembling with trepidation.

The Emperor had long been occupied with military affairs; since ascending the throne, his mind has remained fixed upon the common people. During the punitive expedition to Liaodong, he was exposed to wind and frost as if combing his hair. Since returning from that campaign, his physical strength has been considerably diminished compared to former times, leading him to harbor anxieties regarding his own life.
Having encountered the Dharma Master, he subsequently set his mind upon the Eightfold Noble Path and fortified himself with the five vehicles; thus, he was restored to health.
He then asked:
"If one wishes to plant roots of merit, what is most beneficial?"
The Dharma Master replied:
"Sentient beings sleep within delusion; were it not for wisdom, they could not be awakened.
For the sprout of wisdom to grow and flourish, the Dharma serves as its nourishment."
"The propagation of the Dharma depends upon the person; therefore, ordaining monks is the most important task.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
On the *jīmǎo* day of the ninth month in autumn, he issued an edict stating:
"In the past, at the end of the Sui dynasty, the imperial rule was lost and the world fell into fragmentation. The four seas were submerged in blood and the eight frontiers boiled like a cauldron.
I, the Emperor, was fated to quell this chaos; I personally trod the edge of battle, braving wind and frost, and spent my nights upon horseback."

Although his condition had not yet fully recovered despite the administration of medicine and tonics, he has only recently begun to regain his health; could this auspicious sign not be attributed to the influence of his merit and virtue?
"It is appropriate that five persons each be ordained at the temples in the capital and throughout all the provinces of the realm; fifty persons should be ordained at Hongfu Monastery.
Calculating the three thousand seven hundred and sixteen monasteries within the empire, this amounts to more than eighteen thousand five hundred monks and nuns ordained.

Prior to this, the monasteries throughout the empire had suffered decay and ruin during the final years of the Sui dynasty, and the ranks of the ordained were on the verge of extinction; through this single transmission, they all became a community of disciples once again.
"How magnificent!
This is why the noble person values correct speech.
The Emperor asked again:

“The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the source from which all Buddhas arise; to hear it and not slander it is a merit that surpasses the gift of one’s own body and life, far exceeding what can be attained through treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”

Furthermore, because its principles are subtle and its words concise, many worthy and enlightened gentlemen have cherished and upheld it; yet it is not known whether the text and meaning of the version translated by previous generations are complete.
The Dharma Master replied, “The merit of this sutra is indeed as Your Majesty has decreed.”
The people of the Western Regions all share this same reverence.
Now, examining the old translation, it is also seen to have slight omissions.
According to the Sanskrit original, it is fully titled "The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā that Can Sever [Delusion]," whereas the old translation simply calls it "The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā."

To clarify that for a bodhisattva, conceptual discrimination constitutes affliction, and that the delusion of such discrimination is as firm as a diamond (*vajra*), it is only the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-prajñā*) expounded in this sutra that can sever it; therefore, it is called "The Diamond Wisdom That Can Sever. Thus, we know that the old translation has lost the first two characters.
Furthermore, as in the following passages, there are instances where one of three questions is missing, one of two verses is missing, or three of nine similes are missing, and so forth.
Among these, the translation of Śrāvastī by Master Kumārajīva is acceptable, whereas that of Bhagavān by Bodhiruci is somewhat deficient.
The Emperor said:
"Since you, Master, already possess the Sanskrit original, you may translate it more thoroughly so that sentient beings may hear it in its entirety.
However, the essence of a sutra lies in its principle; there is no need to embellish the phrasing at the expense of deviating from the meaning."
Therefore, he has now newly translated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, relying closely upon the Sanskrit original.
Upon its presentation, the Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the tenth month of winter, the imperial carriage returned to the capital, and the Dharma Master also accompanied it back.

Previously, an imperial edict had been issued for the relevant authorities to construct a separate establishment to the west of the Ziwai Hall at the Northern Gate, which was named the Hongfa Monastery.
Upon his arrival, he resided there.
During the day, the Emperor would detain him for conversation; at night, he would return to the monastery to translate the scriptures.

He further translated the ten-fascicle *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* by Vasubandhu, the ten-fascicle commentary by Asvabhāva Bodhisattva, the one-fascicle *Pratītyasamutpādāryamārga-sūtra*, and the one-fascicle *Śata-dharmavidyāmukha-śāstra*.
On the day of Wushen, the Crown Prince again issued a proclamation, saying:

"The construction of Ci'en Monastery is nearing completion; its magnificent halls are about to be finished, yet the number of monks remains insufficient. I have humbly received an imperial decree to ordain three hundred monks and specially invite fifty Great Virtuous Ones (Mahāsattvas) to together attend the divine abode for the performance of the Way."

The newly established monastery should be named Daci'en Monastery; a separate Translation Hall shall be constructed, featuring magnificent rainbow-colored beams and ornate coffered ceilings, painted with clouds and mist, with jade pedestals, bronze bases, golden rings, and flower-patterned mats—all rendered exceptionally beautiful—to invite the Dharma Master to move there for his translation work, while he simultaneously assumes the administrative leadership of the monastery.
Having received the imperial decree appointing him as the *upādhyāya* (abbot), the Dharma Master submitted a memorial of refusal, stating:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang submits this.

Having humbly received the imperial decree appointing me as the *upādhyāya* of Ci'en Monastery, I respectfully hear this gracious command; my mind and spirit are at a loss for words. With bated breath and trembling, I am deeply moved by awe and trepidation."
I, Xuanzang, am devoid of scholarly achievement and my religious practice is empty and sparse; yet I dare vow to exhaust myself entirely, hoping only to provide brilliant assistance.

Relying upon the Imperial majesty, I have traveled to distant lands to seek the Way. The sūtras and śāstras I have obtained shall now be translated by imperial decree. My sincere hope is that the stream of the Dharma may gradually moisten all things, nourishing the prosperity of the imperial throne, while the holy teachings are propagated and proclaimed, bringing glory to the annals of history.

In the past, Xuanzang braved perilous paths and long suffered from chronic ailments; now that my feeble steed’s strength is exhausted, I fear I shall not complete my studies. To fail the nation’s grace would be an unforgivable offense.
Having been appointed to oversee monastic affairs, I have instead incurred severe reproach; like fish and birds whose natures are altered, I have lost my way between flight and submersion.

I humbly submit that Your Highness, the Crown Prince, possesses innate benevolence and filial piety, and your love and reverence arise from the depths of your heart. Moved by the sorrow of the wind-blown trees and bound by the pain of the cold spring, you have established this monastery to propagate great blessings. To govern the assembly of the Dharma requires one of capable talent; to employ someone unfit for the task will inevitably lead to failure and downfall.

I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s sagely mind may look afar, illuminating the meritorious causes for the propagation of the Dharma; and that Your Compassionate Grace may descend in full measure, examining the loyal sincerity of this humble and vulgar servant. Thus, the Sangha shall be free from the fault of regret or remorse, and both fish and birds shall attain the natural course of their flight and submersion.
Unable to bear the utmost intensity of my sincere entreaty, I respectfully submit this memorial to state my circumstances, prostrating myself in trepidation.

On the *wuchen* day of the twelfth month, an imperial edict was again issued for Wangzong, Prince of Jiangxia and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, to lead the nine divisions of music; Song Xingzhi, Magistrate of Wannian, and Pei Fangyan, Magistrate of Chang’an, were each to lead the musicians within their respective counties, along with the banners and canopies of the various monasteries, all to ensure the utmost solemnity and magnificence.
On the day of Jisi, at dawn, they gathered at the street of Anfumen Gate to welcome the sacred image and escort the monks into the Great Ci'en Monastery.

Upon arrival, these were displayed along the main thoroughfare: there were over fifteen hundred carriages adorned with brocade and embroidery, featuring performances of dragons, fish, banners, and acrobatics, as well as more than three hundred canopies and curtains.

Prior to this, more than two hundred embroidered and painted images, two statues made of gold and silver, and five hundred banners of gold-threaded brocade and silk had been kept overnight at Hongfu Monastery. Together with the scriptures, images, and śarīra relics that the Dharma Master had brought from the Western Regions, these items were escorted out from Hongfu Monastery, placed upon curtained seats and various carriages, and proceeded while positioned in the center.

Furthermore, on both sides before the image, large chariots were each magnificently adorned; atop these chariots, long poles were erected with banners suspended from them, and behind the banners, the Lion King Spirits and others served as the vanguard for the ceremonial procession.

Furthermore, fifty precious jeweled carriages were adorned for the great virtuous ones to ride in; next, the monastic community of the capital city held incense and flowers, followed by hymns of praise. Next, the civil and military officials each led their retinues in formal ranks as attendants. On both sides, the nine divisions of music from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices played, followed in succession by the musical ensembles of the two counties. Banners, pennants, bells, and drums resounded in a tumultuous clamor, dazzling the eyes and floating through the air, shaking the metropolis with their brilliance. Gazing at them, one could not see where they began or where they ended.

The Crown Prince dispatched the Commandant Wei Zhi Shaozong and the Deputy Commandant Wang Wenxun to lead over a thousand troops from the Eastern Palace as manual laborers; he also issued an edict sending the Grand Master of the Imperial Secretariat Li Qianyou as the Chief Commissioner to coordinate with the Commandant of the Martial Guard for inspection and supervision.
The Emperor, accompanied by the Crown Prince and the ladies of the inner palace, stood upon the pavilion of Anfu Gate holding incense burners and watched him depart with great joy.
Those who observed from the streets numbered hundreds of millions.

When the scriptures and images reached the temple gate, by imperial decree, the Duke of Zhao, the Duke of Ying, and the Minister of the Secretariat, Lord Chu, were ordered to lead them in with an incense burner. They were installed within the main hall, while the Nine Divisions of Music, the "Breaking the Array" Dance, and various theatrical performances were performed in the courtyard; once these were concluded, they returned.
On the day of Renshen, he was about to ordain monks.
On the day of Xinwei, the Crown Prince went out with his retinue and guards to stay overnight at his former residence.

At dawn the following day, he proceeded from the south of the temple in a procession of ceremonial insignia; upon reaching the gate, he dismounted and entered on foot, accompanied by the hundred officials.

Having paid homage to the Buddha, he led fifty virtuous monks to meet him and explained his intentions regarding the construction of the temple; as he spoke, his voice was choked with sobs, moving others to deep sorrow.
Onlookers, courtiers, and the monks were all moved to tears. Observing the depth of his filial devotion, one could say he was a Shun of the present age.

Having finished speaking, he ascended the eastern pavilion of the hall and ordered Zhang Xingcheng, the Junior Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to proclaim an edict of grace to remit the sentences of all prisoners currently incarcerated within the capital region. Thereafter, he shaved his hair, observed the fast, and bestowed rolls of silk upon the princes, dukes, and those below them.
Retiring from the presence of others and descending from the pavilion to prostrate before the Buddha, he toured the corridors and halls with his consorts.
Upon reaching the Dharma Master’s quarters, he composed a five-character poem and posted it on the door, saying:
"Ceasing my carriage to gaze upon the Hall of Blessings, I cast my eyes across the imperial capital."
The Wheel of Dharma turns as it contains the sun; the flower-canopy flies up, meeting the clouds.
Verdant mist perfumes the exquisite pavilion; vermilion clouds illuminate the precious robes.
The banners join their rainbow-hues from afar; beyond the void, their splendors are clearly distinguished.
"Tranquil and detached, he ascends to the Ten Stages; spontaneously attaining realization, he reunites with the Three Refuges.
Having finished his contemplation, he returned to the palace.

At that time, both the clergy and the laity were filled with joy, congratulating one another with mutual comfort. There was no one who did not sing of the profound wind’s renewed flourishing and the re-erection of the Bequeathed Dharma, a phenomenon unprecedented since ancient times.
On that day, an imperial decree was issued summoning the Dharma Master back to the Northern Gate.
In the fourth month of the summer of the twenty-third year, the Emperor traveled to Cuiwei Palace, and both the Crown Prince and the Dharma Master accompanied him.

Once he had arrived, apart from matters of administrative disposition, they discussed only the profound mysteries and the Way, inquiring about the retribution of cause and effect, as well as the lingering fragrance and ancient traces of the former sages of the Western Regions; in all cases, he responded by citing the scriptures.
The Emperor received this with deep faith and conviction, frequently rolling up his sleeves and sighing, "I met my Master too late; I have not been able to extensively promote Buddhist affairs.
Although the Emperor was slightly unwell when he departed from the capital, his divine majesty and sagacious concern did not diminish from what they had been in the past.
On the *jisi* day of the fifth month, he suffered a slight headache, and the Dharma Master was invited to stay overnight in the palace.
On the *gengwu* day, the Emperor passed away at the Hanfeng Hall.
At that time, the news was kept secret; the funeral procession returned to the capital, where the mourning rites were announced and the body was encoffined in the Taiji Hall.

On that day, the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne beside the cypress coffin; after the year had passed, he changed the era name to Yonghui. The people of the ten thousand regions wailed in grief as if they had lost their own parents.
The Dharma Master returned to Ci'en Monastery.
From that time forward, he devoted himself exclusively to translation, never wasting even a moment.
Each day he established his own schedule of work; if during the day there were matters that prevented him from fulfilling it, he would certainly continue by working through the night.

Only after the second watch did he set down his pen; having finished transcribing the scripture, he again prostrated to the Buddha and performed circumambulation. At the third watch he slept briefly, and at the fifth watch he rose again to read and recite the Sanskrit original, marking the sequence with vermilion ink in preparation for the translation the following morning.

Every day after the midday meal, at the second watch of the evening, he expounded upon new sutras and śāstras. Monks from various provinces who had come to study would constantly arrive to resolve their doubts and request explanations of the meaning.
Furthermore, having learned that he held the office of *upādhyāya*, they would also come to consult him regarding monastic affairs.

Furthermore, there were internal attendants sent to manage meritorious works; they produced ten sets of the entire Tripitaka and fashioned more than two hundred statues adorned with lacquered cloth and precious materials, all while being instructed to follow the Master’s every movement.

As evening fell, more than a hundred disciples within the monastery all requested his instruction and admonition; they filled the corridors and overflowed the verandas, yet he answered and directed them all without omission.
Although he was surrounded by a convergence of myriad affairs, his spirit remained composed and relaxed, without any obstruction or stagnation.

He continued to discuss with various virtuous men the established doctrines of the sages of the Western regions and the divergent views of the various schools, as well as his own experiences as a youth traveling among the lecture halls; they engaged in lofty discourse and spirited conversation until the end without ever showing fatigue or weariness. His precision, agility, and physical vigor surpassed those of ordinary men to such an extent.

Furthermore, numerous kings, high ministers, and officials frequently came to pay their respects and perform repentance; he welcomed and guided them all, leading them to resolve their minds for enlightenment, such that none failed to abandon their pride and ostentation, reverently praising him with solemnity.

On the *rén-yǐn* day of the first month in the spring of the second year, Jia Dunshe, Prefectural Governor of Yingzhou; Li Daoyu, Prefectural Governor of Puzhou; Du Zhenglun, Prefectural Governor of Guzhou; and Xiao Rui, Prefectural Governor of Hengzhou, were in the capital for the annual assembly of officials. During their leisure from official business, they exhorted one another to visit the Master to request and receive the Bodhisattva Precepts.

The Dharma Master immediately conferred them upon him and extensively expounded for him the practices of a bodhisattva, exhorting him to serve his sovereign with utmost loyalty and to treat those beneath him with compassion and love.
The assembled officials were filled with joy and took their leave.

On the day of Gui-mao, each of us contributed pure wealth to jointly compose this letter and dispatch an envoy to visit the Dharma Master, expressing our gratitude for having heard the teachings on the precepts.
The letter states:

"We have humbly heard that although the body does not require food, the Tathāgata accepted the offering of Cunda; and although the Dharma has nothing to be sought, Vimalakīrti complied with the invitation of Śrīgupta. In both cases, it was to manifest the eternal nature of the ultimate principle and to demonstrate the non-duality of the ordinary and the sage."

Furthermore, this is to respond to sentient beings according to their capacities and to propagate the Way through provisional forms; those who act thus manifest their sincerity in honoring the Dharma, while those who receive it cultivate the merit of practicing dāna. How could this be said to involve a mind preoccupied with self and other, or emotions stained by fame and profit?

Looking back with reverence, we consider that he had cultivated the roots of virtue over many lifetimes, not merely under three, four, or five Buddhas. He profoundly penetrated the characteristics of dharmas and was well-versed in the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Having uniquely awakened to the True Doctrine, he traveled far to seek out sacred traces: he journeyed to the Pure Land of Mount Kukkutapāda and bathed in the clear currents of the Ganges River. Entering the profound Dharma-realm, he sought out spiritual friends; he recovered the ultimate texts from after a hundred generations and explored the mysterious purport from before a thousand years.
Acting as a bridge and raft for all classes of beings, he is neither harsh nor obscure; he bestows his gifts equally upon all, without priority or sequence.

Sentient beings are obscured by their ignorance and deluded regarding the two kinds of emptiness; they revolve through the three realms of existence like silkworms entangling themselves in their own cocoons, or like the wheel of a well that never ceases its turning.

Although they may follow the teachings to give rise to faith, attain understanding according to their conditions, prostrate in refuge, and uphold even a single four-line verse, they remain hidden from view while practicing silent meditation; they loathe suffering and seek eternal bliss, yet they remain distantly stuck in ignorance and are closely mired in the obscurity of ultimate truth. They have not yet awakened to the fact that Buddha-nature resides within themselves, nor do they realize that all objective realms are but consciousness-only. Their minds are not without grasping, and their conceptualizations involve both existence and non-existence; thus, they cannot enter the Eightfold Right Path by means of the Eightfold Wrong Path, nor can they traverse the non-path to reach the Buddha-way.
It is like attempting to cross the sea without a ford, or facing a wall with nothing to see.
Yesterday, taking advantage of a momentary interval in my affairs, I was finally able to pay my respects; you graciously received me and conferred upon me the Bodhisattva precepts.

Bestowing upon them the unprecedented Dharma, they are inspired to give rise to the mind of the Unsurpassed Way; in a single thought-moment, they shatter the boundless, and the four minds reach their ultimate limit at the end of time. The seed of Bodhi arises from within the afflictions of worldly toil; how could the metaphor of a lotus blooming amidst fire suffice to describe it?

I have come to know that the nature of the Tathāgata is itself the mundane world; at the moment of nirvāṇa, it is no different from saṃsāra. To practice prajñā is itself non-practice, and to attain that bodhi is, conversely, non-attainment.
Suddenly, by means of a minor capacity, I was granted the opportunity to hear the Great Teaching; receiving it upon the crown of my head and reflecting upon it, I felt immeasurable joy.
Now, among the six perfections, the giving of Dharma is supreme;
and among the three types of venerable positions, the teacher occupies one of them.
The Great Compassion that benefits all beings is like the sun and moon, which are without personal intent;

yet, looking up to receive this illumination and cherishing the grace bestowed upon me, I feel a sense of gratitude akin to that of the heliotrope and the mugwort, which naturally turn toward the light.

While the Great Being’s sacrifice of his own body upon hearing the Dharma is beyond my aspiration to emulate, the young boy’s offering of soil upon seeing the Buddha is an act I venture to hope to approximate.
I respectfully send these humble offerings to express my devotion, as detailed in the separate letter.

I pray that you will regard my sincerity, cultivate this field of merit, and accept this modest gift, bestowing upon it whatever grace you deem fit. May it be like falling dew adding to the sea, deepening it along with the Bohai;
or like drifting dust gathering on a mountain, becoming eternally firm together with Mount Sumeru—lasting and vast. How fortunate, how fortunate!
The spring chill remains severe; we pray that you maintain your well-being in all your movements and activities.
We respectfully send this brief letter, with nothing further to report.
Jia Dunshe and others bow in reverence.
Such was the admiration he inspired among the court elites.

In the third month of spring in the third year, the Dharma Master intended to construct a stone stūpa on the sunny side of the main gate of the monastery to enshrine the scriptures and images he had brought from the Western Regions; his intention was to ensure that, as human lifespans are transient, the original texts would not be lost or scattered, and furthermore, to protect them from the danger of fire.
The stupa was designed to be thirty zhang in height, intended to manifest the lofty foundation of this great kingdom and to serve as a site for the ancient traces of Śākyamuni.
As he was about to undertake its construction, he submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor.
The imperial messenger, Li Yifu, Shesheren of the Chancellery, informed the Dharma Master, saying:
"The stupa you are constructing is of great scale; I fear it will be difficult to complete in its entirety. It would be better to construct it using bricks."

Furthermore, I do not wish for the Master to undergo such hardship; I have now issued an imperial decree that the deceased’s clothing and belongings from the Eastern Palace, the Inner Quarters, the Yeting, and six other palaces shall be provided to assist you, which will be sufficient to complete your task.
Thereupon, bricks were used, and the work was moved once again to the Western Courtyard.
Each side of the foundation for the stupa measured one hundred and forty feet; following the architectural system of the Western Regions, it did not adhere to the traditional Chinese style.
The stupa has five tiers, including the *cakra* and the *āmalaka*, reaching a total height of one hundred and eighty feet.
At the center of each tier there are śarīra relics, numbering either one thousand or two thousand per level, totaling more than ten thousand grains in all.
The upper story consists of chambers made of stone.

On its southern face stand two steles inscribed with the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka" and the "Record" composed by the Two Sages; these characters were the calligraphy of Chu Suiliang, Duke of Henan and Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day the foundation of the stupa was laid, the Tripitaka Master himself set forth his sincere vows, stating briefly:

"I, Xuanzang, reflect that my merit is meager; though born in this world, I did not encounter the Buddha in person. Yet, by virtue of slight roots of goodness, I have been permitted to hear the teachings of the Semblance Dharma. Were I to have lived during the Final Dharma, to whom could I have turned for refuge?"

Furthermore, I rejoice that I was able to leave the household life at such a young age; I have personally witnessed sacred signs, and having cherished the Dharma since childhood, I have devoted my ears to its profound teachings.
When I hear of the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas, I contemplate emulating them as if I could not reach their level;
when I hear of the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, I take it as my ideal, holding it in reverence within both body and mind.
Therefore, I have followed the venerable lineages of masters and consulted extensively with those who had attained realization.

Truly, it was through the Western inspiration of Emperor Ming’s dream that the True Teaching was transmitted to the East; yet, as the path was obstructed and the distance long, the teachings could not be conveyed in their entirety. Consequently, various schools arose, each vying for its own tenets, and many remained mired in the dualistic doctrines of permanence and annihilation.

Factionalism and jealousy toward those who differ have caused a departure from the principle of the single flavor; consequently, later students look upon one another, not knowing where to turn for guidance.

For this reason, they face Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with deepening sorrow and emulate Sadāprarudita by resting only briefly; they secretly pray for spiritual protection while openly relying on the majesty of the state, resolving to depart from the realm of a single lifetime and cast themselves into a place of ten thousand deaths.
Wherever there were sites of sacred traces, he paid full homage to the lingering spirits; wherever there were those who propagated the Dharma, he sought out everywhere their correct teachings.
Passing by a single location, he grieved for what he had not yet seen;
encountering a single word, he rejoiced in what he had not yet heard. Therefore, with the remaining resources of his life and body, he transcribed whatever was missing or incomplete.
Having fulfilled his sincere vow, he returned to his native land; fortunately, during this era of peace and enlightenment, an imperial edict granted him permission to translate [the scriptures].

The former Emperor’s Way transcended that of the Golden Wheel-turning King, and his fame resounded like the Jade Drum; he flourished the Dharma in the Age of the Semblance Dharma, truly receiving the sacred mandate. Furthermore, he bestowed his divine inspiration, personally composing the "Preface" to the Tripiṭaka. Now, His Majesty, while lecturing on the Way in the Spring Palace, has again composed the "Record" to extol the Sage. This may be called a double radiance joined like two jade disks, their brilliance shimmering in continuous splendor. The imperial decrees hang like the Seven Luminaries, and their resonant tones harmonize with the nine-part music of the *Sheng*.
From the White Horse Monastery in the Eastern Capital to the Western Ming and the Cao Tang, the flourishing of translation and transmission can by no means be compared to this.

Yet, because sentient beings have met with diminished fortune, we have all lost our celestial protector. Fearing that the Sanskrit manuscripts of the Tripiṭaka might perish and be neglected, and that the sublime writings of the two sages might fall into silence and oblivion, I have reverently honored this stupa to enshrine the Sanskrit texts and erected a grand monument to engrave this "Preface" and "Record. I hope that it may stand majestically through eternal kalpas, that the thousand Buddhas may behold it together, and that these hallowed traces, in their vibrant splendor, shall remain as firm as the two polarities of heaven and earth.
At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master personally carried baskets and hampers, transporting bricks and stones; after two full cycles of labor, the work was completed.
On the day of Yimao (the second day) of the fifth month of summer, the Mahāyāna masters Guṇaprabha and Prajñādeva from the Mahābodhi Monastery in Central India sent a letter to the Dharma Master.

Jñānaprabha was thoroughly proficient in the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings, as well as in non-Buddhist texts, the four Vedas, and the treatises on the five sciences; he was the foremost disciple of Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, and scholars throughout the five regions of India all revered him as their master.

Huìtiān was thoroughly versed and well-versed in the eighteen schools of the Hīnayāna; his virtue as a teacher and guide was likewise highly esteemed by them, and while the Dharma Master was traveling through the Western Regions, they constantly engaged in mutual study and refinement together.

Although he had achieved merit through his partial teachings, he had not yet applied his mind to the Vaipulya scriptures; because he clung to these biased views, the Dharma Master constantly rebuked him.
At the time of the Dharma assembly at Kanyākubja, he was again deeply humbled and defeated, and he likewise submitted in shame.

Since our parting, he has held me in reverent admiration without forgetting; he has therefore dispatched the śramaṇa Fachang of the same monastery to deliver this letter, along with hymns of praise and two rolls of fine cotton, his desire to extol my virtues being most profound.
The letter read:

"From the Venerable Hui-tian, who dwells at Mahābodhi Monastery on the Vajrāsana of the World-Honored One—subtle, wondrous, and auspicious—and is surrounded by a great assembly of learned ones, this letter is sent to the Upādhyāya Mokṣa of the Great Country of China, who has exhaustively mastered the subtle refinements of the immeasurable Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras:
We respectfully inquire after your well-being and wish you freedom from illness and affliction."

I, the Bhikṣu Hui Tian, have now composed the *Praise of the Buddha’s Great Supernatural Transformations*, as well as various sūtras, śāstras, and treatises on inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*). These are now being sent with the Bhikṣu Fa Zhang. Furthermore, the venerable Ācārya Jñānaprabha, who is immeasurably learned and of great virtue, likewise sends his greetings as before. The Upāsaka Rishou bows his head in salutation.

I now send you a pair of white cotton cloths together with this letter to demonstrate that my mind is not empty of devotion; do not be surprised by their small quantity due to the great distance of the journey—please accept them.
Should you require any sūtras or śāstras, please record their titles and send them back; I shall have them transcribed and sent to the Venerable Moksācārya. Please be informed of this.
Such was the way he was admired by those far away.
In the second month of the spring of the fifth year, Fachang took his leave to return home and requested a reply.
The Dharma Master provided an answer, along with gifts for his correspondence.
The letter was transcribed in identical script and presented for imperial review; only then was it entrusted to the envoys. The text read:
"The Bhikṣu Xuanzang of the Great Tang Kingdom respectfully composes this letter before the presence of the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānaprabha of Magadha in Central India."
From the moment we parted, more than ten years have passed in an instant.
Our realms are vast and distant, and not a word from you has been heard.
My feelings of longing and affection increase and entangle themselves with every passing day.
When that Bhikṣu, Dharmadīrgha, arrived and was granted an audience, he inquired after my well-being; my eyes suddenly cleared as if I were beholding his venerable countenance in person.
The joy surging within me is difficult to describe with pen and ink.
The seasons are gradually warming; I wonder how you have been since your letter was sent.

Furthermore, upon the return of the envoy last year, I learned that the Great Dharma Master, the Treasury of the True Dharma, had passed away. I offer my inquiries with a grief so profound it cannot be contained.
Alas! It may be said that the boat has sunk in the sea of suffering and the eyes of devas and humans have been extinguished; how could such a pain of displacement and loss have come so swiftly!

Yet, because the Treasury of the True Dharma had planted blessings in former days and established merit over long kalpas, he was able to manifest a magnificent nature of profound harmony and display a grand talent of noble distinction. He succeeded to the virtue of Āryadeva and inherited the brilliance of Nāgārjuna; he rekindled the torch of wisdom and once again raised the banner of the Dharma.

It extinguishes the blazing fires upon the mountains of depravity, damns the surging floods of the inverted sea, guides the exhausted travelers to the place of jewels, and reveals the Great Vehicle to the deluded masses. Vast and expansive, lofty and majestic, it is truly the main pillar and beam of the Dharma-gate.

Furthermore, regarding the teachings of the three vehicles—both the provisional and the ultimate—as well as the heterodox texts concerning annihilationism and eternalism, there were none that he did not store within his breast and master through thorough cultivation in his mind.
