He could eloquently expound upon the most convoluted passages and ensure that even the most obscure principles were clearly revealed. Consequently, both those within and outside the Buddhist fold took refuge in him, and he became the preeminent leader of India.
Furthermore, you were most earnest and skillful in your guidance, never wearying by day or night; like a public well whose vessel fills itself, you poured forth inexhaustibly.

In the past, Xuanzang, while seeking the Way, was privileged to attend upon you and receive your instructions. Although I am but dull and ignorant, I have nonetheless somewhat benefited from your influence, like a tangle of weeds straightened by proximity to flax.
When he took his leave to return to his native city, his entrustment was particularly profound; those earnest words remain as if still ringing in my ears.

I had just hoped that he would enjoy a secure longevity and assist in promoting the profound Dharma, yet who would have thought that in a single morning he would suddenly depart for all eternity? As I reflect upon his eternal passing, my grief is truly unbearable.

I humbly reflect that you, Dharma Master, have long received sublime instruction and early gained entry into the inner sanctum; the sentiment of longing and attachment must be difficult for you to bear—what can be done, what can be done?
Such is the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); what indeed can be done? I pray that you will exercise self-restraint.
In the past, when the Great Awakened One’s radiance was hidden, Kāśyapa succeeded him in proclaiming the great enterprise;
when Śāṇakavāsin passed away, Upagupta expounded his noble principles.

Now that the General of the Dharma has returned to the Truth, the Dharma Master shall succeed him in these duties. We pray only that your pure words and wondrous eloquence may flow eternally throughout the four seas, and that your adornment of merit and wisdom may endure forever with the Five Mountains.

Of the sūtras and śāstras that Xuanzang brought with him, more than thirty works, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, have already been translated; however, the translations of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Nyāyānusāra* are not yet complete, and they will certainly be finished this year.

On this day, may the Holy Person of the Great Tang Emperor enjoy ten thousand blessings, and may all lands be peaceful and secure. With the compassion of a Cakravartin King, you propagate the transformation of the Dharma King; the sutras and treatises produced have all been graced by Your Majesty’s divine pen with prefaces, ordered for transcription by the relevant authorities, and circulated throughout the realm, such that even neighboring states now follow and practice them.

Although we dwell at the end of the Age of Images, the brilliance of the Dharma teachings remains harmonious and serene, no different from the transformation wrought in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī; I humbly pray that you will take this to heart.
Furthermore, while crossing the Xin River previously, I lost one load of scriptures; their titles are recorded below as follows. If you have any news of them, please send them along.
I also enclose a small gift for your worship; I pray that you will graciously accept it.
"The journey is so far that I could not bring much; do not disdain its meager quantity.
Xuanzang bows his head in greeting.
He further replied in a letter to Dharma Master Huìtiān, saying:
“From the Bhikṣu Xuanzang of the Great Tang Kingdom, respectfully addressed to the feet of the Tripiṭaka Master Huītian of Mahābodhi Monastery:
It has been some time since we parted, and my longing for you grows ever deeper.”
Since my voice cannot reach you, I have no way to console your longing and thirst for me.
Now that the Venerable Bhikṣu Dharmadīrgha has arrived, I have received your letter and respectfully acknowledge your well-being, which increases my joy.

Furthermore, I have received two rolls of white cotton cloth and one fascicle of hymns; as your intentions are so generous, I, of meager virtue, feel ashamed that I am unworthy of them, and I tremble with awe.
As the seasonal energies gradually harmonize, I wonder how your physical well-being has been since you received my letter.

I imagine that you have integrated the doctrines of the hundred schools into your mind and settled your thoughts upon the nine divisions of the scriptures; you raise the banner of the True Dharma to welcome those who seek the ancestral source, and beat the drum of victory to humble those opponents clad in armor. You soar before kings and lords and prevail over the ranks of the eminent and talented; thus, you must experience much joy and serenity.

I, Xuanzang, am mediocre and debased, and my physical strength has already declined; furthermore, as I reflect upon your virtue and revere your benevolence, I find only that my hardships have accumulated.
Formerly, while traveling abroad, I had the honor of beholding your radiant countenance there.
At the assembly at Kuśinagara, they again engaged in a formal debate.
Faced with various kings and hundreds of thousands of followers, they were to determine the relative depth of their respective positions.

He established the principles of the Mahāyāna, while he [the opponent] upheld the tenets of the Śrāvaka teachings; in the course of their back-and-forth exchanges, there was inevitably a disparity in the tone and force of their arguments.
I strive to preserve the correct principle rather than protect human sentiment, and for this reason, we have repeatedly encountered friction.
Yet, after leaving the assembly, my mind soon became clear and expansive.
That you, the messenger, still transmit the Dharma Master’s letter expressing thanks and repentance—how persistent is your attachment!

The Dharma Master is rich in learning and refined in expression; his resolve is firm and his conduct far-reaching. The waters of Lake Anavatapta cannot compare to the majesty of his waves, and the pure mani-jewel falls short of matching his brilliance. As a model for those who follow, he is truly a man of superior character. I pray that you will exert yourself in these excellent precepts and propagate the True Dharma.

As for the ultimate reach of principle and the pinnacle of discourse, nothing surpasses the Mahāyāna; it is only regrettable that the Dharma Master has not yet attained deep faith—what is meant by being so attached to the sheep and deer carts while discarding the white ox, or cherishing common crystal while rejecting the *sphatika* gem? O illustrious and virtuous one, why do you remain so mired in such delusion?

Furthermore, this body, like an unbaked clay vessel, is fragile and fleeting, difficult to preserve; you ought to swiftly resolve upon the Great Mind and adorn your right view, lest you find yourself sighing in regret only at the moment of death.

Now that the envoy has returned to his country, I respectfully offer these words in lieu of my personal sincerity, along with a small gift; this is intended merely to express gratitude for your kind intentions, rather than to fully exhaust my profound heart.
Please be informed:

on the day of my previous return, while crossing the Sindhu River, I lost one load of scriptures. I have now recorded their titles as listed separately; I request that you send them along with this letter.
I am unable to provide a detailed account of other matters.
Respectfully presented by the Bhikṣu Xuanzang.

*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili (Huilì), with annotations by Shi Yanzong (Yàncóng).

Beginning from the third month of the first year of the Xiǎnqìng era, when the inscription for the Ci'ēn Monastery was completed, until the first month of the third year, when [the Emperor] returned to the Western Capital in the imperial carriage. From the third month of spring in the first year of Xiǎnqìng, on the day *guīhài*, the Imperial Composition of the Inscription for the Dàcí'ēn Monastery was finished.

At that time, Xu Jingzong, the Minister of Rites, dispatched an envoy to deliver the inscription for the stele to the Dharma Master. Furthermore, an official decree was issued from the Court of State Ceremonial to the monastery.
On the day of Jiazi, the Dharma Master led the assembly of the monastery to the imperial palace to offer his thanks, saying:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks."
Having received the official dispatch from the Court of State Ceremonial, we humbly received the Imperial Edict, wherein Your Majesty personally wielded the divine brush.
The stele inscription composed for the Great Ci’en Monastery has now been completed; its sagely grace descends upon us, and the Imperial words shine down with profound illumination.

The Gate of Mystery becomes ever more profound, and the companions of the Dharma find increased glory; I stand upon the vast earth feeling ashamed, and bear the weight of the high heavens with little strength.
Xuanzang has heard that once the creative work of the Transformer has been spread among all things to establish its teachings, the Way of the Sage likewise reveals its inner sentiment through words.
Thus, while the painting of trigrams and the hanging of written texts were but empty discourses on material forms;
and the establishment of hexagrams and the differentiation of images did not transcend the boundaries of the mundane realm.
Yet the virtue of Fuxi (the Sovereign of Xīhuáng) is still praised in antiquity, and the legacy of King Jī (King Wen) likewise stands uniquely lofty in later generations.
How could this compare to opening up things and accomplishing affairs, elucidating the Eightfold Path to manifest its brilliance;
explaining the Way and establishing discourse, verifying the Three Insights to guide the common people?

Its principles exhaust what lies beyond heaven and earth, and its sentiments encompass what is outside the sun and moon; when comparing their merits and demerits, this [Buddhist teaching] is truly preeminent.

We humbly submit that Your Majesty, the Emperor, wields the Golden Wheel as you govern and rides the Jade Calendar as you seize the opportune moment; your transformation overflows across the four continents, and your benevolence extends throughout the nine realms.

Your Way encompasses that of the Sage, and your merit flourishes like that of the Divine; you possess manifold talents through innate knowledge, and your natural endowment is derived from Heaven’s ultimate perfection.
At first, moved by grief for her bridal mirror, she established a temple; soon thereafter, she raised a supreme banner and further propagated the literary precepts.

As for her celestial blossoms bursting forth and her sagely compositions surging like waves—she swallowed the ocean of brushes to conceive the Dragon Palace, and eclipsed the forest of words to encompass the Crane Tree.
Internally it encompasses the Eight Piṭakas, and externally it scrutinizes the Six Classics; it is profound yet canonical, vast yet subtle.

Thus, the vestiges of the Jetavana Grove are made ever loftier by being entrusted to precious thought, and the lingering fragrance of the Nairañjanā Garden remains unobscured by means of these exquisite compositions.
Not only does this work suppress the illusions of dreams and illuminate the paths of delusion, but it surely serves as a mold for the four heavens and a vessel that encompasses the three realms.

As for Xuanzang, my words and deeds are unworthy of note, yet I have humbly joined the ranks of the monastic community; having repeatedly received your gracious favor, I have always considered myself most fortunate.
I am once again deeply indebted for Your Majesty’s gracious favor; to encounter the flourishing of the Semblance Dharma fills me with both shame and joy, which truly stir my heart.
Unable to contain my profound sense of veneration, I have respectfully come to the Court.
"I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude.

On the day of Yichu, the Dharma Master further reflected that His Majesty’s civil and cultural brilliance was bestowed by Heaven; being sagely and versatile, his literary elegance surpassed that of the Lord of Wei, and his calligraphy likewise excelled that of the Sovereign of Han.

The Dharma Master, seeing that the inscription was a sacred composition and that its calligraphy was also expected to be by a divine hand, went to the Imperial Palace to request that the Emperor write it himself.
His memorial read:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang and others state:..."
I humbly submit that in responding to phenomena and manifesting signs, the divine function is universally comprehensive;
in establishing teachings according to the times, the sagely achievement is fully realized.

Thus we know that only when both sun and moon shine brightly does one reach the ultimate limit of their celestial course across the sky; only when all plants and trees flourish together does one exhaustively realize the virtue of their beauty upon the earth.

I humbly submit that Your Majesty, the Emperor, possesses wisdom that encompasses all things and benevolence that moistens the three realms; having magnified the glorious transformation of the state, you have further expounded the profound wind of the Dharma.

You hold the Daoism of King Mu of the Zhou in contempt, for his appreciation of the "Ode of the Jade Pond" was in vain; and you treat the veneration of the Law by Emperor Ming of Han with disdain, for his opening of the White Horse Temple was merely a hollow gesture.

Thereupon, he humbly descended with celestial writs to propagate far-reaching and profound principles, using them to carve upon magnificent jade tablets so that these flourishing precedents might long endure.
Like the sounding of the Six Excellencies or the radiance of the Five Planets, he unfolded his ultimate aspirations to move the common people and extended his great vows to rectify the age.
How could he merely assist the True Suchness (tathatā) in its hidden depths and manifest its profound mysteries?

Although his elegant discourse has been fully expressed and the jade-green tablets are about to be engraved, the silver hooks of his calligraphy have not yet been inscribed, and the vermilion characters remain concealed within.

Thus, when the music of Kui has already been mounted upon the sounding-boards, how could the melodies of the common village befit such a setting? Once the land of Long has been bathed in daylight, what use is there for the light of a torch?

Were it not for Ya and Kuang tuning the pitch-pipes, and Xihe taking charge of the chariots, how could the great sound of the Dharma-drum be raised, or the radiant colors of the Sun of Wisdom be augmented?

Venturing upon this principle, I venture to make this humble request: I beseech Your Majesty to perfect these existing merits by inscribing them with Your Divine Calligraphy. In this way, the excellence of these works may soar above the clouds, surpassing the traces of former kings, and the marvel of the "hanging dew" script may spread its fragrance to future sages.
With a resonance like gold and a vibration like jade, you awaken the multitude of deluded beings;
with the soaring of a phoenix and the coiling of a dragon, you shall open the eyes of the many who are blind.
How could this merely serve to perpetuate the Image-Dharma (the Buddhist teachings), such that all living beings receive its most profound grace?
Truly, I have also been able to offer some assistance to this enlightened era, so that the ancestral altars may enjoy eternal blessings.

As for Xuanzang, my understanding is dull and shallow; though I have falsely counted myself among the ranks of the monastic forest, I am fundamentally ashamed of my limited learning and have often failed in my observance of the Vinaya. Yet, I have been humbly honored by Your Imperial Words and have undeservedly received such high praise.
Although my alarm and trepidation are extreme, leaving me with no place to set my face, I have for many days maintained a diligent sincerity and uplifted my heart in earnest devotion.
Venturing once more to trouble you with these words, I harbor feelings as conflicting as ice and fire.
The memorial was submitted but not accepted.
On the jingyin day, the Dharma Master petitioned again, saying:

"Yesterday, I was honored by the receipt of Your Majesty’s celestial composition; my joy and gratitude were beyond measure. Yet, as Your Divine Calligraphy has not yet been granted, my longing remains unfulfilled."

I humbly submit that those who climb the wondrous tree of glory must surely smile as they emit their fragrance; those who kneel before the precious jade peak likewise unfold their abundance and bestow their luster.

I venture to hope that Your Majesty, holding the balance of justice and grasping the essence of purity, governs with ease in great tranquility; that your sagely thoughts, like fine brushstrokes, look down upon and concentrate many arts.
The Great Plan (Hongfan) shone forth from the surging waters of Luo, and the "Cursive Sage" (Caosheng) flourished by the side of the pond.
I, Xuanzang, reverently receive the former grace, holding the *ruohua* flower before the golden mirror;
I venture to hope for subsequent favor, awaiting the shadow of the cassia tree beneath the silver hook.
How could it be merely that these joined jade disks revolve together and their linked splendors are looked up to?

I also fear that were it not for Your Majesty’s celestial calligraphy, there would be no means to suspend this writing like the sun and moon; only your exquisite patterns can fully unfold the subtle and profound traces.
"My soul hastens and my head bows low; this is not what I dare to hope for. Overwhelmed by accumulated distress, I venture to present this petition at the risk of death.
Upon the submission of this memorial, the Emperor was just then wielding his divine brush.
Having received the Emperor’s permission, the Dharma Master was overcome with joy and celebration.
He submitted a memorial of thanks, stating: “The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.”
I have humbly received the Imperial decree granting permission for Your Majesty’s own calligraphy to be inscribed upon the stele of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
As the imperial edict has arrived and Your compassionate grace has been lavishly bestowed upon me, I am overwhelmed with reverence and trepidation, not knowing how to respond.
Xuanzang has heard that when a powerful crossbow is drawn to the full, even a flying squirrel cannot trigger its mechanism;
when a great bell conceals its sound, a slender blade of grass cannot produce its resonance.
Yet, I did not expect that the sun and moon, by their very presence, would cause their light to turn toward the Gate of Emptiness.
The rain moistens the vast clouds, thereby manifesting its response within the profound temple;
this is what we aspire to, for how could it have been our original design?

We humbly observe that Your Majesty treads upon the wings of the sun and moon and ascends the pivot of the universe; grasping the tally, You succeed to the Mandate. You follow the example of Xuanyuan and surpass that of Shun; you encompass the legacy of Xia and swallow up the power of Yin. You unfold the myriad subtleties to mold the age, and consolidate manifold talents to illuminate the customs of the people.
Within the nine provinces, all have already been bathed in the breeze of benevolence; beyond the four heavens as well, they have been moistened by profound transformation.

Thus, regarding the Dharma that serves as a bridge across the stream, were it not for the Most Holy One, its source could not have been elucidated; and as for the work of subtle assistance, were it not for the Ultimate Person, how could its traces have been spread?

Although the utmost limit of honoring the distant ancestors naturally moves the celestial heart, one may still pray for profound divine protection; thus, Your Majesty has turned Your imperial gaze toward us, bestowing Your sublime words upon us in their entirety. These already surpass the rarest treasures of past ages, and as these secret traces are about to be revealed, they will exceed even the most priceless jewels.
Among all classes of beings, there are none who do not rejoice and revere this.

Yet, for those followers of the Brahma-vehicle, their joy and exultation redouble; to dream of the vast music of the Heavenly Carriage is no marvel compared to this, and to obtain the crest-jewel of a Wheel-Turning King—how could it be considered more precious than this?
I hope it shall be engraved upon enduring stone to be established within this blessed courtyard; thus may those deluded beings, though currently benumbed, have their ears and eyes opened.

May the torch of the Dharma flourish and be transmitted to future generations, so that those who behold these precious characters and gaze upon these silver calligraphic strokes may awaken to Bodhicitta this very day;
and by reciting these forceful compositions and exploring their profound mysteries, they may realize Prajñā in this very place.
Though kalpas may exhaust the smallest mustard seed, the brilliance of beauty endures forever;
though seas may shift and mulberry fields return, the flourishing legacy of noble conduct remains undecaying.
I, Xuanzang, am of humble origin and have long felt deficient in my religious practice; now that I have been ordained, I aspire to propagate the profound Way.
In traveling to Kapilavastu, I originally relied upon the Imperial transformation; now that I have undertaken this translation, I further receive the encouragement of the Court.
During the era of Zhenguan, I was undeservedly bathed in profound compassion, and since the Yonghui period, I have again been graced by extraordinary favor.
The two sovereigns have deigned to bestow their encomiums with their own brushes; these sacred compositions from two reigns have conferred upon me the utmost honor and adornment.
Reflecting upon my own ignorance and inferiority, I am truly filled with apprehension and trepidation.
The sincerity of repaying this kindness has not been forgotten from dusk until dawn.
Yet, as the depth of this grace is vast and immense, how could a mere drop of water suffice as recompense?
Since the bounty bestowed is as great as Mount Song, it cannot be thanked for with but a speck of dust.

I can only rely upon the power of various wisdoms to employ them in boundless ways, thereby augmenting the auspicious legacy of the imperial mausoleums and assisting in the strengthening of the foundation for seven hundred years.
I am unable to contain the utmost depth of my reverent devotion.
I respectfully enclose this memorial of thanks, presented by the Palace Attendant, Your Servant Wang Junde, for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
Having lightly presumed upon Your Majesty’s august presence, I am deeply trembling with fear.

On the eighth day of the fourth month of summer, after the Great Emperor had completed the calligraphy for the stele and the artisans had finished carving it, and as it was about to be sent to the temple, the Dharma Master, feeling both humbled and grateful for the Imperial benevolence, did not dare wait passively for its arrival. He therefore led the assembly of the Ci’en Monastery, along with the monks and nuns of the capital, each preparing canopies, precious curtains, banners, and flowers, and together proceeded to the Fanglin Gate to welcome it.
By imperial decree, the nine divisions of music from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices were dispatched, accompanied by musicians from the two counties of Chang’an and Wannian.

Among the banners, even the lowest rose above the clouds and mists; among the streamers, even the shortest brushed against the Milky Way. There were over three hundred such items in total, with more than a hundred musical wagons.
On the evening of the seventh day, they gathered at the Xianfu Gate Street in the western part of the city.
That night it rained, and on the eighth day, the roads were impassable; by imperial decree, the journey was temporarily halted, and the Dharma Master was invited to enter the palace.
On the tenth day, the weather was clear and beautiful; by imperial decree, the ceremonial arrangements were ordered to be set out as before.

At dawn on the fourteenth day, the procession finally set forth; banners, streamers, and other regalia were displayed in succession from Fanglin Gate to Ci’en Monastery, filling the thirty li between them with a brilliant splendor.
The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate tower to gaze upon it with great delight; more than a million men and women from the capital came to watch.

On the fifteenth day, seven monks were ordained and a vegetarian feast was prepared for two thousand monks. Nine divisions of music were performed before the Buddha Hall, and the assembly did not disperse until evening.
On the sixteenth day, the Dharma Master again went with his disciples to the Imperial Court to offer thanks for the stele’s arrival at the monastery.
The memorial read:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang and others state:..."

On the fourteenth day of this month, we humbly received the imperial decree to deliver the Imperial Calligraphy for the Stele of the Great Ci’en Monastery, along with the performance of the Ninefold Music as an offering.
As the sun of Yao shines its light, it first increases the brilliance of the torch of wisdom; as the ocean of Shun flows its waves, it further suffices to broaden the stream of the Dharma.

The magnificent stele was erected upon the craggy cliff, its celestial inscription brilliantly illuminating the scene; it resembled the hues of a rosy cloud reflecting off a sacred mountain, or as if a cluster of shimmering constellations were descending upon a celestial peak.
All those present, both monastics and laypeople, rushed forward like lightning or clouds, gazing upon it with such awe and joy that they felt they had experienced something never before known.

I humbly submit that when the Eight Trigrams were inscribed and the Six Lines were appended, when laws were fashioned by observing birds and the classics were spread after weeping for the Qilin, the noble deeds of the Sages were fully manifested therein. It was intended to provide a track for things and leave a model for posterity, establishing instruction according to the times, molding all living beings, and elevating moral influence.
Thus, while the stone inscriptions of the First Emperor of Qin merely glorified the rites of *feng* and *shan*,
and the stele carvings of the Wei sovereigns did nothing more than record the achievements of great feasts,

they still claimed their titles were loftily superior to those of a hundred kings; yet how could these compare to Your Majesty’s own composition of sagely verse and the humble opening of your immortal calligraphy?

The resonance of the golden music unfolds its cadence, and the silver hooks display their brilliant traces; he probes the Dragon Palace to establish the Three Mysteries and surpasses the Phoenix Script to exhaust the eight calligraphic styles. He gallops with his thoughts like spring waves rising, and distills the autumn dew to manifest his uniqueness.

He expounded the wondrous principles of the Mahāyāna and praised the profound mysteries of the Six Pāramitās; his transformation reached across the three thousandfold world-systems, and his fame soared beyond ten billion lands.

The subtle words of the Nairañjanā Garden were further illuminated through the Emperor’s own composition, while the Bodhisattvas of the Bamboo Grove were rendered even more venerable by means of His divine brush.

Consequently, the Brahmins were led to take refuge in his heart; they severed the net of doubt and received his reverent instruction. Pāpīyān transformed his thoughts, prostrating the mountain of heterodoxy and devoting himself to the Way.

How could this merely mean that those within the gates of the mundane dust first awakened from their confusion regarding the direction, or that guests lingering in the dream of existence would transcend the limits of suffering?
Since the teaching of the Image Period gradually spread to the East, nearly six hundred years have passed; yet the flourishing of its propagation has never equaled that of the present time.

Even when Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty experienced a spiritual resonance, he still sought counsel from Fu Yi; and when the Ruler of Wu took refuge in the [Buddhist] tradition, he still examined his doubts with Kan Ze.

From this point onward, there has been none worthy of praise; yet, transforming beings according to conditions, he alone is commended for his illustrious destiny. That doing good must be met with response has firmly established a majestic and flourishing foundation. Like a King of the Golden Wheel whose divine achievements are unfathomable, he is like a Sovereign of the Jewel Crown whose blessings shall endure forever.

Xuanzang and his companions have, through our own delusions, been unworthily favored by imperial grace; we have had the good fortune to enter the profound academy. Now that the compassionate clouds spread once more and the Dharma drum resounds again, the transformation of the Three Insights has flourished and the gate of the Eightfold Path remains forever open. Yet, reflecting upon ourselves, we are neither sincere nor earnest, having received encouragement and guidance in vain. Looking up to the high heavens, we are grateful for the bestowed benefits; looking down at the deep valleys, we harbor feelings of shame.
"Unable to contain our utmost sincerity of reverent veneration, we respectfully approach the palace gate to present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
When the stele arrived, the relevant officials constructed a separate stone pavilion in the northeast corner in front of the Buddha Hall to house it.

The residence featured double-tiered arches and layered rafters; its cloud-patterned lintels and ornate ridgepoles were illuminated by golden flowers shining downward, while precious bells gleamed above, and the dew-dish atop the immortal’s palm was identical to those on sacred stupas.
The Great Emperor was skilled in regular, clerical, cursive, and running scripts, and he was especially refined in *feibai* (flying white).

His stele was inscribed in the running script, and he further employed the *feibai* style for the four characters "Xianqing First Year," both of which reached the pinnacle of spiritual subtlety and wonder.
Those who came to view it numbered several thousand each day.
Officials of the third rank and above in the civil and military services submitted petitions requesting permission to make rubbings, which was granted.

Since the cessation of the use of knotted cords and the rise of written characters, the two seal scripts (Zhuan) have differed in form, and the regular (Kai) and cursive (Cao) styles have diverged in their momentum. With the "hanging needle" and "dangling dew," the "cloud mist" and "prostrate wave," as well as the epigraphic inscriptions on stone, the *changzhang* script, the eight-part script, and the clerical (Li) script—each of these ancient styles possessed its own strengths and weaknesses, such that none could achieve universal excellence.

For instance, Emperor Yuan of the Han was praised for his excellence in clerical script; Cao Cao of Wei was skilled in cursive and running scripts; Zhong Yao was proficient in the three styles; Wang Zhong excelled in the eight-part script; Liu Shao and Zhang Hong gained renown through the flying-white script; and Cai Yong and Zhao Mengfu left their names as "Sages of Cursive."
Only the General of the Household (Zhonglang) and the Right Army Commandant (Youjun) possessed a partial convergence of various excellences, yet even they could not achieve perfection.
Thus, when Wei Wenxiu saw the calligraphy of the two Wangs, he remarked:
"The two Wangs may indeed be called skilled, but they are not yet masters of the art of writing."

If his celestial calligraphy is so preeminent and soaring, lush and vigorous, encompassing the manifold styles of ancient sages and exhausting the many talents of former philosophers—serving as the "springtime" of the brush and a rare harmony among all texts—it is truly to our Sovereign that such merit must be attributed.

In his youth, the Dharma Master devoted himself to listening to and studying the teachings; later, while traveling to the Western Regions, he crossed the Ling Mountains and the Snowy Ranges, whereupon he contracted a cold-related illness that repeatedly caused his heart to seize with pain, leading him through many hardships and sufferings.
For several years now, I have relied on medicine to keep my condition under control.
This past summer, in the fifth month, while seeking coolness due to the heat, my old ailment was provoked, and for a time it seemed I would not survive.

Both the clergy and the laity were filled with anxiety and apprehension; the Secretariat reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict dispatching the Imperial Physician-in-Attendance for Superior Medicine, Jiang Xiaozhang, and the Acupuncturist, Shangguan Zong, to provide specialized care, and ordered that all required medicines be supplied from within the palace.
The messengers at the northern gate were dispatched several times each day to observe the weather and relay news.
Even regarding his place of rest and sleep, he ordered the most skilled attendants of the inner bureau to arrange everything.
His cherishing [of the child] was such that even a compassionate father toward his only son could not exceed it.
Xiaozhang and others attended to him with medical care, never leaving his side day or night; only after five days did he recover, and the hearts of those both inside and outside were at ease.
Having received the Imperial favor, the Dharma Master presented a memorial of thanks on the following day, stating:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.
Xuanzang has been unskilled in self-care, and my chronic cold ailment has flared up again, nearly reaching a critical stage; I was almost about to depart from this auspicious era."
By the grace of Heaven, moved by compassion, a skilled physician was sent down; as soon as the acupuncture and medicine were applied, I was granted recovery.

My failing years have been halted at their end, and my dispersed spirit has been restored from its point of dissolution. I behold once more this flourishing age and may again follow the enlightened guidance—not merely that the chronic ailments of the *gao* and *huang* are forever severed, but that my physical tissues are perpetually harmonized.

Reflecting upon my own mediocrity and insignificance, I have repeatedly been graced by extraordinary favors; yet, as the benefits bestowed are profound while my life is fragile, I know not how to repay them.
I can only rely on the power of wisdom, hoping thereby to requite these hidden blessings.
Xuanzang remains physically weak and exhausted, and is as yet unable to proceed to the Imperial Palace to offer his thanks; he is overcome with the utmost sense of awe and gratitude.
He has respectfully dispatched his disciple Dachengguang to present this memorial for Your Majesty’s information.
The Emperor read the memorial and dispatched the attendant Wang Junde to inquire after the Dharma Master, saying:

"Since you have recently taken medicine, your physical strength must surely be weak and depleted; I request that you take good care of yourself and refrain from exerting your mental faculties for the time being."
The Dharma Master, having received the Imperial inquiry, was overcome with the utmost joy and trepidation, and again submitted this expression of gratitude:
"I, the Śramaṇa Xuanzang, state:

I have been beset by the accumulation of karmic burdens, which has brought upon me the suffering of illness; in the space of a single breath, I was nearly separated from Your Majesty’s enlightened reign."

Suddenly, we have been graced by the Emperor and Empress’s descent of compassionate thoughts and their concern for our very lives; heavenly messengers have arrived repeatedly, exceeding ten times our comfort, and divine medicine has stooped to save us, as if we had encountered a single pill.
Having drunk from and bathed in Your Sacred Benevolence, my deep anguish has been dispelled; having received Your medical care, I have finally attained recovery.
Who would have expected that the soul already departed would be summoned by the Supreme Deity, and that a life destined for early end would be renewed by the Great Furnace?
Reflecting inward upon my own meager and humble nature, how could I be worthy of this? I beat my breast in profound shame; words are insufficient to express it.
How could I ever be enough to repay such extraordinary grace? I would grind my insignificant body to dust, yet still there would be no thanks sufficient.
I now hope to exert myself in this ritual recitation, exhausting my body and mind, to repay your incomparable grace and slightly to stifle my boundless debt of gratitude.
Feeling a sense of profound thankfulness beyond measure, I respectfully submit this memorial to express my thanks.

"Joy and fear are intertwined, leaving me utterly at a loss for what to do; I deeply regret having troubled Your Majesty’s hearing and vision, and I prostrate myself in increasing awe and trepidation.
Furthermore, in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial edict was issued stating:
"Laozi is my ancestor; his name, rank, and titles ought to precede those of the Buddha."

At that time, several hundred people, including the Venerable Fachang of Puguang Monastery and the Venerable Puying of Zongchi Monastery, presented their grievances at the imperial court, yet they did not receive a rectification of their situation.

After the Dharma Master returned to his country, he repeatedly submitted petitions to the throne, which were granted for deliberation; however, before these could be finalized, Emperor Wen passed away.
In the sixth year of the Yonghui era, an imperial edict was issued:
"When Daoists or monks commit offenses whose circumstances are difficult to ascertain, they may be investigated and adjudicated according to secular law."

Officials in remote regions were unfamiliar with the intent of the imperial edicts; regardless of the magnitude of the matter, they frequently employed stocks and canes, causing extreme humiliation and dishonor.

The Dharma Master was constantly concerned about this, and as he grew increasingly frail due to illness, fearing he might never again behold the Emperor’s countenance, he entrusted someone to submit a memorial regarding the two aforementioned matters, stating that they were not conducive to the state's well-being:
"Xuanzang’s life hangs by a thread, and I fear I shall not have the opportunity for further words. I respectfully submit this petition while prostrated upon my pillow in trepidation."
The imperial decree was sent to inform him, saying:
"We have heard what you have reported.
However, as for the titles and positions within the Buddhist Way, these were determined by the previous dynasty; the matter must be deliberated."
The imperial decree stating that he should conform to secular customs was immediately issued for his dismissal and retirement.
"The Master should set his mind at ease and take strengthening medicine," [the Emperor said].
On the twenty-third day, an imperial edict was issued, saying:
"The Daoist teachings are pure and void, and the Buddhist scriptures are subtle and profound; all things rely upon them as a bridge and ferry, and they are revered by the three realms.

Recently, however, because the Dharma has declined and people have become corrupt, many violate the precepts and regulations. We have provisionally relied upon secular laws to issue punishments and warnings, hoping thereby to stop evil and encourage good; it is not that we slight the Dharma on account of human failings."
However, since those such as the clergy already possess established regulations, it would likely cause unnecessary trouble and disturbance to impose further penalties upon them.
Therefore, the previous order requiring Daoist priests, Daoist nuns, monks, and nuns to follow secular law in cases of transgression should be suspended.
"There must have been some transgression; it is fitting that you comply with the established regulations.
Having received this imperial grace, the Dharma Master submitted a memorial to the palace to express his gratitude, saying:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.
I have humbly received the Imperial Decree, which restores the provisions for monks and nuns who have committed offenses to follow the ancient statutes, rather than being subject to secular law.

This unexpected bounty has suddenly been bestowed upon the monastic community, and this immeasurable grace has once again descended upon the dark abode of the Dharma. To bask in its radiance and bathe in the Way is truly a source of glory; yet, as I stand constrained upon the earth and reflect upon my own person, I can only feel an ever-increasing sense of awe and trepidation.

I humbly submit that since the Dharma King has passed away, the teachings of the Image Age have been transmitted in emptiness; thus, the rules for honoring and perpetuating them are entrusted to enlightened sovereigns.

I prostrate in thought before Your Majesty, the Emperor: you occupy the pinnacle of the precious throne and ride the Golden Wheel of Righteousness. You look with favor upon this Śākya teaching and harbor a deep resolve to propagate it. You consider that while those who have cast off adornment at the Gate of the Profound differ outwardly from worldly customs, and though their emotions may be entangled in the five turbidities and their observance of the precepts often deficient, they wear the three robes upon their bodies, and the field of merit remains therein.
He has severed the dense net of jade-like regulations and spread forth broad benevolence;
he has trusted the upright words from the golden mouth and granted this dedication.

Thus, the celestial deities are surely filled with joy and respond with auspicious omens; how could it merely be that his fellow monks cherish his kindness, for he has further added steadfastness and integrity.

If anyone should turn their back on this act of leniency and bring calamity upon themselves, they would be violating the solemn decree of the Great Master and failing the profound compassion of the Holy Sovereign. All you enlightened spirits should naturally mete out punishment; why wait for the statutes of the secular court before sentencing them for their wickedness and folly?

I, Xuanzang, am of mediocre and dull capacity, yet I have been unworthily included within the stream of the Dharma. Whenever I receive your vast grace, I harbor feelings of shame and trepidation; now, receiving once more this extraordinary reward, my anxiety and awe are redoubled.
However, as I have recently been afflicted by illness, I have been unable to attend at the palace in accordance with custom.

I did not expect that the light of the sun and moon would still shine upon shards and rubble, nor that the bounty of clouds and rain would surely moisten even the weeds and brambles.
Overwhelmed by gratitude and trembling with awe, joy and a sense of profound sincerity converge within me; I am unable to contain the utmost depth of my devotion, whether in life or death.
"I respectfully submit this letter of thanks for your notification.
The matter is of great importance while my person is of humble station; thus, I am unable to express it fully.
Having received the imperial permission, the Dharma Master subsequently carried out the reburial.
The ceremonial arrangements for his funeral procession were all provided by public funds.
At that time, more than ten thousand monastics and laypeople from the Luoyang area attended.

Later, Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei dynasty moved the capital from Dai to Luoyang and constructed the Shaolin Monastery on the northern side of Mount Shaoshi. Following the variations in the terrain’s elevation, it became known as the Upper Terrace and the Lower Terrace, comprising twelve courtyards in total.
To the east it rests upon Mount Song, facing south toward Shaofeng Peak; to the north it relies on lofty ridges, encompassing three rivers.

Towering crags rise steeply, and flying springs wind and reflect one another. Pine and ruan creepers intertwine with bamboo, while cassia, cypress, and various fine woods stand in lush profusion. Majestic yet elegant, serene and empty, it is truly a most excellent place within this realm.

The western terrace is the most exquisite and beautiful; it was the place where Bodhiruci translated the scriptures and also the site where Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra practiced seated meditation, where a stupa containing his preserved remains can still be seen.
At the end of the Daye era, a band of rebels attempted to burn it down with fire, but they failed; rare treasures from near and far remained intact.
To the northwest of the temple, at the foot of a ridge below Guoshi County and in Fenghuang Valley to the southeast of Chen Village—also known as Chenbao—is the birthplace of the Dharma Master.
On the twentieth day of the ninth month of autumn, the Dharma Master requested entry into Shaolin Monastery for the purpose of translation.
His memorial read:
“The Śramaṇa Xuanzang says:”
Xuanzang has heard that the path to Bodhi is far, and those who travel it must rely on provisions;
the river of birth and death is deep, and those who cross it must depend upon a boat or raft.
These "provisions" consist of the sublime practices of the Three Studies and the Three Wisdoms, and are not of the same kind as grain ground overnight.
The boat and raft are the pure practices of the eight patiences and eight contemplations; they are not merely for those who rely on a double-planked vessel.
Thus, the Buddhas, possessing them, ascend to the other shore, while ordinary beings, lacking them, sink into birth and death.
Consequently, throughout the vast and boundless triple world, all drift upon the river of the seven outflows;
across the immense four modes of birth, all are submerged by the waves of the ten entanglements.

Without exception, they swirl like billows and revolve like mist; their minds are bewildered and their wills intoxicated. They endure until the exhaustion of kalpas as vast as stone tablets without weariness, and remain ever more firm even when the mustard-seed cities are consumed.
It was truly lamentable that he did not know how to mount the three vehicles to emerge from the burning house, or to ride the Eightfold Path to reach the Jewel Monastery!

It is not merely that the autumn wind stirs my spirit to deep sighing; it is surely more than just the feelings of Confucius, such that I have never failed to set aside my meal when eating, or to startle awake while sleeping.

I, Xuanzang, have often reflected that this body is a provisional conglomeration of manifold conditions, impermanent from moment to moment. Even the trees on a riverbank or the vines over a well cannot adequately illustrate its precariousness and fragility; a city of Gandharvas or water bubbles cannot serve as metaphors for its lack of solidity. Therefore, I expect my end at any moment morning or night, placing no hope in long duration.
Yet, as the years flow like a stream, my sixtieth year has already arrived with sudden haste.
Reflecting on this rapid passage, the remainder of my life may well be foreseen.

Furthermore, in my youth, I sought the Dharma and traveled in search of teachers and friends across various kingdoms; there was no place I did not pass through, and the distances were so vast that my physical strength was utterly exhausted.
In recent years, my physical strength has further declined.
Looking at my shadow and observing the passing light, how much longer can I remain?

Since my provisions for the journey are not yet sufficient and the road ahead grows ever shorter, there is no day that I do not lament this; though I set it down in brush and ink, it cannot be fully expressed.

Yet, though my life is of little value, I have been fortunate enough to encounter a sagely sovereign; I have received the extraordinary favor of the previous dynasty and am indebted for Your Majesty’s exceptional grace. I have long been bathed in this profound benevolence throughout the passing of years and months.

As for the increase in titles and the enhancement of value, the spreading of renown and the soaring of fame—flying without wings and sitting atop the Milky Way—he received the fourfold offerings and surpassed the splendor of his peers; even seeking among the ancients, such a thing had never occurred before.
What virtue or merit do I, Xuanzang, possess to have reached this point?

It is entirely due to the vast and moistening grace of Your Majesty’s imperial favor and the compassionate descent of the sun and moon, which have caused this common "swallow-stone" to be treated as a treasure and this feeble "stallion" to be deemed worthy of honor. As I reflect upon myself within, I can only feel profound shame and humility.
Furthermore, to harm excess and loathe fullness is truly the refined intent of former sages;
to have few desires and know contentment is likewise the sincere teaching of all Buddhas.

Examining myself, Xuanzang finds my learning and practice to be empty and void, and my reputation and conduct to be unworthy of praise. It is not fitting that I should continue to presume upon Your Majesty’s compassionate grace for long.

I humbly beg to resign my office and spend the remainder of my life in the mountain forests, where I shall engage in ritual recitation and walking meditation to repay your patronage and encouragement.

Furthermore, I am grateful that Your Majesty, in the dignity of a Cakravartin King, has spread the transformation of the Dharma King, ordering that all the scriptural texts obtained from the Western Regions be translated.
Xuanzang, unworthy as I am, have been humbly entrusted with this deficient capacity and have presumptuously assumed this responsibility.
Having received the Imperial decree, I have remained restless day and night.

To date, I have translated more than six hundred fascicles, all of which constitute the essential tenets of the Tripiṭaka and the four Āgamas, and the pivotal keys of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

It is a forest and marsh for the stages and practices of both ordinary beings and sages, and a sea and wetland for the eighty thousand Dharma gates; the Western Regions praise it as a scripture that stabilizes the nation and its regions.

Whatever textual meaning one requires, there is nothing that cannot be found within it—like choosing timber from Mount Denglin, where one finds whatever size is needed, or gathering treasures from the seashore, where one takes whatever shape is desired. As a source for scholars, this work serves as a fitting model.
I, Xuanzang, employ this to repay the grace of the state; truly, it cannot be fully exhausted, yet I still hope for even one ten-thousandth part of it.

However, in severing and subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*), concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) must necessarily support one another, like the two wheels of a chariot; if either is lacking, it is insufficient.
As for such matters as investigating and savoring the sutras and śāstras, these belong to the study of wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā);
as for relying on forest retreats to sit in meditation, these belong to the study of concentration (samādhi-śikṣā).

Since my youth, I have been able to apply myself with some degree of mastery to the meaning of the teachings, yet I have had no leisure to settle my mind within the four dhyānas and nine meditative attainments.

I now wish to entrust my thoughts to the gates of dhyāna and clarify my mind in the waters of samādhi, to restrain the wild restlessness of the monkey-like emotions and to tether the galloping of the mental imagery; were I not to withdraw my traces into the mountains, this could not be accomplished.

I have humbly learned that in this province, Mount Songgao and Mount Shaoshi possess overlapping ridges and peaks; their crags and gullies abound in wonders. They harbor wind and clouds and encompass both benevolence and wisdom. Fruits and medicinal herbs flourish there, while the *luo* and *bie* vines provide a pure and empty atmosphere. Truly, these are the famous mountains within the seas and the divine peaks within the realm.

Within this area, there are further monasteries such as Shaolin Monastery and Xianju Monastery; all of them span and rest upon rocky crags, winding through and encircled by forests and springs, where Buddhist rites are solemn and majestic, and the chambers and buildings are secluded and profound.
This is precisely where the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty translated the scriptures; it is truly a place one may rely upon for the practice of dhyāna and contemplation.

Furthermore, even two retired scholar-officials of the Han dynasty understood to return to the sea and decline honors, and even commoners like Chao Fu and Xu You knew to dwell in the truth and preserve their simplicity. How much more so for Xuanzang, who has left the household life for the sake of the Dharma yet remains stalled amidst the marketplace—this pure wind stirs my soul, and as I reflect on it, my sense of shame increases.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty’s brilliance surpasses the seven luminaries, and your illumination reaches the depths of the nine dark realms.

I beseech you to grant favor to this humble sincerity and deign to grant your permission, allowing me to sever ties with the clamor and dust of the common world, withdraw my traces from among men, and join the herds of deer and the flocks of wild ducks and cranes. May I dwell upon a fragment of stone and take shelter beneath the shade of a single tree, guarding the restless monkey of the mind and contemplating the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Thus, may the thieves of the four Māras and the nine fetters have no means to break in, while the mind of the five patiences and ten stages may be successively induced. This shall serve as a gradual path toward Bodhi and a virtuous cause for reaching the other shore. Externally, I shall not burden the imperial wind; internally, I shall increase my spiritual practice. To be permitted to conclude my life in this manner would be the ultimate grace of Heaven.
If you would condescend to grant your favor, then the noble integrity of Huiyuan of Mount Lu may be emulated, and the pure reputation of Daolin of Mount Shan may be continued.
Furthermore, I hope that amidst the intervals of your meditative contemplation, you might occasionally engage in translation; I am filled with the utmost joy and aspiration.
"I respectfully approach the palace to present this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal.
Having lightly provoked Your Imperial Majesty’s august authority, I am filled with profound trepidation.
When the Emperor read the memorial, he did not grant his permission.
On the twenty-first day of that month, a divine brush spontaneously produced a letter stating:

"I have examined your memorial and understand your desire to conceal your traces among the crags and springs, emulating the legacy of Hui-lin and Hui-yan to bridge the past, and entrusting your thoughts to meditative stillness to emulate the standards of Daoyi and Kumārajīva to mark the present. As I look up to and draw from your refined character and virtuous influence, I truly hold you in the highest esteem."
My own karma is empty and my learning meager; I have not fathomed the lofty and profound.
Nevertheless, based on my shallow understanding and limited hearing, I have seen no reason for this to be acceptable.

You, Dharma Master, serve as a bridge and raft for the three realms and draw forth beings of the four modes of birth; your wisdom is as bright as the lamp of the mind, and your concentration is as still as the water of the will.
It is not obscured by the sensory objects of the insentient world; how could it be startled by the waves of consciousness?
If the Way and its Virtue can be dwelt within, why need one seek the layered ridges of Mount Taihua?
If emptiness and stillness can be taken as a dwelling, why need one dwell solely among the deep crags of Mount Shaoshi?
I hope you will restrain these words and no longer present such requests.
Then, the great recluse within the marketplace and the court will not only be as esteemed as the sages of antiquity;
the vast benefit of your insights and learning shall be even more precious for this very age.
Since the imperial decree had ordered that the memorial be withheld, [the Emperor] did not dare speak further.
Having received the imperial missive, the Dharma Master submitted a letter of thanks, saying:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks."
The envoy, Officer Li Junxin, has arrived and graciously bestowed upon me a handwritten imperial edict.

Your silver calligraphy is more beautiful than vermilion script; your sagely compositions flourish like the *Hetu* diagram. Its grandeur bears the forms of peaks and mountains, while its lush vitality draws forth the spirit of wind and clouds.

I did not expect that at the close of autumn I would behold the elegance of spring blossoms, nor that while dwelling between the Yi and Luo rivers I would suddenly gaze upon the treasures of Kunlun and Mount Jing.
Holding them in my hands and facing them with joy, I dance and leap for gladness.
In the past, Ji Zhong received a letter from the Lord of Wei that spoke only of our separation;
Huiyuan was honored by a letter from the Emperor of Jin that merely ordered him to be provided with rice.
I have not yet seen words that combined the principle of emptiness and stillness with the instruction on the great recluse’s state within the marketplace.
I firmly know that the Sage Ruler’s mind encompasses both the ultimate truth and the mundane world, synthesizing all that exists and embracing all that is non-existent.
He surpasses Fuxi and Xuanyuan, rising even higher, and outstrips Cao Cao and Ma Yuan, reaching ever further.

However, as for Xuanzang, one whose nature is like unbleached silk, he especially fears the dye of crimson and indigo; one whose body is like a creeping vine, he truly longs for the pine and the *qǐ* tree.

He hopes to dwell amidst the mist and clouds at Shaoshi Mountain and find companionship among the springs and rocks in the valleys of Songshan, thereby fulfilling his desire to avoid drowning while ultimately realizing his vow to prevent fire.

Therefore, I venture to exhaust my ignorance and, at the risk of death, present this to Your Majesty’s hearing; I pray that the compassion of your molding and shaping will not exclude the wild ducks and swallows, and that the bounty of your clouds and rain will not abandon even the spiders and insects.
Yet, Your Majesty’s brilliant edict has descended upon us, yet you have not deigned to grant your gracious consent.
Instead, you have bestowed further favors and rewards, graciously conferring this luster and honor upon us.
Our five emotions tremble with fear, and we do not know how to maintain ourselves.
Having already withdrawn my previous words, I did not dare to request further.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude, feeling only increased trepidation.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month of winter, the first birthday of Prince Foguang, the Dharma Master again presented a set of dharma robes to Prince Foguang.
The memorial states:
"I, the śramaṇa Xuanzang, submit this.

I have heard that when orchids flourish in a purple garden, those who pass by them are inevitably joyful; when cassias grow luxuriantly by a green stream, those who encounter them are filled with delight."
If even the grasses and trees are thus, how much more so for human beings, and especially for the progeny of the Sage!

We humbly reflect that Your Majesty and the Empress, possessing the countenance of divine wisdom and embracing the virtue of Heaven and Earth, have pacified and governed the realm and nurtured all living beings like children.
Furthermore, he extensively constructed monasteries and widely promoted the accumulation of merit.
This augments the eternal and unchanging enterprise of the imperial destiny and assists the adamantine and firm causes of the sovereign’s mandate.

Since they have been wonderfully and skillfully cultivated through perfuming and practice, it has caused the imperial crown prince’s spiritual faculties to flourish daily, while the Prince of Lu’s noble excellence becomes ever more manifest.

Prince Fuguang’s precocity grows increasingly radiant; this may truly be called surpassing the Zhou and transcending the Shang, rivaling the height of the Yellow Emperor, a source of celebration for ten thousand years for son after son and grandson after grandson.
I, Xuanzang, though unworthy and of humble station, have had the fortune to occasionally meet with Your Majesty and others; my private heart leaps with joy, truly filled with delight and gladness.

Today being the day of the Prince of Buddhist Radiance’s first birthday, according to ritual there is the custom of presenting congratulations; I have therefore, following my own simple sincerity, respectfully offered this set of Dharma robes.

I humbly pray that the myriad deities may protect the Prince and a hundred blessings may support him; that he may enjoy peace and harmony in both waking and sleeping, and that his nursing and nourishment may be perfectly regulated.
May he cause the Three Jewels to flourish and long endure, subdue the four Māras, practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva, and continue the work of the Tathāgata.
It does not surpass the jade calyxes and celestial branches, its brilliance and vitality flourishing in such abundance that my joy reaches its utmost limit.
I respectfully submit this memorial along with the robe for Your Majesty’s perusal.
Having lightly offended Your Imperial Majesty’s august presence, I am filled with profound trepidation and remorse.
At that time, the Dharma Master was engaged in translation at Jici Palace without ceasing for even a moment; his accumulated fatigue developed into an illness.

He submitted a memorial to the Emperor, who, upon hearing of it, was displeased and immediately dispatched the court physician Lü Hongzhe to deliver an imperial decree of consolation to the Dharma Master.
The Dharma Master, moved beyond measure by both grief and joy, submitted a memorial of thanks, saying:
"I, the śramaṇa Xuanzang, address Your Majesty.
The envoys Lü Hongzhe and others have arrived, proclaiming Your Majesty’s decree to offer me consolation regarding my ailment and granting me permission to go outside for convalescence."
Your compassionate decree has suddenly arrived, and this feeble frame has been roused; yet, in the presence of Your Imperial Majesty, I feel as though I am placed within ice-cold springs.
Xuanzang’s self-restraint has been misplaced, and my ailments continue to accumulate.

Since parting from Your Imperial Footsteps, my entanglements have redoubled; my heart is pained and my back is stifled with distress, my bones ache and my flesh suffers agony. Eating and sleep have utterly ceased, and my breath grows ever fainter. Fearing that some unforeseen calamity may occur, I worry it might defile the palace precincts.
I intended to go abroad and hide myself away in a ravine, yet fearing I might disturb Your Majesty’s august hearing, I did not dare immediately report my departure.
Thus, following your inquiry, I went out to the monastery; however, as my illness grew more severe due to this exertion, my heart was also severed from this enlightened age.
Thereupon, Zhang Dezhi, a physician of the Imperial Medical Bureau, performed acupuncture treatment for him; consequently, his condition gradually improved, and he was able to preserve his life.
Reflecting upon the crime of his unauthorized actions, he anticipated the punishment of being ground to powder and smeared with ink.

I humbly reflect that the brilliance of the sun and moon has long been aware of my folly and clumsiness, and the bounty of the rivers and seas has always granted me indulgence and forbearance; how could I transfer this fortune to one so insignificant as myself, or bend the laws of the established code for such a case?
I hope to extend the principles of public justice to harmonize the Office of the Censorate; I would rather face a light sentence in a wrongful prison than await the executioner’s axe.

Yet, even with my waning spirit and decaying body, I am still bathed in the radiance of Your Majesty's grace. As I touch my breast to express my gratitude, I shall engrave this upon my very flesh and bones.

Reflecting upon my own condition, I am prostrate and ill, no longer as I was in ordinary times; though my worries may be as humble as those of a commoner, they exhaust all the hopes of my remaining life.
My only regret is that while the profound grace [of Your Majesty] remains unanswered, my final days have already failed me first.
Looking up with reverence to the Emperor’s diligence, he personally underwent the hardships of the hunt at Jiang, intending to inspect military exercises and his heart set on training the troops.

Having already manifested benevolence in releasing the Qilin, he further secured merit by receiving the Phoenix; thus, joy gathers from far and near, and happiness unites above and below. With Fenghou clearing the dust and the Mountain Deity guarding the wilds, I respectfully consider that your every movement is surely attended by the utmost auspicious omens.
Shen Nü was cautioned for ten days’ journey and returned within a single day;
the humble [Han] Xuan traveled with his eight swift steeds and turned back when he was but close by.
Your Majesty’s carriage may wait; my eternal longing will find solace therein. Yet as I reflect on these matters, I am filled with trepidation and fear that I shall ultimately fall into ruin.
I am overcome with the utmost dread and trepidation.
I respectfully submit this memorial to await my punishment and report these matters.
In my state of confusion and anxiety, I have lost all sense of direction; I prostrate myself to await Your Majesty’s decree.
The Emperor read the memorial with great joy.

After three days had passed, he dispatched an envoy to welcome the Dharma Master into the palace, providing him with the four types of offerings and entertaining him for several days. He then issued an edict to send the Dharma Master back to Jicui Palace, where he was once again commissioned to perform his translations.
In the twelfth month of winter, the palace at Luoyang was renamed the Eastern Capital.

Dissatisfied with the narrowness of its administrative domain, the Emperor divided Fan-shui from Zhengzhou and He-yang from Huaizhou to the east, and abolished Guozhou to the west; he then annexed the counties of Yi-yang, Yong-ning, Xin-an, and Mian-chi, all of which were made subordinate to it.
The Dharma Master, because his native district had become increasingly illustrious, composed a formal letter of congratulation, saying:
"The śramaṇa Xuanzang speaks.
I have humbly heard that the Chunsou mansion was bestowed upon Qin, as the High God portended the establishment of the Golden City."
The tortoise diagram was presented to Xia, and within the central realm, the Jade Spring was first glimpsed.
Thus we know that the foundation of spiritual blessings rests here, and the imperial way is clearly manifest therein.
Prosperity and renown arise from these distant divinations; it is for this reason that the glorious light reveals its destined era.
Truly following the Way, one must surely abide by these principles.
We humbly observe that the Emperor and Empress weigh matters with discernment and govern the people with impartiality.
At this most profound and central of sites, you have halted your imperial progress in accordance with the ancient tours of inspection.
Relying on the magnificent scale of the ancient regulations, he established the outer walls modeled after the capital of Hao;
yet, still cherishing the ideal of a humble palace, he deemed the labor of the previous construction excessive,
and mindful of restraining restlessness, he felt concern for the ease of rising at dawn.

Were it not for the unification of the Chinese and the barbarians and the equalization of labor services and taxes, how could the Imperial Favor have been so long retained and the imperial edicts so brilliantly issued?
Thus, when the decree was first promulgated, the mountains and rivers underwent a profound transformation;
as the new regulations began to take effect, the mists and clouds shifted their hues with a vibrant luster.

The soaring eaves are bright under the sun, and the imperial thoroughfare is clear and fresh; divine intentions respond with spiritual resonance, and the eternal order of human relations is profound and harmonious.
Were one to compose a poem on the fish of Wuchang, they would rejoice at migrating to the royal city;
they vie to emulate the cranes of Yunting, wishing to attend the imperial carriage.
The reliance upon Jin and Zheng was already too narrow, and the strategies of Liu and Zhang were even more limited.
The former kings were cramped and constrained, with Feng and Luo opening up in succession; our sovereign, however, encompasses all within his embrace, establishing both Yi and Xian simultaneously.
The lineage of the Qilin shall flourish and the imperial mandate endure for a long time; thus, you may feast in the Pingle Hall to the east and gaze upon the Jianzhang Palace to the west.
May you linger to play the sheng flute to prolong your longevity, and as you thrive amidst the aquatic plants, let your praises flow in song.
Vast and impartial is the ultimate justice; lofty and sublime, it is rarely described.
I, Xuanzang, am but useless timber unable to be of service, and my fear grows ever deeper.
Yet, in the outskirts of the Three Rivers, I have unworthily been granted the favor of my native village.
A thousand-year fortune has culminated in the establishment of this new capital.
Though my humble thatched door remains obscured, my lowly life still endures;
I rejoice to be enrolled among those beneath the imperial chariots, feeling no shame for having once been beyond the frontier passes.
Moreover, the auspicious occasion of Guangzhai is a cause for shared joy far and near;
that His Majesty is at ease is a singular favor bestowed upon those of humble station.
We cannot contain our utmost delight and jubilation.
"I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude for Your Majesty’s knowledge.
In the first month of the spring of the third year, the Imperial carriage returned to the Western Capital,
and the Dharma Master also followed him back.
The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty,
Scroll Nine The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Da Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang Dynasty,
Scroll Ten
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huili and annotated by Shi Yancong.

From the first month of the third year of Xianqing, when [the Master] followed the imperial carriage from Luoyang back to the Western Capital, until his passing at Yuhua Palace in the second month of the first year of Linde. From the first month of the third year of Xianqing, when the imperial carriage returned to the Western Capital from the Eastern Metropolis, the Dharma Master also returned with it. [The period covered is: From the first month of the third year of Xianqing, when he followed the imperial carriage from Luoyang back to the Western Capital, until his passing at Yuhua Palace in the second month of the first year of Linde. In the first month of the third year of Xianqing, the imperial carriage returned to the Western Capital from the Eastern Metropolis, and the Dharma Master likewise returned with it.
In the seventh month of autumn, there was again an imperial decree for the Dharma Master to relocate to Ximing Monastery.
The monastery had been constructed on the nineteenth day of the eighth month of autumn in the first year, under the cyclical sign Wuzi.
Previously, an imperial decree had been issued stating:

"The former residence of Prince Pu in the Yan Kang Ward shall be used to construct one Buddhist monastery and one Daoist observatory each for the Crown Prince; command the Dharma Master to inspect the sites."
He returned and reported that the site was too narrow to accommodate two establishments; therefore, they decided to build the temple there altogether, while the monastery was moved to Puning Ward.
Construction began first on the temple, and by the sixth month of summer that year, the building work was completed.
The temple faces three hundred and fifty paces and its circumference spans several li.
Broad thoroughfares run to its left and right, while residential quarters flank its front and rear.
Green locust trees line its exterior, and clear waters flow through its midst; grand and imposing, it is the foremost among the benevolent shrines of the capital.

The corridors, halls, pavilions, and terraces soar and startle as they reach toward the Milky Way; their golden door-ornaments and decorated rafters dazzle with the brilliance of the sun and the glow of the dawn clouds.
There are ten courtyards in total, comprising more than four thousand rooms.
The magnificence of its adornments surpassed even those of the Tóngtài Monastery of the Liáng dynasty or the Yǒngníng Monastery of the Wèi dynasty.

By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were first instructed to select fifty monks of great virtue (dàdé) and one attendant for each; subsequently, one hundred and fifty novices (tóngzi) were further ordered to undergo an examination of their studies and conduct in preparation for ordination.
On the thirteenth day of that month, a vegetarian feast was established at the temple to ordain monks, and the Dharma Master was commissioned to oversee the ordination.

On the fourteenth day of the seventh month in autumn, the monks were welcomed into the temple; their ceremonial deportment, banners, canopies, music, and other arrangements were exactly in accordance with the protocols used for entering Ci’en Monastery and welcoming the stele.
By imperial decree, Ximing Monastery was ordered to provide the Dharma Master with a superior room and ten newly ordained śrāmaṇeras, including Haihui, to serve as his disciples.

Because the Great Emperor held the Dharma Master in high esteem during his previous reign, after ascending the throne, his veneration and respect increased even further. Imperial envoys and court officials visited him constantly to offer greetings and consolation. He bestowed upon him more than ten thousand pieces of cotton cloth, silk, and brocade, as well as several hundred items of dharma robes, inner garments, and *kāṣāya* cloths. Having received these, the Dharma Master used them all to construct stupas for the state and to produce scriptures and images; he distributed them to the poor and to foreign Brahmin guests, dispersing them immediately as they were received, without storing anything away.
He made a vow to create ten koṭis of images—one koṭi being one hundred million—and they were all successfully completed.

As the *Prajñāpāramitā* is held in high esteem in the Eastern Land, although it had been translated in previous dynasties, it was not yet complete; thus, the people again requested that he translate it thoroughly.

However, as the *Prajñāpāramitā* section is vast and the capital is full of distractions, and furthermore, as human life is impermanent, he feared it would be difficult to complete; he therefore requested that the translation take place at Yuhua Palace.
The Emperor granted his permission.

Consequently, in the tenth month of winter in the fourth year, the Dharma Master departed from the capital for the Yu Hua Palace, accompanied by the virtuous monks who were translating the scriptures and his disciples; all provisions and services were provided exactly as they had been in the capital, and upon arrival, he was settled in the Susongcheng (Solemn Sincerity) Court.
In the first day of the first month of the spring of the fifth year, he began the translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The Sanskrit original consisted of a total of two hundred thousand stanzas; as the text was so vast, his disciples frequently requested that it be abridged. The Master, wishing to comply with their wishes, intended to eliminate redundancies and repetitions, following the example of Kumārajīva’s translations.

Having formed this thought, during the night in a dream, there immediately occurred an extremely terrifying event as a warning: he saw himself either riding through perils and treading upon precipices, or being attacked by a fierce beast; only after breaking into a sweat and trembling with fear did he manage to escape.
Having awakened, he was struck with alarm and fear; he spoke to the assembly and returned to relying on the extensive translation.
During the night, he then saw all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emitting light from between their eyebrows, which illuminated and touched his own body, leaving his mind and spirit serene and at ease.

Furthermore, the Dharma Master personally saw himself holding flower lamps to make offerings to the Buddhas, or ascending a high seat to preach the Dharma for the assembly, surrounded by many people who praised and paid him reverent homage.
