The Dharma Master responded with composed eloquence; [his opponents] all entered his domain, grasped his spear, seized his point, and struck against his shield, yet each one failed to maintain their footing and stood with open mouths in reverent submission. They acclaimed him as a man of Heaven-endowed talent, difficult to match in debate.
When King Śīlāditya and the others saw him, they were filled with joy and clapped their hands; all of them knelt on their elbows and touched his feet, offering precious treasures as alms.
After the assembly concluded, he further studied Sanskrit script, as well as various sūtras and śāstras.

From the teachings of the Vaipulya scriptures on Mount Vulture Peak and the "half-character" texts of the Deer Park, as spoken throughout the Tathāgata’s single lifetime, down to the works composed by later sages such as Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and Vasubandhu, as well as the eighteen heterodox schools including the Mahīśāsaka and others, and the divergent tenets of the five Nikāyas—he has extensively searched and researched them all, penetrating their essential meanings and mastering their texts.

Furthermore, regarding the traces of the Buddha’s presence in the world—such as the Forest of Firmness at Nirvāṇa, the Bodhi tree where he subdued Māra, the exalted Kālūpagiri Stūpa, and Mount Naga where he left his shadow—he personally proffered his respects to them all, beholding their spiritual wonders in full detail, leaving nothing out.

The Dharma Master’s aspirations having been fulfilled and his studies and surveys completed, he was about to return to his native land. He consequently transcribed more than six hundred works of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, commissioned seven images, and obtained over one hundred grains of śarīra relics. On the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the spring in the nineteenth year of the Tang dynasty, he arrived back in Chang’an.
Monastics and laypeople rushed forward to welcome him, the entire city emptied its markets to do so.
At that moment, the mist and smoke cleared away, the scenery was magnificent and the breeze fresh; jeweled canopies filled the streets, and flowered banners obscured the sun.
Auspicious clouds hang their luster above the heavens, dense and profuse;
the common people sing praises upon the thoroughfare, a deep and resonant murmur.
Hereupon, perverse winds are suddenly stilled, and the sun of wisdom shines forth with renewed brilliance.

Although he did not encounter the World-Honored One as He descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, this journey alone is sufficient to be a source of glory and beauty for a thousand years.
During his travels, the Dharma Master traversed tens of thousands of li, enduring every kind of hardship and peril.

As for the mountains of parched shade and frozen cold, the ravines of surging waves and turbulent currents, the miasma of virulent poisons and black winds, and the herds of *śarabhas*, *siṃhas*, *vṛkas*, and *śālāvṛkas*—these were all regions where Faxian lost his companions and places where Zhiyan was left behind; they are lands never trodden by Ban Chao and never visited by Zhang Hai.

The Dharma Master traveled alone and solitary, yet with unyielding composure; he spread the Tang wind beyond the Eight Rivers and propagated the nation’s transformation throughout the Five Indias. He caused the kings and lords of distant realms to direct their hearts toward the imperial capital, and the chieftains of far-off lands to look up in reverence toward the celestial path. While this was indeed the peerless achievement of the Dharma Master, it was also due to the power of the Sagely Court’s flourishing destiny and its spiritual resonance.

The Emperor grasps the Dragon Chart to compile the calendar and accords with the "Red Decree" to rule as sovereign; he slaughters the whales and swine to deliver all living beings, dispelling the clouds and mists to bring radiance to the sun and moon.

He rectified the collapsing pillars of the four intermediate directions and stilled the surging currents of the vast ocean; he re-established Heaven and Earth and once again exercised the power of creative transformation.
His ninefold achievements encompassed those of the Yu and Xia dynasties, and his seven virtues surpassed those of the Cao and Liu houses.

The seas are calm and the rivers clear; the seasons are harmonious and the years are bountiful. Those far away are not without obedience, and those nearby are not without peace. Heaven is perfected and earth is leveled; humanity rejoices and the spirits are pleased.
Furthermore, as the sovereign’s brilliance shone forth in accordance with the correct, the significance of the "Three Virtues" flourished;
as the ministers were loyal and diligent, the song of "How Excellent! was truly justified.

Subsequently, his achievements reached the limits of the vast earth and his virtue moved the High Heaven: purple mushrooms displayed their beauty upon the jade steps, and magnificent fruits formed their blossoms upon the vermilion pavilions.

Furthermore, it is like the auspicious stone of Xizhou and the jade tally of Song County, which recorded the millennium of the Sage Ruler and manifested the vocation of the Crown Prince as his successor.
These verses of a talent as rare as phoenix feathers and this text for the Buddha-field of the Sovereign have remained unopened throughout ten thousand ages, only to emerge now under our Emperor.
Is this not because the luminous spirits assist his virtue and the profound heavens bestow their blessings?

Furthermore, as he directs his mind toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fortifies the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), he recalls the countenance of the Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) and dwells upon the teachings by the Ajitavatī River. Thus, it has caused his preserved remains and dark-blue hair to appear with radiant splendor, while the sublime scriptures and eminent monks arrive together in mutual brilliance.

The clouds of compassion spread across the six directions, and the Dharma drum resounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system. Heavenly flowers fly alongside the auspicious winds, and emerald mists share their fragrance with the incense smoke; thus, those worldly men submerged in the flowing currents look toward the distant shore with renewed hope, while the guests who tread the profound path of pure emptiness perceive the Three Emptinesses as no longer remote.

What is called the "southern pointer" opens the way so that those in confusion may know the directions, and when the autumn wind sweeps through the forest, the myriad pipes spontaneously harmonize their sounds.

Such was the profound virtue of the Dharma Master; such was his meeting with this auspicious time. How could he be compared to Fayu and Fotudeng, who cherished the Way yet encountered the cruelty of Shi Le and Shi Hu, or to Daoan and Kumārajīva, who transmitted the scriptures during the corrupt reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing?

When comparing their depth, they are like the water of a roadside puddle set against the rivers and lakes; when contrasting their brilliance, they are like the morning sun compared to the glow of a firefly.
Formerly, when Zhong Jue arrived, Emperor Wen of Wei offered a poem to praise him;
when the divine sparrow appeared, Jia Kui presented a eulogy to discuss its marvel.

If even for such lowly creatures as birds and beasts the ancients still composed songs and verses, how much more so for the Master’s imperishable divine merit and his great achievement as a pillar of the Dharma—how could one remain silent during this enlightened age and fail to offer praise and description?

Establishing myself in these studies, I feel ashamed before the sages of the past; my virtue does not equal that of the predecessors. I do so merely because I have equally been moistened by the transformation of the Dharma and have humbly joined the ranks of its followers. My feelings of admiration and longing exceed those of ordinary people by a hundredfold; therefore, I have exerted my efforts despite my mediocrity and folly to briefly present this transmission.

As for the beauty of his pure character and noble reputation, and his achievements that surpass the past and illuminate the future, these shall properly be treated by distinguished masters of the brush; they cannot be detailed here in full.
I hope that the discerning gentleman will accept my intention without derision.
The eulogy says:
“When life’s inspiration is severed and the Great Sage has transferred his spirit, it is only the wise man who can truly carry on his legacy.”
Aśvaghoṣa first sang forth the melody, and Āryadeva later expounded it; as the sun was about to set, the bright moon appeared.
How majestic is this Dharma Master! Truly a man of integrity, he stands far above gods and men, untethered by the dregs of the mundane world.
He exhausted the profundity of the profound mysteries and investigated the principles of Confucianism; he was as pure as a bright pearl and as fragrant as hui-herbs and zhi-grass.
Lamenting the omissions in the scriptures and doubting the errors in their meanings, he committed his life to seeking them out, braving dangers and treading upon treacherous paths.
Vast and expansive is his capacity, stalwart and sincere is his devotion; he has spread his excellence throughout the Western Region and returned all merit to the Eastern Pavilion.
Now that we have encountered a sage-ruler—none other than our Sovereign—the jade mirror is once again suspended and the pearl casket is restored to order.
The Three Vehicles having been expounded and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* simultaneously proclaimed, the Sun of Wisdom is made to shine even more brightly upon what was once obscure.

As for me, I am but a mediocre and insignificant person, fortunately permitted to join the ranks of the multitude; raised from my youth within a humble thatched door, I have neither been refined nor polished.
"I look up to these high mountains and thirst for these clear streams; I wish to climb and rely upon them, comparing myself to a creeping vine.
Shi Yancong’s commentary states:

"I have observed that since Buddhism first crossed over to the East, tens of thousands of men of talent and wisdom have abandoned their homes to enter the Way. Among them, few have been able to excel in both [secular and religious] virtues, though there are one or two who possess such beauty."

As for matters such as his vision, hearing, countenance, and speech; his extensive learning and powerful memory; his disregard for life and high regard for the Way; his distant journeys to remote frontiers; his integrity as firm as pine and bamboo; his noble resolve surpassing metal and stone; and how he caused the multitudes of heroes to change their minds and the Holy Sovereign to turn his light toward him—all these are fully recorded in the Tripiṭaka.

Furthermore, I have heard that during the height of the summer, the body of the Tripitaka Master never became moist with sweat; during the depths of the bitter cold, his countenance did not appear haggard or distressed. Moreover, he neither stretched nor yawned, and neither sneezed nor coughed. Since we have not yet fully ascertained his spiritual rank, how can we presume to fathom the level of his sagehood?
Furthermore, when Beigong manifested illness, auspicious signs were profuse; on the day he was about to pass away, his countenance was radiant and serene—this, too, is difficult to fathom.

More than a month after his passing, someone arrived carrying powdered sandalwood incense and requested that the Tripiṭaka Master’s body be anointed according to the customs of the Western Regions, but the assembly would not permit it.
The man changed his expression and said, "I shall submit a separate memorial; if you masters do not permit it, I request that you record this report for submission to the throne.
The assembly followed his lead.
When the coffin was opened and the remains exhumed, people perceived a wondrous fragrance like the scent of lotuses. They questioned one another in astonishment, and all said it was just so.

The previous person had removed the outer shrouds and left only the undergarments; when the assembly beheld that the Tripiṭaka Master’s countenance was as if he were alive, they all cried out in grief and gazed upon him together.

After he had applied fragrant ointments to the deceased, dressed the body for burial, and the coffin was already closed, he suddenly vanished; the multitude suspected him to be a celestial being (*deva*).
Examining his long-standing aspirations through the Tripiṭaka and investigating his recent traces, who else but a Mahāsattva could have been like him?
"O my fellow practitioners, may you fortunately aspire to emulate his example;
exert yourselves!"—From the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Great Ci'en Monastery of the Great Tang*, Scroll Ten.
